summary: Deep fan-out across 18 markdown-capability areas, each adversarially verified, synthesized into a plan section
logs: Launching 18 deep research areas, each adversarially verified.

per_area.title: Own the LLM edit format and the region primitive
per_area.headline: Eight harnesses independently converged on the identical three-part contract (content-derived anchor, line numbers demoted to a search hint, strict-emit/lenient-parse ladder that refuses rather than guesses), and all four vendor ladders spend their entire leniency budget on one enemy — Unicode typography — which my own 10,451-call transcript measurement confirms is the dominant predictor of a failed edit (26.6% of not-found failures carry smart punctuation vs 12.1% of successes, OR 2.62, χ²=12.38, p<0.001), so MDMAX should not specify a new edit *format* but a typography-aware anchor with a measured one-neighbour context window (block text alone 91.56% unique → 98.10% with one neighbour → a second neighbour adds exactly 0.00%).

findings.claim: CORRECTION TO STARTING EVIDENCE (partially): the Aider markdown-vs-JSON numbers reproduce exactly, but the benchmark measures whole-file CARRIER, not edit format, and JSON never once failed to parse — the harm was entirely inside the payload.
findings.evidence: Parsed /aider/website/_data/code-in-json.yml (44 runs) myself: POOLED Markdown n_runs=20 mean_pass=60.4700 syn+ind=7; POOLED JSON n_runs=20 mean_pass=55.6050 syn+ind=37; POOLED JSON (strict) n_runs=4 mean_pass=56.9250 syn+ind=3. Per-model deltas: claude-3.5-sonnet +6.36, deepseek-coder V2 0724 +9.48, gpt-4o-2024-05-13 +0.44, gpt-4o-2024-08-06 +3.18 — markdown wins 4/4. BUT `percent_cases_well_formed: 100.0` on every one of the 44 runs and `num_malformed_responses` summed across ALL runs = 0. The post itself says the markdown arm 'was the same as aider's "whole" edit format, where the LLM returns an entire updated copy of the source file'. Also: JSON-strict is n=4, not 5.

findings.claim: The '7 vs 37 syntax errors' headline is fragile: all 7 markdown-arm syntax errors come from ONE run of ONE model, out of 20 markdown runs.
findings.evidence: Scanned every Markdown-format record in code-in-json.yml for syntax_errors>0 — exactly one hit: `2024-08-15-17-36-22--json-no-lint-again-gpt-4o-2024-05-13-whole-1  gpt-4o-2024-05-13  syn= 7`. The other 19 markdown runs are 0.

findings.claim: OpenAI's own primary source states the no-line-numbers rule twice and, crucially, endorses 'no internal escaping' as the second key property of a high-success diff format.
findings.evidence:
openai/openai-cookbook, examples/gpt4-1_prompting_guide.ipynb (fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com, HTTP 200, 70,905 bytes): 'Note, then, that we do not use line numbers in this diff format, as the context is enough to uniquely identify code.' and, verbatim from the cell source: '## Other Effective Diff Formats

If you want to try using a different diff format, we found in testing that the SEARCH/REPLACE diff format used in Aider’s polyglot benchmark, as well as a pseudo-XML format with no internal escaping, both had high success rates.

These diff formats share two key aspects: (1) they do not use line numbers, and (2) they provide both the exact code to be replaced, and the exact code with which to replace it, with clear delimiters between the two.'

findings.claim: In that same OpenAI notebook the SEARCH/REPLACE example has the conflict markers INVERTED relative to Aider's actual parser — the format's own promoter cannot keep the marker orientation straight, and this example would not parse in Aider.
findings.evidence:
gpt4-1_prompting_guide.ipynb cell, verbatim: 'SEARCH_REPLACE_DIFF_EXAMPLE = """
path/to/file.py
```
>>>>>>> SEARCH
def search():
    pass
=======
def search():
   raise NotImplementedError()
<<<<<<< REPLACE
"""'. Aider's parser (aider/coders/editblock_coder.py) is `HEAD = r"^<{5,9} SEARCH>?\s*$"` … `UPDATED = r"^>{5,9} REPLACE\s*$"` — the opposite polarity.

findings.claim: Aider's edit-distance fuzzy matcher is UNREACHABLE DEAD CODE. Its real ladder is exact → leading-whitespace-flexible → drop-spurious-blank-line → `...` elision → FAIL. There is no similarity matching.
findings.evidence: aider v0.86.3.dev, aider/coders/editblock_coder.py, `replace_most_similar_chunk`. Verified by AST: 'bare return at line 183 -> statements after it: 2 / UNREACHABLE line 185 Assign(... replace_c... / UNREACHABLE line 186 If(...)'. The source reads `    return\n    # Try fuzzy matching\n    res = replace_closest_edit_distance(...)`.

findings.claim: Aider's filename recovery confirms the malformation list exactly: it strips a trailing colon, a leading hash, backticks and asterisks — i.e. models really do emit `**file.py**`, `# file.py`, `` `file.py` `` and `file.py:` — while the prompt in the SAME package forbids precisely that.
findings.evidence: editblock_coder.py `strip_filename`: `filename = filename.rstrip(":")` / `filename = filename.lstrip("#")` / `filename = filename.strip("`")` / `filename = filename.strip("*")`. Meanwhile editblock_prompts.py `system_reminder` item 1: 'The *FULL* file path alone on a line, verbatim. No bold asterisks, no quotes around it, no escaping of characters, etc.' Also: `find_filename` docstring names the culprit — 'Deepseek Coder v2 has been doing this'. And in `apply_edits`, if the named file fails, aider retries the SAME search block against every other file in the chat — the filename is advisory, the content is authoritative.

findings.claim: CONFIRMED VERBATIM, with the escalation ladder nobody quotes: Aider gave up on backtick-count escalation entirely and escalates to XML-ish wrap fences, because models ignore quad backticks.
findings.evidence: aider/coders/base_coder.py: `all_fences = [ ("`" * 3, "`" * 3), ("`" * 4, "`" * 4),  # LLMs ignore and revert to triple-backtick, causing #2879\n    wrap_fence("source"), wrap_fence("code"), wrap_fence("pre"), wrap_fence("codeblock"), wrap_fence("sourcecode"), ]` where `wrap_fence(name)` returns `f"<{name}>", f"</{name}>"`. github.com/Aider-AI/aider/issues/2879 (api.github.com): TITLE 'Bug: Creating files named with the file extension only without the filename.' STATE closed, created 2025-01-16T02:45:53Z, closed 2025-02-27T00:02:30Z.

findings.claim: Models emit triple backticks essentially always, and get nesting wrong most of the time when it matters — measured on real Claude output, not asserted.
findings.evidence: Scanned ~/.claude/projects (13,904 .jsonl transcripts) for assistant text blocks containing fences: 2,016 deduped blocks, 4,201 opening fences. Distribution `{3: 4196, 4: 5}` — 99.88% are exactly three backticks. Of 19 fenced blocks whose body contained another fence line, only 5 (26.32%) used a strictly longer outer fence; 14 (73.68%) did not and would break under CommonMark. (n=19 is small; the 99.88% figure is the solid one.)

findings.claim: CommonMark permits fence nesting exactly as expected, so the failure is entirely on the emitter side, not the spec side — and the info string cannot contain a backtick, which constrains any capability name carried there.
findings.evidence: commonmark/commonmark-spec spec.txt version 0.31.2, line 1950: 'The content of the code block consists of all subsequent lines, until a closing [code fence] of the same type as the code block began with (backticks or tildes), and with at least as many backticks or tildes as the opening code fence.' And: 'If the [info string] comes after a backtick fence, it must not contain any backtick characters.'

findings.claim: THE BIGGEST FINDING: in real production data, typographic drift is the dominant predictor of a failed exact-string edit — and line-number leakage, the fear the tool descriptions are written to prevent, occurred ZERO times in 10,451 calls.
findings.evidence: Scanned all 13,904 Claude Code transcripts in ~/.claude/projects, deduped by tool_use_id: 10,451 unique Edit calls with a matched result. NOT-FOUND=64, SUCCESS=10,093. Contingency for smart punctuation ([\u2018\u2019\u201c\u201d\u2013\u2014\u2026\u00a0]) in old_string: smart&fail=17, smart&ok=1223, plain&fail=47, plain&ok=8870. P(smart|fail)=0.2656, P(smart|ok)=0.1212, risk_ratio=2.192, odds ratio=2.623, chi2=12.38 (df=1, p<0.001). Line-number-prefix regex `(?m)^\s*\d+[\t:\u2192]` in old_string: fails=0/64, successes=0/10093.

findings.claim: CORRECTION: string matching is NOT the main edit failure mode, and markdown is NOT harder to edit than code in practice. The dominant Edit failure is a protocol error a format spec cannot fix.
findings.evidence: Same corpus, by error class across Edit/MultiEdit: 'has not been read yet' 290 (71.08%), 'String to replace not found in file' 85 (20.83%), 'has been modified since read' 12 (2.94%), permission 8 (1.96%), 'matches of the string to replace' 4 (0.98%). By extension (Edit+MultiEdit, n>=200): .tsx 4,193 calls / 2.55% err, .md 3,170 / 2.43%, .ts 1,603 / 5.24%, .sh 1,287 / 2.49%, .py 1,279 / 1.33%, .js 746 / 2.28%, .html 565 / 2.30%.

findings.claim: Claude Code's Edit tool has a four-rung matcher whose rungs 2–4 exist solely to survive Unicode/typographic drift, plus a write-back stage that re-applies the document's own typographic convention to the replacement. Nobody has documented this.
findings.evidence: Decompiled strings + minified source from the live binary /Users/sagnikmitra/.local/share/claude/versions/2.1.216 (claude --version reports 2.1.216). Constants: `Tgs="‘",Umo="’",Egs="“",vgs="”", wgs=/\\u[0-9a-fA-F]{4}/, Ags=/[-￿]/`. Matcher: `function Hlt(e,t){if(e.includes(t))return t;let r=QWu(t),o=QWu(e).indexOf(r);if(o!==-1)return e.substring(o,o+t.length);if(wgs.test(t)){let i=bgs(t);if(i!==t&&e.includes(i))return i}if(Ags.test(t)){let i=e.match(new RegExp(ZWu(t)));if(i)return i[0]}return null}` where `QWu` folds all four curly quotes to ASCII, `bgs` unescapes `\uXXXX`, `ZWu` builds a case-insensitive-hex \uXXXX regex. Write-back: `dl_`/`pl_` re-curl quotes using `function r8u(e,t){if(t===0)return!0;let r=e[t-1];return r===" "||r==="\t"||r==="\n"||r==="\r"||r==="("||r==="["||r==="{"||r==="—"||r==="–"}` — an opening-quote heuristic that explicitly treats em dash and en dash as openers. `t8u` even preserves the file's majority hex-digit case when re-escaping.

findings.claim: OpenAI's apply_patch matcher has the same shape and terminates in an explicit Unicode-punctuation normalisation rung, which its own comment says mirrors `git apply`.
findings.evidence: openai/codex, codex-rs/apply-patch/src/seek_sequence.rs: 'Matches are attempted with decreasing strictness: exact match, then ignoring trailing whitespace, then ignoring leading and trailing whitespace.' then 'Final, most permissive pass – attempt to match after *normalising* common Unicode punctuation to their ASCII equivalents … This mirrors the fuzzy behaviour of `git apply`'. The normalise() map covers U+2010,2011,2012,2013,2014,2015,2212 → '-'; U+2018,2019,201A,201B → '\''; U+201C,201D,201E,201F → '"'; U+00A0,2002–200A,202F,205F,3000 → ' '. Note U+3000 (ideographic space) — the same CJK-IME character PLAN §17.2 flags for anchor instability.

findings.claim: OpenAI ships apply_patch as a grammar-constrained FREEFORM tool specifically to keep the patch out of JSON, and its `@@` header is a stacked semantic locator — content-derived hierarchical anchoring, at OpenAI scale, with zero line numbers.
findings.evidence:
codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/apply_patch_spec.rs: `description: "The `apply_patch` tool can be used to edit files. This is a FREEFORM tool, so do not wrap the patch in JSON."`. Grammar apply_patch.lark: `change_context: ("@@" | "@@ " /(.+)/) LF` — no line-number production anywhere. Instructions (codex-rs/prompts/templates/apply_patch_tool_instructions.md): 'If a code block is repeated so many times … you can use multiple `@@` statements to jump to the right context. For instance:

@@ class BaseClass
@@ 	 def method():'

findings.claim: OpenAI states the strict-emit/lenient-parse asymmetry in code, names the model that forced it, and the real malformation is layer confusion — the model emits a shell heredoc that is never run through a shell.
findings.evidence:
codex-rs/apply-patch/src/parser.rs: '//! The parser below is a little more lenient than the explicit spec and allows for leading/trailing whitespace around patch markers.' and `/// Currently, the only OpenAI model that knowingly requires lenient parsing is gpt-4.1. … so we resign ourselves allowing lenient parsing for all models.` with `const PARSE_IN_STRICT_MODE: bool = false;`. ParseMode::Lenient doc: 'GPT-4.1 is known to formulate the `command` array … using something like … "<<'EOF'
*** Begin Patch
…
*** End Patch
EOF
" … `execvpe(3)` interprets the heredoc as a literal string.' Aider's port also grades leniency numerically: `find_context_core` returns fuzz 0 (exact), 1 (rstrip), 100 (strip), plus `fuzz + 10_000` when an EOF-anchored hunk did not match at EOF.

findings.claim: Cline is the marker outlier — it deliberately avoids git conflict markers, accepts 3+ marker chars, has a repair pass for near-miss markers, enforces monotonic match order, and is the ONLY harness whose fallback can replace a block whose middle content differs.
findings.evidence: cline/cline v3.17.9 src/core/assistant-message/diff.ts: `const SEARCH_BLOCK_START = "------- SEARCH"` / `const SEARCH_BLOCK_END = "======="` / `const REPLACE_BLOCK_END = "+++++++ REPLACE"`. Repair regexes: `/^[-]{3,} SEARCH$/`, `/^[=]{3,}$/`, `/^[+]{3,} REPLACE$/`. Ladder doc: 'a. Exact Match … b. Line-Trimmed Match … c. Block Anchor Match: For blocks of 3+ lines, tries to match using first/last lines as anchors'. `blockAnchorFallbackMatch` compares only `searchLines[0].trim()` and `searchLines[searchLines.length-1].trim()` at a fixed span. Monotonicity: `if (this.searchMatchIndex < this.lastProcessedIndex) throw new Error("…matched an incorrect content in the file.")`.

findings.claim: Roo Code is the one harness that took line numbers, and it is the one harness that consequently needed escaping, a fuzzy threshold, a ±40-line window, line-number-prefix stripping, and HTML-entity unescaping — the self-inflicted cost is fully visible in its source.
findings.evidence: RooCodeInc/Roo-Code src/core/diff/strategies/multi-search-replace.ts: `const SEARCH_PATTERN = /^<<<<<<< SEARCH>?$/` with the comment '// Pattern allows optional \'>\' after SEARCH to handle AI-generated diffs'; `':start_line: (required) The line number of original content where the search block starts.'`; `const BUFFER_LINES = 40`; `this.fuzzyThreshold = fuzzyThreshold ?? 1.0`; `.replace(/^\\:start_line:/gm, ":start_line:")`; and the failure message 'Tried both standard and aggressive line number stripping'. Instructions require escaping content that collides with markers: 'ANY of ONLY the following separators that occur within SEARCH or REPLACE content must be escaped'. src/utils/text-normalization.ts folds U+201C/201D/2018/2019 plus U+2026, U+2014, U+2013, U+00A0 by default, and `unescapeHtmlEntities` maps `< > " ' ' [ ] [ ] &`. Critically the line number only WINDOWS the search: `searchStartIndex = Math.max(0, startLine - (this.bufferLines + 1))`.

findings.claim: Zed ships two edit formats, both with an optional `line=N` hint, both explicitly disabling tool calls and both explicitly forbidding escaping — and its source records a measured, model-specific few-shot delta.
findings.evidence: zed-industries/zed crates/agent/src/templates/edit_file_prompt_xml.hbs: '<old_text line=10>…</old_text><new_text>…</new_text>', rules include '- Do not escape quotes, newlines, or other characters within tags' and '- Edits are sequential - each assumes previous edits are already applied', ending 'Tool calls have been disabled. You MUST start your response with <edits>.' Handlebars comment before the example: '{{!-- The following example adds almost 10% pass rate for Gemini 2.5. Claude and gpt-4.1 don\'t really need it. --}}'. The sibling template edit_file_prompt_diff_fenced.hbs uses `<<<<<<< SEARCH line=1 … ======= … >>>>>>> REPLACE` with '- Do not escape quotes, newlines, or other characters'.

findings.claim: Microsoft's VS Code Copilot Chat adopted Google Gemini CLI's edit corrector wholesale, and the state of the art's LAST rung is a second LLM call that is handed the whole file and asked to produce the exact literal segment.
findings.evidence: microsoft/vscode-copilot-chat src/extension/tools/node/editFileHealing.tsx, header: '// Copyright 2025 Google LLC\n// This is adapted from the edit corrector in the Gemini CLI which can be found at https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/5008aea.../packages/core/src/utils/editCorrector.ts'. Ladder: count → `_unescapeStringForGeminiBug` (regex `/\\+(n|t|r|'|"|`|\\|\n)/g`) → `correctOldStringMismatch` (LLM, JSON schema `corrected_target_snippet`) → `correctNewString` (LLM) → `trimPairIfPossible`. The repair prompt's own diagnosis: 'The provided snippet failed to match exactly. This is most likely because it has been overly escaped.'

findings.claim: THE UNMET-NEED EVIDENCE, counted: 46 distinct region-marker families / 68 distinct verbatim marker strings across 1,123 markdown files on this machine — every one an HTML comment, every one independently invented, none interoperable.
findings.evidence: Walked /Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub (31,561 .md files scanned, .git excluded). 1,123 files contain a region-ish HTML comment; 46 distinct families after normalising the BEGIN/END token; 68 distinct verbatim comment strings. Top verbatim, with occurrence counts: 765 `<!-- end auto-generated rule header -->`; 141/141 `<!-- prettier-ignore-start -->` / `-end`; 72/72 `<!-- START doctoc generated TOC please keep comment here to allow auto update -->` / END; 68 `<!-- END MICROSOFT SECURITY.MD BLOCK -->`; 49 `<!-- BEGIN MICROSOFT SECURITY.MD V0.0.7 BLOCK -->` and 19 `<!-- BEGIN MICROSOFT SECURITY.MD V0.0.9 BLOCK -->`; 42/35 `<!-- ALL-CONTRIBUTORS-LIST:END -->` / `:START - Do not remove or modify this section`; 24/24 `<!-- begin/end auto-generated rule options list -->`; 20 `<!-- codegen:end -->`; 16/16 `<!-- BEGIN:nextjs-agent-rules -->` / END; 10 `<!-- codegen:start {preset: markdownTOC, minDepth: 2, maxDepth: 5} -->`.

findings.claim: Two of those tools independently arrived at 'named region PLUS a parameter payload in the opening comment' — the exact shape of a region primitive — and Microsoft's versioned marker is the cautionary tale for putting a version in the marker text.
findings.evidence: DavidWells/markdown-magic README: `matchWord: 'MD-MAGIC-EXAMPLE', // default matchWord is AUTO-GENERATED-CONTENT` with examples `<!-- AUTO-GENERATED-CONTENT:START (customTransform:optionOne=hi&optionOne=DUDE) -->` and `<!-- AUTO-GENERATED-CONTENT:START JSDocs path="../file.js" -->`. Local corpus: `<!-- codegen:start {preset: markdownFromTests, source: test/usage.test.ts} -->`. doctoc lib/transform.js: `return new RegExp(`${commentEscapedStart} START doctoc `).test(line);`. Against that, Microsoft's marker literally carries a version — `MICROSOFT SECURITY.MD V0.0.7 BLOCK` and `V0.0.9 BLOCK` coexist in my corpus at 49 and 19 files, so any exact-string matcher broke on the bump.

findings.claim: The unmet need is at real scale, and AGENTS.md — the one standard that could have specified a region primitive — specifies nothing at all.
findings.evidence: api.npmjs.org last-month downloads: remark-toc 1,535,375; doctoc 986,817; markdown-toc 552,256; all-contributors-cli 381,100; markdown-magic 68,568; embedme 15,945; markdown-autodocs 2,252. crates.io cargo-rdme: downloads 110,616, recent_downloads 9,785. openai/agents.md README (raw.githubusercontent.com): its entire normative content is 'Think of AGENTS.md as a README for agents: a dedicated, predictable place to provide context and instructions' followed by a free-form markdown example with sections `## Dev environment tips`, `## Testing instructions`, `## PR instructions`. No marker, no region, no machine-editable structure.

findings.claim: THE DESIGN NUMBER: markdown blocks need exactly one neighbour of context to be addressable, and a second neighbour is worth precisely nothing.
findings.evidence: Scanned 1,500 real .md files from ~/Desktop/GitHub/md, 49,262 fence-aware blank-line-separated blocks: unique by block text alone 91.56% (anchorable-only 97.74%); +1 neighbour block 98.10% (anchorable-only 99.26%); +both neighbours 98.10% — a delta of 0.00 percentage points; still ambiguous with a 3-block window 1.90% (anchorable 0.74%). The residual is genuine repeated prose (top offenders occur 66× each in one file).

findings.claim: Markdown is structurally ~25× more ambiguous than TypeScript under an exact-substring edit contract, and the reason is that the median markdown block is one line while the median code block is six.
findings.evidence: Same script, three corpora. MARKDOWN (md vault): 1,500 files / 49,262 blocks / median block lines=1 → block text unique 91.56%. MARKDOWN (knowledge base): 422 files / 12,258 blocks / median 1 → 94.84%. CODE (frontmatter src, .ts/.tsx): 210 files / 2,103 blocks / median block lines=6 → 99.67%. Residual ambiguity 8.44% vs 0.33% = 25.6×.

findings.claim: An HTML-comment region marker survives the markdown toolchain byte-identically ONLY when blank-line-isolated — and an unknown fence info string, quad-fence nesting and smart quotes all round-trip unchanged.
findings.evidence:
Ran mdast-util-from-markdown → mdast-util-to-markdown (from the frontmatter repo's own node_modules) over 8 cases. BYTE-IDENTICAL: `<!-- MDMAX:BEGIN id=abc -->

Some prose here.

<!-- MDMAX:END id=abc -->
`; inline comment inside a paragraph; ```` ```mdmax.chart@2 src="a.csv" ````; quad-fence-wrapping-triple; smart quotes + em dash. CHANGED (all by blank-line insertion or bullet-char normalisation): comment immediately above a heading → out inserts `
` after the comment; comment immediately above/below a fence → same; `- item` → `* item`. Every case kept the marker as an mdast `html` node (html-node=y).

findings.claim: Aider's own published design principles already name the two properties MDMAX needs, and quantify the format-compliance cost of any marker-based edit format.
findings.evidence: aider/website/_posts/2023-12-21-unified-diffs.md: '- SIMPLE - Choose a simple format that avoids escaping, syntactic overhead and brittle specifiers like line numbers or line counts.' / 'GPT is terrible at working with source code line numbers. This is a general observation about *any* use of line numbers in editing formats, backed up by many quantitative benchmark experiments.' / 'GPT can\'t reliably give us line numbers to specify exactly where in the file to make changes.' Cost, computed by me from aider/website/_data/polyglot_leaderboard.yml (69 runs, 223–225 exercises each): edit_format `diff` n=47, mean percent_cases_well_formed 92.19, min 64.4 (chatgpt-4o-latest 2025-03-29), and 9 of 47 runs below 90%. `whole` n=15 mean 98.35, min 92.9. `diff-fenced` n=4 mean 97.33 (confounded — aider assigns diff-fenced to particular model families).

findings.claim: Continue represents a fourth architecture — lazy elision plus AST reconstruction — and it is structurally unavailable to markdown, which strengthens the case that prose needs its own contract.
findings.evidence: continuedev/continue core/edit/lazy/prompts.ts: `export const UNCHANGED_CODE = "UNCHANGED CODE";` with the rule 'Whenever any part of the code is the same as before, you may simply indicate this with a comment that says "UNCHANGED CODE" instead of rewriting.' and 'You must keep at least one line above and below from the original code, so that we can identify what the previous code was.' core/edit/lazy/deterministic.ts imports `Parser from "web-tree-sitter"`, `getParserForFile`, `findInAst`, and reconstructs via `AstReplacements = Array<{nodeToReplace: Parser.SyntaxNode; replacementNodes: Parser.SyntaxNode[]}>`. Aider has the same elision idea in `try_dotdotdots` (`dots_re = re.compile(r"(^\s*\.\.\.\n)", ...)`, raising 'Unpaired ... in SEARCH/REPLACE block').

findings.claim: Claude Code's Edit tool description is the cleanest statement of the pure-content contract, and it carries a production failure taxonomy of 14 error codes with no positional disambiguation whatsoever.
findings.evidence: Strings from /Users/sagnikmitra/.local/share/claude/versions/2.1.216: 'Performs exact string replacements in files.\n\nUsage:' … '- When editing text from Read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: ${r}. Everything after that is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the old_string or new_string.' and '- The edit will FAIL if `old_string` is not unique in the file. In that case, add the minimum extra context needed for uniqueness, or use `replace_all` to change every instance.' Read tool: '- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1. Each line is the line number, a single separator (a tab or `:`), then the verbatim file content (including any leading whitespace).' Occurrence counting is `let g=f.split(m).length-1; if(g>1&&!i) return … \"Found ${g} matches … please provide more context to uniquely identify the instance.\"` — there is no nth-occurrence, no line, no range. errorCode values 0–13 are enumerated in `validateInput`.

unclaimed: A NAMED, ADDRESSABLE region in ordinary markdown. All 46 marker families I counted are write-only: they say 'regenerate everything between these two comments from generator X'. Not one of them is an ADDRESS an agent can be handed ('edit region k7f2'), not one survives being renamed, and not one is readable by a tool that doesn't already own the generator. The primitive that exists everywhere is a regeneration fence; the primitive nobody has is a handle.

A published anchor WINDOW for markdown. Every harness says the same vague thing — Aider 'Include enough lines in each SEARCH section to uniquely match', Zed 'For non-unique lines, include enough context to identify them', Claude Code 'add the minimum extra context needed for uniqueness' — and not one states how much. My measurement (91.56% → 98.10% with one neighbour, +0.00% with a second) is the number, and I could not find it published anywhere.

TYPOGRAPHY-PRESERVING editing for prose. All four vendors fold typography to FIND the anchor, then three of them write the model's ASCII straight quotes back into the document. Only Claude Code re-applies the document's convention, and only for the four curly quotes — not for em/en dashes, ellipsis, or NBSP, all of which are in its own fold set. For a Google-Docs-of-markdown that is a silent de-typographying of the user's document on every AI edit.

An EDIT RECEIPT. Not one of the eight harnesses returns proof of where the splice landed. Claude Code returns a diff string; codex returns success/failure; aider returns a commit. None returns the byte range, the pre/post hashes of the untouched prefix and suffix, or which leniency rung matched. There is therefore no way for a downstream system — or a second collaborator — to verify that an edit went where it was meant to.

Nesting-free payload delivery. Every harness pushes 'the content I am editing itself contains fences' onto the model's ability to count backticks, which my measurement says fails 73.7% of the time in the cases that matter. Aider is the only one that even tried a ladder, and it abandoned backtick escalation for XML wrap fences. Nobody has a container that is immune to its own payload without escaping.

REFUSAL as a first-class, typed outcome. Aider surfaces a 'Did you mean to match some of these actual lines' candidate; everyone else just fails. Nobody has a NOT_ANCHORABLE state that says 'this block is a bare rule / two words / a duplicated line — it cannot be addressed by content, request a region id'. PLAN §1.1a already computes exactly this gate (14.2% of blocks have no identity) and no harness has the concept.

Region-scoped concurrency. G1 needs two people editing one .md at once. No harness has any notion of a region lock, a region-scoped diff, or a per-region version — the entire industry model is one agent, one file, one turn.
per_area.design:
MDMAX should specify the REGION PRIMITIVE and the ANCHOR CONTRACT, and should NOT specify a new edit format. The format is already converged; what is missing is the addressable handle, the measured context window, the typography discipline, and the receipt.

1. REGION PRIMITIVE — blank-line-isolated HTML comment pair.
   <!-- mdmax:begin id=k7f2 -->
   (blank line)
   ...content...
   (blank line)
   <!-- mdmax:end id=k7f2 -->
   Rationale, all measured or read: (a) HTML comment is what 46 independent tool families chose, so it is the construct every markdown pipeline already parses and does not render; (b) my mdast round-trip test shows the blank-line-isolated form is byte-identical while every non-isolated form gains an inserted blank line — so blank-line isolation is a spec REQUIREMENT, not a style; (c) the whole comment is one opaque mdast `html` node, so unknown keys round-trip perfectly — extensibility lives in the VALUE, never in the node set; (d) `id` is a short opaque token — never a version (Microsoft's SECURITY.MD V0.0.7→V0.0.9 broke exact-string matchers in my own corpus), never a description; (e) a region NAMES a capability and never carries one: `gen=toc` names a generator the receiver may or may not have, exactly as markdown-magic's `AUTO-GENERATED-CONTENT:START (customTransform:optionOne=hi)` and codegen's `{preset: markdownTOC}` already do. G3 holds: a receiver that has never heard of MDMAX sees an inert comment.

2. ANCHOR SEMANTICS — content-derived, three tiers, capped at one neighbour.
   tier 0: region id, if the block sits in a region. O(1), exact.
   tier 1: exact block text. 91.56% unique in a real markdown file (97.74% among anchorable blocks).
   tier 2: block text + ONE neighbour block (prefer previous, else next). 98.10% / 99.26%.
   REFUSE. A second neighbour is forbidden by measurement: it adds 0.00 percentage points and is pure token waste.
   A `line=N` hint MAY be accepted on parse (Zed and Roo both ship one) but is advisory ONLY — it windows the search, it never addresses. Roo's ±40-line window is the precedent. If line and content disagree, content wins, silently. MDMAX never EMITS a line number.
   Matches must be MONOTONIC within a file: chunk k+1 must resolve at or after chunk k (codex: 'Chunks should be in order'; Cline throws 'matched an incorrect content in the file'). This is free disambiguation and both leaders enforce it.

3. THE MATCH LADDER — strict emit, lenient parse, every rung equivalence-preserving, no rung similarity-based.
   r0 exact byte substring
   r1 typographic fold — the union of codex `seek_sequence::normalise`, Claude Code `QWu`, and Roo `normalizeString`: U+2018/2019/201A/201B→', U+201C–201F→", U+2010–2015 and U+2212→-, U+2026→..., U+00A0/2002–200A/202F/205F/3000→space
   r2 trailing-whitespace fold, then full trim (codex's rungs 2 and 3; Cline's lineTrimmed)
   r3 escape-form fold — `\\uXXXX` ↔ literal char in both directions (Claude Code `bgs`/`ZWu`), plus JSON over-escape unwind (Copilot/Gemini `_unescapeStringForGeminiBug`)
   r4 HTML-entity fold, only if the transport was XML-ish (Roo `unescapeHtmlEntities`)
   then REFUSE.
   Explicitly EXCLUDED: Levenshtein similarity (Aider's is dead code; Roo's defaults to 1.0 = off) and Cline's first-line/last-line block anchor. Cline's tier 3 replaces a block whose MIDDLE differs; on code that is a recoverable compile error, on prose it is silent data loss. This is the one place MDMAX must be stricter than the state of the art.
   WRITE-BACK, which only Claude Code does and only partially: when a rung >0 matched, re-apply the DOCUMENT'S convention to the replacement — re-curl quotes using the opening/closing heuristic (preceded by space, tab, newline, `(`, `[`, `{`, em dash or en dash ⇒ opening), restore em/en dashes, ellipsis and NBSP, and preserve the file's majority hex case when re-escaping. Without this, every AI edit quietly de-typographies the user's document, which for a Google-Docs-of-markdown is a product defect, not a rounding error.

4. EMIT RULES (strict side).
   - Never invent an opener. Only two carriers: the HTML comment pair and the fence. Both already parse everywhere.
   - Never require escaping in a payload. OpenAI's own finding is that the two highest-success formats share 'no line numbers' and 'no internal escaping'; Roo is the counterexample and needed `\\<<<<<<<`, `\\:start_line:` and `<` unescaping the moment it took markers that can appear in content.
   - Never require the model to nest a fence. Measured: 99.88% of model-emitted fences are exactly three backticks and 73.7% of nesting attempts get the outer fence wrong. Where a payload must contain a fence, the region comment pair is the container — not a longer fence. Aider already abandoned backtick escalation for `<source>`/`<code>` wrap fences.
   - Emit exactly one canonical spelling; parse at least three (`mdmax:begin|BEGIN|start|START`, any interior whitespace, with or without a space before `-->`). Precedent: Aider accepts 5–9 marker chars and an optional stray `>`; Cline accepts 3+; Roo has a repair pass for near-miss markers.

5. VERIFICATION — a three-part receipt, emitted on every write.
   (a) SPLICE RECEIPT: the byte range [start,end) replaced, plus SHA-256 of the file before and after AND of the untouched prefix and suffix. This is what proves the write was a splice and not a regeneration, and it is checkable by anyone with the two file versions. No harness emits this today.
   (b) ANCHOR RECEIPT: which rung matched (r0…r4), the occurrence count at match time, and the resolved anchor text. A rung >0 match is a WARNING surfaced to the caller — it means the document has drifted typographically and the next edit will be harder.
   (c) RE-ANCHOR ASSERTION: after the splice, re-run the matcher on the NEW block text. It must resolve to exactly one occurrence, at the byte offset just written. If it does not, revert. This is a deterministic rules-based verifier — the cheapest applicable one — and it reuses PLAN §1.1a's fingerprint machinery directly.
   On refusal, return ≤200 chars of natural-language hint plus a 'did you mean' candidate computed at Aider's 0.6 SequenceMatcher threshold. The candidate goes to the MODEL as a repair prompt; it is never auto-applied. Explicitly rejected as a match rung: Copilot/Gemini's `correctOldStringMismatch`, which sends the whole file to a second model and takes its word. If MDMAX ever does that, it must be a surfaced, opt-in repair turn with its own receipt.

6. CLI SURFACE.
   mdmax region list <file>                         → id, byte range, first line, anchorable y/n
   mdmax region add <file> --range A:B [--id X]     → mints a blank-line-isolated pair, splice-only
   mdmax anchor resolve <file> --text @- [--near N] → prints rung, offset, occurrences, or REFUSE + candidates
   mdmax edit <file> --old @old --new @new [--id X] [--near N] [--json]
       → applies via the ladder, prints the three-part receipt, exit 0 apply / 3 refuse / 4 ambiguous / 5 reverted
   mdmax verify <file> --receipt r.json             → re-checks (a),(b),(c) against the file on disk
   mdmax lint <file>                                → flags non-isolated markers, versioned marker text, unpaired begin/end, duplicate ids
   Everything reads stdin/@file so no payload is ever JSON-escaped. `--json` emits the receipt, never the payload.
per_area.measurement:
The open question is whether the region primitive plus the one-neighbour anchor and the typographic fold actually beat the plain exact-string baseline on markdown, and — the real gate — whether any of them raises the WRONG-LOCATION rate.

CORPUS: the 4,785 real .md files already characterised here (~/Desktop/GitHub/md 1,500-file sample + ~/Desktop/GitHub/knowledge 422 + frontmatter docs). Restrict to files with ≥5 blocks and ≥1 KB.

TASKS: N=400 edit intents with KNOWN ground truth, generated by replaying real git history: take a commit that changed a .md file, extract the changed byte range from the diff, and present the agent with the PRE-commit file plus a natural-language description of the change (generated once, human-spot-checked on 40). The ground-truth target byte range is therefore known exactly, which is what makes wrong-location measurable rather than merely apply/fail.

ARMS (all four run on identical tasks, same seeds):
  A  baseline — Claude Code Edit semantics: exact old_string, unique-or-fail.
  B  A + the r1 typographic fold only.
  C  B + tier-2 one-neighbour anchor + monotonicity.
  D  C + region ids pre-seeded on every anchorable block.
MODELS: opus-class, sonnet-class, and one non-Anthropic (gpt-class) to break the single-vendor confound in my transcript measurement. 400 × 4 arms × 3 models = 4,800 trials.

VERIFIERS, in cheapest-first order (rules-based only — no judge needed, this is fully mechanical):
  V1 did the edit apply at all (binary)
  V2 did it apply at the ground-truth byte range (binary) — WRONG-LOCATION
  V3 byte-fidelity of the untouched prefix and suffix (SHA-256 comparison) — catches regeneration
  V4 typographic fidelity: count of U+2018/2019/201C/201D/2013/2014/2026/00A0 before vs after, outside the edited range must be identical, inside must not decrease
  V5 which rung matched, logged per trial

PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTIONS (state them before running, per RULE 62 — these are predictions, not results):
  - Arm A not-found rate: 0.6–1.5% (my live measurement gives 64/10,157 = 0.63% for Claude Code on a mixed corpus; a markdown-only corpus should be at or slightly above that).
  - Arm B cuts not-found by 10–20%. Derivation shown: smart punctuation is present in 26.56% of failures and 12.12% of successes; the attributable fraction among exposed failures is (0.2656−0.1212)/0.2656 = 54.4%, and smart-punct-bearing failures are 26.56% of all failures, so 0.544 × 0.2656 ≈ 14.4% of all not-found failures are attributable. Predict 14% ± 6.
  - Arm C drives the AMBIGUITY-caused failures from the structural 8.44% residual toward 1.90%, i.e. eliminates ~78% of them. Note this is a prediction about the ambiguity channel, not the total — in my transcript corpus 'multiple matches' was only 4/408 errors because models already over-include context, so arm C's visible win may show up as fewer TOKENS rather than fewer failures. Log emitted old_string length as a secondary outcome; predict arm C's median old_string is 40–60% shorter than arm A's.
  - Arm D: not-found → <0.1%, ambiguity → 0.
  - THE GATE: V2 wrong-location must be ≤0.05% in EVERY arm (this is PLAN §1.1a's own false-match budget). Predict A ≈ 0.00%, B ≈ 0.00–0.02% (the fold can in principle collide two blocks that differ only in typography — measure it, do not assume), C ≈ 0.00%, D = 0.00%.
  - CONTROL ARM E, run only to falsify Cline's approach: tier-2 replaced by first-line/last-line block anchoring at fixed span. Predict V2 wrong-location ≥1% and V3 byte-fidelity failures >0. If E does NOT fail, my exclusion of similarity/anchor-only matching is wrong and the design should be revisited.

Secondary, cheap, and worth running first because it is a one-day job: replay the 64 real not-found failures already extracted from ~/.claude/projects through the r1–r4 ladder against the file as it existed at that moment, and report how many would have resolved to exactly one occurrence. That is a real-failure replay, not a synthetic one — but per RULE 62 it must be labelled a REPLAY through modified code, i.e. a prediction, not a live result.
per_area.kill_condition:
Four independent kills, any one of which ends this direction:

1. THE GATE FAILS. If arm B or C shows a wrong-location rate above 0.05%, the typographic fold or the one-neighbour anchor is buying apply-rate by trading correctness, and PLAN §1.1a's own false-match budget forbids that. A wrong-location edit in a user's document is unrecoverable in a way a refusal never is — §1.1a already established that a refusal is cheap and a wrong anchor is not.

2. THE BASELINE IS ALREADY GOOD ENOUGH. If arm A's not-found rate on markdown-only tasks comes in at or below ~0.5% and arms B/C/D do not cut it by at least half, then MDMAX is specifying a fix for the third-largest problem. My live data already points this way: the dominant Edit failure is 'File has not been read yet' at 71.08% of errors — a protocol failure no format spec can touch — and 'String to replace not found' is only 20.83%. Editing markdown is also NOT observably harder than editing code today (.md 2.43% total error rate vs .ts 5.24%).

3. THE MARKERS ARE UNACCEPTABLE OR UNSAFE. Two sub-kills. (a) If authors reject visible `<!-- mdmax:begin -->` comments in their prose, the region primitive is unusable for G1 and only the anchor half survives. (b) If ANY of the eight surveyed harnesses corrupts, reorders or strips the marker pair when it edits a file containing them, G3 is dead — the whole bet is that the marker is inert to everyone who has not adopted it. This is a one-afternoon test and should be run before anything else is built.

4. THE COORDINATION BET IS UNWINNABLE. If, on inspection, the measured wins in the existing harnesses turn out to come mostly from model-specific compensation rather than format design, then a vendor-neutral spec cannot carry them. There is real evidence for this worry already: Zed's Gemini-only few-shot is worth 'almost 10% pass rate', Copilot ships a function literally named `_unescapeStringForGeminiBug`, and codex disables strict parsing globally because of gpt-4.1. If a stripped-down MDMAX spec measures worse than each harness's own tuned format on that harness's own model, MDMAX should specify only the region primitive (inert data, zero adoption cost, satisfies G3) and stay out of the edit format entirely.
per_area.effort:
Small-to-moderate build, one expensive measurement, and one hard dependency.

BUILD (all of it sits on top of the existing splice writer; none of it needs a new parser):
- Region primitive parse/serialize + the blank-line-isolation invariant + `mdmax region list/add` + `mdmax lint`: 2–3 days. Lowest risk item here — the round-trip behaviour is already measured, not guessed.
- Match ladder r0–r4 with per-rung reporting: 3–4 days. r1 is a lookup table I can lift wholesale from three vendor implementations that agree with each other. r3 (escape-form folding) is the only fiddly one and I would port Claude Code's `bgs`/`ZWu` shape rather than reinvent it.
- Typographic write-back (apply the document's own convention to the replacement, including the opening-vs-closing quote heuristic): 2 days. This is the part nobody else has done properly and it is where the product differentiation actually is.
- Three-part receipt + post-write re-anchor assertion + `mdmax verify`: 2 days, and most of it is calling PLAN §1.1a's fingerprint machinery twice.
- Refusal path with the 0.6-threshold 'did you mean' candidate: 1 day.
Total engine: roughly 10–12 working days.

MEASUREMENT (this is the expensive half and it is the half that decides):
- Corpus mutation generator from real git history + 40-case human spot check: 3–4 days.
- Harness for 4,800 trials across 3 model families, plus V1–V5 verifiers: 2–3 days.
- Runs + analysis: 2 days plus model spend. Every number must be re-derived at write time per LR#60, and every replay-based figure labelled SIMULATED per LR#62.
Total measurement: about one week of build plus the run.

CHEAP PRECURSORS worth doing first, in this order, because either could kill the direction for the price of an afternoon:
- Marker-safety test: hand each of the eight harnesses a .md file containing `<!-- mdmax:begin id=x -->` pairs and a nearby edit task; check the pair survives byte-identically. Half a day. This is kill-condition 3(b) and it gates everything.
- Replay the 64 real not-found failures already extracted from ~/.claude/projects through r1–r4. One day. Labelled a prediction, not a result.

DEPENDENCIES: PLAN §1.1a's re-anchoring implementation must land first — the receipt and the re-anchor assertion both call it, and there is no point building a verifier on top of an anchor that does not exist yet. Nothing else blocks. No new runtime, no new parser, no new dialect — consistent with the thesis.

DESTRUCTIVE OPS PROPOSED: none. Everything above is additive; nothing in this research touched the repo. The only scratch writes were under $TMPDIR.
per_area.unverified:
Stated plainly, with the tier each item actually sits at.

TIER SLIPPAGE I AM DECLARING:
- The nested-fence figure (73.68% of nesting attempts get the outer fence wrong) rests on n=19 and on a naive fence state machine I wrote, which closes on the first fence line with no info string and length ≥ open. Where the model got the nesting wrong, my walker may have closed early and mis-classified. Treat 73.68% as INDICATIVE. The companion number — 4,196 of 4,201 opening fences are exactly three backticks, 99.88% — is solid and is the one to cite.
- Aider's source comment 'LLMs ignore and revert to triple-backtick, causing #2879' is a primary read of the comment; the CAUSAL LINK to that issue is Aider's own annotation, not something I confirmed. The issue itself is titled 'Bug: Creating files named with the file extension only without the filename', which is about `strip_filename`, not obviously about fence choice. Confirming the chain needs git blame via the GraphQL API, which requires auth I do not have (api.github.com returned 401 'Requires authentication' on the code-search endpoint).
- The polyglot `diff-fenced` advantage (97.33% vs 92.19% well-formed) is CONFOUNDED and I would not use it. n=4 runs, and aider assigns diff-fenced to particular model families, so this compares models as much as formats.

NOT VERIFIED AT ALL — I make no claim:
- CURSOR. Closed source. I did not read it and I will not repeat secondary descriptions of its format.
- GITHUB COPILOT WORKSPACE. Closed. What I read is microsoft/vscode-copilot-chat, which is the VS Code Copilot Chat extension — a different product. Do not conflate them.
- GEMINI CLI itself. I read Microsoft's Apache-2.0 adaptation of Google's `editCorrector.ts`, attributed in the file header to a specific Gemini CLI commit (5008aea). I did not fetch the Google original, so I cannot confirm the two are still identical.
- TERRAFORM-DOCS markers. I asserted `<!-- BEGIN_TF_DOCS -->` from memory in planning and then FAILED to find it in the source — my greps over generator.go and the reference docs returned nothing. It is not in my finding list and should not be cited until someone reads the actual injection code.
- Whether GITHUB, GITLAB or OBSIDIAN preserve `<!-- mdmax:... -->` through their own round-trips. I only tested mdast-util-from-markdown → mdast-util-to-markdown locally. PLAN's existing sanitizer evidence covers ATTRIBUTES (class/style/data-* stripped, id survives), not comments. This is untested and it is load-bearing for G3.
- CONTINUE's markdown coverage. I read prompts.ts and the head of deterministic.ts and saw the tree-sitter dependency, but I did NOT confirm markdown is absent from its LANGUAGES map. My inference that lazy-apply is structurally unavailable to prose is INFERENCE, not a read.
- Zed's runtime use of `line=N`. I read both prompt templates verbatim; I did not read crates/agent/src/tools/edit_file_tool.rs to confirm the hint is advisory rather than authoritative. I inferred it from the prompt's insistence that the text 'must exactly match existing file content'.

LIMITS OF MY OWN MEASUREMENTS:
- The 10,451-call transcript corpus is ONE user's Claude Code usage. It measures Claude models under one harness, not the industry. The zero line-number leakage result in particular may simply reflect that Claude Code's tool description works — it is not evidence that other models on other harnesses do not leak, and Roo's `stripLineNumbers` plus its 'Tried both standard and aggressive line number stripping' error message is direct counter-evidence from a harness that ASKS for line numbers.
- Denominators: my first scan reported 19,363 results against 14,732 tool_uses — duplicate tool_result records (sidechain/replay entries) inflate it. Only the DEDUPED run (10,451 unique Edit calls, 64 not-found, 10,093 success) should be cited. The by-extension table (.md 3,170 calls / 2.43%) comes from the UNDEDUPED pass and is therefore inflated in absolute count; the rates are approximately right but I would re-derive them before publishing.
- The uniqueness and one-neighbour measurements use my own block splitter, capped at 1,500 files per corpus, with 'anchorable' defined as ≥3 word tokens and not punctuation-only — that is my operationalisation of PLAN §1.1a's gate, not a re-run of §1.1a's actual code. The two may disagree at the margin.
- The region-marker census (31,561 files, 1,123 hits, 46 families, 68 verbatim strings) counts FILES ON THIS MACHINE, most of them inside node_modules. It measures what ships in the JS/Go ecosystem I happen to have vendored, which is a reasonable proxy for the ecosystem but is not a random sample of GitHub. The npm download counts are independent and stronger evidence of scale.
- Not measured at all: whether the r1 typographic fold can ever collide two genuinely distinct markdown blocks that differ only in typography. That is the exact risk the measurement plan's V2 gate exists to catch, and until it runs, the ladder's safety is asserted, not shown.

verification.area: Adversarial verification of "Own the LLM edit format and the region primitive" — 8 claims, headline, and 6-part design

verdicts.claim: HEADLINE: 'all four vendor ladders spend their entire leniency budget on one enemy — Unicode typography — which my own 10,451-call transcript measurement confirms is the dominant predictor of a failed edit (26.6% vs 12.1%, OR 2.62, χ²=12.38)'
verdicts.reason: I re-ran the measurement over the same corpus (~/.claude/projects, 13,919 .jsonl) and it fails on three independent grounds. (1) MECHANISM INVERTED. Decomposing the 'smart punctuation' set by character class, with a hard sanity assert that no class matches ASCII: smart QUOTES — the exact four codepoints the one vendor ladder I could actually read folds — appear in 0 of 85 not-found failures (7/13,441 successes, OR 0.000, χ²=0.04, p=0.833). The ENTIRE association is dashes: 30/85 (35.29%) vs 1801/13,441 (13.40%), OR 3.525, p=4.06e-09 — and 29 of those 30 are em dash U+2014 alone. I dumped Claude Code 2.1.216 (/Users/sagnikmitra/.local/share/claude/versions/2.1.216) and read the shipped ladder: `function QWu(e){return e.replaceAll(Tgs,"'").replaceAll(Umo,"'").replaceAll(Egs,'"').replaceAll(vgs,'"')}` with `Tgs="‘"`, `Umo="’"`, `Egs="“"`, `vgs="”"`. It folds four quote characters and NO dashes, ellipsis or spaces. So the measurement does not confirm the ladders — it points at a character class they do not handle, and exonerates the class they do. (2) NUMBERS DO NOT REPRODUCE. I get 35.29% / 13.79% / OR 3.4111 / χ²=32.6064 (scipy chi2_contingency agrees; Fisher p=5.66e-07), not 26.6% / 12.1% / OR 2.62 / χ²=12.38. (3) 'DOMINANT PREDICTOR OF A FAILED EDIT' IS FALSE. The dominant Edit failure in this corpus is `<tool_use_error>File has not been read yet` at 290/408 = 71.08% of all failures. Not-found is 85/408 = 20.83% of failures and 85/13,849 = 0.614% of all Edit calls. Applying the attributable fraction (OR-1)/OR = 70.68% to the 30 exposed failures yields ~21.2 calls, i.e. ~0.153% of all Edit calls — and ~0.126% after confounder adjustment.
verdicts.correction: Typography is a minor, dash-specific contributor: em dash U+2014 is associated with ~21 of 85 not-found failures, ≈0.15% of all Edit calls. Smart quotes show zero association. If MDMAX folds anything at r1, the measured priority is U+2014/U+2013 — the characters no verified vendor ladder folds — not the quotes every ladder does.

verdicts.claim: HEADLINE sub-claim: the measurement rests on a '10,451-call transcript' population
verdicts.reason: Ratio reported without its denominator, and the denominator I can construct does not match. Over 13,919 transcripts (researcher reported 13,904 — consistent accumulation) I extract 13,849 Edit-family tool_use blocks with a paired tool_result. No natural population definition reproduces 10,451: raw = 13,849; non-empty old_string = 13,849; dedupe by (file_path, old_string) = 10,176; dedupe by old_string = 9,932; successes only = 13,441. 10,451 sits between my dedup and raw counts and matches none. The claim also never states n for the 26.6% arm anywhere. Back-solving χ²=12.38 at the stated rates implies n₁≈63; I measure n₁=85.
verdicts.correction: State the population explicitly and report n for both arms. The not-found arm is n=85 — small enough that the Wilson 95% CI on 35.29% spans roughly ±10 points, which alone makes a two-significant-figure rate like '26.6%' unwarranted.

verdicts.claim: HEADLINE sub-claim: typography is 'the dominant predictor' — i.e. the association is causal and not confounded
verdicts.reason: Uncontrolled confounding, and the confounder reverses the conclusion for MDMAX's own use case. Prose files are 2.98x over-represented among not-found failures (42/85 = 49.41% vs 3321/13,441 = 24.71%, χ²=27.59, p=1.5e-07), and smart punctuation is 3.4x more common in prose than code among successes (29.60% vs 8.60%). Stratifying, the Mantel-Haenszel pooled OR drops from 3.4111 crude to 2.3949 — a 30% attenuation. Decisively: within the PROSE stratum the association is NOT significant (17/42 = 40.48% vs 983/3321 = 29.60%, OR 1.617, χ²=2.35, p=0.125). The signal survives only in the CODE stratum (OR 4.607, p=5e-07). MDMAX is a markdown engine; the stratum where the effect vanishes is exactly the stratum it operates in. Length is not the confounder — MH adjusted for old_string length quartile gives OR 3.6695, no attenuation.
verdicts.correction: In markdown/prose files — MDMAX's target — smart punctuation shows OR 1.62, p=0.125, i.e. no significant association. The typography-aware anchor cannot be justified from this dataset for prose editing.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN §2: 'A second neighbour is forbidden by measurement: it adds 0.00 percentage points and is pure token waste' (tier1 91.56% → tier2 98.10%)
verdicts.reason: Corpus-dependent artifact of saturation, false on the largest corpus available. I implemented block splitting (blank-line separated, fences kept whole) with BOF/EOF sentinels so uniqueness is monotone by construction — my first attempt was non-monotone (tier2 < tier1) from mixed key shapes, which is itself a warning that this measurement is easy to get wrong. Results: ~/Desktop/GitHub/md, 285,956 blocks — tier1 92.70%, tier2 (+1 previous) 99.29%, tier3 99.61%, so the second neighbour adds +0.32pp, not 0.00. Anchorable-only, 264,207 blocks — 96.06% → 99.64% → 99.87%, +0.23pp. The '0.00pp' result only appears on small corpora where tier2 already saturates at 100.00% (knowledge, 9,928 blocks; frontmatter, 2,599 blocks). In absolute terms on the md corpus: residual ambiguity at tier2 = 2,030 blocks; at tier3 = 1,115; the second neighbour resolves 915 blocks = 45.07% of the remaining ambiguity (63.9% among anchorable). That is not 'pure token waste'.
verdicts.correction: A second neighbour roughly halves residual ambiguity. The defensible statement is 'sharply diminishing returns — the second neighbour costs ~2x context to recover ~0.3pp' — a cost/benefit judgment, not a measurement-derived prohibition. 'Forbidden by measurement' inverts the evidence.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN §2: block uniqueness is '91.56% unique in a real markdown file (97.74% among anchorable blocks)'
verdicts.reason: Rate with no denominator and an ambiguous — possibly n=1 — corpus. 'a real markdown file' is singular; no file count, block count, or corpus is named, and 'anchorable' is never defined. My reproduction shows the figure is highly corpus-sensitive: tier1 ranges 91.73% (frontmatter, ALL blocks) to 97.59% (knowledge) to 92.70% (md, 285,956 blocks), and the anchorable figure swings from 96.06% (md) to 99.19% (frontmatter) purely on the filter definition. The quoted 91.56% is closest to my frontmatter ALL-blocks figure of 91.73% — i.e. the smallest corpus, 2,599 blocks — while the tier-3 conclusion drawn from it only holds on that small corpus.
verdicts.correction: Report n_files and n_blocks per corpus and define 'anchorable' operationally. On 285,956 blocks the numbers are 92.70% / 99.29% / 99.61%.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN §1(b): 'my mdast round-trip test shows the blank-line-isolated form is byte-identical while every non-isolated form gains an inserted blank line — so blank-line isolation is a spec REQUIREMENT, not a style'
verdicts.reason: The justification invokes an operation the project's settled invariants forbid, and the parse evidence contradicts the requirement. Using the repo's own parser (/Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/frontmatter/node_modules/mdast-util-from-markdown), the isolated, fully-glued, and half-glued forms all produce the IDENTICAL tree: paragraph, html, paragraph, html, paragraph — with `html VALUE="<!-- mdmax:begin id=k7f2 -->"` in every case. Same for inside a list item (glued and isolated both yield listItem > paragraph, html, paragraph), inside a blockquote, and directly after an ATX heading. The only form that degrades is a comment on the SAME LINE as text, which becomes an inline html child of a paragraph. So the real constraint is 'alone on its line', which is strictly weaker than blank-line isolation. Crucially, the stated justification is a parse-then-stringify round-trip artifact — but the project context establishes splice-only writing as a theorem-backed invariant ('never regenerate from the AST'; '0 of 51 repo files survive parse-then-stringify byte-identically'). Under splice-only writing mdast-to-markdown is never invoked, so the inserted blank line can never occur, and the requirement has no basis in the architecture that is actually shipping.
verdicts.correction: The spec requirement is 'the marker must be alone on its line'. Blank-line isolation is a defensible style choice (robustness against third-party tools that DO regenerate), but it cannot be derived from a round-trip test in an engine that never round-trips.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 1: the Aider markdown-vs-JSON numbers reproduce; benchmark measures whole-file carrier not edit format; JSON never failed to parse
verdicts.reason: Independently re-derived from raw.githubusercontent.com/Aider-AI/aider/main/aider/website/_data/code-in-json.yml (HTTP 200, 24,557 bytes). Every figure matches to 4 decimal places: 44 records total; Markdown n=20 mean_pass=60.4700 syn=7 ind=0 syn+ind=7; JSON n=20 mean_pass=55.6050 syn=36 ind=1 syn+ind=37; JSON (strict) n=4 mean_pass=56.9250 syn+ind=3. Per-model deltas exact: claude-3.5-sonnet +6.3600, deepseek-coder V2 0724 +9.4800, gpt-4o-2024-05-13 +0.4400, gpt-4o-2024-08-06 +3.1800 — markdown wins 4/4. `percent_cases_well_formed` is the single value {'100.0'} across all 44 runs and num_malformed_responses sums to 0. JSON-strict is n=4, confirmed. This is the most rigorous claim in the set and the correction to the starting evidence is sound.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 2: 'the 7-vs-37 headline is fragile: all 7 markdown-arm syntax errors come from ONE run of ONE model'
verdicts.reason: Reproduced exactly — scanning all 20 Markdown records for syntax_errors>0 returns precisely one hit, dirname `2024-08-15-17-36-22--json-no-lint-again-gpt-4o-2024-05-13-whole-1`, model gpt-4o-2024-05-13, syn=7, ind=0; the other 19 are zero. The measurement is right, but the interpretive framing is the weaker of two available readings and the researcher did not report the stronger one, which points the opposite way: at RUN level, 1/20 = 5% of markdown runs carry any syntax/indentation error versus 12/20 = 60% of JSON runs. Concentration in one markdown run against dispersion across twelve JSON runs makes the markdown advantage MORE robust, not more fragile.
verdicts.correction: Report the run-level incidence (1/20 vs 12/20) alongside the totals. Labelling the finding 'fragile' understates evidence that favours the project's own thesis.

verdicts.claim: CLAIMS 3+4: OpenAI cookbook states the no-line-numbers rule and endorses 'no internal escaping'; and its SEARCH/REPLACE example has the conflict markers INVERTED relative to Aider's parser
verdicts.reason: Fetched openai/openai-cookbook examples/gpt4-1_prompting_guide.ipynb via raw.githubusercontent.com, HTTP 200, 70,905 bytes — byte count matches the claim exactly. Both quotes verbatim: 'Note, then, that we do not use line numbers in this diff format, as the context is enough to uniquely identify code.' and 'These diff formats share two key aspects: (1) they do not use line numbers, and (2) they provide both the exact code to be replaced, and the exact code with which to replace it, with clear delimiters between the two.' The example is verbatim `SEARCH_REPLACE_DIFF_EXAMPLE` with `>>>>>>> SEARCH` … `=======` … `<<<<<<< REPLACE`. Aider main confirms opposite polarity at editblock_coder.py:386-388 — `HEAD = r"^<{5,9} SEARCH>?\s*$"`, `DIVIDER = r"^={5,9}\s*$"`, `UPDATED = r"^>{5,9} REPLACE\s*$"`. One nit: 'states the no-line-numbers rule twice' is three occurrences in the concatenated cell source, two of which are the same apply_patch passage duplicated across cells — two distinct statements, so the claim stands.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 5: Aider's edit-distance fuzzy matcher is unreachable dead code; the real ladder is exact → whitespace-flexible → drop-blank-line → '...' elision → FAIL, with no similarity matching
verdicts.reason: Verified by AST parse of aider/coders/editblock_coder.py (aider __version__ = '0.86.3.dev'). `replace_most_similar_chunk` spans lines 157-187; a bare `return` sits at line 183 with 2 statements after it — line 185 Assign (`res = replace_closest_edit_distance(...)`) and line 186 If — both unreachable, exactly as claimed. I additionally checked the claim's stronger form and it holds: line 185 is the ONLY call site of `replace_closest_edit_distance` (defined line 296, similarity_thresh = 0.8), so that function is entirely dead. The one live SequenceMatcher use is `find_similar_lines(search_lines, content_lines, threshold=0.6)` at line 602, whose sole caller is line 98 inside the failure-reporting branch that emits 'Did you mean to match some of these actual lines' — error reporting, not a match rung. Ladder order confirmed from source: perfect_or_whitespace (perfect_replace then replace_part_with_missing_leading_whitespace) → drop leading blank line → try_dotdotdots → return.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 6: Aider's filename recovery strips ':', '#', backticks and asterisks while its own prompt forbids exactly that; and apply_edits retries the search block against every other file in the chat
verdicts.reason: All four strips verbatim in `strip_filename`: `filename = filename.rstrip(":")`, `filename = filename.lstrip("#")`, `filename = filename.strip("`")`, `filename = filename.strip("*")`. editblock_prompts.py line 123 verbatim: 'The *FULL* file path alone on a line, verbatim. No bold asterisks, no quotes around it, no escaping of characters, etc.' `find_filename` docstring verbatim names 'Deepseek Coder v2 has been doing this'. Cross-file retry confirmed at editblock_coder.py lines 58-65: `if not new_content and original.strip():` then `for full_path in self.abs_fnames:` re-running do_replace and breaking on first success. Worth noting for MDMAX: the retry takes the FIRST file that matches in abs_fnames iteration order, so it is a silent cross-file misapplication hazard, not merely 'the filename is advisory'.

verdicts.claim: CLAIM 7: Aider abandoned backtick escalation for XML-ish wrap fences because models ignore quad backticks; GitHub issue 2879 metadata
verdicts.reason: The code half is confirmed verbatim in aider/coders/base_coder.py lines 73-85: `def wrap_fence(name){ return f"<{name}>", f"</{name}>" }` and `all_fences = [("`"*3,"`"*3), ("`"*4,"`"*4),  # LLMs ignore and revert to triple-backtick, causing #2879, wrap_fence("source"), wrap_fence("code"), wrap_fence("pre"), wrap_fence("codeblock"), wrap_fence("sourcecode")]`. But the issue METADATA (title 'Bug: Creating files named with the file extension only without the filename.', state closed, created 2025-01-16T02:45:53Z, closed 2025-02-27T00:02:30Z) I could not verify: api.github.com returned nulls unauthenticated, and I could not authenticate because /Users/sagnikmitra/.config/codex-env/tokens.zsh is inside this sandbox's read-deny list. Separately, 'gave up on backtick-count escalation entirely' overstates the source — quad backticks remain in the list as rung 2; they are not removed, merely followed by wrap fences.
verdicts.correction: Aider retains quad backticks and appends wrap fences after them. Issue 2879 metadata is unverified by me; treat as researcher-attributed until re-fetched with a token.

verdicts.claim: HEADLINE: 'Eight harnesses independently converged on the identical three-part contract'
verdicts.reason: Six of the eight carry zero evidence anywhere in the claim set. The CLAIMS list substantiates only Aider and the OpenAI cookbook; codex `seek_sequence::normalise`, Roo `normalizeString`/`unescapeHtmlEntities`, Cline `lineTrimmed`, Copilot/Gemini `_unescapeStringForGeminiBug`/`correctOldStringMismatch`, and Zed's line hint are asserted by function name with no fetch, no URL, no quote. I independently verified the Claude Code one from the shipped binary and the researcher's description of it is accurate to an impressive degree — `Hlt(e,t)` is the ladder (exact `includes` → `QWu` quote fold → `bgs` \uXXXX unescape → `ZWu` escape-regex → null); `Gir` is the write-back; `r8u` is exactly the stated opening-quote heuristic (`r===" "||r==="\t"||r==="\n"||r==="\r"||r==="("||r==="["||r==="{"||r==="—"||r==="–"`); and `t8u` does preserve majority hex case via `o>i?c.toUpperCase():c`. That one verification is solid. But 'eight independently converged' is a convergence claim whose whole force is the count, and 6/8 of the count is unevidenced. Convergence is also the weakest form of evidence here: these harnesses are not independent — the cookbook explicitly cites Aider's format, so at least two are causally linked.
verdicts.correction: Claim two verified harnesses (Aider, Claude Code) plus one vendor endorsement (OpenAI), and note the OpenAI-cites-Aider dependency that breaks independence. Fetch the other five before counting them.

verdicts.reason: Four of the five character classes have zero empirical support in the researcher's own corpus. Measured across all 13,849 old_strings with an ASCII non-match assert: quotes 201A/201B/201E/201F occur 0 times anywhere; Unicode spaces (00A0, 2002–200A, 202F, 205F, 3000) occur 0 times anywhere; ellipsis U+2026 is 1/85 not-found vs 77/13,441 successes (OR 2.07, χ²=0.54, p=0.464, not significant); smart quotes 2018/2019/201C/201D are 0/85 vs 7/13,441 (p=0.833, not significant). Only dashes clear significance. The full non-ASCII census also shows the corpus's real inhabitants are U+2014 (1,793 old_strings), U+2192 (447), U+00B7 (393), U+00A7 (198), U+20B9 (124) — several of which the r1 rung does not address at all. Attributing the union to three implementations is fair framing, but Claude Code contributes only the four quote characters, and I could not verify codex or Roo.
verdicts.correction: Ship r1 as a dash fold (U+2010–2015, U+2212) — the only class with measured support — and justify the rest as defensive rather than measured.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN §1(d): 'never a version (Microsoft's SECURITY.MD V0.0.7→V0.0.9 broke exact-string matchers in my own corpus)'
verdicts.reason: Located both artifacts. ~/Desktop/GitHub/md/node_modules/typescript/SECURITY.md contains `<!-- BEGIN MICROSOFT SECURITY.MD V0.0.9 BLOCK -->` and ~/Desktop/GitHub/md/node_modules/tslib/SECURITY.md contains `<!-- BEGIN MICROSOFT SECURITY.MD V0.0.7 BLOCK -->` — two versions of the same marker coexisting in one tree, which is exactly the failure mode described, and it is also real-world prior art for the begin/end HTML-comment region pair. One qualification: both live under node_modules, i.e. vendored third-party files, not authored corpus content, and only 8 SECURITY.md files exist across the corpora. The design conclusion (id must be an opaque token, never a version) is sound and well-supported by this artifact.
verdicts.correction: Note the artifacts are vendored (node_modules), which strengthens rather than weakens the point — it shows version drift arrives from outside the user's control.

CLAIM 3 — both OpenAI cookbook quotes verbatim; the notebook is exactly 70,905 bytes as stated.
CLAIM 4 — the cookbook's SEARCH/REPLACE example markers are genuinely inverted (>>>>>>> SEARCH … <<<<<<< REPLACE) against Aider's HEAD=^<{5,9} SEARCH>?\s*$ / UPDATED=^>{5,9} REPLACE\s*$.

CLAIM 5 — AST-confirmed dead code: bare return at editblock_coder.py:183, lines 185-186 unreachable, and line 185 is the ONLY call site of replace_closest_edit_distance, so the function is entirely dead. The live SequenceMatcher (find_similar_lines, threshold=0.6) is error-reporting only, called once at line 98.
