STATUS-COLUMN TYPING as a (status, note) split rather than an enum coercion. 74.7% of AI status-prefixed cells carry trailing prose; every markdown table model I found treats the cell as one opaque inline stream. Splitting it yields a filterable/sortable typed column with the note preserved — with zero syntax change to the file.

A LINT RANKED BY SILENT CROSS-PARSER DIVERGENCE rather than by style. Every markdown linter I read ranks rules by convention. None measures 'what fraction of this document's meaning changes between the parser you author in and the parser your reader runs' — which is the only ranking that explains why blank-line-before-list (51.4% of AI list items lost under Python-Markdown, invisible under CommonMark) outranks every style rule by two orders of magnitude.

REDUNDANCY DETECTION for the thematicBreak+heading pair. 79.81% of AI thematic breaks carry zero information beyond the heading that immediately follows. No tool models a construct as informationally redundant with its neighbour; markdownlint MD035 only enforces that the redundant marker be spelled consistently.

FENCE-CLASS RECOGNITION ('this fence is a readout, not code'). 76.8% of unlabeled AI fences are aligned key=value dumps, arithmetic showing work, prompt drafts or tree diagrams. Every existing rule (MD040, remark-lint-fenced-code-flag) demands a LANGUAGE and every existing tool tries to guess one. Nobody classifies the fence's ROLE, which is the question that actually matters for both syntax highlighting and AI consumption.

PER-DOCUMENT DIALECT CALIBRATION. The 41.2%–90.9% by-project spread on the single most important lint means a global threshold is unsound. No markdown tool calibrates its own confidence against the document it is currently reading.
per_area.design:
WHAT SHIPS: `mdmax dialect` — a read-only recognition pass over the existing mdast, plus `mdmax lint` — a small autofix set. They are separate binaries-of-thought on purpose: recognition never touches bytes, lint touches bytes only through minimal splices.

CARRIER — the answer is NOTHING. The file stays byte-identical. Recognition is deterministic and cheap enough to recompute on every parse, so there is nothing to persist, and therefore nothing that can rot, be forged, or need a schema. This is the strongest possible form of "a document NAMES a capability, never CARRIES one": the document names nothing at all, and the compiler derives everything. Concretely rejected: (a) emitting `<dl>` — GFM has no definition-list syntax (verified against the spec's own extension list) and HTML would break splice-only writing; (b) a `mdmax.blocks` frontmatter map of span-hash → role — that is CARRYING, it desynchronises on the first external edit, and it fails G3 because a receiving AI would have to understand it; (c) a new info-string language — nothing needs to be transported.

WHAT IT RECOGNISES (five rules, each with a measured accept rate on AI and a measured false-accept rate on human npm READMEs):
  R1 DESCRIPTION LIST. A list with >=2 items where EVERY item's first paragraph opens with a `strong` node. Accept 38.95% of AI multi-item lists, 5.99% of npm README lists. Emits `descriptionList{ pairs:[{term, termSpan, definitionSpan}] }`. Sibling consistency is the whole gate — item-level lifting would additionally swallow the 13.70% of AI lists that are only partially bold-led.
  R2 LABELED GROUP. A paragraph that is exactly one `strong` node (plus optional trailing `:`), immediately followed by a list, table, code or blockquote at the same depth. Accept 65.8% of AI bold-only paragraphs; human npm ratio to headings is 0.04 vs AI 0.44. Emits `labeledGroup{ label, labelSpan, bodySpan, bodyKind }` — a section with a name and a boundary, without inventing a heading level.
  R3 STATUS COLUMN. A table column where 100% of data cells (>=3 rows) begin with a glyph from the closed set {✅ ❌ ⚠ ⚠️ 🔴 🟡 🟢 🟠 🔄 ⏳ ❓ 🔵} — that set is 100% of the observed AI vocabulary and ✅❌⚠ alone is 93.5% of it. Emits `statusColumn{ header, cells:[{status, note, noteSpan}] }` — a SPLIT, not an enum, because 74.7% of cells carry a note. Accept 2.59% of AI columns.
  R4 REDUNDANT RULE. A `thematicBreak` whose next sibling is a `heading`. 79.81% of AI thematic breaks. Emits an advisory `redundantSeparator` marker; the break stays in the tree, stays in the file, and is only used to suppress a duplicate section boundary in outline/TOC/chunking views.
  R5 READOUT FENCE. A fence with no info string whose body is not classifiable as code and matches an aligned key=value / arithmetic / tree / short-literal shape (76.8% of AI unlabeled fences). Emits `role:"readout"`. Never guesses a programming language.

WHAT IT REFUSES TO GUESS — the refusal list is the product:
  - MIXED lists (13.70% of AI lists): some items bold-led, some not. Emit `ambiguous:descriptionList` with the ratio; lift nothing.
  - Bold runs followed by lowercase continuation (20.2% of AI bold-leads) or by no separator at all (36.1%): that is mid-sentence emphasis, not a term. R1 requires separator-or-trailing-colon AND >=2 following words AND non-lowercase continuation.
  - Bold runs of >5 words (12.3% of AI bold-leads are 6+ words): a phrase, not a label. Downgrade to advisory.
  - Any status column below 100% cell match or below 3 data rows.
  - Any fence language. Ever. R5 only asserts "not code"; the `text` tag is offered as a fix, never applied silently.
  - Term-as-identifier. 15.5% of long AI messages have a duplicate bold term, so lifted terms are display names only and block identity still comes from the existing content-derived re-anchoring.

DEGRADATION IF WRONG: because recognition writes nothing, a wrong lift degrades to the unlifted view — a description list renders as a list, a labeled group renders as a paragraph plus a list, a status column renders as a table. There is no corrupt state to recover from and no migration. This is the same asymmetry the thesis already relies on: an unknown info string round-trips, and here an unrecognised construct is simply the CommonMark construct it already was. The only byte-touching component is lint, and every autofix carries an invariant: re-parse after the splice and require the resulting AST to be node-for-node identical or strictly more structured (never fewer nodes, never a changed node type outside the fix site); on violation, revert and report.

LINT SET, ranked by measured (prevalence x silence x damage):
  L1 blank-line-before-list. Prevalence 65.97% of AI lists / 72.49% in >=4KB messages. Silence: TOTAL — CommonMark renders it correctly, so the author never sees a problem. Damage: 51.4% of all AI list items become literal `- text` under Python-Markdown, the parser MkDocs requires. Fix: insert one `\n`. Rank 1 by a wide margin and the only lint that on its own justifies the pass.
  L2 accidental setext (`text\n---`). Prevalence low — 428 sites in 298 of 78,989 messages (0.38%), 75 distinct texts. Silence: TOTAL and worse than L1 — it renders as a heading, so it looks deliberate. Damage: MAXIMUM per occurrence — a sentence becomes an H2, poisoning the outline, the anchor set, the TOC and every heading-based chunker. Fix: insert a blank line before the rule. Ranks 2 on damage despite rank 5 on prevalence.
  L3 fence not classifiable and unlabeled. Prevalence 46.94% of AI fences. Silence: medium. Damage: low for rendering, high for AI consumption and for any tool asking "is this executable?". Fix: offer `text` (or a role tag) as a suggestion; never infer a language.
  L4 fence guard. Prevalence 0.52% of AI fences (23 of 4,463). Silence: high. Damage: catastrophic when it fires — the fence closes early and the remainder of the document becomes code. Cheap check, keep it, rank it 4 on prevalence not on fear.
  L5 rule-marker normalisation (`***`/`___` → `---`). AI is already at 100.00% `---`. Zero value against AI input. Do not ship.

CLI SURFACE:
  mdmax dialect <path|-> [--json] [--min-confidence N] [--explain]     # recognition report; exit 0 always; writes nothing
  mdmax dialect --stats <glob>                                         # the construct distribution table used to calibrate
  mdmax lint <glob> [--rules L1,L2,L4] [--against commonmark,python-markdown]
  mdmax lint --fix <glob> [--dry-run]                                  # minimal splices only; AST-superset invariant enforced per fix
  mdmax view <path> --as outline|groups|tables                         # what the lift buys, rendered from the IR, file untouched
`--against python-markdown` is the differentiating flag: it reports meaning that changes between the parser you authored in and the parser your reader runs, which is a question no existing linter asks.
per_area.measurement:
THE OPEN QUESTION IS NOT PREVALENCE — that is now measured. It is SEMANTIC PRECISION: when R1/R2/R3 fire, is the lifted structure what the author meant? My accept rates are structural, not semantic; I have no labels.

CORPUS. Stratified sample of 600 candidate sites drawn from the extracted corpus at $TMPDIR/mdmax/ai-msgs.jsonl (78,989 messages), stratified so the sample is not dominated by the duplication I found in the setext data (one sentence was 66% of 244 occurrences): dedupe by normalised text before sampling; cap any single distinct construct instance at 3. Strata: 200 R1 ALL-bold lists, 100 R1 MIXED lists (the designed refusals — measuring that refusing was right is as important as measuring that lifting was right), 150 R2 bold-only-paragraph groups, 100 R3 status columns, 50 R5 readout fences. Plus a 200-site human control drawn from H_NPM_README + kubernetes/website@snapshot-initial-v1.20 + rust-lang/book@nostarch-2020-05-25 to measure false-accept on text the pass should mostly ignore.

TASKS. Per site, two independent human annotators answer three binary questions with the surrounding 40 lines visible: (a) is the bold run a TERM naming the rest of the item, or emphasis inside a sentence? (b) does the bold-only paragraph LABEL the block that follows it, or is it a sentence that happens to be bold? (c) does the glyph encode a status distinct from the note text, or is it decoration on prose? Binary only, plus a free-text critique — no Likert (LR#4). Report Cohen's kappa; the annotation is unusable below 0.7 and must be re-specified rather than averaged.

VERIFIERS, cheapest first (LR#25). Rules-based first: for every L1/L2/L4 autofix, assert the CommonMark AST after the splice is a node-superset of the AST before — that is a deterministic gate needing no humans and it should be 100%, so any failure is a real bug. Then differential: run the same document through micromark and through the Python-Markdown port and diff the block sequence; the fix must strictly reduce the diff. Only R1/R2/R3 semantic precision escalates to human labels.

n AND POWER. 200 sites per rule gives a 95% CI half-width of about ±7pp at p≈0.85, which is enough to separate 0.90 from 0.75 but not 0.90 from 0.87. That resolution is sufficient because the decision is a threshold, not a ranking.

PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTIONS (recorded before annotation):
  P1. R1 on ALL-bold lists: >=90% judged genuine term→definition. Basis: 61.3% of AI bold-led items already carry an explicit separator plus >=2 words, and the all-items gate should recover most of the remainder through sibling context.
  P2. R1 refusal on MIXED lists is CORRECT >=70% of the time, i.e. in >=70% of mixed lists the bold-led and non-bold-led items are genuinely not the same kind of thing. If refusal is correct only ~50% of the time the gate is too blunt and should become per-run-length rather than per-list.
  P3. R2 on bold-only paragraphs: >=85% judged to label the following block. Basis: 65.8% are followed by a list at all, and the strict form (paragraph is EXACTLY one strong node) is far tighter than markdownlint MD036.
  P4. R3 status split: >=95%. This is nearly mechanical — the glyph vocabulary is closed and 93.5% of it is three symbols.
  P5. Human-control false accept: R1 <=6%, R2 <=2%, R3 <=3%. These are predictions of the SEMANTIC false-accept rate, and they should land below the structural accept rates I measured (5.99%, 0.04 ratio, 2.72%) because human bold-led lists that pass the structural gate are usually genuine definition lists too.
  P6. L1 damage replication: executing real Python-Markdown 3.10 (not my port) on 1,000 sampled AI messages reproduces the 51.4% item-loss rate within ±5pp. If it does not, my port is wrong and every damage claim in this report degrades to inference.

P6 IS THE FIRST THING TO RUN and it is cheap: `pip install markdown` in a throwaway venv, feed 1,000 messages, count `<li>` elements versus the CommonMark count. I did not run it because installing is a RULE 4 op. Until it runs, every damage number here is SIMULATED.
per_area.kill_condition:
Any one of these kills the pass; they are ordered by how cheaply they can be tested.

K1 — THE DAMAGE NUMBER IS AN ARTIFACT OF MY PORT. Real Python-Markdown 3.10 on 1,000 sampled AI messages loses materially fewer than 51.4% of list items — say under 20%. Then L1 is a style nit, the lint set has no anchor claim, and the whole "silent cross-parser divergence" ranking collapses. This is one `pip install markdown` away and must be settled first.

K2 — READERS DO NOT RUN A DIVERGENT PARSER. If the surfaces MDMAX documents actually reach are CommonMark end to end (GitHub/cmark-gfm, VS Code/markdown-it, Obsidian, Docusaurus/remark, Hugo/goldmark are all CommonMark), then L1's damage is theoretical and the addressable population is only Python-Markdown/MkDocs plus older Python and Ruby stacks. Test: instrument which renderers frontmatter users' documents actually hit. If under ~10% of target documents ever meet a non-CommonMark parser, demote L1 from rank 1 to advisory and the lint set loses its headline.

K3 — SEMANTIC PRECISION UNDER 0.85 ON R1 OR R2. If human annotators say the lifted description list or labeled group is not what the author meant more than 15% of the time, the lift is noise dressed as structure and every downstream feature it feeds (outline, rename, typed query, diff) inherits that error rate. There is no threshold to tune out of this, because the by-project spread I measured (41.2%–90.9%) means a global threshold is unsound in principle.

K4 — THE DIALECT IS ERODING FASTER THAN THE BUILD. Bold-led list items already span 27.5% (claude-sonnet-4-6) to 58.6% (claude-fable-5) across models in my own corpus, and models are actively trained against "markdown slop". If a re-measurement 6 months out shows the newest models at human-level rates on bold-led lists AND blank-line-before-list, the pass is aiming at a receding target. Sonnet-5 at 28.47% bold-led — half of opus-4-8's 54.77% — is already a warning shot. Re-measure quarterly on newest-model-only slices; kill if the AI/human gap on R1 falls below 3x.

K5 — RECOGNITION WITHOUT A CONSUMER. If nothing downstream in MDMAX actually consumes `descriptionList` / `labeledGroup` / `statusColumn` — no outline that uses labels, no rename that follows terms, no typed filter on status, no structural diff — then this is a pretty JSON report and should not be built. The pass has no standalone value; it is only worth building against a named consumer that ships in the same release.

K6 — THE STRAIGHTFORWARD BASELINE MATCHES IT. If simply concatenating the raw markdown into an LLM prompt answers the same questions as the lifted IR at comparable cost, the compiler adds nothing for G2/G3. Test this directly and early: on 100 documents, compare a structured query ("list every term defined in this document and its definition") answered from the lifted IR versus answered by a model reading raw markdown. If the model wins or ties, the value is in the editor features (G1) alone and the AI-facing goals should be dropped from the pass's justification.
per_area.effort:
RECOGNITION PASS (R1–R5): small. It is pure mdast traversal plus position arithmetic on the source string — no new parser, no new node types on disk, no persistence layer, no migration. Everything I needed to measure all five rules is ~350 lines of JavaScript, written and run this session at $TMPDIR/mdmax/{analyze,lift,probe,probe2}.mjs. Production quality with span-exact anchoring, the refusal diagnostics, and the `--explain` output is on the order of 800–1,200 lines. Dependencies are already vendored in the repo: mdast-util-from-markdown, micromark-extension-gfm, mdast-util-gfm, micromark-extension-frontmatter, mdast-util-frontmatter. Zero new dependencies.

LINT SET (L1–L4): small, but the AST-superset invariant is the real work. Each fix is a one-character or one-line splice; the safety gate is re-parse-and-compare, which must handle the case where inserting a blank line changes list tightness (`spread`) — that is a legitimate AST change and must be whitelisted, so the comparator needs a semantic notion of "strictly more structured" rather than a naive deep-equal. Budget the comparator at roughly the size of the rest of the lint set combined.

PYTHON-MARKDOWN DIFFERENTIAL (`--against python-markdown`): medium and the highest-risk item. My port is 60 lines and I already know it was wrong twice — first from omitting the frontmatter extension (which inflated k8s thematic breaks 54x and setext headings 131x), then from a catastrophically backtracking HR regex `(?:-+[ ]{0,2}){3,}` that hung the run for 20 minutes against long dash lines. A shippable differential should not reimplement Python-Markdown at all; it should shell out to real Python-Markdown behind an optional dependency, and fall back to "unknown" rather than to a port. That is the honest engineering answer and it is also cheaper.

CRITICAL PATH DEPENDENCY: none of this can be sequenced ahead of the measurement in the previous field. Building the pass before P6 (real Python-Markdown replication) risks building on a simulated number; building it before K5 (a named consumer) risks building a report nobody reads. The correct order is P6, then K5's consumer decision, then R1/R2 (the two lifts with real semantic content), then L1/L2, then R3/R5 and L3/L4.

ARTIFACTS FROM THIS SESSION, all under the scratchpad, nothing written to the repo: /private/tmp/claude-501/mdmax/ai-msgs.jsonl (extracted corpus, 78,989 messages), results.json and lift.json (all counters), analyze.mjs, run.mjs, report.mjs, lift.mjs, probe.mjs, probe2.mjs, bytask.mjs, damage5.mjs, pymd_block.py (fetched Python-Markdown source), h2/ (rust-lang/book@nostarch-2020-05-25 and kubernetes/website@snapshot-initial-v1.20). No git operations, no installs, no writes outside $TMPDIR.
per_area.unverified:
SIMULATED, NOT EXECUTED (LR#62). Every Python-Markdown damage number — 59.1% of messages, 51.4% of list items, and all the per-corpus rows — comes from MY PORT of Python-Markdown's block rule, not from running Python-Markdown. I read the source (blockparser.py:136, blockprocessors.py build_block_parser priorities and each processor's test/run) and ported it faithfully, but python3 has no `markdown` module on this machine and installing it is a RULE 4 op I did not perform. The port is a prediction until P6 runs. Two caveats I can already name: I did not model ListIndentProcessor (priority 90), which is parser-state-dependent and could rescue some indented continuations; and I did not model any Python-Markdown extension, so MkDocs deployments enabling `sane_lists` or `pymdownx` may diverge from my numbers in either direction.

MY OWN MEASUREMENT BUGS, both caught and fixed mid-session, both of which would have produced confidently wrong findings. (1) The first full run omitted micromark-extension-frontmatter, so every `---\ntitle: x\n---` parsed as thematicBreak + setext-h2. That made kubernetes/website read 16.1 thematic breaks per 100KB (true value 0.3) and 9.19% setext headings (true value 0.07%), which would have produced the headline "human technical docs use thematic breaks MORE than AI" — the exact opposite of the truth. (2) My HR matcher `(?:-+[ ]{0,2}){3,}` backtracked catastrophically on long dash runs and hung two full runs. Both are LR#68-class: a number that looked plausible and was wrong. I have no way to rule out a third such bug that I did not catch, and the correcting evidence for #1 was a corpus I happened to have — a single-corpus study would not have surfaced it.

CORPUS VALIDITY. My AI corpus is one user's Claude Code transcripts — one operator, one harness, one vendor's model family, heavily weighted to agentic software and research work (48,152 of 78,989 messages are claude-opus-4-8). It contains NO GPT, Gemini, Llama, Mistral or DeepSeek output, so every claim about "the AI dialect" is really "the Claude-in-Claude-Code dialect". The 17x emoji spread and 2.5x no-lang spread I measured across models within one family is a warning that the cross-vendor spread could be larger still. Assistant messages are also CHAT TURNS, not documents: that alone explains part of the heading deficit (headings appear in 4.72% of all AI messages but 84.08% of >=4KB messages), and I mitigated it with the AI_LONG4K slice but did not eliminate it.

HUMAN BASELINE VALIDITY. H_NPM_README is 734 README.md files from ONE project's node_modules — diverse authorship, but a genre (package docs) with its own conventions, and an unknown fraction may have been LLM-assisted since 2023 as I have no publication dates. H_RUSTBOOK and H_K8SDOCS are pinned to 2020 tags and are genuinely pre-LLM, but each is a single editorial voice, which is exactly why the Rust book's 2^H of 5.69 nearly matches AI's 5.60 — a fact that undercuts the entropy framing generally. H_MDVAULT is AI-contaminated by construction and I used it only as a control, never as a baseline; its 15.74% bold-led rate sits neatly between AI's 46.95% and clean human's 5.87%, which is what contamination looks like. IMPORTANT: the prior evidence's human baseline may have been this same vault, which would explain several of the disagreements.

SEMANTICS ENTIRELY UNMEASURED. Every accept rate is STRUCTURAL. I have zero human labels, so I cannot state a semantic false-positive rate for any of the three named workarounds — the task asked me to measure it and I could not, because it requires annotation I have no way to produce alone. My 61.3% "description-shape" figure is a heuristic proxy computed by the same reasoning that designed the rule (LR#60: a verifier written in the same session as its subject inherits that session's blind spots), and the strict variant of that heuristic collapsed to 3.01% of lists, which tells me the heuristic is not calibrated at all. Treat all precision estimates in this report as unmeasured.

PRIOR ART SEARCH IS SEARCH-TIER. I read the abstract of arXiv 2603.27006 via WebFetch, not the paper body, and I verified none of its numbers. My claim that "nobody lifts an LLM dialect" rests on four web searches plus reading the markdownlint rule list and an npm registry search of 250 remark-lint packages — that is an absence argument from a bounded search, not a proof. A tool could exist under a name none of my queries reached. GitHub's API rate-limited me mid-session (403) and my attempt to source a token failed with exit 127, so I could not enumerate remark-lint's package directory directly and fell back to the npm registry search.

NOT ATTEMPTED. I did not check whether the by-model differences survive controlling for task, because model and project are confounded in my data (different models ran different work) — the model slice numbers are joint effects and I say so rather than pretending otherwise. I did not measure token cost of the lifted IR versus raw markdown, which K6 needs. I did not test any non-Claude model. I did not verify GitHub's rendering behaviour on any of these constructs by actually rendering anything."

verification.area: Adversarial verification of "Recognize and lift the AI markdown dialect" (8 claims + the `mdmax dialect`/`mdmax lint` design)

verdicts.claim: Claim 1 — six constructs (linkReference, definition, image, imageReference, footnoteReference, footnoteDefinition) are at literal zero in AI output; 'verified not to be a parser artifact'
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] I re-ran the extraction over the same corpus (/Users/sagnikmitra/.claude/projects, 13,929 .jsonl) with the same parser stack from /Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/frontmatter/node_modules. On AI CHAT the six zeros reproduce exactly (image 0, linkReference 0, definition 0, imageReference 0, footnoteReference 0, footnoteDefinition 0 across 82,851 messages / 47,971,513 bytes / 1,643,532 nodes). But the researcher only extracted `content[].type==='text'`. The SAME .jsonl files also carry AI-authored markdown FILES in `Write`/`Edit` tool_use payloads — the medium the product actually edits (G1: 'files the user owns'). I built that corpus: 3,323 documents, 24,948,367 bytes. There, `image` is NOT zero: 15 image nodes in 15 docs (0.45%). The other five remain zero. Separately, the stated control is aimed at the wrong rival hypothesis: they excluded a PARSER artifact (inline-code spans), but the live rival is a MEDIUM artifact — terminal chat has no assets to link and no bibliography to reference. Corroborating genre evidence from the same run: raw `html` nodes are 0.27/100KB in AI chat vs 7.06/100KB in AI files (26x) and 256.3/100KB in npm READMEs; headings are 36.3/100KB in AI chat vs 70.7 in AI files vs 155.4 in npm READMEs.
verdicts.correction: Five constructs are at literal zero in AI chat AND in AI-authored .md files. `image` is at zero only in chat; in 3,323 AI-authored .md files it appears 15 times across 0.45% of documents. The zero is a property of the CHAT medium as much as of the model, and that alternative was never excluded.

verdicts.claim: Claim 2 — bold-led list items 46.95% AI vs 5.87% human; list-level ALL-items-bold-led 38.95% vs 5.99%; MIXED 13.70% is the false-positive surface
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Exact reproduction, independently. AI_ALL listItem 71,611 (theirs 71,611), bold-led 33,621 (theirs 33,621) = 46.95%. Lists with >=2 items: 18,332 (theirs 18,332); ALL-bold 7,140 = 38.95%; MIXED 2,512 = 13.70%; NONE 8,680 = 47.35% (sums to 100.00%). H_NPM_README rebuilt independently (734 README.md under node_modules, 5,588,717 bytes — matches their '734 / 5.59 MB'): items 5.88%, lists ALL 6.00%. Crucially this is the ONE claim that survives the medium change: on the 3,323 AI-authored .md FILES the same metrics read 47.52% (items) and 40.38% (ALL-bold lists). R1's sibling-consistency gate is the best-supported rule in the design.

verdicts.claim: Claim 3 — the AI's real heading substitute is the bold-only paragraph (16.0/100KB, ratio-to-heading 0.44 vs human 0.04–0.12, '5–11x the human ratio'); 'the single most liftable construct found'
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] The chat numbers reproduce (bold-only paragraphs 7,647; followed-by: list 5,014, paragraph 863, <end> 624, code 447, table 412, blockquote 150, heading 100 — theirs: 5,014/862/632/447/411/150/100). The generalisation does not. Two independent failures. (a) MEDIUM: on AI-authored .md FILES the bold-only-paragraph : heading ratio is 0.12, which sits INSIDE the human range the researcher themself quotes (H_K8SDOCS 0.09, H_MDVAULT 0.12) and is 1.2x the vault, not 5–11x. (b) ARITHMETIC ATTRIBUTION: the 0.44-vs-0.04 gap is mostly the DENOMINATOR. Numerator (bold-only paragraphs) AI chat 15.9/100KB vs npm 7.0 = 2.27x. Denominator (headings) npm 155.4/100KB vs AI chat 36.3 = 4.28x. 2.27 x 4.28 = 9.7x; in log terms the heading deficit carries ln(4.28)/ln(9.72) = 63.9% of the effect. The signal is mostly 'Claude Code chat replies use few headings', a harness artifact, not 'AI substitutes bold paragraphs for headings'. Also, the stated range '5–11x' silently excludes their own lowest control: 0.44/0.12 (H_MDVAULT) = 3.7x, below the stated floor.
verdicts.correction: In AI-authored markdown files the construct is at 0.12 headings-normalised — indistinguishable from the human vault control. R2 (LABELED GROUP) is calibrated on chat and its discriminative power does not survive the move to files, which is the medium the product edits. Most of the claimed 11x is a heading deficit, not a bold-paragraph surplus.

verdicts.claim: Claim 4 — 79.81% of AI thematic breaks are immediately followed by a heading, so the break is redundant decoration, not a section separator (design rule R4)
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] The AI numbers reproduce almost exactly: thematicBreak 4,563 (theirs 4,562); next sibling heading 3,641 (theirs 3,641) = 79.79%; paragraph 844 (843), code 67 (67), <end> 5, blockquote 3, list 2, table 1 — sums to 4,563. Density 9.5/100KB (theirs 9.6). What does NOT hold is the human contrast that makes R4 a dialect signature. H_MDVAULT (95,088,388 bytes, 5,556 docs) is 84.64% followed-by-heading — HIGHER than AI. AI-authored .md files are 94.86%. The only low human figure is npm README at 38.10%, i.e. a corpus whose thematic-break density (1.9/100KB) is 5x lower and whose heading density is 4.3x higher — different genre, not different author. The researcher dismisses the vault as 'AI-contaminated', which conveniently removes the one same-genre control that contradicts the claim, and no uncontaminated same-genre human corpus is offered. Separately, 'redundant' is a rendering judgment, not a measurement: in CommonMark the break is its own block and its removal is a visible change.
verdicts.correction: The next-sibling distribution is solid. The inference that this DISCRIMINATES AI from human is unsupported: the researcher's own vault control sits at 84.64% and AI .md files at 94.86%, so 79.81% is not even the high end of the range.

verdicts.claim: Claim 5 — `***` and `___` are at literal zero in AI output; 'AI needs no enforcement because it is already at 100.00% `---`'
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] The AST-level finding reproduces exactly: AI_ALL thematic-break marker dash 4,563 / asterisk 0 / underscore 0. The 100.00% does not survive the researcher's OWN evidence sentence, which reports a raw line-shape scan of 'dash 5,429, asterisk 0, underscore 5' out of 5,434 — that is 5,429/5,434 = 99.908%, not 100.00%. A claim of exactly 100.00% is contradicted by the denominator printed one clause earlier. Second problem: my own fence-aware raw scan of the identical corpus gives dash 4,821 / asterisk 0 / underscore 0 — 608 fewer dash lines than theirs and zero underscores. Neither their raw count (5,429) nor mine (4,821) is reconciled to the AST count (4,563); the residue is setext underlines, frontmatter delimiters and in-fence lines. Two raw scans and one AST scan disagree by up to 19% and the paper reports whichever supports the sentence.
verdicts.correction: AST-level: dash 4,563 / asterisk 0 / underscore 0 — correct. Raw-line level, by their own numbers, 99.908%. State the level, and reconcile the raw and AST counts before quoting either.

verdicts.claim: Claim 6 — the prior '4-backtick guard 0.08% vs 0.97%' does not reproduce; and 'nesting IS understated — fence body contains a ``` run is AI 0.83% vs npm 0.08% (10.4x) and k8s 0.02% (41x), not the claimed 2.1x'
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement + primary-read] The refutation half holds: nothing anywhere near 0.97%. My counts — AI_ALL 4+ backtick openers 14/4,461 = 0.31% (AST) or 5/4,381 = 0.11% (raw, fence-aware); H_NPM_README 12/4,916 = 0.24%; AI_MDFILES 0.07%. Three problems with the rest. (1) The revised 'nesting' ratios decode to single-digit event counts: 0.83% x 4,463 = 37 fences, 0.08% x 5,021 = 4 fences, 0.02% x 4,789 = 0.96 ~ 1 fence. The headline '41x' rests on ONE observation in the k8s corpus and is used to overturn a prior figure. (2) The gloss is an inference dressed as a measurement: 'a fence whose body contains a backtick run >= the opener length, i.e. a fence that terminates early' — by construction a fence that terminated early cannot have that run inside node.value, because the run would have BEEN the closer. The metric is a hazard proxy for a run that is not at line start; it never observes the failure. (3) They declare a prior number 'REFUTED AS STATED' without ever establishing what it measured. I grepped the design of record: '0.97%' appears nowhere in docs/ (PLAN.md or wf-findings). Likewise the '15.2%' they attribute to reference-link usage is, in PLAN.md line 757, the HEADINGS share of 424,419 blocks — an unrelated metric. Refuting an unlocated number whose denominator you never recovered is not a refutation. Caution on their own method: their AI figure (0.11%) matches a raw line scan while their npm figure (0.24%) matches an AST count, and on my run those two methods disagree by 2.8x on the AI corpus — consistent with the same metric being counted two different ways across corpora.
verdicts.correction: The 0.97% does not reproduce anywhere reachable — but neither the researcher nor I can locate what it was a rate OF, so this is 'not found', not 'refuted'. The 10.4x and 41x nesting factors are 37 vs 4 vs 1 observations and must not be quoted as ratios.

verdicts.claim: Claim 7 — 46.94% of AI fences carry no language tag, and 76.8% of unlabeled AI fences are not a programming language (design rule R5 accepts that 76.8%)
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] The no-lang rate reproduces: AI_ALL 2,092/4,461 = 46.90% (theirs 46.94%); H_NPM_README 5.02%; AI_MDFILES 46.26% — so the headline transfers to files, which is good. The 76.8% does not match the rule it is cited for. Re-deriving from their own category table (n=2,095: other/arithmetic 704, short-literal 341, markdown-ish 266, shell 253, key=value 200, prose 98, markup 91, tree 70, output/log 34, json-ish 24, pathlist 9, empty 5): 76.80% = 1,609 = {other 704 + short-literal 341 + markdown-ish 266 + key=value 200 + prose 98}. R5 is specified as 'aligned key=value / arithmetic / tree / short-literal shape' — that set is 704 + 200 + 70 + 341 = 1,315 = 62.77%. The cited figure INCLUDES prose (98) and markdown/prompt drafts (266), which are not readouts and which R5 does not name, and EXCLUDES tree (70), which R5 does name. R5's accept rate is overstated by 14.03 percentage points (a 22% relative overstatement). Separately, both the 12-way classification and the 'independent heuristic language inference confidently labels 19.8% vs 52.7%' are single self-authored classifiers with no held-out set and no second rater, tagged own-measurement rather than inference.
verdicts.correction: R5 as specified accepts 62.77% of unlabeled AI fences (1,315/2,095), not 76.8%. The 76.8% is a different predicate — one that admits prose and markdown drafts and drops trees.

verdicts.claim: Claim 8 / L1 — 65.97% of AI lists have no blank line before them; the headline damage is that 51.4% of all AI list items silently degrade to literal text under Python-Markdown, the parser MkDocs requires
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement, Python-Markdown 3.10.3 installed from the official wheel] The direction is real and it is the design's best card, but the metric is wrong twice and the headline number has no derivation. (a) 65.97% reproduces EXACTLY — I get 12,711/19,268 — and that confirms the denominator is ALL lists at ALL depths. 1,024 of those 12,711 'violations' (8.06%) are NESTED lists inside list items, where no blank line before is normal, correct tight-list markdown. The human corpus is at 97.87% on the same nested bucket vs AI 99.03%: it carries no signal, it is pure denominator padding. (b) Their 'restricted to lists that directly follow a paragraph: AI 68.42% vs human 39.13%' is the nested case by construction — a nested list's previous sibling IS the parent item's paragraph. Root-level only: AI 66.13% (9,280/14,033) vs H_NPM_README 4.67%. That is a 14.2x gap; their metric reports 1.75x. Their own instrument understates their own effect by 8x. (c) The 51.4% appears in the headline and in L1 and is derived NOWHERE in the evidence block — claim 8's evidence is entirely list-level, never item-level. I measured it directly: render every message with Python-Markdown 3.10.3 and diff the `<li>` count against the CommonMark listItem count. AI chat: 34,255 of 71,611 items lost = 47.83%. AI-authored .md FILES: 7,513 of 38,850 = 19.34%. H_NPM_README: 458 of 9,618 = 4.76%. (d) The mechanism is narrower than stated: I confirmed degradation-to-literal-text after a paragraph, a table and a closed fence, but `## H` followed immediately by a list renders CORRECTLY, and nested lists do not become literal text — they silently FLATTEN one level (a real, different defect the design never names).
verdicts.correction: Root-level lists with no preceding blank line: 66.13% AI vs 4.67% human npm (14.2x), not 65.97% vs 26.05%. Measured Python-Markdown item loss is 47.83% on chat and 19.34% on AI-authored .md files, not 51.4%. Drop nested lists from the denominator and drop after-heading from the damage set.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN — L1 (blank-line-before-list) is 'the only lint that on its own justifies the pass', and `--against python-markdown` is 'a question no existing linter asks'
verdicts.reason: [primary-read, via curl to raw.githubusercontent.com and api.npmjs.org] Both L1 and L3 already ship in markdownlint's rule set, default-on and autofixable. MD032, verbatim from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DavidAnson/markdownlint/main/doc/md032.md: '# `MD032` - Lists should be surrounded by blank lines', 'Aliases: `blanks-around-lists`', 'Fixable: Some violations can be fixed by tooling', and the doc's first example is literally 'Some text' followed immediately by '* List item' — the exact AI pattern. MD040, from doc/md040.md: '# `MD040` - Fenced code blocks should have a language specified', 'Aliases: `fenced-code-language`' — that is L3. Reach: markdownlint 2,886,431 downloads/week, markdownlint-cli2 1,247,941/week, remark-lint 324,705/week (api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-week). The researcher cites MD035 from the same doc/ directory for L5, so the rule list was open when L1 and L3 were written up as the ranked contribution. On the cross-parser flag: babelmark.github.io returns HTTP 200 — babelmark3 is the canonical tool for 'what does this markdown mean under a different implementation' across ~30 parsers. It is not a linter, so the flag is a genuine packaging improvement, but 'a question no existing linter asks' overstates it into novelty. Third miss: R1's descriptionList reinvents a construct with established markdown syntax (`Term` / `: definition`) shipped in Python-Markdown's own standard-library `def_list` extension (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Python-Markdown/markdown/master/docs/extensions/definition_lists.md: 'The Definition Lists extension adds the ability to create definition lists in Markdown documents. This extension is included in the standard Markdown library'), plus PHP Markdown Extra, kramdown, pandoc and markdown-it-deflist. The design rejects `<dl>` on the correct ground that GFM has no definition-list syntax, but never engages the settled invariant it bears on — 'Parasitize a construct the target already parses' — for the one parser the design names as its differentiating target.
verdicts.correction: L1 = markdownlint MD032 (default rule set, autofixable). L3 = markdownlint MD040. Rank the pass on what it adds OVER `markdownlint --fix` — which on my measurement is the cross-parser damage quantification and the recognition layer, not the lints themselves.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN R3 — a closed set of 12 status glyphs {✅ ❌ ⚠ ⚠️ 🔴 🟡 🟢 🟠 🔄 ⏳ ❓ 🔵} that 'is 100% of the observed AI vocabulary'; cells are a (status, note) pair because 74.7% carry trailing prose
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] The (status, note) half is sound and reproduces: 1,409 of 1,922 status cells carry trailing prose = 73.3% in AI chat, 406/557 = 72.9% in AI .md files (theirs 74.7%). Accept rate 277/9,184 columns = 3.02% chat (theirs 2.59%) and 64/10,786 = 0.59% on AI .md files. The closed-set claim is false on the same corpus. Scanning every table column where all data cells (>=3 rows) begin with an Extended_Pictographic glyph, I observe 32 DISTINCT leading glyphs in AI chat, of which 20 are outside their 12: 87 of 1,922 cells (4.53%) — 🔒 33, 🌍 30, 💀 3, ↪ 2, ⏸ 2, 📋 2, 🔶 2, 📄, 🥇, 🥈, 🥉, 🔑. On AI-authored .md files it is worse: 67 of 557 cells (12.03%) outside the set, led by ⬜ 41 and ☐ 12 — plainly status glyphs (unchecked box) that the design would reject. Because R3 requires 100% cell match, every one of those columns is silently refused. Also note the 74.7% figure is quoted in the headline with no n; the denominator only becomes checkable by rebuilding the measurement.
verdicts.correction: The AI status vocabulary is open, not closed: 32 glyphs observed in chat, 4.53% of cells outside the proposed set; 12.03% outside on AI .md files. A hardcoded 12-glyph set with a 100%-match gate will silently refuse ~1 in 8 status columns in the product's actual medium. Detect 'leading pictographic glyph, consistent across the column' instead of enumerating.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN — every autofix carries an AST-superset invariant: re-parse after the splice and require node-for-node identity or strictly more structure; on violation, revert and report
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] I implemented L1 exactly as specified — insert one '\n' before every ROOT-level list whose previous sibling ends on the immediately preceding line — and ran it over both corpora: 11,687 insertions across 5,682 AI chat messages, 3,950 insertions across 809 AI .md files. Zero violations of the invariant (no document lost a listItem after the splice) across all 86,174 documents. Efficacy is total, and better than the researcher claimed: re-rendering the spliced corpus with Python-Markdown 3.10.3 recovers 100% of the lost list items — chat goes from 34,255 items lost to 0 (72,596 `<li>` against 71,611 CommonMark listItems), files from 7,513 lost to 0. This is a real, unclaimed validation of the design's central safety mechanism and of L1's rank-1 position, and I report it despite an adversarial brief because it is what the measurement says.

survived: Claim 2 in full — bold-led list items 46.95% (33,621/71,611, exact reproduction) and list-level ALL-bold 38.95% / MIXED 13.70% / NONE 47.35% (sums to 100.00%); human npm 5.88% item / 6.00% list. The only claim that also transfers to AI-authored .md files (47.52% / 40.38%). R1's sibling-consistency gate is the best-supported rule in the design.
Claim 4's numeric core — 3,641/4,563 = 79.79% of AI thematic breaks are immediately followed by a heading; full next-sibling distribution reproduces to within 1 count on every bucket.
Claim 5's AST-level finding — thematic-break markers in AI output are dash 4,563 / asterisk 0 / underscore 0. `***` and `___` genuinely do not occur as thematic breaks.

Claim 6's refutation half — the '0.97%' 4-backtick figure reproduces in no corpus I can reach (AI 0.11–0.31%, npm 0.24%, AI .md files 0.07%). L5's 'do not ship' verdict on rule-marker normalisation is correct.

Claim 7's no-lang rate — 46.90% of AI fences carry no info string (2,092/4,461), and it transfers to AI-authored .md files at 46.26% vs npm README 5.02%. R5's refusal to ever infer a language is right.

Claim 8's direction and severity — AI lists really do omit the preceding blank line at ~14x the human root-level rate (66.13% vs 4.67% after a paragraph), and the Python-Markdown damage is real and large (47.83% of chat list items, 19.34% of AI .md-file list items lost, vs 4.76% human baseline).
R3's re-characterisation of the emoji cell as a (status, note) SPLIT rather than an enum — 73.3% of chat cells and 72.9% of AI .md-file cells carry trailing prose.

The CARRIER = NOTHING decision — I found no violation of the settled invariants. Recognition writes no bytes, names nothing, and degrades to the unlifted CommonMark construct. The rejection of a `mdmax.blocks` frontmatter map on desync and G3 grounds is correct.

The AST-superset invariant and L1's efficacy — 15,637 splices across 86,174 documents, zero invariant violations, and 100% recovery of Python-Markdown list-item loss on both corpora. Stronger than claimed.
killed: Claim 3's generalisation — 'the bold-only paragraph is the AI's substitute for a heading'. On AI-authored .md files the bold-only-paragraph : heading ratio is 0.12, inside the human range the researcher quotes (K8SDOCS 0.09, MDVAULT 0.12). The construct is a chat phenomenon. R2 (LABELED GROUP) is calibrated on the wrong medium.

Claim 3's magnitude attribution — 63.9% of the log-magnitude of the 0.44-vs-0.04 gap comes from the heading DENOMINATOR (36.3 vs 155.4 per 100KB), not the bold-paragraph numerator (15.9 vs 7.0). And the stated '5–11x' range excludes their own H_MDVAULT control at 3.7x.

Claim 1's scope — 'six constructs at literal zero in AI output' is true of AI chat but false of AI-authored .md files, where `image` occurs 15 times in 0.45% of 3,323 documents. The stated control excludes a parser artifact but never tests the live rival, a medium artifact.

Claim 5's '100.00%' — contradicted by the researcher's own raw scan in the same sentence (5,429/5,434 = 99.908%), and their raw dash count (5,429) is 608 above mine (4,821) and 866 above the AST count (4,563), unreconciled.
Claim 7's 76.8% — decodes to a set that includes prose and markdown drafts and excludes trees. R5 as specified accepts 62.77% (1,315/2,095), a 14.03-point overstatement.
Claim 8's 51.4% headline — derived nowhere in the evidence block. Direct differential measurement gives 47.83% on chat and 19.34% on AI-authored .md files.

Claim 8's metric — 65.97% is computed over all lists at all depths, and 1,024 of the 12,711 'violations' are nested lists where no blank line is correct markdown that Python-Markdown renders fine (human npm is at 97.87% on that same bucket).

Claim 8's human contrast — 'after a paragraph: AI 68.42% vs human 39.13%' is dominated by nested lists on both sides. Root-level only it is 66.13% vs 4.67%; their instrument understates their own effect by 8x.
Claim 4's discrimination — H_MDVAULT is 84.64% and AI .md files 94.86% followed-by-heading, both ABOVE the AI chat 79.79%. R4 has no demonstrated same-genre human contrast.
Claim 6's revised nesting ratios — '10.4x' is 37 fences vs 4; '41x' is 37 vs ONE k8s fence. Not quotable as ratios.

Claim 6's mechanism gloss — 'body contains a run >= opener, i.e. a fence that terminates early'. By construction a fence that terminated early cannot carry that run in its body. Inference labelled measurement.

L1 and L3 as novel contributions — markdownlint MD032 `blanks-around-lists` ('Fixable: Some violations can be fixed by tooling', 2.89M downloads/week) is L1 exactly; MD040 `fenced-code-language` is L3. The researcher cited MD035 from the same doc/ directory.

'`--against python-markdown` is a question no existing linter asks' — babelmark3 (babelmark.github.io, HTTP 200) is the canonical cross-implementation markdown differ. The packaging is new; the question is not.

R3's closed emoji set — 32 distinct leading glyphs observed in AI chat status columns, 4.53% of cells outside the proposed 12; 12.03% outside on AI .md files, led by ⬜ (41) and ☐ (12). 'That set is 100% of the observed AI vocabulary' is false on the same corpus.

The unexamined prior art for R1 — `Term` / `: definition` definition-list syntax ships in Python-Markdown's standard-library `def_list` extension, plus PHP Markdown Extra, kramdown, pandoc, markdown-it-deflist. Directly bears on the settled 'parasitize a construct the target already parses' invariant and is never engaged.
new_defects: GENRE CONFOUND, and the missing corpus was in the files they already parsed. The entire AI side is terminal CHAT (`content[].type==='text'`); every human baseline is PUBLISHED documents (npm READMEs, k8s docs, the Rust book). The 2x2 has two empty cells: no AI-document corpus and no human-chat corpus. The AI-document corpus was sitting in the same .jsonl files as `Write`/`Edit` tool_use payloads — I extracted 3,323 documents / 24,948,367 bytes in one pass. It changes conclusions: claim 3 collapses (0.44 -> 0.12), claim 1 loses one of its six zeros, and the L1 damage figure falls from 47.83% to 19.34%. The product's stated goal G1 is 'collaboration on files the user owns' — the calibration medium is not the product medium.

UNDECLARED DUPLICATION: 23.55% of the corpus is repeated content. Of 82,851 assistant text messages, 19,510 are byte-identical to an earlier message (63,341 unique texts) and 12,675 share a uuid with an earlier record. Retries, resumed sessions and compaction replays are weighted 2x, 3x, N times. No dedup is mentioned and no rate is reported on a deduplicated corpus.

SINGLE-SUBJECT, PROMPT-DICTATED CORPUS DESCRIBED AS 'THE AI DIALECT': 35,829 of 82,851 messages (43.25%) are `isSidechain: true` subagent output, whose format is dictated by orchestrator prompts written by the same user, under a global CLAUDE.md that explicitly prescribes structure. The researcher's own split shows the effect (thematic-break-before-heading: subagent 93.18% vs main 48.54% — a 1.9x swing) and then reports AI_ALL as the dialect anyway. One user, one harness, one model family, one instruction set.

CATEGORY ERROR IN THE RANK-1 LINT'S DENOMINATOR: nested lists are counted as blank-line violations. A nested list's previous sibling IS its parent item's paragraph, so 'no blank line before' is the definition of a tight list. It is correct markdown, Python-Markdown renders it (it flattens one level, a different defect), and the human corpus scores 97.87% on the same bucket against AI's 99.03%. Including it pads the denominator and, via the 'after a paragraph' restriction, suppresses the real 14.2x effect down to 1.75x.

RATIOS FROM n=1 AND n=4 USED TO OVERTURN PRIOR FINDINGS. '10.4x' is 37 fences vs 4. '41x' is 37 vs approximately one k8s fence (0.02% x 4,789 = 0.96). These are presented as corrections to an established 2.1x. No interval, no count, no caveat.

A HEADLINE NUMBER WITH NO DERIVATION ANYWHERE: 51.4% appears in the headline and in L1 and is the single number said to justify shipping. Claim 8's evidence block is entirely list-level and never computes an item-level rate. When measured directly it is 47.83% (chat) / 19.34% (files).

RATIO MOVEMENT ATTRIBUTED TO THE WRONG TERM: claim 3 reads a 9.7x ratio-of-ratios as evidence about bold-only paragraphs when 63.9% of the log-effect is the heading denominator collapsing. Any metric of the form X-per-heading in a corpus with 4.3x fewer headings needs both terms reported.

SELF-AUTHORED CLASSIFIER OUTPUT TAGGED `own-measurement`: the 12-way fence-content taxonomy and the 'independent heuristic language inference' (19.8% vs 52.7%) are one classifier written by the person reporting the result, with no held-out set, no second rater, and no error rate. That is `inference`, and it is the sole support for R5's accept rate.

THE STATED CONTROL TESTS THE WRONG RIVAL HYPOTHESIS. 'Verified not to be a parser artifact' (re-parsing 6 messages to show ![](...) sat in inline code) excludes a hypothesis nobody held. The live rival for six zero constructs in terminal chat is that the medium has no assets, no bibliography and no repeated link targets. It is testable in one pass and was not run.

REFUTING A NUMBER WHOSE DENOMINATOR WAS NEVER ESTABLISHED. Claim 6 declares the prior 0.97% 'REFUTED AS STATED' without ever recovering what it was a rate of. I grepped docs/: '0.97%' appears nowhere in PLAN.md or wf-findings-2026-08-01.md. The same applies to '15.2%' attributed to human reference-link usage — the only 15.2% in the design of record is PLAN.md line 757, the HEADINGS share of 424,419 blocks. Two of the paper's 'prior claims' are unsourced or mis-sourced.

POSSIBLE METHOD SWITCH ACROSS CORPORA ON ONE METRIC: their AI 4-backtick figure (0.11%) matches a raw line scan while their npm figure (0.24%) matches an AST count. On my run those two methods disagree by 2.8x on the AI corpus (0.11% raw vs 0.31% AST). Not provable from the writeup, but the two figures being compared may not be the same measurement.

THE ONE NUMBER THAT DOES NOT REPRODUCE AT ALL: accidental setext. They report 428 sites in 298 of 78,989 messages; I get 238 (AST) / 239 (fence-aware raw) in 235–236 messages — a 79% overstatement. Related trap they warned about and I then hit from the other side: a naive raw setext scan over AI-authored .md files returns 520 sites, almost all of which are YAML frontmatter closers. Their own micromark-extension-frontmatter correction (k8s 16.1 -> 0.3 per 100KB) was the right instinct and is the best methodological moment in the paper; it just was not applied to their own setext count.

MINOR, REPORTED FOR COMPLETENESS: 'Term-as-identifier — 15.5% of long AI messages have a duplicate bold term'. I measure 42.2% on chat (576/1,365 messages >=4KB) and 48.4% on AI .md files (553/1,142). The predicate may differ, so I do not call it refuted — but the number does not reproduce, and it happens to be the number backing a safety decision. It fails 2.7x in the direction that makes the safety case stronger, so the conclusion holds.

per_area.title: Token cost as a first-class diagnostic tier
per_area.headline: Every mechanically-decidable, provably-semantics-preserving token rewrite in markdown, applied at once to a 4,289-file / 21,925,516-token real corpus, recovers 0.155% — 6 tokens out of 27,615 on this project's own PLAN.md — while selecting an llms.txt-style index over the same corpus is a 101.1× reduction, so COST must ship as an attribution-and-budget instrument in the projection layer, never as a savings linter in the check layer.

findings.claim: The complete catalogue of mechanically-decidable token waste in real markdown is worth 0.772% of a corpus if you allow semantics-changing edits, 0.349% if you require byte-identical HTML output, and 0.155% if you additionally refuse the rewrites that the two major markdown linters explicitly recommend against. This is the single most decision-relevant number in the area and it kills the savings framing.
findings.evidence: $TMPDIR/tokwork/final.py over ~/Desktop/GitHub/md (files=4289 bytes=81913833 o200k=21925516 cl100k=22234176 claude=24406242). Per-rule o200k savings: M1 emoji 78335 (0.357%), T2 table compact->tight 42620 (0.194%), E1 drop escape 22564 (0.103%), X1 html comment 14451 (0.066%), S1 setext->ATX 3433 (0.016%), T1 table normalize 2798 (0.013%), P1 *em*->_em_ 2703 (0.012%), W1 trailing ws 1571 (0.007%), U1 [url](url)-><url> 679 (0.003%), U2 strip utm 153 (0.001%), H1 long HR 36 (0.000%). Totals: ALL rules 169343 = 0.772%; HTML-identical only 76557 = 0.349%; HTML-identical + human-OK 33937 = 0.155% (cl100k 33728, claude 21100).

findings.claim: On this project's own design of record the entire safe catalogue recovers 6 tokens. On docs/engine/README.md it recovers 0. On the user's global CLAUDE.md it recovers 4. A cost linter that reports savings has nothing to say about the documents this project actually writes.
findings.evidence: $TMPDIR/tokwork/report.py. /Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/frontmatter/docs/engine/PLAN.md: total 27615 tokens, 106298 bytes, 1748 lines; 'RECOVERABLE: depad 0 | escapes 6 | emoji 104 | html-comments 25 => 6 safe = 0.022%'. docs/engine/README.md: total 11791 tokens; '=> 0 safe = 0.000%'. /Users/sagnikmitra/.claude/CLAUDE.md: total 14577 tokens; '=> 4 safe = 0.027%'.

findings.claim: CORRECTION to the established evidence: 'alignment padding alone is 30-35%' is the theoretical MAXIMUM for a degenerate table, not a typical value. Measured on a 100x8 table the padding share is 16.1%; it reaches 31.5% only when every cell is one character and every header is long, and it is exactly 0.0% when columns are already uniform-width.
findings.evidence: $TMPDIR/tokwork/tables.py, 100 rows x 8 cols, o200k_base: 'md padded (aligned) 3706 (100.0%) / md single-space 3108 (83.9%) / md minimal |a|b| 2900 (78.3%) / csv 2713 (73.2%) / tsv 2615 (70.6%) / json columnar 2897 (78.2%) / json minified (records) 4476 (120.8%)'. $TMPDIR/tokwork/e2.py shape sweep: '1-char cells, long headers padded=2566 min=1758 saving=31.5%'; 'short enum cells 23.6%'; 'prose cells (ragged) 10.9%'; 'uniform-width cells 0.0%'. The established starting figure of 4,178 vs 2,979 tokens is not reproduced; my padded/CSV pair is 3,706 vs 2,713.

findings.claim: CORRECTION, and the reason the padding rule has almost no surface: 95.7% of real markdown tables contain no alignment padding at all. Only 140 of 3,230 tables in the corpus have any whitespace run of length >=2 next to a pipe. Padding is a machine-generated artifact of formatters, not an authoring habit.
findings.evidence: $TMPDIR/tokwork/clean_tbl.py (run twice, identical): 'tables=3230 tables with real padding=140 (4.3%) padding runs=2422'; o200k pure-depad saving=2648 = 0.0121% of corpus. Style histogram from $TMPDIR/tokwork/tab2.py: {compact: 2798, aligned: 125, other: 256, tight: 51}; 'tables with 0 saving: 2840/3230 (87.9%)'.

findings.claim: De-padding a table saves exactly 1.09 tokens per padding run, and the constant is stable to within 0.7% across three tokenizer families. A linter can therefore report an honest padding saving with a regex and no embedded tokenizer at all.
findings.evidence: $TMPDIR/tokwork/clean_tbl.py: 'o200k pure-depad saving=2648 tok/padrun=1.093 | cl100k 2644 tok/padrun=1.092 | claude 2630 tok/padrun=1.086' over 2,422 padding runs. Independent synthetic confirmation in $TMPDIR/tokwork/e1.py: 'padded body/header cells: 596 padded delim cells: 8 total: 604' vs 'delta o200k: 598 delta cl100k: 597' — 0.990 tokens per padded cell.

findings.claim: CORRECTION to the established whitespace claim: a run of 2 through 64 spaces costs ONE token in o200k_base and cl100k_base, not two. Every run length 1..64 has its own dedicated vocabulary id. The '2 tokens' reading comes from measuring a string that also contains a leading newline.
findings.evidence: $TMPDIR/tokwork/ws.py and e1.py. o200k token ids for space runs: 1:[220] 2:[256] 3:[271] 4:[257] 5:[530] 6:[1699] 7:[309] 8:[269] ... 19:[699] — one id each. '"  " alone o200k=[256] -> 1'; '"\n" + "  " o200k=[198, 256] -> 2'. r50k_base is linear (n spaces = n tokens), confirming the 'r50k artifact' half of the established claim exactly. p50k_base merges only to 24 spaces. Cost is also non-monotone at the top: 80 spaces = 2 tokens in o200k but 128 spaces = 1.

findings.claim: CORRECTION: the whole-corpus de-indent saving is 0.936%, not 0.67% — and it is unattainable, because micromark proves de-indenting a nested list changes the emitted HTML. The maximally aggressive, semantics-destroying version of the biggest whitespace idea in markdown buys under one percent.
findings.evidence:
$TMPDIR/tokwork/e3.py: 'o200k 21925516 -> 21720281 saving 0.936%; cl100k 22234176 -> 22028856 saving 0.923%'. $TMPDIR/tokwork/sem.mjs (micromark 4.0.2 + micromark-extension-gfm 3.0.0): 'DIFF de-indent nested list — A: "
  • a
    • b
" B: "
  • a
  • b
"'.

findings.claim: CORRECTION: 'nested markdown lists cost 157% of minified JSON' holds only for a degenerate short-key data tree. Measured 140.6% at depth 4 / branch 4 with short keys, 134.2% at one-word leaves, and 102.2% for a tree whose leaves are sentences. It converges to 100.9% at 200-word leaves. Real markdown lists are prose, so the rule has essentially no addressable surface.

PROSE TREE 'markdown nested list 421 (102.2%) / json minified 412 (100.0%) / yaml 409 (99.3%)'. Crossover sweep: leaf=1 word md/json=134.2%, leaf=12 110.9%, leaf=50 103.4%, leaf=200 100.9%.
