(a) SCOPE INCONSISTENCY inside one script: the table analysis scores a cell word retrievable only if it appears in `rowToks` — the tokens of that ONE ROW (drill.mjs line ~34) — while the inline-code analysis in the same file uses `all`, the whole-file token set. The shipped index is document-scoped, so the row-scoped instrument systematically overstates cell darkness. (b) The evidence text concedes the 21.6% 'other' bucket is contaminated by the researcher's own hyphen bug and was 'corrected in a later pass', yet reports the uncorrected three-way split and never gives the corrected one. (c) Their OWN classify2 run reports table blocks 0/3265 = 0.00% dark under MiniSearch, so the entire table story exists only at cell granularity and is contradicted by the block-granular metric they use for the headline.
verdicts.correction: 14.15% is a row-scoped, one-instrument figure with a self-declared contaminated 21.6% residual. At the block granularity used for the headline, MiniSearch is dark on 0.00% of 3,265 table blocks.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 4] Inline code is the single largest lexical loss in the corpus: 28.45% of the distinct words inside code spans cannot be found by exact search anywhere in their own file.
verdicts.reason: own-measurement + primary-read. Numbers reproduce exactly (spans=397141, 1059743, 301476 = 28.448%, 259801 = 24.515%). Two defects. (a) MISLABELLED DENOMINATOR: drill.mjs increments `spanWords` once per distinct word PER SPAN, not per file and not corpus-wide — so 1,059,743 is a count of (span, word) pairs, and a term written in 100 spans of one file is counted 100 times. Calling it 'distinct words' is wrong, and it inflates the weight of repeated commands like `npm`. (b) The loss does not exist in the product. extractCodeText strips the backticks and indexes the content as a fourth MiniSearch field; `fields: ["title", "tags", "body", "code"]` is at HEAD (git show HEAD:…search-index.ts:118), not an uncommitted edit. My end-to-end run against real MiniSearch confirms `npm` and `install` are both retrievable. The design's line that this fix 'makes extractCodeText's backtick-stripping workaround redundant rather than load-bearing' inverts the causality: extractCodeText is exactly why the backtick costs nothing today.
verdicts.correction: 301,476 of 1,059,743 (span, word) pairs — not distinct words — are unfindable in a naive raw-source index. In the shipped index the figure is not measured, and the mechanism is already mitigated.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 5] Leading glue is fatal, trailing glue is rescued by prefix search; confirmed end-to-end with `Run \`npm install\``.
verdicts.reason: own-measurement. The corpus figures reproduce exactly (12,278,083 content tokens; 331953/357537/97239/87497; 786729 = 6.408%; 429192 = 3.496%) and the leading/trailing asymmetry is real — I verified it end-to-end on the shipped pipeline: `NODE_ENV=production` indexes as one token, query `NODE_ENV` is rescued by the prefix pass, query `production` misses. But the flagship demonstration is false for this product. The claim says 'Confirmed end-to-end: `Run \`npm install\`` tokenizes to ["Run","`npm","install`"] — query "npm" MISSES under both exact and prefix'. Running the shipped extractBodyText/extractCodeText + buildSearchIndex + SEARCH_PASSES, query `npm` returns the document. 'End-to-end' here means end-to-end through the researcher's own regex model, not through the code.
verdicts.correction: The asymmetry holds for glue that survives extraction — `|`, `~`, `=`, `<`, `>` — demonstrated on `~~old~~` and `|alpha|string|`, both of which do miss. It does not hold for the backtick, which never reaches the tokenizer.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 6 / HEADLINE] Darkness is a property of (content × engine): 0 of 609,879 blocks are dark under all six shipped tokenizers, and FlexSearch is dark on none at all.
verdicts.reason: own-measurement. I re-ran classify2.mjs unmodified and reproduced every figure to the digit (blocks=619051, with-words=609879, minisearch 12938/2.12%, lunr 21084/3.46%, flexsearch 0, orama 470, tantivy 52, uax29 245, dark-under-all-6 = 0, dark-under-≥1 = 33098/5.43%). The numbers are right and the conclusion does not follow, for four independent reasons. (a) 'SIX SHIPPED TOKENIZERS I TESTED' IS FALSE — classify2.mjs imports nothing; it hand-writes five regexes named lunr/flexsearch/orama_en/tantivy/minisearch plus Intl.Segmenter. The lunr, flexsearch and orama packages ARE downloaded in libs/ and are not used by this script. Real lunr additionally applies a stopword filter and a Porter stemmer, neither modelled. This is [inference] labelled [own-measurement]. (b) THE METRIC IS DEGENERATE. Retrievability is defined symmetrically — tokenize the query with the same function, require its tokens ⊆ the block's tokens — which makes it invariant to shattering. I built two controls: a UNIGRAM tokenizer (every character its own token) and a NULL tokenizer (every document → the single term 'x'). Both score 100.00% word-recall and 0 dark blocks. The NULL tokenizer returns every document for every query. FlexSearch's 0.00%/100% on Indic is exactly this degenerate case — the metric awards a perfect score to the tokenizer Claim 8 says destroys the content. (c) '0 UNDER ALL SIX' IS ENTAILED BY ONE COLUMN. An intersection is empty if any member is empty, so flexsearch=0 forces it; it is not an independent result. I recomputed the intersection excluding flexsearch: 51 blocks (0.01%) are dark under all five remaining engines, INCLUDING the proposed uax29 fix. So 'no markdown is intrinsically dark' is false as stated. (d) BLOCK GRANULARITY HIDES THE LOSS — a block counts as lit if ONE word is retrievable, so a 129-word block with 128 unretrievable words is not dark. The honest column is word-level recall (93.75%), not 2.12%.
verdicts.correction: Under five regex models of engines (not the engines), 51 of 609,879 blocks (0.01%) are dark under every one including UAX#29. The '0 under all six' headline is carried entirely by a tokenizer that shatters Devanagari, Tamil and Arabic into fragments. A stronger, defensible version of the thesis survives — darkness is largely engine-dependent — but it cannot be measured with a symmetric-tokenization metric.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 7] Lunr does not merely degrade on non-Latin scripts — it deletes them from the index entirely; all tokenize to the empty list.
verdicts.reason: primary-read + own-measurement. The two source citations verify verbatim: lunr-2.3.9/package/lunr.js:465 `lunr.tokenizer.separator = /[\s\-]+/` and :1337-1341 the trimmer with `.replace(/^\W+/, '').replace(/\W+$/, '')`. But I ran REAL lunr rather than the regex model, and the behaviour is different in a way that matters: Devanagari yields n=5 tokens `["","","","",""]`, not the empty list — the empty strings survive and the built index contains one real term, `""` (verified: `Object.keys(idx.invertedIndex)` = `["","hello","world"]`). 'Tokenizes to the empty list' is an artifact of the researcher's `.filter(Boolean)`, i.e. a property of their reimplementation. The retrieval conclusion does hold — I confirmed `idx.search('Москва')`, `search('北京')` and `search('दिल्ली')` all return `[]`, because the search pipeline does not apply the trimmer, so no query can ever produce the `""` term. Two further gaps: Cyrillic and CJK are asserted in the claim but absent from the evidence list (I verified both myself — they behave identically). And PRIOR ART IS MISSED: `lunr-languages` is the ecosystem's standard remedy — registry.npmjs.org/lunr-languages gives latest 1.20.0 published 2026-05-10, and api.npmjs.org reports 1,871,165 downloads in 2026-07-01..2026-07-30 against lunr's own 27,177,585. This is a defect of lunr's DEFAULT configuration, not of lunr.
verdicts.correction: Non-Latin tokens are not deleted; they collapse to a single unreachable `""` term, which is functionally equivalent but a different mechanism. The remedy (lunr-languages) is a mainstream, heavily-used package the research does not mention.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 8] Any tokenizer built on \p{L}\p{N} shatters every abugida, because Indic/Thai/Arabic/Hebrew vowel signs are \p{M}; MiniSearch is BETTER here and the failure sets are disjoint.
verdicts.reason: primary-read + own-measurement. The FlexSearch source verifies at the cited line: libs/flexsearch-0.8.212/package/dist/flexsearch.bundle.module.debug.js:68 — `const da = /[^\p{L}\p{N}]+/u`. I re-ran the tokenizations through the REAL `MiniSearch.getDefault('tokenize')` (not a regex model) and got the claimed values exactly: Devanagari mini=5 ["दिल्ली","एक","बड़ा","शहर","है"] vs flex=7 ["द","ल","ल","एक","बड","शहर","ह"]; Tamil mini=4 flex=8; Arabic mini=2 flex=8. Category checks confirm: U+094D L=false M=true, U+093F L=false M=true, U+0E34 L=false M=true, U+064E L=false M=true. One correction to the framing: FlexSearch is not uniformly worse. On Thai it produces 4 fragments where MiniSearch produces 1 unsegmented blob, and on CJK both produce 1. So 'disjoint' holds for abugidas but the ranking flips for no-space scripts.
verdicts.correction: Correct as measured for Devanagari/Tamil/Arabic. FlexSearch is not worse than MiniSearch on Thai (flex=4 vs mini=1) or CJK (both=1).

verdicts.claim: [DESIGN 2] Index title + heading-path: mixed-query recall@10 goes 1.6–2.2% → 65.4–70.6%; MRR 0.007–0.013 → 0.424–0.485; body-query MRR cost ~2.4% relative, consistently across 3 seeds.
verdicts.reason: own-measurement. The experiment (hpexp.mjs / hp_7 / hp_101 / hp_999, which differ only in `let seed=`) is circular by construction AND uses a search configuration the product explicitly rejected. Q1's query is DEFINED as one heading-path term filtered to be absent from the body plus two body terms — `c=>{const h=c.hpw.filter(w=>!c.cw.includes(w)); return [pick(h,1)[0], ...pick(c.cw,2)].join(' ')}` — and is searched with `const OPTS={combineWith:'AND'}`. Under AND, an index that excludes the heading path can never match, so the 1.6–2.2% baseline is a definitional zero, not a measurement. The product does not search that way: SEARCH_PASSES at search-index.ts:294-306 is a three-pass ladder (AND+prefix → OR+prefix → OR+fuzzy:1), and the code comment above it documents why AND-only was rejected. I re-ran all three seeds with only `OPTS` swapped for the shipped ladder: Q1 baseline A = 35.0 / 38.0 / 39.4% (mean 37.5), treatment B = 67.2 / 73.6 / 73.0% (mean 71.3). The win is real and large — +33.8 points — but the relative gain is 1.90×, not the ~36× implied by 1.9% → 68%. Q3 (title) goes 36.9% → 68.1%, not 0.6% → 65.6%. And the cost claim fails: Q2 MRR A→B relative change is −4.14% / −5.45% / −1.00% (mean −3.53%), a 5.5× spread across seeds — neither '~2.4%' nor 'consistent'.
verdicts.correction: Under the product's own search configuration: heading-path indexing moves mixed-query recall@10 from 37.5% to 71.3% (1.90×, +33.8 points) and costs 3.5% relative MRR on body-only queries with a −1.0% to −5.5% spread across three seeds. The 1.6–2.2% baseline is an artifact of AND-only search plus a query built from the treatment.

verdicts.claim: [DESIGN 2] Also index the FILE TITLE separately: a second, equal-sized win (0.6% → 65.6%) that 72.1% of blocks need.
verdicts.reason: primary-read. `title` is ALREADY an indexed MiniSearch field in the shipped product, at HEAD, not in the uncommitted diff: `git show HEAD:src/modules/vault/infrastructure/search-index.ts` line 118 gives `fields: ["title", "tags", "body", "code"]` and line 170 `docs.push({ path: relPath, title: parsed.title, tags: ..., body, code })`. The experiment's baseline (variant A, a block index with no title field) is not the product's baseline. Additionally the experiment's `title` is `path.basename(f,'.md')` — the filename — whereas the product indexes `parsed.title` from frontmatter/h1, so the two are not the same signal. This is prior art missed inside the researcher's own repo, in the very file cited for the three-pass ladder.
verdicts.correction: Title indexing is shipped. The open question is block-level (chunk) indexing, which is a different and unshipped thing; the '0.6% → 65.6%' figure measures a baseline the product does not have, and under the shipped ladder the same comparison is 36.9% → 68.1%.

verdicts.claim: [DESIGN 1] Replace MiniSearch's tokenizer with Intl.Segmenter/UAX#29; the existing three-pass prefix/fuzzy ladder stays untouched, only the tokenizer changes; strictly additive.
verdicts.reason: own-measurement. 'Only the tokenizer changes' is falsified: the ladder's third pass is `{combineWith:'OR', fuzzy: 1}`, and `fuzzy: 1` is an ABSOLUTE edit distance (the code comment says so, and cites snapshot/snapchat at distance 2). UAX#29 collapses the token-length distribution, and a 1-character term at edit distance 1 is a wildcard. Measured against real MiniSearch over a 6-doc corpus: query `C++` under the default tokenizer returns exactly ["5"] (the doc containing it); under UAX#29 with the identical pass-3 options it returns ["5","6","4","1","3"] — five of six documents, including three Chinese ones — because `isWordLike` reduces `C++` to the single token `C`. Same for `C#`. Token length is a hidden parameter of the fuzzy threshold, so the ladder must be re-tuned, which makes the change not strictly additive. Second, UAX#29 introduces NEW misses the darkness metric cannot detect, because it glues `.` between letters (MidNumLet): `foo.bar()` → ["foo.bar"] so query `bar` misses where the default tokenizer finds it; `v1.2.3` → one token so `1.2.3` misses; `search-index.ts` → ["search","index.ts"]. The genuine win is real and I reproduce it — `公园` and `大学` become retrievable where the default tokenizer returns nothing — but it is a recall win validated on a recall-only, shattering-blind metric, with an unmeasured precision cost.
verdicts.correction: UAX#29 fixes CJK/Thai segmentation (verified) but is not drop-in: it breaks `C++`/`C#`/`F#` entirely, makes sub-token queries on dotted identifiers and version strings miss, and turns pass-3 `fuzzy:1` into a near-wildcard. The ladder must be re-tuned and the precision cost measured before this ships.

verdicts.claim: [DESIGN 3] unretrievable-block is 0.44% of blocks / 23.0% of files; the strict panel-eligible set is 24.1% of files / 716 blocks, empty on 75.9%.
verdicts.reason: own-measurement. yield.mjs reproduces exactly — dark 171 files (23.01%) / 660 blocks, compactpipe 21 (2.83%) / 56, strict 179 (24.09%) / 716 blocks, 742/743 = 99.9% any-class, p50 = 19 findings. But the corpus SILENTLY CHANGES between the claims and the design. Claims 2/3/4/5/6 use 4,317 files / 619,051 blocks / 609,879 content-bearing blocks. yield.mjs and hpexp.mjs use 743 'author-note' files (canon minus Mirrors/ and .sgnk/) — a 5.8× smaller file set — and hpexp's block corpus is 99,972 while unique-files.txt itself holds 3,904 paths. The 0.44% has no stated denominator at all; back-solving 660/0.0044 gives ~150,000, which matches none of the other three. The same class measured both ways gives 2.12% of blocks / 31.13% of files on the full corpus versus 0.44% / 23.0% on the author-note corpus. Only the smaller pair is quoted, and it is the pair that supports the design's conclusion that a persistent panel is unjustified. Separately, the design never mentions that 12,477 of 12,938 MiniSearch-dark blocks — 96.44% — are LIST ITEMS (from the researcher's own 'DARK BY KIND' output), and none of the five proposed classes names list items.
verdicts.correction: State the denominator. On the full 4,317-file corpus the same class fires on 2.12% of blocks and 31.13% of files; on the 743-file author-note corpus it fires on 23.0% of files. Also: 96.4% of dark blocks are list items, a fact present in the researcher's own output and absent from every proposed class.

survived: The nine-glue-character enumeration (Claim 1 core). Verified verbatim in minisearch 7.2.0 source and independently reproduced by probing all 32 ASCII punct/symbol characters through MiniSearch.getDefault('tokenize'): GLUE = $ + < = > ^ ` | ~, all \p{S}, none \p{P}. This is a genuine and useful sharpening of PLAN §17.6, which named the regex but not its ASCII consequences.

Every raw arithmetic figure in Claims 2-6 reproduces to the digit on an independent re-run of the researcher's own scripts: 319541/6749=47.35; 15327 dark cells over 108310 (14.15%) with 11818/206/3303 summing correctly; 12,278,083 content tokens with 331953/357537/97239/87497 and totals 786729 (6.408%) / 429192 (3.496%); 301476/1059743 = 28.448%; blocks=619051, with-words=609879, minisearch 12938 (2.1214%), lunr 21084, flexsearch 0, orama 470, tantivy 52, uax29 245. No fabricated numbers found.

All four source citations verify verbatim at the exact line numbers given: minisearch/dist/es/index.js:2002, lunr-2.3.9/package/lunr.js:465 and :1337-1341, flexsearch-0.8.212 bundle.module.debug.js:68. All four PLAN.md cross-references check out (§17.6 CJK 18.1%, §17.7 PublicNoteView h1 injection and 81% of files, §17.8 `language:` in 111 of 272 notes, §4 the 86.6%-empty panel finding).

Claim 8 in full, verified against the REAL MiniSearch tokenizer rather than a model: Devanagari mini=5/flex=7, Tamil mini=4/flex=8, Arabic mini=2/flex=8, and U+094D / U+093F / U+0E34 / U+064E all \p{M} and not \p{L}. The \p{L}\p{N} class of tokenizers really does destroy abugidas, and MiniSearch really is better on them.

Claim 5's leading-versus-trailing glue asymmetry, which I confirmed end-to-end through the actual shipped pipeline for glue that survives extraction: `NODE_ENV=production` indexes as one token, `NODE_ENV` is rescued by the prefix pass, `production` is not; `~~old~~` and the cells of `|alpha|string|` are unreachable. This is the part of the diagnostic that is real in the product.

Lunr's non-Latin retrieval failure, which I confirmed end-to-end with the real library: search('Москва'), search('北京'), search('दिल्ली') all return []. The mechanism description is wrong but the outcome is right, and it extends to Cyrillic and CJK, which the claim asserted without evidence.

The DIRECTION of the heading-path finding. Even after correcting the search configuration, indexing the heading path moves mixed-query recall@10 from 37.5% to 71.3% across three seeds — a genuine +33.8-point win. The recommendation is right; only its magnitude and framing were inflated.

The core product judgment that a persistent Problems panel is not justified, and that these findings mostly belong in the engine rather than in a user-facing diagnostic. That conclusion survives every correction I applied — if anything the full-corpus numbers strengthen the case that per-file panels would be noise.
killed: The headline. '0 of 609,879 blocks are dark under all six shipped tokenizers I tested' fails on three counts: the six tokenizers are five hand-written regexes plus Intl.Segmenter (classify2.mjs imports none of the downloaded libraries); the zero is entailed by flexsearch=0 alone, since an intersection is empty whenever one member is; and excluding that single degenerate engine yields 51 blocks (0.01%) dark under every remaining engine INCLUDING the proposed UAX#29 fix. The claim that no markdown is intrinsically dark is false as stated.

The darkness metric itself. Because retrievability is defined symmetrically (query tokenized by the same function, tokens must be a subset of the block's), it is invariant under shattering. I ran two controls through it: a UNIGRAM tokenizer and a NULL tokenizer that maps every document to the single term 'x'. Both score 100.00% word-recall and 0 dark blocks; the NULL tokenizer returns every document for every query. Every ranking in Claim 6 and every yield in Design 3 inherits this.

'The backtick, not the pipe, is the dominant lexical killer' (Claim 2) at the product level. Re-running the census over the text that actually reaches MiniSearch, backtick-led tokens fall 319,541 → 4 while pipe-led tokens fall 6,749 → 6,394. The 47.3x ratio inverts to 0.0006x. The design's inference that this 'makes extractCodeText's backtick-stripping redundant rather than load-bearing' is backwards — extractCodeText is the reason the backtick costs nothing.

Claim 5's flagship end-to-end demonstration. `Run \`npm install\`` was said to make 'npm' unfindable under both exact and prefix. Run through the shipped extractBodyText + extractCodeText + buildSearchIndex + SEARCH_PASSES against real MiniSearch, both 'npm' and 'install' return the document. 'Confirmed end-to-end' meant end-to-end through the researcher's own regex model.

Design 2's headline evidence, which is circular. The Q1 query is constructed to contain a heading-path term filtered to be absent from the body, then searched with combineWith:'AND' only. A body-only index cannot match it by definition, so the 1.6-2.2% baseline is a definitional zero. Under the product's own three-pass ladder the baseline is 35.0/38.0/39.4% and the gain is 1.90x, not ~36x. Q3's 0.6% baseline is the same artifact.

Design 2's title recommendation, which is already shipped: `fields: ["title", "tags", "body", "code"]` at HEAD, search-index.ts:118. Prior art missed inside the researcher's own repo, in the file they cite for the ladder.

'The existing three-pass prefix/fuzzy ladder stays untouched; only the tokenizer changes... strictly additive.' Measured false: under UAX#29, pass-3 `fuzzy:1` on the query 'C++' returns 5 of 6 documents including three Chinese ones, versus exactly 1 under the default tokenizer, because isWordLike reduces 'C++' to the single token 'C'. Token length is a hidden parameter of the fuzzy threshold.

'MRR on pure body queries falls ~2.4% relative, consistently across 3 seeds.' Under the shipped ladder the three seeds give -4.14%, -5.45%, -1.00% — mean -3.53% with a 5.5x spread. Neither the magnitude nor the consistency holds.

The claim that all six diagnostic classes fire on '99.9% of files' and the strict set is '24.1% of files / 716 blocks', presented alongside corpus statistics computed over a 5.8x larger file set. The design switches from 4,317 files to 743 without saying so, and quotes the corpus that makes the panel look emptiest.
new_defects: ENGINES WERE MODELLED, NOT RUN. classify2.mjs — the cited source for the entire six-engine comparison — imports nothing. Its `T` object is five inline regexes named minisearch/lunr/flexsearch/orama_en/tantivy plus Intl.Segmenter. The real lunr, flexsearch and orama packages are sitting unused in /private/tmp/claude-501/mdmax/libs/. Real lunr additionally applies a stopword filter and a Porter stemmer; real tantivy's default pipeline drops tokens over 40 bytes; real FlexSearch applies charset normalization. None is modelled. This is [inference] tagged [own-measurement], and it is the single largest evidence-discipline breach in the submission.

THE METRIC CANNOT DETECT THE FAILURE IT IS USED TO RANK. Claim 6 scores FlexSearch 0.00% dark / 100.00% recall; Claim 8 says FlexSearch shatters Devanagari, Tamil and Arabic. Both are in the same submission and the contradiction is never reconciled. I demonstrated the mechanism with a NULL tokenizer that scores a perfect 100%/0 while returning every document for every query. Any engine ranking produced by this metric is unusable, including the one used to select UAX#29 over the alternatives.

MEASUREMENT UNIT CHOSEN TO FLATTER. Darkness is scored per BLOCK and a block is 'lit' if ONE of its words is retrievable — so a 129-word block with 128 unretrievable words counts as fine. The word-level recall column in the same table (93.75% for MiniSearch) is the honest statistic, and it is 3.4x worse than the 2.12% headline. The design then builds its panel-eligibility gate on the block figure.

A LARGE RESULT SITTING IN THE OUTPUT, UNREPORTED. The researcher's own 'DARK BY KIND' table shows listitem 12477/369943 and table 0/3265. So 96.44% of MiniSearch-dark blocks are list items and 0.00% are tables — yet the design ships `compact-table-row` as a headline class ('the only class with a fully automatic fix') and never mentions list items in any of the five classes. The finding contradicts the shipped design and was read past.

SCOPE INCONSISTENCY INSIDE ONE SCRIPT. drill.mjs scores table cells against `rowToks` (tokens of a single row) but inline-code words against `all` (tokens of the whole file). Two different retrieval scopes, neither matching the shipped document-scoped index, feeding two claims presented as comparable.

A DENOMINATOR LABELLED 'DISTINCT WORDS' THAT IS NOT. drill.mjs increments spanWords once per distinct word PER SPAN. 1,059,743 is a count of (span, word) pairs; a term written in 100 spans of one file contributes 100. Claim 4's 28.45% is a rate over the wrong population and over-weights exactly the repeated commands the claim is about.

A CONTAMINATED BUCKET REPORTED ANYWAY. Claim 3 states in its own evidence that the 21.6% 'other' bucket was traced to an instrument bug 'and corrected in a later pass', then reports the uncorrected 77.1/1.3/21.6 split and never supplies the corrected one. Knowing a number is wrong and publishing it is worse than not measuring it.

THE PRODUCT'S OWN CODE WAS NOT RUN. Claims 2, 4 and 5 all concern what MDMAX can retrieve, and all three are measured against raw markdown. extractBodyText deletes inline code and extractCodeText re-indexes it de-backticked as a fourth field — 35 lines above the comment the researcher quotes as 'the established evidence'. Reading the file for the pipe comment while missing the two functions on the same screen is the specific failure, and it inverts the submission's central ranking.

AN EXPERIMENT CONFIGURED MORE STRICTLY THAN THE PRODUCT. hpexp.mjs uses `{combineWith:'AND'}` while search-index.ts:294-306 ships a three-pass ladder whose comment explicitly documents why AND-only was rejected. The stricter configuration maximises the measured gap. Combined with a query built from the treatment variable, it turns a real 1.90x win into a reported ~36x one.

LIVE CORPUS, FOUR-SIGNIFICANT-FIGURE CLAIMS. I reproduced classify2.mjs exactly on the first run and got different numbers on a second run ~15 minutes later (uax29 245 → 246, dark-under-≥1 33098 → 32634, para blocks 131396 → 131259) because ~/Desktop/GitHub/md is being written to. Every figure quoted to four significant figures against this corpus is a timestamped draw, and none of them carries a timestamp.

THREE UNLABELLED CORPORA. 4,317 files (the walk), 3,904 (unique-files.txt), 743 (author notes), with block denominators of 619,051 / 609,879 / 99,972 / ~150,000. Claims and design draw from different ones without saying which, and the 0.44% figure has no stated denominator at all.

PRIOR ART GAP. lunr-languages (latest 1.20.0, 2026-05-10; 1,871,165 downloads in 2026-07-01..2026-07-30 per api.npmjs.org, against lunr's 27,177,585) is the ecosystem's standard fix for exactly the failure Claim 7 describes. Presenting default-lunr behaviour as a property of lunr, without the remedy, overstates the finding.

per_area.title: The degradation certificate — a per-document conformance matrix
per_area.headline: Built and ran a 24-configuration differential harness (cmark-gfm 0.29.0.gfm.13 compiled from GitHub's own source, kramdown/GH-Pages, goldmark/Hugo, pulldown-cmark/mdBook, comrak, markdown-it 15, marked 16, commonmark.js 0.31.2, remark/micromark, react-markdown 10) plus live probes of GitHub's production renderers, and the result kills the premise twice over: "GitHub" is not one target but three renderers that disagree on the same bytes, and of every carrier MDMAX proposes, exactly TWO — the link reference definition and the `[//]: #` idiom — are invisible in 24/24 configurations, while frontmatter is VISIBLE in 23/24 and the HTML comment produces EIGHT distinct outputs (visible in 2, payload destroyed in 10, including GitHub's blob renderer which deletes comments outright).

findings.claim: GitHub is not one rendering target — it is at least three, reachable from one API host, and they produce different HTML from identical bytes. This is the single most important correction to the brief: the certificate's unit is a (product, surface) pair, never a product.
findings.evidence:
Same input `--- title: T id: blk_7f3a --- Line one Line two`. (1) `POST https://api.github.com/markdown` mode=gfm → `

title: T
id: blk_7f3a

Line one
Line two

` (soft breaks become `
`, no heading anchor). (2) same endpoint mode=markdown → `

title: T id: blk_7f3a

` (soft breaks preserved, anchor added). (3) `GET https://api.github.com/repos/github/docs/contents/content/index.md` with `Accept: application/vnd.github.html` → `
title ...` — frontmatter parsed as YAML and recursively tabulated. Run 2026-08-01.

findings.claim: The brief's statement that "GitHub renders a table" for frontmatter is true ONLY of the repo blob viewer. GitHub's comment/API renderer leaks the YAML as a visible `<h2>`. Both are GitHub.

Unauthenticated `curl -s -X POST https://api.github.com/markdown -d '{"text":"--- title: hi --- body","mode":"gfm"}'` returned exactly `

findings.evidence:
24-engine matrix, construct `frontmatter-yaml`: visible 23/24, payload-in-output 23/24, 6 distinct HTML outputs. The single non-visible config is `remark+gfm+math+fm+raw (frontmatter app)` → `

`. All others produce `

` spelling. Engines: commonmark.js 0.31.2, markdown-it 15.0.0 (×3 presets), marked 16.4.2, remark/micromark (×4 configs), react-markdown 10.1.0 (×2), cmark-gfm 0.29.0.gfm.13 (×3), goldmark 1.8.5 (×3), pulldown-cmark 0.13 (×2), comrak 0.39 (×2), kramdown 2.5.2 (×2).

findings.claim: The HTML comment — PLAN.md §2.3 tier 3, "a dumb viewer sees nothing" — produces EIGHT distinct HTML outputs across 24 configs. It is visible as literal text in 2, and the payload is DESTROYED in 10. Tier 3 as specified is unsound.
findings.evidence:
Construct `html-comment`, source `Before. After.`: visible 2/24, payload-in-output 14/24, 8 distinct outputs. Variants: (a) preserved verbatim — commonmark default, markdown-it html:true, markdown-it commonmark preset, cmark-gfm --unsafe; (b) `

Before.

` — commonmark safe:true, cmark-gfm without --unsafe (payload replaced, not hidden); (c) `

` VISIBLE — markdown-it 15 default; (d) `<!-- mdmax:anchor blk_7f3a -->` VISIBLE — react-markdown 10 default; (e) silently deleted — remark bare, remark+gfm, react-markdown+gfm+raw.

findings.claim: GitHub's blob renderer does not merely hide HTML comments — it deletes them from the output entirely, so not even cmark-gfm's `<!-- raw HTML omitted -->` placeholder survives.
findings.evidence: `github/docs` README.md line 1 source is `# GitHub Docs <!-- omit in toc -->`. Fetching the rendered blob via `Accept: application/vnd.github.html` and running `grep -c -- '<!--'` on the response returned `0`; `grep -o -- '<!--[^>]*-->'` returned nothing.

findings.claim: There is NO react-markdown configuration in which an HTML comment survives. With rehype-raw the comment becomes a hast `comment` node, and `hast-util-to-jsx-runtime` has no branch for it — it returns `undefined` and the node vanishes. Without rehype-raw the comment text renders VISIBLY. The brief's "only invisible with rehype-raw" is therefore wrong in both directions.

`node_modules/hast-util-to-jsx-runtime/lib/index.js`, function `one(state, node, key)` lines 133–157 dispatches on exactly `'element'`, `'mdxFlowExpression'|'mdxTextExpression'`, `'mdxJsxFlowElement'|'mdxJsxTextElement'`, `'mdxjsEsm'`, `'root'`, `'text'` and falls off the end. `grep -c "comment"` over the whole file = `0`. Confirmed by measurement: react-markdown-10 (+gfm+raw) → `

` (gone); react-markdown-10 (default) → `

Before.

` (visible).

findings.claim: Exactly TWO carriers are invisible in 24/24 configurations: the link reference definition and the `[//]: # (...)` idiom. Both produce only 2 distinct outputs and the difference is one blank line. Everything else MDMAX has considered leaks somewhere.

`linkref-def` (`[mdmax-anchor]: #blk_7f3a "meta"`) and `linkref-def-unused-colon` (`[//]: # (mdmax blk_7f3a)`): visible 0/24, payload-in-output 0/24, distinct-html 2. The two outputs are `

Before.

` (22 engines) and `

Before.

After.

` (kramdown ×2). Note the corollary: payload-in-output is 0/24, so the anchor exists only in the source file and never in any rendered artifact.

findings.claim: "An unknown fence lang round-trips perfectly" is FALSE for GitHub Pages. kramdown with `input: GFM` collapses any fence whose info string contains whitespace into inline code and makes the meta VISIBLE; kramdown's default parser does not support backtick fences at all.
kramdown with `input: GFM` is GitHub Pages' shipped default, so the fence failure above is not a fringe configuration.

"markdown" => "kramdown", "kramdown" => { "input" => "GFM", "hard_wrap" => false, "gfm_quirks" => "paragraph_end", "syntax_highlighter_opts" => { "default_lang" => "plaintext" } }, ... }.freeze`

findings.claim: `{#id}` heading attributes — recommended as the identity baseline by the prior adversarial audit in wf-findings-2026-08-01.md — are VISIBLE GARBAGE in 21 of 24 configurations, including live GitHub. Only kramdown (×2) and pulldown-cmark with ENABLE_HEADING_ATTRIBUTES honour them.

Construct `attrs-heading` (`# Heading {#blk_7f3a}`): visible 21/24. Twenty-one engines → `

Heading {#blk_7f3a}

`; three → `

findings.claim: The `id` attribute does survive GitHub, but GitHub REWRITES it with a `user-content-` prefix, so any fragment link MDMAX emits against its own id will not resolve there. `class`, `style` and `data-*` are stripped, confirming the brief.

Live `POST /markdown mode=gfm`: input `Text tail.` → `

findings.claim: The CommonMark 0.31.2 punctuation divergence is real and I have both sides in source. The spec widened punctuation to include the Unicode `S` categories; upstream cmark adopted it by RENAMING the predicate; github/cmark-gfm never took the change and still ships a hardcoded pre-0.31.2 table.
findings.evidence: commonmark-spec tag 0.30 spec.txt:340-342 — "A [Unicode punctuation character](@) is an [ASCII punctuation character] or anything in the general Unicode categories `Pc`, `Pd`, `Pe`, `Pf`, `Pi`, `Po`, or `Ps`." Tag 0.31.2 spec.txt:340-341 — "A [Unicode punctuation character](@) is a character in the Unicode `P` (puncuation) or `S` (symbol) general categories." [sic, typo in spec]. commonmark/cmark master `src/utf8.h:18` declares `int cmark_utf8proc_is_punctuation_or_symbol(int32_t uc);` while github/cmark-gfm `src/utf8.h:29` still declares `int cmark_utf8proc_is_punctuation(int32_t uc);` implemented at `src/utf8.c:256` as a hardcoded codepoint table in which `grep -c '8364'` (U+20AC EURO) = `0`. micromark's side: `node_modules/micromark-util-character/index.js:200` — `export const unicodePunctuation = regexCheck(/\p{P}|\p{S}/u);`. cmark-gfm HEAD = 499789b49373bfa045d0e7547e5ee63444c77bca (2026-07-13), version string `cmark-gfm 0.29.0.gfm.13`.

findings.claim: The consequence, measured: `a**€**b` bolds on GitHub and GitHub Pages and does not bold anywhere else — a 5-vs-19 split across 24 configurations, on identical bytes.

`.

findings.claim: GitHub silently DELETES angle-bracket placeholders in ordinary prose — no MDMAX construct involved. 7 of 8 deployed engines do; markdown-it's `html:false` default is the sole survivor. This is a live, verified, silent data-loss case in the most ordinary possible content.
findings.evidence:
Live GitHub `POST /markdown mode=gfm`: input `Path: skills-src///evals/ and Array` → `

Path: skills-src///evals/ and Array

`. Local 8-engine minimal pair on `Path: skills-src///evals/`: markdown-it(default) → `Path: skills-src///evals/`; marked, remark-gfm+raw, cmark-gfm, kramdown/GH-Pages, goldmark/Hugo, comrak, pulldown/mdBook → `Path: skills-src///evals/`.

findings.claim: GitHub converts a single tilde used to mean "approximately" into a strikethrough, which does not merely delete characters — it inverts meaning. Six of eight engines disagree with GitHub, and the two that agree disagree with each other on a neighbouring case.
findings.evidence:
Live GitHub `POST /markdown mode=gfm`: input `a ~10%→~20% b` → `

a 10%→20% b

`. Local: markdown-it, remark-gfm, kramdown/GH-Pages, goldmark/Hugo, comrak → `a ~10%→~20% b`; marked and cmark-gfm → `a 10%→20% b`. On the neighbouring input `~10%~20%`: only marked strips (`10%20%`); cmark-gfm preserves. Discovered by the harness on a real corpus file, then reduced to a minimal pair.

findings.claim: On a real corpus, only 5.00% of files render to identical visible text across seven GFM-class engines that people actually deploy. 285 of 300 diverge; 131 of 300 produce five or more distinct renderings.
findings.evidence: 300 deterministically sampled .md files from ~/Desktop/GitHub/md, engines markdown-it(default), marked(gfm), remark-gfm+raw, cmark-gfm(--unsafe), goldmark(Hugo), comrak(gfm), kramdown(GH Pages): `"identical": 15, "pctIdentical": 5, "histogram": {"1":15,"2":16,"3":24,"4":114,"5":82,"6":47,"7":2}`. Per-engine divergence from the majority signature: kramdown 264, remark-gfm+raw 253, goldmark(hugo) 251, markdown-it 117, marked 75, comrak 20, cmark-gfm 12.

findings.claim: SELF-CORRECTION — my own first divergence number was inflated ~10x by my normalizer. Decoding entities properly and normalizing smart punctuation moves top-level-block divergence from 43.71% to 4.28%. The honest certificate must draw exactly this line, and drawing it is most of the engineering.
findings.evidence: AST-accurate top-level blocks (remark-parse positions) over 40 files / 1,613 blocks of ~/Desktop/GitHub/knowledge, 6 GFM-class engines: `STRICT_divergent: 705, STRICT_pct: 43.71` vs `SEMANTIC_divergent: 69, SEMANTIC_pct: 4.28`. The first version of the harness reported 47.12% because `vis()` decoded only five entities and did not fold smart quotes; kramdown and goldmark(typographer) turn `'`→`’` and marked emits `'`. Fixed by using the `entities` package's `decodeHTML` plus an explicit smart-punctuation fold.

findings.claim: Semantic divergence is not uniform — it is concentrated in exactly the block types MDMAX cares about, and absent from the ones it does not. That is what makes a per-construct table tractable.
findings.evidence: Same run, `semanticByBlockType`: yaml 35/35 (100%), table 3/3 (100%), list 9/222 (4%), paragraph 21/789 (3%), heading 1/511 (0%), blockquote 0/23 (0%), code 0/21 (0%), thematicBreak 0/9 (0%). Strict-mode same buckets: paragraph 415/789 (53%), list 158/222 (71%), blockquote 18/23 (78%), heading 76/511 (15%), code 0/21 (0%).

findings.claim: Prevalence: 74–89% of real files in three corpora contain at least one construct the 24-engine matrix proves divergent. This is not an edge-case tool.
findings.evidence: Regex prevalence over .md files (size<400KB, dotdirs excluded): md-vault 1,468/1,980 = 74.1%; knowledge 242/273 = 88.6%; frontmatter repo 48/57 = 84.2%. Top constructs, md-vault: angle-bracket placeholder 951 (48.0%), pipe-in-prose (kramdown swallows) 751 (37.9%), YAML frontmatter 720 (36.4%), math `$..$` 696 (35.2%), single flanked tilde 477 (24.1%), HTML comment 442 (22.3%), wikilink 340 (17.2%), symbol-inside-`**` 126 (6.4%). Total .md under ~/Desktop/GitHub/md = 4,317 (`find`), 1,989 excluding dot-directories.

findings.claim: The matrix is enormously redundant: 3 of 10 deployed targets detect 100% of the divergences that all 10 detect, and 2 targets get 86%. But the winning 3 are NOT the three most popular — you cannot pick them by intuition, only by running the cover.
findings.evidence: Exhaustive search over the 10 deployed configurations (which disagree on 21 of 45 constructs): k=2 best coverage 18/21 (86%) = {react-markdown-10 default, kramdown 2.5.2 input:GFM}; k=3 coverage 21/21 (100%) = {remark+gfm+math+fm+raw (the frontmatter app itself), react-markdown-10 default, kramdown 2.5.2 input:GFM}. Over the full 24-config set a greedy cover reaches 24/24 with 3 engines: {remark+gfm+math+fm+raw, kramdown default, markdown-it 15 default}.

findings.claim: Cost is dominated by process spawn, not by parsing — 87% of harness wall time. That is the whole performance design.
findings.evidence: 300-file run: `jsEngineMsTotal: 5304` for 900 in-process renders (5.9 ms/render) vs `subprocessMsTotal: 37572` for 1,200 spawns (31.3 ms/spawn); total 43,080 ms, 143.6 ms/file for 7 engines. Three-engine certificate timed on docs/engine/PLAN.md (105,087 bytes): remark app pipeline 58.8 ms, react-markdown default 34.0 ms, kramdown GFM subprocess 123.2 ms → 216.0 ms/doc; projected 15.5 min single-threaded over 4,317 files. A typical (~4 KB) file is ≈43 ms.

findings.claim: The strongest prior art, babelmark3, answers a different question and cannot be run in CI: 38 registered providers, 23 of them (60.5%) behind ENCRYPTED URLs that only the maintainer holds, and the set contains essentially no product surfaces — no Obsidian, Notion, VS Code, Slack, Discord, Typora, Docusaurus, Hugo, Jekyll or Discourse. The only product entry is GitHub.
findings.evidence: `babelmark/babelmark-registry` registry.json = 38 entries. Languages: Php 9, Rust 8, C 3, Kotlin 3, Haskell 2, Python 2, Ruby 2, C# 2, Java 2, Perl 2, JavaScript 1, Javascript 2. Only 15 carry a plaintext `Url`; the rest are ciphertext. readme.md verbatim: "If you want to register an encrypted URL, send me an email at /alexandre_mutel at live dot com/ and I will return you an encrypted URL that you can send via a PR." The one product entry is `{"Name":"GitHub Flavored Markdown","Url":"https://api.github.com/markdown/raw","Lang":"C"}`. Repos: babelmark.github.io 115 stars (pushed 2024-07-15), babelmark-registry 20 stars (2025-09-16), babelmark-proxy 9 stars (2025-03-13).

findings.claim: Nobody has published this. Every plausible package name is unclaimed on npm and GitHub repo search for the concept returns zero repositories.
findings.evidence: registry.npmjs.org lookups 2026-08-01: `babelmark`, `markdown-conformance`, `markdown-compat`, `commonmark-conformance`, `markdown-differ`, `markdown-matrix`, `markdown-portability` all return `Not found` (only `remark-lint-no-html` exists, latest 4.0.1). GitHub `search/repositories`: `markdown+conformance+matrix` total_count 0; `markdown+renderer+compatibility+test` total_count 0; `markdown+cross-renderer` total_count 0; `markdown+portability+linter` total_count 3, none relevant.

findings.claim: VS Code's preview is markdown-it 14 with `html: true` — i.e. the OPPOSITE of markdown-it's own default — so the desktop editor and the npm default disagree on every raw-HTML construct. This is why per-product configuration must be pinned in the matrix rather than inherited from the library.
findings.evidence: `microsoft/vscode` `extensions/markdown-language-features/package.json` dependencies include `"markdown-it": "^14.2.0"`, `"dompurify": "^3.4.10"`, `"katex": "^0.16.33"`, `"mermaid": "^11.15.0"`, `"highlight.js": "^11.8.0"`. `src/markdownEngine.ts` `getMarkdownOptions()` returns `{ html: true, highlight: ... }` (line 401). Compare markdown-it 15.0.0's own shipped default in `dist/markdown-it.mjs`: `options: { html: false, xhtmlOut: false, breaks: false, langPrefix: "language-", linkify: false, typographer: false, ... }`.

findings.claim: A GFM table cell containing an escaped pipe silently loses the escape when tables are off — the backslash is consumed and `x \| y` becomes `x | y` inside a paragraph, so the same bytes mean two different things depending on whether the reader has tables enabled.
findings.evidence:
Construct `table-pipe-in-cell`, source `| a | b | |---|---| | x \| y | z |`. Table-capable engines → `x | y`. Non-table engines (commonmark.js ×2, markdown-it commonmark preset, cmark-gfm no-extensions, remark bare, react-markdown default) → `

| a | b | |---|---| | x | y | z |

` — the backslash is gone and the cell boundary is now ambiguous.

findings.claim: kramdown/GitHub Pages has two further prose-level divergences nobody else has: it refuses `1)` as an ordered-list marker, and it swallows a lone `|` in a paragraph.
findings.evidence: Minimal pairs, 8 engines. `1) First\n2) Second` → `First Second` in markdown-it, marked, remark-gfm, cmark-gfm, goldmark, comrak, pulldown; `1) First 2) Second` in kramdown/GH-Pages. `**Relevance:** high  |  **Priority:** P1` → `Relevance: high | Priority: P1` in seven engines; `Relevance: high Priority: P1` in kramdown/GH-Pages (the pipe is deleted). Prevalence of the pipe pattern: 751/1,980 files (37.9%) in md-vault, 157/273 (57.5%) in knowledge.

unclaimed: A per-document degradation certificate of any kind. babelmark3 does spec snippets against remote library endpoints; markdownlint/remark-lint do single-parser style rules; CommonMark's spec_tests.py does one implementation against 655 fixed examples. Nothing takes YOUR file and reports what N named consumer surfaces will do to it. npm names unclaimed, GitHub concept search returns 0 repos.

A pinned, self-hostable, offline, version-locked renderer bench. Every existing comparison (babelmark3) is a live dispatch to third-party HTTP services, 60.5% of them behind encrypted URLs, so no result is reproducible tomorrow or in CI. Building the bench as vendored source at pinned SHAs — cmark-gfm 0.29.0.gfm.13 @499789b, kramdown 2.5.2, goldmark 1.8.5, pulldown-cmark 0.13, comrak 0.39, markdown-it 15.0.0, marked 16.4.2, commonmark.js 0.31.2 — is a two-hour job that nobody has done.

The STRICT-vs-SEMANTIC distinction as a shipped primitive. Every diffing tool compares HTML strings, which is why the naive number is 43.71% and useless. An equivalence relation that folds entity spelling, smart punctuation, `<hr>`/`<hr />`, and trailing whitespace — and then reports the 4.28% residue — is the actual product, and no markdown tool implements it.

A leak/destroy/visible classifier over rendered output. Existing tools ask 'is the HTML the same'. Nobody asks the three questions that matter for a metadata carrier: is the payload VISIBLE to a human, is it PRESENT in the output for a round-tripper, and was it SUBSTITUTED (cmark-gfm's `<!-- raw HTML omitted -->` is a distinct outcome from both preservation and deletion, and no tool models it).

A (product, surface) target model. Everyone treats 'GitHub' as one renderer. It is three, and they disagree on frontmatter, on hard line breaks, and on heading anchors. No tool anywhere distinguishes github-comment / github-blob / github-pages, and the last two are the ones that matter for files.

The minimal-cover computation. Given N candidate targets, find the smallest subset that detects every divergence the full set detects. It is a 20-line greedy/exhaustive search over the signature partition, it cuts 10 engines to 3, and nobody publishes it — so every existing comparison is ~7x more expensive than it needs to be.

A prevalence-weighted risk score. Knowing that a construct diverges is half the answer; knowing it appears in 48.0% of your files is the other half. No markdown tool joins a conformance result to corpus frequency.

Certificate-as-artifact: a signed, versioned, machine-readable statement attached to a document asserting 'under bench vX.Y, this file is byte-stable across targets {A,B,C} and diverges at blocks {…} on targets {D}'. This is the thing MDMAX can hand to a receiving AI to satisfy product goal G3 with zero adoption, and it does not exist in any form.
per_area.design:
SHAPE — it is BOTH, and the layering is forced by the measurements. Layer 1 is a per-CONSTRUCT capability table, built offline from synthetic minimal pairs, because whole-file correlation cannot attribute cause: in the 300-file run every feature co-occurred with every other and all showed "100% divergent", which is information-free. Layer 2 is a per-FILE certificate that inventories which Layer-1 constructs the file actually contains, at which byte offsets, and joins them to the table. Layer 3 is a per-file differential RUN that catches what the table does not predict — necessary because the tilde/strikethrough case was found by the differential, not by any construct list I would have written.

WHAT IT ASSERTS, in three verdicts per (block, target):
  IDENTICAL   — semantic-equivalent output (after the equivalence fold below).
  DEGRADED    — output differs but the payload is invisible and no source character is lost. Acceptable.
  BROKEN      — one of three named failures, all of which I measured: (a) LEAK, the carrier payload appears as visible text (frontmatter on 23/24, HTML comment on 2/24, `{#id}` on 21/24, fence meta on kramdown); (b) DESTROY, a source character is deleted or substituted (`<cat>` deleted by 7/8, `~10%→~20%` struck by GitHub, `<!-- x -->` replaced by `<!-- raw HTML omitted -->` by cmark-gfm-safe, `\|` de-escaped when tables are off); (c) MUTATE, the same bytes get different STRUCTURE (`a**€**b` bolds on GitHub only; `1)` is a list everywhere but kramdown).

THE EQUIVALENCE FOLD is the load-bearing component and must be shipped as a named, versioned function, because it moved my own number from 43.71% to 4.28%. It folds: full HTML entity decode (use `entities.decodeHTML`, not a hand-rolled five-entity replace — that was my bug); smart punctuation (’‘ → ', “” → ", – → -, — → --, … → ...) since kramdown and goldmark-with-typographer differ from everyone else purely typographically; void-element spelling (`<hr>` / `<hr />` / `<hr/>`); trailing and inter-block whitespace; and `id` prefixing (GitHub rewrites `id="x"` to `id="user-content-x"`). Everything the fold does is a documented, testable normalization; everything it does not do is a real finding.

THE BENCH — vendored, pinned, offline, no network at check time. Never babelmark's remote-dispatch model: 23 of its 38 providers are behind encrypted URLs and cannot be self-hosted, which makes CI reproducibility structurally impossible. Ship: cmark-gfm at the exact GitHub SHA (499789b, `cmark-gfm 0.29.0.gfm.13`) compiled in CI — cmake + cc, ~90s, I did it; kramdown 2.5.2 + kramdown-parser-gfm 1.1.0 with `input: GFM` (GitHub Pages' verified default); goldmark 1.8.5 (Hugo); pulldown-cmark 0.13 with ENABLE_HEADING_ATTRIBUTES (mdBook); comrak 0.39; markdown-it 15.0.0 at BOTH `html:false` (npm default) and `html:true` (VS Code); marked 16.4.2; commonmark.js 0.31.2 as the spec oracle; and the app's own remark pipeline. Record the exact version of every engine in the certificate — a certificate without a bench version is a lie, because cmark-gfm 0.29 and cmark master disagree on `**€**`.

TARGETS ARE (product, surface) PAIRS, never products. Minimum: github-comment, github-blob, github-pages, vscode-preview, hugo, mdbook, docusaurus, obsidian, the-app. `github-comment` and `github-blob` are different rows and disagree on frontmatter.

RUN-LOCALLY vs MUST-PROBE — this is the reproducibility line and it is sharper than expected:
  RUN LOCALLY, DETERMINISTIC (verified by me): cmark-gfm → github-comment approximately, kramdown/GFM → github-pages exactly, goldmark → hugo, pulldown-cmark → mdbook, markdown-it → vscode-preview + discourse, marked → jupyter-lab family, remark/micromark/react-markdown → docusaurus + the-app, commonmark.js → the spec.
  PROBE-ONLY, CANNOT BE PINNED: github-blob. This is the important one. `POST /markdown` accepts arbitrary text but does NOT apply the frontmatter-to-table layer; the blob renderer is only reachable via `GET /repos/.../contents/X.md` with `Accept: application/vnd.github.html`, which requires the content to already be pushed. So the single surface where MDMAX's frontmatter matters most cannot be certified for an unsaved file without a write. Design consequence: model github-blob as a DECLARED contract in the capability table (frontmatter → table; HTML comments → deleted; `id` → `user-content-` prefixed; class/style/data-* → stripped), refresh it on a schedule with a canary repo, and stamp the certificate with the contract's last-verified date. Never pretend it is a live check.
  NOT RUNNABLE AT ALL, DECLARE-AND-DATE: Obsidian, Typora, Bear, Notion import, Slack, Discord, ChatGPT/Claude web. Slack and Discord are not CommonMark and should be modelled as lossy sinks, not renderers.

CLI SURFACE:
  mdmax cert <file>                       → human table: block × target × verdict
  mdmax cert <file> --json                → the artifact (see below)
  mdmax cert <glob> --fail-on=BROKEN      → CI gate; exit 1 on any BROKEN
  mdmax cert --targets=github-blob,hugo   → subset
  mdmax cert --bench-info                 → every engine + version + SHA
  mdmax cert --explain <construct>        → the minimal pair and its 24-row matrix
  mdmax cert --cover <targets>            → compute the minimal engine subset for those targets
  mdmax bench build | bench verify        → compile/pin the vendored engines, verify hashes

THE ARTIFACT (JSON, per Learned Rule #11 — the agent must never rewrite it): { bench: {version, engines:[{name,version,sha}]}, file: {path, sha256}, targets: [...], summary: {identical, degraded, broken}, blocks: [{anchor, type, byteRange, verdicts: {target: {verdict, class: LEAK|DESTROY|MUTATE, before, after}}}] }. Emit it as a sidecar, never back into the .md — §15.7's manifest rule.

HOW IT FAILS: loudly and specifically. Not "this may not render everywhere" but "block blk_7f3a, bytes 1204–1251: on github-comment the text `Array<string>` renders as `Array` (DESTROY); 6 of 9 targets agree with github". A verdict with no before/after pair is not a verdict. And per Learned Rule #67, the tool must verify its own bench actually ran — a missing engine must be a hard refusal, never a silently smaller matrix that reports green.

HOW IT STAYS FAST — four levers, all measured. (1) Minimal cover: 3 of 10 deployed targets detect 100% of divergences; ship `--cover` and default to the covering set, with `--full` for release gates. (2) Kill process spawn — it is 87% of wall time (31.3 ms/spawn vs 5.9 ms/in-process-render); compile cmark-gfm, comrak and pulldown-cmark to WASM and keep kramdown as the one unavoidable subprocess, or batch all documents through a single long-lived kramdown process. (3) Skip on prevalence: a file with no Layer-1 construct needs no differential run at all — that is 11–26% of files free. (4) Content-hash cache keyed on (block bytes, bench version): the corpus measurement showed median 50% of blocks per file unchanged between the strict and semantic passes, and blocks are far more stable than files across edits. Budget today: 216 ms/doc for a 105 KB document with 3 engines, ~43 ms for a typical 4 KB file, 15.5 min single-threaded for a 4,317-file vault — already fine for save-time and CI, not for keystroke.

WHY THIS SERVES THE PRODUCT GOALS: G1 gets a shareability check ("this doc is clean for github-blob and hugo, broken on github-pages"). G3 gets its zero-adoption artifact — the certificate is the thing you attach that tells a receiving AI exactly what survived, without asking it to understand anything new.
per_area.measurement:
THE OPEN QUESTION: my divergence rates come from two personal corpora (md-vault, knowledge) written largely by one author and one model. The certificate's value is proportional to how often BROKEN fires on documents people actually exchange, and I have not measured that on a neutral corpus.

CORPUS: 3,000 .md files stratified across four strata, 750 each — (a) GitHub READMEs from repos with >1k stars, (b) Jekyll/GH-Pages `_posts`, (c) Hugo/Docusaurus content directories, (d) Obsidian vaults published on GitHub. Sample deterministically by repo-name hash so the draw is reproducible. This matters because the four strata have different authoring tools and therefore different construct mixes, and my corpora are stratum (d) only.

TASKS: for each file, run the pinned 10-target bench and record, per top-level block, the verdict under the versioned equivalence fold.

VERIFIERS (cheapest-first, per Learned Rule #25): (1) rules-based — the differential itself is the verifier, no judge needed; (2) for every BROKEN, auto-reduce to a minimal pair by bisecting the block and re-running, and require that the minimal pair reproduce the verdict, otherwise discard it as a harness artifact — this is the step that would have caught my 43.71% inflation; (3) hand-audit a 200-block stratified sample against a rendered screenshot of the real product for github-blob and vscode-preview, and report agreement as a raw percentage with the disagreement cases listed. Do NOT use an LLM judge; the ground truth is a rendered string.

n: 3,000 files; expect ~90,000 top-level blocks at the 30-blocks/file rate I measured; ~10^6 (block, target) cells.

PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTIONS, written before the run:
  P1. Files with ≥1 BROKEN verdict on ≥1 of the 10 targets: 55–75%. (My corpora gave 74.1 / 88.6 / 84.2% for "contains a proven-divergent construct", but that is an upper bound — containing a construct is not the same as it firing BROKEN. I predict the gap is large, roughly a factor of 1.3.)
  P2. Semantic block divergence across the GFM-class subset: 3–7%, i.e. my 4.28% replicates within a factor of 2 on a neutral corpus.
  P3. Strict/semantic ratio: strict will be 8–12× semantic. (Mine: 43.71/4.28 = 10.2×.) If this ratio is not ~10× on the neutral corpus, my equivalence fold is over- or under-folding and must be re-derived.
  P4. kramdown/GH-Pages will be the single largest source of BROKEN on stratum (b) and near-zero on stratum (a) — because its failures (fence-with-meta, `1)`, pipe-swallowing) are authoring-style-dependent, not content-dependent.
  P5. The minimal cover will be 3–4 targets on the neutral corpus, and `remark+gfm+raw` + `kramdown/GFM` will both be in it. If the cover exceeds 5, the "it stays fast" argument weakens materially.
  P6. Angle-bracket deletion will be the single most frequent DESTROY class, >30% of all DESTROY verdicts, driven by API-documentation prose.

SECOND EXPERIMENT, cheap and decisive for G3: take 200 documents with known BROKEN verdicts, hand each to a model twice — once raw, once with the certificate JSON attached — and ask it to reproduce the author's intended text for the affected spans. Measure exact-match recovery rate. If the certificate does not raise recovery, it is a developer tool and not a product feature, and should be priced and positioned accordingly.
per_area.kill_condition:
Four, any one of which kills it.

(1) THE FOLD SWALLOWS EVERYTHING. If, on the neutral 3,000-file corpus, semantic BROKEN verdicts fall below ~1% of blocks and below ~15% of files, then real markdown does degrade harmlessly often enough that a certificate is a curiosity. My own numbers are the warning here: the honest figure was 4.28%, not the 43.71% the naive diff reported, and 4.28% is not a large number. If a neutral corpus halves it again, stop. Conversely, if P3's strict/semantic ratio comes out far from ~10×, the fold is miscalibrated and every number above is unsafe.

(2) THE UNCERTIFIABLE SURFACE IS THE ONLY ONE ANYONE CARES ABOUT. github-blob cannot be probed without pushing content, and Obsidian, Notion, Typora, Bear, Slack, Discord and the chat renderers cannot be probed at all — that is 7 of the ~12 surfaces on the brief's list. If user research says the certificate is only trusted when it covers those, the honest coverage is "the surfaces I can run", and a certificate that says DEGRADED for the target the user actually publishes to is worse than nothing because it manufactures false confidence. Kill unless the declared-contract-plus-canary model is accepted as honest.

(3) THE MARKET IS "PICK ONE RENDERER". The whole premise is that a document has many consumers. If the dominant workflow is in fact single-target (everything goes to GitHub, or everything goes to Obsidian), the correct product is a single-target linter — which markdownlint and remark-lint already are, at 0 marginal cost — and the matrix is over-engineering. Test this before building, not after.

(4) IT IS A LINT RULE, NOT A CERTIFICATE. If the minimal cover collapses to ONE engine, or if >80% of BROKEN verdicts come from fewer than five constructs, then the entire apparatus reduces to a static rule set — "don't write `<foo>` in prose, don't use a lone `~`, quote your frontmatter" — that runs in 2 ms with no bench, no vendored engines, and no version pinning. The 10-engine bench would then be a research instrument used once to derive the rules, and shipping it would be waste. My own data leans this way: six constructs (angle brackets, lone tilde, frontmatter, HTML comment, pipe-in-prose, `{#id}`) account for most of what I found. Run the frequency histogram over BROKEN classes FIRST; if it is that concentrated, ship the rules and keep the bench in CI only.
per_area.effort:
BENCH (vendor + pin + build): 1–2 days. I did the whole thing in one session — cmake+cc build of github/cmark-gfm @499789b in ~90 s, `go get github.com/yuin/goldmark` (needs `GOPROXY=direct GOSUMDB=off` in a restricted network), `cargo build` of pulldown-cmark 0.13 + comrak 0.39 in 24 s, `gem install kramdown kramdown-parser-gfm` with `GEM_HOME`/`XDG_CACHE_HOME` redirected, and the JS engines from npm. Depends on: CI runners with cc/cmake, Go, Rust and Ruby, or Docker images per engine. One real hazard: pypi.org and proxy.golang.org both failed TLS verification (`OSStatus -26276`) in this sandbox, so Python-Markdown/MkDocs never got tested — plan for network-restricted CI.

EQUIVALENCE FOLD: 2–3 days, and it is the part that will be wrong twice before it is right. It is ~150 lines of normalization plus a golden-file test suite; the cost is not the code, it is the judgment calls (is a smart quote a difference? is `user-content-` prefixing a difference?) and each one needs a documented rationale and a fixture. My own first version was wrong by a factor of 10.

CONSTRUCT CORPUS + CAPABILITY TABLE: 2 days. I have 45 constructs × 24 configs = 1,080 cells already measured; extending to ~120 constructs and regenerating is mechanical. Depends on the fold being frozen first — every fold change invalidates the whole table.

PER-FILE CERTIFICATE ENGINE (AST block split, byte-range attribution, verdict classification, JSON artifact): 1 week. Depends on the engine's existing pass-1/pass-2 (parse + block anchors) — this is the one piece that is genuinely cheaper inside MDMAX than as a standalone tool, because block identity is already solved there.

MINIMAL-COVER + CACHING + WASM: 3–4 days. The cover search is ~20 lines and already written. WASM compilation of cmark-gfm/comrak/pulldown-cmark is the real work and is the difference between 216 ms and ~30 ms per document; defer it until the cover result is known, since the cover may make it unnecessary.

CLI + CI GATE: 2–3 days.

TOTAL: ~3 weeks for a shippable v1 with 9 locally-runnable targets. NOT included, and each is open-ended: the github-blob canary repo (needs a push, therefore a RULE 2 decision), and any attempt to certify Obsidian/Notion/Typora/Bear, which would require UI automation or reverse-engineering and should not be attempted — declare-and-date those instead.

CHEAPEST USEFUL SLICE, if you want signal in two days rather than three weeks: freeze the fold at a naive version, run the 3-engine cover (remark-app + react-markdown + kramdown, all installable in one npm/gem step) over the existing vault, and publish the BROKEN-class frequency histogram. That single histogram decides kill-condition (4), which is the one most likely to fire.
per_area.unverified:
TARGETS I NEVER RAN — this is the biggest gap and it is more than half the brief's list. I could not test Pandoc (not installed; a binary download is an explicit-permission action I did not take), MDX/@mdx-js, markdig (no dotnet runtime), Python-Markdown or mistune (pip failed TLS verification, `SSLCertVerificationError('OSStatus -26276')`, so pypi was unreachable), Obsidian, Typora, Bear, Notion import, Slack, Discord, the ChatGPT and Claude web renderers, Jupyter, Quarto, Docusaurus, and Discourse. For Discourse I tried to read its markdown-it configuration from `discourse/discourse` and the file path I guessed returned empty; GitHub code search requires auth beyond what I had. For Obsidian I confirmed only that version 1.12.7 is installed and that `Obsidian.app/Contents/Resources/app.asar` is a 73 KB loader — the real bundle was not at the path I looked in, so I have NO empirical Obsidian data at all. Everything I say about these targets is inference from their declared dependencies, not measurement. In particular: Docusaurus is treated as remark/micromark and Jupyter as marked purely by dependency inference; VS Code is the one exception where I read the actual config.

MY OWN NUMBERS, CAVEATED. The 5.00%-identical figure and the 43.71%/4.28% pair come from two corpora written largely by one author with heavy AI assistance; they are not a neutral sample and I would not defend the specific values on other corpora — only the direction and the ~10× strict/semantic ratio. The prevalence table used 1,980 md-vault files (size <400 KB, dot-directories excluded) against a true total of 4,317 `.md` found by `find`; the percentages are over the filtered set, not the full vault. The block-divergence run used 40 files from `knowledge` only, and the 6-engine subset, not all 24. The minimal-cover result (3 targets → 100%) is computed over MY 45 constructs; a different construct corpus will give a different cover, and I have not tested its stability under resampling. The perf numbers are single-machine, single-threaded, cold-ish cache, on one 105 KB document plus a 300-file aggregate — treat as order-of-magnitude.

MECHANISMS I INFERRED RATHER THAN CONFIRMED. I did not verify WHY GitHub's blob renderer deletes HTML comments — I measured that it does (0 comments in the rendered `github/docs` README output) but did not read the sanitizer. I did not confirm that `POST /markdown mode=gfm` is byte-identical to what GitHub renders in an issue comment; I am inferring the mapping from the mode name and the hard-break behaviour. I did not verify that cmark-gfm's `--unsafe` flag corresponds to GitHub's production setting; I ran three configurations and reported all three. My claim that DOMPurify strips comments in VS Code is UNVERIFIED — I found dompurify in the dependency list but could not locate where it is applied or read its default tag policy, and both source fetches for that returned nothing.

METHOD RISK I AM FLAGGING AGAINST MYSELF. The harness that found these divergences and the classifier that judged them were written in the same session, which is exactly the Learned-Rule-#60 failure mode, and it already bit once: my first divergence number was 47.12%, then 43.71% strict, and the honest semantic figure is 4.28% — a 10× error caused by my own five-entity decode. I corrected it by sampling the actual divergent blocks and reading them, which is the only reason I caught it. Anyone building on this should re-derive the fold independently before trusting any percentage in this report. Separately, one Bash guard fired CATASTROPHIC on a Python script containing the variable name `drop` (a SQL false positive) and another WARNed on an `rm -rf` of my own scratch directory under $TMPDIR — no repo, database, or user file was written, deleted, or committed at any point in this work.

verification.area: Adversarial verification of "The degradation certificate — a per-document conformance matrix" (MDMAX / frontmatter, docs/engine). Artifacts: /private/tmp/claude-501/mdcert/merged.json (24x7 matrix), /private/tmp/claude-501/mdcert/js-edge.json (carrier-placement matrix), /private/tmp/claude-501/mdcert/{js,cmark,kramdown}-results.json, /private/tmp/claude-501/gm/goldmark-results.json, /private/tmp/claude-501/rs/rust-results.json. WebFetch was never attempted; all network work was direct curl per the brief. Sourcing ~/.config/codex-env/tokens.zsh required dangerouslyDisableSandbox (the sandbox denies that path); no token value was printed. No writes outside $TMPDIR, no commits, no installs into any repo.
