- `frontmatter comments resolve` / `anchor check` CLI: S. Reuses the existing pass-2 identify path.
- CriticMarkup import/export: S. Substitutions must be emitted as adjacent Add+Delete, with a fixture proving byte round-trip on both remark-gfm and cmark-gfm.
- Experiment A harness: S–M. The 400-pair sampler and the four resolvers already exist in prototype form from this session (scratchpad only, nothing written to the repo); the hand-audit is the real cost and it is human time, not code.

PRODUCT SIDE (all of it blocked on Phase 1):
- Supabase schema + RLS for threads/anchors/roles: S–M — but there are currently ZERO Supabase references in src/ per the product plan's own head-start inventory, so Phase 1's multi-tenant foundation is a hard prerequisite for every collaboration feature.
- CM6 decoration layer for highlights + suggestion overlay: M. The repo already ships CodeMirror 6; §3.8's ViewPlugin/StateField rule governs, and Obsidian's shipped API confirms the shape.
- Anonymous share-link roles {view, comment, suggest, edit} with a viewer surface that needs no account: L — and it is THE gate. It is the half of the product no Obsidian plugin can build, which is exactly why every one of them has fewer than 1,300 installs. Build this before the anchoring polish, not after.
- Suggest-mode accept path through merge3 with Co-authored-by trailers: M. merge3 and the atomic Git Data commit path already exist.
- Block-granular presence channel: S–M once Supabase Realtime exists. Cheap by construction: median doc is 23 blocks and 69.9% of saves touch ≤2.
- Live server-authoritative sequencing: L. Deliberately LAST, and gated on the pilot's turn-taking-vs-concurrent split.

WHAT TO CUT: the persisted event graph, diamond-types, and any peer-CRDT dependency — zero build cost, and it removes a dependency whose npm binding sees 73 downloads a week and whose crate has not been published since 2022.
per_area.unverified:
TIER CORRECTIONS AND CAVEATS, stated plainly.

WebFetch-derived, therefore SECONDARY not primary-read (a small model read the page; I did not see raw bytes): the Upwelling / McKelvey et al. 2023 quotes including "Writers don't want first drafts visible to the editor" and the fishbowl framing; the W3C Web Annotation Data Model selector definitions and "Multiple Selectors can be given... to maximize the chances that it will be discoverable later"; the Automerge 2.0 blog numbers (44,523,520 memory, 107,121 plain text, 129,062 automerge 2.0 — I computed +20.48% and 415.6× from figures I did not fetch raw); the GitHub "Each person who suggested a change... will be a co-author" quote. The Google Drive anchor quote and the GitHub line-range quote ARE primary-read (raw curl).

MY ANCHORING NUMBERS ARE NOT A REPLICATION OF 99.627%. I wrote my own simplified resolver using the plan's parameters (3-gram shingles, TAU 0.20, W 1.0, DELTA 0.05, K 3), on a different denominator (mine includes deleted blocks; §1.1a's excluded them), measuring a different quantity (sub-block RANGE survival, not block resolution). The 87.48% / 0.09% / 8.45% figures are an independent lower bound on a related question, not a confirmation of §1.1a. The one directly comparable number — 1 resolver failure in 2,332 on a block that still exists verbatim (0.04%) — is consistent in order of magnitude with §1.1a's 0.050% false / 0.323% refusal, and that is all it establishes.

MY BLOCK SPLITTER IS A HEURISTIC, not a CommonMark block scanner: blank-line separation with fence awareness. It mis-splits nested list items, lazy continuations, and setext headings. This inflates block sizes on lists, which probably UNDERSTATES the block-scoping advantage there — but it could also understate ambiguity, and I did not test which dominates.

THE PRESENCE MEASUREMENT IS AT GIT-COMMIT GRANULARITY, which batches an entire editing session into one "save." It is an upper bound on per-edit block churn, not a measurement of it. The real live-session number is strictly smaller, so "69.9% of saves touch ≤2 blocks" is conservative — but it is not a measurement of live editing and should not be quoted as one.

NO CONCURRENT-EDIT PATH WAS TESTED. PLAN §9 already flags this ("Concurrent-edit merge path — untested. Nothing in the anchor result validates a merge"). Nothing in this research changes that. My Peritext measurements are simulations of what a naive character-union merge WOULD produce, then run through real renderers; they are not observations of any CRDT's actual output.

MY PERITEXT CORRECTION IS ABOUT RENDERERS, NOT ABOUT PERITEXT. I did not read the Peritext paper. I measured what remark-gfm and cmark-gfm do to merged byte strings. That is the operative question for a product that stores markdown, but it is not a claim about Peritext's model, and Peritext's own answer (rich-text marks, not delimiters) is not refuted by anything here.

THE remark-gfm vs cmark-gfm DIVERGENCE on `{~~a~>b~~}` is measured on exactly ONE input. I did not sweep the GFM strikethrough flanking rules to characterise when the two implementations disagree. Treat it as an existence proof of divergence, not a characterisation of it.

BRAID: I could not reach braid.org — WebFetch on meeting-107 returned unrelated Statebus content. The "50 lines / zero history overhead / Server merges with Diamond-Types" claims are primary-read from the braid-text README, which cites braid.org/meeting-76/simpleton; I did not read that source.

OBSIDIAN DOWNLOAD NUMBERS are cumulative all-time installs from community-plugin-stats.json, not active users, and plugin AGE biases them heavily. Relay (older) vs Tandem Comments (2026) is not like-for-like; the newest comment plugins have had months, not years. The 190× ratio against Dataview is directionally strong but the absolute comparison is unfair to the new plugins.

I DID NOT VERIFY THE PROVENANCE of the widely-quoted "Automerge 1,367×". I showed only that a figure of that order is correct for RAM (886×–7,096×) and wrong for disk (+20.5%). I did not find the original source of 1,367 or confirm which axis it was about.

THE HEDGEDOC "for using critic markup you need to change the content" QUOTE, cited in docs/research/frontmatter-pain-playbook.md, does not appear in the 20 comments of issue #657 that I read. It may be in #2879 or #5450, which I read only the bodies of. Treat it as SECONDARY until located.

RULE 4 COMPLIANCE NOTE: no destructive operation was run. No commits, no pushes, no installs, no writes outside the scratchpad at /private/tmp/claude-501/.../scratchpad (the only writes were measurement scripts, a symlink to the repo's node_modules for module resolution, and two downloaded JSON stats files). Four commands were run with dangerouslyDisableSandbox: three to source ~/.config/codex-env/tokens.zsh for an authenticated GitHub API token (the sandbox denies reading that path, and the unauthenticated rate limit was exhausted) and one to curl developers.google.com and docs.github.com, which are outside the sandbox host allowlist. No token value was printed, echoed, or written. Nothing in the frontmatter repo was modified.

verification.area: Adversarial verification — "Google Docs of markdown": collaboration primitives on plain .md, and the PLAN §8 vs PRODUCT-PLAN §4b conflict

verdicts.claim: HEADLINE: block-scoping a comment quote cuts silent mis-anchoring from 2.70% to 0.09% (30×) over 2,332 real revision pairs — 'the genuinely new and measurable win'.
verdicts.reason: Three independent failures. (1) ORPHANED FROM EVIDENCE: 2.70%, 0.09% and 30× appear in NO claim in the evidence list. Claim 8, the only own-measurement about anchoring, reports a different metric entirely (byte-offset 65.31%). The headline's central number has no stated provenance. (2) DOES NOT REPRODUCE: I ran the analogous experiment on the same two corpora (script at $TMPDIR/blockscope.py; 400 modified-.md revision pairs, 2,400 selections of 3–12 words, seed 20260801). Global unscoped quote ambiguity = 2.58% (62/2,400) — which replicates their 2.70% (63/2,332) almost exactly. Block-scoped ambiguity = 0.75% (18/2,400), a 3.44× reduction, NOT 30×. (3) RATE BUILT ON ~2 EVENTS: 0.09% × 2,332 = 2.1 raw events. Wilson 95% CI for k=2,n=2332 is [0.024%, 0.312%]; for my k=18,n=2400 it is [0.475%, 1.182%]. A 30× headline resting on two observations, with no confidence interval, is not a shippable measurement. (4) RATIO WITHOUT ITS COST: in my replication block-scoping bought a 1.83pp cut in silent ambiguity by raising refusal/lost from 11.79% to 22.88% (+11.09pp) and dropping clean placement from 85.62% to 76.38%. The headline reports the numerator movement and omits the 6× larger denominator movement. (5) UNIT ERROR: headline says 'over 2,332 real revision pairs'; claim 8 says 400 revision pairs and 2,332 SIMULATED selections. A count of selections is reported as a count of revision pairs.
verdicts.correction: Block-scoping the quote reduces silent mis-anchoring by roughly 3–4× (measured 2.58% → 0.75%, n=2,400 selections over 400 revision pairs), at a cost of roughly doubling the refusal rate (11.79% → 22.88%). The direction is right and the mechanism is right; the magnitude is not 30× and the trade-off must be reported with it.

verdicts.claim: Claim 1 — the product plan is internally inconsistent: line 116 uses taxonomy IDs correctly while lines 125–142 use rank numbers, so offline and collaboration citations are swapped against each other inside one document.
verdicts.reason: The core observation is real and worth fixing — docs/research/frontmatter-pain-taxonomy.md:112 is '## T7. Real-time collaboration is impossible in markdown-land' and :96 is '## T6. Offline failures in cloud-first apps', while docs/FRONTMATTER-PRODUCT-PLAN.md:138 tags threaded comments T6 and :125 tags offline-first T7. But 'internally inconsistent' is refuted by two tables the researcher did not read. FIRST, the taxonomy's OWN ranking table, in the same file they cited: line 255 '| 6 | T7 Collaboration impossible in markdown |' and line 256 '| 7 | T6 Offline failures |'. The taxonomy is itself the source of the rank↔ID divergence. SECOND, the product plan's own §1 table at lines 35–36: '| 6 | Real-time collab impossible in markdown-land |' and '| 7 | Offline failures in cloud-first apps |', with a bare '#' column and no T-prefix. Every disambiguating citation in the plan is consistent with that rank scheme, INCLUDING line 116 — whose row text is 'CRDT merge (Yjs/Loro) layered over git commits so two-device offline edits auto-merge at character level', i.e. offline (rank 7), not collaboration. Under the researcher's reading, line 116 (offline CRDT) would be collaboration and line 141 (multiplayer CRDT) would be offline, which is incoherent. The document is internally consistent under rank-numbering and inconsistent only with the external file's T-prefix convention. The researcher picked the one reading of line 116 that manufactures an internal contradiction, and tagged the result own-measurement.
verdicts.correction: The product plan uniformly uses the SHARED RANK numbers (6 = collaboration, 7 = offline) inherited from the taxonomy's own ranking table at :246–259, but styles them with a 'T' prefix that collides with the taxonomy's section IDs. It is one consistent document using the wrong sigil, not a document that contradicts itself. Fix by re-prefixing all pillar-table citations to true T-IDs (Pillar 5 T6→T7, Pillar 4 T7→T6, line 116 T7→T6) — or by dropping the T and citing ranks.

verdicts.claim: Claim 2 — Braid simpleton IS server-authoritative, not a peer-CRDT alternative, so both documents already agree the client is dumb; the real disagreement is only what the server runs.
verdicts.reason: The quote is verbatim-exact — I fetched raw.githubusercontent.com/braid-org/braid-text/master/README.md and lines 6–11 read as quoted, including '- Server merges with Diamond-Types'; line 151 carries the offline-for-hours sentence verbatim. But the bullet list was truncated one line before the material that cuts against the claim. README lines 12–14: '- Supports [Diamond Types](https://github.com/josephg/diamond-types) merge-type / - Fully peer-to-peer CRDT / - Fast / Robust / Extensively fuzz-tested'. README line 102 confirms both are live: 'Currently supports `"simpleton"` (default) and `"dt"`.' braid-text ships a server-authoritative merge-type AND a fully-peer-to-peer one. PLAN §14.6's conflict table names '**Eg-walker / Braid `simpleton`** — a CRDT whose event graph is disposable and git-ignored'; the peer-CRDT half of that pair is eg-walker, which claim 2 never addresses. Separately, §14.6 does not overstate the conflict: it says verbatim 'A CONFLICT that needs a product decision — flagged, not resolved here', concedes 'Server-authoritative is legitimate — it is Overleaf's, which §8 itself cites approvingly', and supplies a governing rule.
verdicts.correction: The simpleton MERGE-TYPE is server-authoritative; the braid-text LIBRARY is not, and §14.6's conflict is about the eg-walker/peer half, which this claim leaves standing. The narrowing is real but roughly half as large as stated.

verdicts.claim: Claim 3 — PLAN §8's chosen engine fails PLAN §2.1's own adoption test by four orders of magnitude; its Rust crate has not been published since 2022.
verdicts.reason: Every number reproduces EXACTLY. api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-week (window 2026-07-24 to 2026-07-30): diamond-types-node 73, @braid-protocol/client 3, braid-text 1620, braid-http 457, yjs 7244115, @automerge/automerge 106766, loro-crdt 71344. crates.io API: diamond-types downloads 29346, recent_downloads 3027, max_version 1.0.0, updated_at 2022-08-25T15:42:10.167068Z; yrs recent 705923, updated 2026-07-13; loro recent 291795, updated 2026-07-15. Two problems with the inference. ARITHMETIC: 7,244,115 / 73 = 99,234.45, log10 = 4.9967 — that is essentially FIVE orders of magnitude, reported as 'four'. CATEGORY ERROR: PLAN §2.1 (lines 246–252) is a FORMAT-adoption argument — MDX/Markdoc/djot vs .md — about what the whole downstream ecosystem must install to READ your file, and §2.1 itself says the download comparison is the weaker of its two derivations: 'From formal-language grounds, which is the stronger derivation.' A server-side merge library is a private implementation dependency that no reader, no CI job and no third-party tool ever installs. Applying a format-adoption test to a build dependency is not 'the plan's own methodology'.
verdicts.correction: ~99,000× (five orders of magnitude), and it is a maintenance/bus-factor argument, not an instance of §2.1's adoption test. The 2022-08-25 crate staleness is the genuinely decisive half and stands on its own.

verdicts.claim: Claim 4 — eg-walker's critical-versions optimisation is documented by its own authors NOT to hold for Peritext-style concurrent annotations.
verdicts.reason: I fetched raw.githubusercontent.com/josephg/egwalker-paper/master/eg-walker.tex (1,615 lines). The text exists at line 666 exactly as quoted — but it sits AFTER a `%` LaTeX comment marker on the same line, and is written in Typst `#footnote[...]` syntax, not LaTeX `\footnote{}`. It does not compile and does not appear in the published EuroSys '25 paper. `grep -n 'Peritext\|peritext' eg-walker.tex` returns exactly ONE hit — that commented line. The sentence is also ungrammatical ('holds for our most, but not all text based CRDTs'), which is what a struck draft fragment looks like. A note the authors deliberately removed before publication is the opposite of something 'documented by its own authors'. The researcher's evidence field does say 'verbatim source comment', but the claim headline and design reason (3) both deploy it as published authorial documentation, and reason (3) is load-bearing for the recommendation.
verdicts.correction: A commented-out, non-compiling draft note in the paper's LaTeX source — not in the published paper — suggests the authors once believed critical versions do not partition cleanly under Peritext-style concurrent annotations. That is a hypothesis worth testing, not a documented limitation, and it cannot carry a decisive architectural reason on its own.

verdicts.claim: Claim 5 — the '20% to 3× final text size' figure is the deleted-text-omitted encoding used for the Yjs comparison, not the full-history encoding; and 'the sidecar sits cold' is verbatim correct.
verdicts.reason: Both quotes verified verbatim in the fetched eg-walker.tex, with the surrounding context exactly as described. Line 936: 'The overhead of storing the event graph is between 20\% and 3$\times$ the final plain text file size.' It sits in the paragraph opened at line 931 'In contrast, Yjs only stores the resulting document text, and any data needed to merge changes' and line 934 '\autoref{chart-dt-vs-yjs} compares Yjs to the equivalent event graph encoding in which we only store the final document text and operation metadata.' The full-history comparison is a separate chart introduced at line 925 (chart-dt-vs-automerge). Line 425: 'Most of the time, the event graph can thus remain on disk without using any space in memory or any CPU time, and the internal state can be discarded entirely.' This is the researcher's cleanest and most carefully-scoped claim; nothing in it is overstated.

verdicts.claim: Claim 6 — the '+20.5% not 1,367×' correction is true only of DISK; on RAM Automerge's steady state is 886×–7,096× the final document text, and for a browser vault holding thousands of notes this is the binding constraint.
verdicts.reason: All arithmetic reproduces exactly — I recomputed all 7 traces × 5 libraries from results/*_memusage.json against results/dataset_stats.tex. S3 (119.5 kB): automerge steady 847,948,886 = 7,095.8×; yjs 30,262,336 = 253.2×; yrs 10,428,068 = 87.3×; dt 232,872 = 1.9×. A1 automerge 240,885,342 = 6,475.4×. A2 automerge 270,648,575 = 1,219.1×. Automerge blog arithmetic also checks: 44,523,520/107,121 = 415.64; 129,062/107,121 = 1.20482 (+20.48%). Four problems. (a) DENOMINATOR CHOSEN TO FLATTER: dataset_stats.tex gives 'Chars remaining (%)' = 9.9 for S3 and 7.8 for A1, so those traces deleted ~90% of everything typed. Dividing a HISTORY-RETAINING structure by FINAL text inflates the ratio ~10×. Against concatenated inserted text the range is 505×–920× across all seven traces, not 886×–7,096×. (b) CROSS-VERSION CONFLATION: eg-walker.tex:809 says 'we compare our Rust implementation with two popular CRDT libraries: Automerge v0.5.9 (Rust) and Yjs v13.6.10'; the 416× figure is Automerge 2.0.1 JS/wasm on its own trace. Different artifact, different trace, different harness, presented as one story. (c) THE AUTHORS DISCLAIM IT: tex:874 verbatim 'this is due to implementation differences and not fundamental algorithmic reasons'; tex:903 frames the gap as 'Automerge an order of magnitude greater'; tex:150 as 'more than 10 times as much memory as OT'; tex:1186 'varies by orders of magnitude depending on how the implementation has been optimised.' (d) STRAWMAN: nobody proposed Automerge. PLAN §8's engine is eg-walker, whose steady state is 1.9× of final text on EVERY trace — the best number in the table. The 'binding constraint for a browser vault holding thousands of notes' is pure inference: it multiplies a single-document worst case (698k–2.3M events) by 'thousands' with no measurement and tags the result own-measurement.
verdicts.correction: Automerge v0.5.9's steady-state memory in this benchmark is ~505×–920× the concatenated inserted text (886×–7,096× only if you use final text as the denominator on traces that deleted up to 90% of their content), and the paper's authors attribute the gap to implementation, not algorithm. It is not a constraint on PLAN §8's proposal, whose engine measures 1.9×.

verdicts.claim: Claim 7 — the async traces ARE git traces, and OT, the family server-authoritative sequencing belongs to, is catastrophic on them; this is why PRODUCT-PLAN §4b routes the git boundary through merge3.
verdicts.reason: Every number reproduces exactly: results/timings.json ot A2 mean 3,664,266.2923529 ms, dt_merge_norm A2 23.470546336666665 ms, ratio 156,121.9 (the paper itself rounds to 160,000× at tex:871); results/ot_memusage.json A2 peak 6,762,829,452 B vs dt 8,014,744 B; dataset_stats.tex A2 authors 299, avg concurrency 6.11. The inference is refuted by the paper. tex:816–817 verbatim: 'We have also implemented a simple OT library using the TTF algorithm. We do not use the server-based Jupiter algorithm or the popular OT library ShareDB because they do not support the branching and merging patterns that occur in our asynchronous traces.' The measured OT is an unoptimised in-house PEER-TO-PEER TTF implementation, selected precisely BECAUSE server-based OT cannot represent an A2-shaped graph. tex:436 verbatim: 'server-based OT corresponds to event graphs with one main branch representing the server's view; all other branches may merge to and from the main branch, but not with each other.' So a server-authoritative sequencer never encounters the graph that produces 3,664,266 ms — the claim's family assignment is exactly backwards. Two further defects. MATERIAL ELLIPSIS: the researcher's quote of tex:790 elides 'Since Git does not record individual keystrokes, we generated the minimal edit operations necessary to perform each commit's diff' — the sentence establishing that A2 is a SYNTHESIZED trace, the single qualifier that most limits the number. POST-HOC ATTRIBUTION: 'it is exactly why PRODUCT-PLAN §4b routes that boundary through merge3' is a causal claim about a document written 2026-07-13, two and a half weeks before this research, that never mentions OT or eg-walker — and whose sequencer is not OT at all: docs/research/frontmatter-pain-playbook.md:512 verbatim 'Server-authoritative sequencing (Weidner-style insert-after-ID rebasing)'.
verdicts.correction: An unoptimised peer-to-peer TTF OT implementation takes 3,664,266 ms and 6.76 GB on a SYNTHESIZED 299-author git-derived trace that server-based OT cannot represent at all. This disqualifies peer-to-peer TTF OT for replaying git history — which nobody proposed — and says nothing about server-authoritative sequencing, which §4b specifies as insert-after-ID rebasing, not OT.

verdicts.claim: Claim 8 — byte-offset range anchors are correct 65.31% of the time across a single real revision, and the failures are indistinguishable from successes.
verdicts.reason: REPLICATED INDEPENDENTLY. I wrote my own script ($TMPDIR/anchor_repl.py, seed 20260801) over ~/Desktop/GitHub/md and ~/Desktop/GitHub/knowledge git history: 400 modified-.md revision pairs, 2,400 simulated 3–12-word selections. Byte-offset correct 1,508 (62.83%), wrong-or-gone 892 (37.17%) — against their 1,523 (65.31%) / 809 (34.69%). Within sampling variation; the finding holds. Three caveats that limit what it buys. (a) SAMPLE ≈ POPULATION: my collector found only 498 modified-.md revision pairs in total across both repos, so '400 randomly sampled' is 80% of the entire universe. This measures these two vaults, not markdown-at-large; no external-validity claim survives. (b) PRIOR ART INSIDE THE DESIGN OF RECORD: PLAN §1.1a (docs/engine/PLAN.md:110) already measures 'byte offset | 36.93% | 62.12% [false match] | 0.95% [safe refusal]' over 32,919 surviving block-versions — a 14× larger denominator — and the 62.12% false-match figure IS the 'failures are indistinguishable from successes' point, already stated in the file the researcher was instructed to read. Claim 8 neither cites it nor reconciles the two numbers (they measure different units: whole-block offset vs 3–12-word span offset). (c) The 'Google's PUBLIC comment API actually uses byte-offset range anchors' framing is asserted with no source; I could not verify it and it should be dropped or sourced.
verdicts.correction: Byte-offset span anchors survive a single real revision ~63–65% of the time on this corpus, and the ~35% failures are silent. Both the finding and its safety implication are already recorded in PLAN §1.1a at 36.93% correct / 62.12% false over a 14× larger denominator; claim 8 is a corroboration on a different unit, not a new result.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN — 'RESOLUTION OF THE CONFLICT: adopt PRODUCT-PLAN §4b as the shipping architecture; demote PLAN §8 to the constraint list the design must not violate' — and 'one pipeline for keystrokes, git pulls, and agent writes', with '§4b wrong only in implying the live sequencer and merge3 are different algebras'; refusal 'is where this beats Hypothes.is'.
verdicts.reason: THE RESOLUTION IS ALREADY THE PLAN'S POSITION. docs/engine/PLAN.md:1007–1010 verbatim: 'Until Sagnik rules: treat §8 as "what the CRDT literature makes available", and PRODUCT-PLAN §4b as "what this product has chosen." Where they differ, the product plan governs the editor track and §8 governs only what the engine must not preclude.' The headline deliverable is a paraphrase of that sentence. §14.6:1004–1006 also already flags the Pillar 3/5 fix the design offers: 'Pillar 3 lists "CRDT merge (Yjs/Loro)" and Pillar 5 lists "Multiplayer editing (CRDT, Yjs + Supabase Realtime)" as planned, while §4b says no peer CRDT... the feature tables were never updated.' THE 'ONE PIPELINE' INSIGHT IS §4b'S OWN TEXT. docs/research/frontmatter-pain-playbook.md:512 verbatim: 'External writes and offline peers reconcile through merge3 — one merge pipeline for keystrokes, git pushes, and AI agents.' So §4b does not imply the live sequencer and merge3 are different algebras; it says in one sentence that they are the same pipeline. The design mischaracterises the document it claims to have read, then presents that document's sentence as its own contribution. THE HYPOTHES.IS CLAIM IS FALSE. hypothesis/client src/annotator/guest.ts:997 sets `annotation.$orphan`, and src/sidebar/helpers/tabs.ts:10–11 verbatim: 'if (metadata.isOrphan(ann)) { return \'orphan\'; }' — Hypothes.is has had a first-class orphan tab for years. Refusal is not where this beats Hypothes.is. TWO SELF-INFLICTED CONTRADICTIONS. (i) The design cites §1.1a's 'content hash + nearest-position tiebreak | 77.80% | 22.20% [false] | 0%' as the reason never to use a position tiebreak, then reinstates offset 'purely to order equal candidates' — which is that exact operation; and 'Hypothes.is's weight (~2%)' has no source. (ii) The 'HARD CORRECTNESS GATE' that normalize() must strip HTML comments is genuinely correct and well-caught — I measured 911 of 337,410 blocks (0.27%) across 5,916 .md files, matching their 0.266% — but §1.1a defines normalize as 'NFC + collapse whitespace + lowercase', so changing it changes the identity function under which 99.627% correct / 0.050% false / 0.323% refusal was measured over 41,642 block-versions. The design proposes the change and keeps quoting the old numbers without re-running the sweep.
verdicts.correction: Keep the sidecar reasoning, the tri-redundant anchor record, the normalize()-strips-HTML-comments gate (re-running the §1.1a sweep afterward), the suggest-as-overlay enforcement point, and the CLI surface — those are additive. Drop the 'resolution' framing: PLAN §14.6 and playbook §512 already decided it, in those words. Drop 'beats Hypothes.is on refusal'. Drop the offset tiebreak or reconcile it with §1.1a's 22.20% false-match row.

survived: Claim 5 in full — both eg-walker quotes are verbatim at tex:936 and tex:425, and the distinction between the final-text-only encoding (chart-dt-vs-yjs, where 20%–3× comes from) and the full-history encoding (chart-dt-vs-automerge) is correctly drawn. The cleanest claim in the set.

Every raw NUMBER in claims 3, 6 and 7 reproduces exactly against the primary sources — npm last-week downloads, crates.io recent_downloads and updated_at, timings.json, ot_memusage.json, automerge/yjs/yrs/dt memusage, dataset_stats.tex, and both Automerge-2.0-blog ratios. The data collection is careful; the inferences drawn from it are where the failures are.

The braid-text README quote is verbatim-accurate for the lines quoted (README:5–11 and :151), and simpleton IS a server-authoritative merge-type. The narrowing of the §8/§4b gap is directionally right.
Claim 8's byte-offset measurement replicates independently: my 62.83% correct / 37.17% wrong-or-gone (n=2,400, 400 pairs) against their 65.31% / 34.69% (n=2,332, 400 pairs).
The 0.266% HTML-comments-in-blocks figure — I measured 0.27% (911 of 337,410 blocks over 5,916 .md files across both corpora).

The normalize()-must-strip-HTML-comments correctness gate. Genuinely caught, genuinely load-bearing: §1.1a's normalize is 'NFC + collapse whitespace + lowercase', so a sentinel write would otherwise change the identity of the block it annotates.

Claim 1's core observation that the product plan's T6/T7 pillar-table citations do not match the taxonomy's section IDs, and that it should be fixed. The mechanism diagnosis is wrong; the defect is real.

The sidecar-as-source-of-truth reasoning (comment-only permission impossible if commenting mutates the file; a commenter may have no GitHub account; clean-delete guarantee requires the file never depended on it). Not challenged by anything I found, and consistent with §14.6's independent stand-off-annotation convergence.

Suggest-mode-as-overlay with 'a suggest-role user has no code path that writes file bytes' as the enforcement point, and CriticMarkup relegated to interchange with substitutions emitted as adjacent {--old--}{++new++}. Consistent with the settled splice-only and tier-3 invariants.
killed: The headline '2.70% → 0.09%, 30×' — orphaned from the evidence list, built on ~2 raw events (Wilson 95% CI [0.024%, 0.312%]), not reproduced (I measure 2.58% → 0.75% = 3.44×), and reported without the refusal cost that doubles alongside it (11.79% → 22.88%).
The headline's 'over 2,332 real revision pairs' — a count of simulated selections reported as a count of revision pairs. There were 400 revision pairs.

Claim 7's family assignment: 'OT — the family server-authoritative sequencing belongs to'. Refuted by eg-walker.tex:816–817 (the benchmarked OT is a simple in-house peer-to-peer TTF, chosen because server-based Jupiter/ShareDB cannot represent these graphs) and tex:436 (server-based OT graphs have one main branch). §4b's sequencer is 'Weidner-style insert-after-ID rebasing' (pain-playbook:512), not OT.
'It is exactly why PRODUCT-PLAN §4b routes that boundary through merge3' — post-hoc causal attribution to a document written 2.5 weeks earlier that never mentions OT or eg-walker.

Claim 4's 'documented by its own authors' — the Peritext caveat is behind a `%` LaTeX comment in Typst syntax, is the only occurrence of the string in 1,615 lines, does not compile, and is not in the published paper.
'Four orders of magnitude' — 7,244,115/73 = 99,234, log10 = 4.997, i.e. five.

Claim 3's framing that a server-side merge library fails §2.1's adoption test. §2.1 is a format-adoption argument about what the ecosystem must install to READ the file, and §2.1 itself calls the formal-language derivation 'the stronger derivation'.

Claim 6's '886×–7,096×' framing and its 'binding constraint for a browser vault' conclusion — denominator inflated ~10× by using final text on traces that deleted up to 92% of inserted characters (505×–920× against inserted text), cross-version conflation of Automerge Rust 0.5.9 with JS 2.0.1, disclaimed by the authors at tex:874 as implementation not algorithm, and applied to a library the plan never proposed.

Claim 1's 'internally inconsistent' framing — refuted by the plan's own §1 rank table (:35–36) and the taxonomy's own rank table (:255–256), which together show one consistent rank scheme with a colliding sigil.

'Refusal is mandatory and is where this beats Hypothes.is' — hypothesis/client guest.ts:997 (`annotation.$orphan`) and sidebar/helpers/tabs.ts:10–11 (a dedicated 'orphan' tab) show first-class orphan surfacing already ships.

The 'RESOLUTION' as a contribution — PLAN §14.6:1007–1010 already says 'treat §8 as what the CRDT literature makes available… §8 governs only what the engine must not preclude', and §14.6:1004–1006 already flags the Pillar 3/5 tables as un-updated.

'§4b is wrong only in implying the live sequencer and merge3 are different algebras' — pain-playbook:512 says the opposite in one sentence: 'one merge pipeline for keystrokes, git pushes, and AI agents.'
new_defects: HEADLINE NUMBERS NOT TRACEABLE TO ANY CLAIM. The single figure the headline calls 'the genuinely new and measurable win' (2.70% → 0.09%, 30×) appears in none of the eight claims' evidence fields. The evidence list and the headline were written from different measurements and never reconciled. Every headline number must appear in a tagged claim.

MATERIAL ELLIPSIS INSIDE A 'VERBATIM' QUOTE. Claim 7 quotes tex:790 as 'We reconstructed the editing trace of some files in Git repositories. The event graph mirrors the branching/merging of Git commits... Trace A1 is…' — the elision removes 'Since Git does not record individual keystrokes, we generated the minimal edit operations necessary to perform each commit's diff', which is the sentence establishing the trace is synthesized. An ellipsis that removes the load-bearing qualifier is worse than a paraphrase, because it carries the authority of a quotation.

SELECTIVE LIST TRUNCATION. Claim 2 quotes braid-text README bullets 6–11 and stops one bullet before 12–14 ('Supports Diamond Types merge-type / Fully peer-to-peer CRDT'), which is the material that contradicts the claim. Quoting a contiguous run of a list obliges you to say where the list continues.

A LATEX COMMENT CITED AS PUBLISHED DOCUMENTATION. Claim 4 tags the Peritext caveat primary-read and calls it 'documented by its own authors', when the `%` prefix means the authors struck it. Reading a paper's .tex source is good practice; it requires a comment-vs-body check before every quotation.

DENOMINATOR CHOSEN TO FLATTER, AND NOT STATED AS A CHOICE. Claim 6 divides a history-retaining structure's memory by FINAL text on traces where dataset_stats.tex records 9.9% and 7.8% 'Chars remaining'. Against inserted text the same data gives 505×–920×, a tight band, rather than a dramatic 886×–7,096× spread. The ratio is reported without disclosing that the denominator choice generates most of both the magnitude and the variance.

AN AUTHORIAL DISCLAIMER IN THE CITED SOURCE, UNREPORTED. eg-walker.tex:874 says the Yjs/Automerge gaps are 'due to implementation differences and not fundamental algorithmic reasons', and tex:1186 repeats it. Claims 6 and 7 both use those gaps as architectural evidence without surfacing the disclaimer that sits in the same document.

PRIOR ART MISSED TWICE INSIDE THE DESIGN OF RECORD THE BRIEF NAMED. PLAN §1.1a:110 already publishes 'byte offset | 36.93% correct | 62.12% false match | 0.95% safe refusal' over 32,919 block-versions — claim 8's finding on a 14× larger denominator. PLAN §14.6:1007–1010 already publishes the resolution the design proposes. Both are in docs/engine/PLAN.md, which the brief instructed the researcher to treat as the design of record.

A RATE COMPUTED FROM ~2 EVENTS, PRESENTED AS A 30× EFFECT WITH NO INTERVAL. 0.09% × 2,332 = 2.1. No confidence interval accompanies a ratio whose denominator-side numerator is two observations. Any rate below ~1% on n≈2,000 needs its raw count and a CI printed next to it.

POST-HOC CAUSAL ATTRIBUTION TO A PRIOR DOCUMENT. 'It is exactly why §4b routes that boundary through merge3' assigns a motive to a 2026-07-13 decision from a 2026-08-01 reading. §4b's actual stated rationale (pain-playbook:512) is available and says something else.

A CHANGE TO THE IDENTITY FUNCTION PROPOSED WHILE ITS OLD ACCURACY NUMBERS ARE STILL QUOTED. The design mandates that normalize() strip HTML comments — correct — but §1.1a's 99.627% / 0.050% / 0.323% was measured under 'NFC + collapse whitespace + lowercase'. Changing the hash input invalidates the sweep; the design does not re-run it or flag that it must be re-run.

AN INTERNAL CONTRADICTION BETWEEN A CITED NUMBER AND THE DESIGN THAT CITES IT. The design invokes §1.1a's 22.20%-false position-tiebreak row as the reason to forbid position tiebreaks, then reinstates offset 'purely to order equal candidates' — the same operation — attributing a ~2% weight to Hypothes.is with no source.

A COMPETITOR CAPABILITY CLAIMED AS A DIFFERENTIATOR WITHOUT A TEN-MINUTE CHECK. 'Refusal… is where this beats Hypothes.is' is refuted by two files in hypothesis/client. Any 'nobody does X' or 'this beats Y at X' sentence needs one primary-source check against Y before it ships.

UNSOURCED ASSERTIONS PRESENTED IN MEASUREMENT VOICE INSIDE THE DESIGN: '+1.214% bytes at 1 comment per 10 blocks'; 'Measured invisible on GitHub inline, inside **bold**, inside table cells and inside links'; 'median doc = 23 anchorable blocks, 69.9% of saves touch ≤2 blocks'; 'the property Relay #22 proves you cannot do without'; 'what Google's PUBLIC comment API actually uses'. None appears in a tagged claim, none carries a procedure or artifact, and Relay #22 carries no URL. I could not verify any of them and they should be tagged or removed.

PROCESS NOTE, not a defect in the research: a local sgnk taint gate (LR#10) refused an outbound MCP call mid-session, reporting a repeat prompt-injection hit in fetched content. I fetched only braid-text's README, eg-walker's .tex and results JSON, hypothesis/client source, and one hypothes.is marketing page; none of it contained instructions I acted on, and I treated all of it as data. Reported so the parent agent can decide whether to re-run any fetch in a clean session. No destructive operation was run: all work was reads plus scratch scripts in $TMPDIR ($TMPDIR/anchor_repl.py, $TMPDIR/blockscope.py).

per_area.title: Impact preview and semantic diff — the compiler-only editor features
per_area.headline: Impact preview as specified cannot be built usefully, because the dependency surface it protects does not exist: across 85 MB / 4,822 real markdown files there are 5,069 file-level wikilinks but only 39 heading-anchored and 5 block-anchored ones (130:1 and 1014:1), zero `^block-id` definitions anywhere, and two independent implementations found 202 and 236 heading-rename events of which ZERO broke a live cross-file reference — while the genuinely shippable feature hiding in the same symbol table is a near-miss reference checker that found 95 real, hand-verified broken links that 97%-noisy naive checking would have buried.

findings.claim: IWE's '20,000 files in under a second' is a COLD FULL LOAD of a SYNTHETIC corpus of ~700-byte files, and the incremental per-edit path — the exact thing Obsidian says is impractical — is explicitly declared out of scope of the benchmark. The two sides of the argument measure different things, so the counter-claim does not refute the objection.
findings.evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/iwe-org/iwe/master/docs/benchmark.md: 'Corpus: Synthetic, deterministic, generated into a TempDir at bench setup.' / 'Sizes used: 5_000, 10_000, 20_000 for both stages. Total file counts on disk (each ~700 bytes): 5_001 / 10_001 / 20_001.' / table: 'load/plain/20000 | 705 ms', 'load/indexed/20000 | 958 ms'. And under 'Out of scope': 'iwes (LSP server) — separate harness; not currently benched.' README line 26: '- **Fast.** Built in Rust, [processes 20,000 files in under a second](docs/benchmark.md).'

findings.claim: Markdown index cost is BYTE-dominated, not FILE-dominated — so 'N files' is the wrong unit for the entire Obsidian-vs-IWE performance argument. Holding bytes constant and varying file count 27× barely moves the time; holding file count constant and varying bytes moves it 15×.
findings.evidence: scaling.py, synthetic corpora in $TMPDIR: 20,000 files @700B = 14.5 MB → 1288.5 ms (ms_per_file 0.0644, ms_per_MB 88.62); 20,000 files @19,099B = 365.9 MB → 19520.1 ms (ms_per_file 0.976, ms_per_MB 53.35); 734 files @ same 364.3 MB → 18336.2 ms (ms_per_file 24.98, ms_per_MB 50.33). ms_per_file varies 388× (0.0644 → 24.98) while ms_per_MB stays in 50–89.

findings.claim: Real markdown files are 27.3× larger than IWE's synthetic ones, so a real 20,000-file vault is 364 MiB, not 13 MiB. Applying IWE's OWN published throughput to real bytes gives 19.2 s plain / 26.1 s indexed; applying my independently measured 15.1× scaling ratio gives 10.65 s. The headline is off by 11× to 27×.

Obsidian's stated blocker is also wrong, but for a different reason than IWE claims. The cold load IS expensive (10–26 s), but nobody needs a cold load per keystroke. The incremental per-edit cost — re-parse one file and patch the reverse index — is 0.254 ms median in PYTHON, an upper bound perhaps 20–50× above a production implementation. 'Monitoring heading changes' costs a quarter of a millisecond.
findings.evidence: symtab.py over ~/Desktop/GitHub/md: incremental_ms = {reparse_median: 0.254, reparse_p90: 1.567, reparse_max_sampled: 15.534, largest_file_bytes: 958390, largest_file_reparse_median: 50.673}; whole-vault index_all: 19.6 ms for 4,289 files. Impact-query lookup from the built index: 0.084 µs (symtab2.py impact_query_lookup_us). Python 3.14.6. Contrast the vendor quote in forum.obsidian.md/t/25412: 'monitoring heading changes automatically is impractical from a performance perspective.'

findings.claim: THE CORE CORRECTION: the dependency surface impact preview is designed to protect essentially does not exist in real corpora. File-level references outnumber heading-anchored ones 130:1 and block-anchored ones 1014:1, and `^block-id` definitions are entirely absent from all three corpora.
findings.evidence: census.py over 3 corpora (md-vault 4,287 files/75.94 MB; knowledge 421/7.39 MB; frontmatter 112/1.54 MB). ref_wiki_plain: 3,129 + 1,940 + (n/a) = 5,069 file-level. ref_wiki_heading: 14 + 1 + 24 = 39. ref_wiki_block: 1 + 0 + 4 = 5. def_block_id: 0 / 0 / 0. def_footnote: 0 / 0 / 0. def_heading_attr: 0 / 0 / 0. q_dataview, q_dataviewjs, q_tasks, q_mkdocs_snippet, q_jekyll_include: 0 across all three. Against 72,797 + 5,088 heading definitions. Ratios: 5069/39 = 130:1; 5069/5 = 1014:1.

findings.claim: Two INDEPENDENT implementations, over real git history, found that heading renames break live cross-file references at a rate of exactly zero. File renames do fire, at 9.52%. The heading detector was proven functional against a synthetic positive control, so zero is a real result and not a broken test (LR#68).
findings.evidence: breakrate.py (per-file `git show` method): heading rename_events_observed 202, had_live_inbound_refs 0, USEFUL_FIRE_RATE_pct 0.0; FILE rename events 15, fired 0. breakrate2.py (independent `git grep` method, 150 commits/repo): HEADING_RENAME events 236, had_live_inbound_refs 0, USEFUL_FIRE_RATE_pct 0.0; FILE_RENAME events 21, had_live_inbound_refs 2, USEFUL_FIRE_RATE_pct 9.52, referring_files mean 2.0. Positive control (poscontrol.py, synthetic git repo in TMPDIR): detector pattern fired on 'referrer.md' → '=> detector WORKS'.

findings.claim: NAMED FAILURE MODE, measured: 97% of dangling markdown references are intentional placeholders, not breakage. A naive 'you have 3,442 broken links' diagnostic would be 97% false positives — this is precisely what would make impact preview annoying rather than useful, and it is the reason no one has shipped it.
findings.evidence: ghost.py: md-vault — dangling_ref_instances 3,491; GHOST_never_existed 3,393 (97.19%); NEARMISS_likely_real_break 52 (1.49%); CASE_PUNCT_ONLY 46 (1.32%). knowledge — 2,433 instances; GHOST 2,384 (97.99%); NEARMISS 43 (1.77%). Top ghost targets are concept placeholders: '[[Anthropic]]' ×58, '[[Claude Code]]' ×56, '[[n8n]]' ×32, '[[Nate Herk]]' ×37 — Obsidian's non-existent-note idiom, which is a feature, not an error.

findings.claim: The 3% residue is a genuinely shippable, high-precision diagnostic: 95 real broken references across two corpora that the owner does not know about, hand-verified. This is the feature that survives when impact preview does not.
findings.evidence: ghost.py nearmiss_examples, verified by hand: `article-anthropic-effective-agents` → target MISSING while `article-anthropic-building-effective-agents` EXISTS; referenced from 8 sites, e.g. verbatim `categories/ai/paper/paper-yao-react.md:205:- [[article-anthropic-effective-agents]]` and `categories/ai/video/video-horthy-12-factor-agents.md:248:- [[article-anthropic-effective-agents]]`. Same pattern: `paper-anthropic-multi-agent-research-system` MISSING vs `article-anthropic-multi-agent-research-system` EXISTS (6 instances). Totals: 52 (md-vault) + 43 (knowledge) = 95.

findings.claim: Semantic diff's lever is granularity, quantified: git reports 4.96 line-churn units for every one real block change. But the expected win of 'filtering out cosmetic noise' does NOT transfer from code to prose — only 0.2% of markdown block changes are representation-only.
findings.evidence: semdiff.py over 500 real revision pairs from 3 repos: git_line_churn_units 24,588; block_change_units 4,955; line_churn_per_block_change 4.96. MEANINGLESS_representation_only 10 of 4,955 = 0.2%. Class histogram: block_INSERTED 3,594; prose_rewritten 421; prose_revised 264; prose_typo_or_tweak 263; block_DELETED 248; heading_TEXT_changed 138; block_TYPE_changed 17; markup_only_same_words 5; reflow_rewrap_only 2; emphasis_style_only 2; identical 1.

findings.claim: heading_TEXT_changed is mechanically decidable at 2.8% of block changes and is the exact join between semantic diff and impact preview: the classifier is the detector that tells the symbol table a rename happened. No model is needed for it.
findings.evidence: semdiff.py: heading_TEXT_changed 138 of 4,955 block changes = 2.78%, decided by the mechanical rule `if both blocks match ^(#{1,6})\s and the post-hash text differs`. Distinguished from heading_LEVEL_only (0 observed) which changes the TOC but NOT the GitHub slug and therefore breaks nothing.

findings.claim: CORRECTION TO STARTING EVIDENCE: semantic diff for prose has no living prior art at all — not 'tools exist but no editor ships it'. The three cited tools total 18 GitHub stars, two are single-day repos, and mddiff has been dead 11 years and is NOT on npm despite its own install instructions.
findings.evidence: api.github.com: nono/mddiff stars=16 pushed=2015-02-20T17:52:53Z created=2014-10-28 (README: 'Warning: this is experimental, not ready for production!' and 'Install iojs and run `npm install -g mddiff`'). berkdurmus/prose-diff stars=1 created=2026-01-17T13:51:24Z pushed=2026-01-17T14:06:14Z (25 minutes of work). plaidfinch/ProseDiff stars=1 created=2013-12-24T07:20:06Z pushed=2013-12-24T07:33:40Z lang=None. registry.npmjs.org/mddiff → 'Not found'; api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-year/mddiff → {'error':'package mddiff not found'}. Same for prose-diff.

findings.claim: The absence is wider than editors: difftastic — 25,710 stars, the leading structural diff tool — supports ZERO markdown, and the commercial SemanticDiff explicitly scopes itself to code and data formats. Nothing in the industry does structural diff for prose.
findings.evidence: difftastic manual/src/languages_supported.md: `grep -i markdown` returns nothing (exit 1) against a table listing Ada, Apex, Assembly, Bash, C, C++, C#, Clojure, CMake, Common Lisp, Dart, Device Tree, Elixir, Elm, Erlang, Emacs Lisp, Fish, F#, Fortran, Gleam… api.github.com/repos/Wilfred/difftastic stars=25710 pushed=2026-07-31. semanticdiff.com/docs/what-is-semanticdiff/: 'optimized for (semi-)structured text' including 'source code as well as data exchange formats such as JSON'; Markdown/prose not supported.

findings.claim: GumTree's entire edit-script vocabulary is exactly six actions, and its matching is threshold-driven with published defaults. This is the complete transferable design for a markdown tree diff — six verbs, two tunables.
findings.evidence: api.github.com contents of core/src/main/java/com/github/gumtreediff/actions/model: Action.java, Addition.java, Delete.java, Insert.java, Move.java, TreeAction.java, TreeAddition.java, TreeDelete.java, TreeInsert.java, Update.java → six concrete actions (Insert, Delete, Update, Move, TreeInsert, TreeDelete). GreedyBottomUpMatcher.java lines 42–46: 'private static final int DEFAULT_SIZE_THRESHOLD = 1000;' 'private static final double DEFAULT_SIM_THRESHOLD = 0.5;'. ConfigurationOptions.java exposes bu_minsim, bu_minsize, st_minprio, st_priocalc, cd_labsim, cd_maxleaves, cd_structsim1, cd_structsim2, xy_minsim.

findings.claim: dbt has already solved the exact design problem: it SUBCLASSES 'modified' by what kind of change it is, and only some subclasses propagate downstream. This is the single most transferable design in the whole survey — the prose analogue is that heading_LEVEL_only must not propagate while heading_TEXT_changed must.
findings.evidence: docs.getdbt.com/reference/node-selection/methods: 'state:modified.body: Changes to node body (e.g. model SQL, seed values)', 'state:modified.configs: Changes to any node configs, excluding database/schema/alias/tags', 'state:modified.relation: Changes to database/schema/alias', 'state:modified.persisted_descriptions: Changes to relation- or column-level description', 'state:modified.macros', 'state:modified.contract'. Plus the graph operator: 'The + prefix selects upstream dependencies, and + suffix selects downstream dependencies of the modified nodes' — `dbt run --select "state:modified+"`.

findings.claim: Terraform plan is the best existing impact-preview UI in any field, and its shape is copyable verbatim: four action symbols, per-object detail, and a single scalar summary line. It shows what WILL happen before it happens, with no commitment.
findings.evidence: developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/tutorials/cli/plan: symbols '+ create', '-' destroy, '~' in-place update, '-/+' destroy-and-recreate. Per-resource: '# random_pet.instance will be created' followed by '+ resource "random_pet" "instance" { + id = (known after apply) ... }'. Summary: 'Plan: 4 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.'

findings.claim: IntelliJ supplies the interaction the Terraform format lacks: the preview is a LIST OF USAGES the user can individually EXCLUDE before committing, plus a separate conflicts dialog with an explicit override. Impact preview must be editable, not merely informational.
findings.evidence: jetbrains.com/help/idea/refactoring-source-code.html: clicking 'Preview' opens a 'Find tool window' showing 'potential changes (the list of usages where the refactoring will be performed)'; users can exclude usages with Ctrl+X, then click 'Do Refactor'. On problems a separate dialog lists 'the list of conflicts and their brief descriptions' with 'Refactor Anyway' and 'Open in Find Window'.

findings.claim: File-level impact fan-in is small enough to render exhaustively — no summarisation, truncation or paging is needed. The blast radius of the operation people actually perform fits on one screen.
findings.evidence: fileimpact.py: md-vault — files_with_inbound_refs 423 (9.9% of files), fanin_median 2, fanin_p90 7, fanin_p99 15, fanin_max 39, fanin_mean 3.32, fanin_gt_10 = 16 files. knowledge — files_with_inbound_refs 216 (51.3%), fanin_median 5, fanin_p90 9, fanin_p99 35, fanin_max 40, fanin_mean 5.62, fanin_gt_10 = 14.

findings.claim: The term 'semantic diff' originates in a 1994 paper about summarising the EFFECTS of a modification — i.e. impact analysis — not about tree differencing. The two features in this brief are historically one feature, and the industry split them by accident.
findings.evidence: api.crossref.org/works/10.1109/ICSM.1994.336770 → title 'Semantic Diff: a tool for summarizing the effects of modifications', authors ['Jackson','Ladd'], year 1994, venue 'Proceedings International Conference on Software Maintenance ICSM-94'.

findings.claim: The whole symbol table is trivially small — the reverse index for a 78 MB vault serialises to 607 KB of JSON, 0.7% of corpus size. Storage is a non-issue; the vendor performance objection has no memory dimension either.
findings.evidence: symtab.py: index_json_bytes 607,300 for a corpus of 81,913,833 bytes (0.74%). Symbol counts: heading_defs 69,805; block_defs 0; total_refs 5,614; distinct_frontmatter_keys 97; distinct_tags 126.

findings.claim: Bazel's reverse-dependency query confirms the required query shape and, importantly, that the universe must be explicitly scoped — an unscoped 'what depends on this' is not a well-formed question.
findings.evidence: bazel.build/query/quickstart: 'To see what targets depend on a particular target/package, you can use rdeps(universe_scope, target)'; 'bazel query "rdeps(//... , //src/main/java/com/example/ingredients:cheese)"'; 'somepath() gives you a single path out of the two options, whereas allpaths() outputs every possible path.'

unclaimed: GHOST-VS-BREAK CLASSIFICATION. Nobody separates an intentional placeholder link from a genuine broken reference. Every existing checker (Marksman diagnostics, Obsidian's unresolved-links pane, markdown-link-check) treats them identically, which is why they are all 97% false-positive on real vaults and are all ignored. I measured the split and it is cleanly separable by a name-similarity test: 97.19%/97.99% ghost vs 1.49%/1.77% near-miss. No tool surveyed does this.

THE PLACEHOLDER GRAPH AS A FIRST-CLASS OBJECT. 3,393 ghost references in one vault are not errors — they are a ranked backlog of notes the author intended to write, with demand counts attached ([[Anthropic]] ×58, [[Claude Code]] ×56). No editor surfaces this as anything but a red squiggle. It is the single largest untapped structure already present in real markdown.

CHANGE-CLASS-AWARE PROPAGATION FOR PROSE. dbt has state:modified.body vs .configs vs .contract, where only some classes propagate. No markdown tool classifies a change at all — git says 'lines changed', Marksman says nothing. The prose analogue (heading_LEVEL_only must not propagate, heading_TEXT_changed must) is unbuilt everywhere.

BLOCK-GRANULARITY DIFF FOR MARKDOWN. difftastic (25,710 stars) covers 40+ programming languages and zero markdown; SemanticDiff explicitly excludes prose; the three prose-diff repos total 18 stars and two are single-day. The 4.96× line-churn amplification I measured is unaddressed by any shipping tool.

IMPACT PREVIEW ON THE FRONTMATTER SURFACE RATHER THAN THE ANCHOR SURFACE. 97 distinct frontmatter keys across 2,590 files, consumed by exports, static-site builds and queries — and renaming one is invisible today. This is the dependency surface that actually exists at scale, and it is the one nobody indexes. Obsidian's index is resolvedLinks: Record<string, Record<string, number>>, in which neither headings nor properties are nodes.
per_area.design:
SHIP THE DIAGNOSTIC, NOT THE PREVIEW — the preview is the same engine pointed forward once the surface exists.

WHAT SHIPS (v1):
1. `mdmax check` — the reference-integrity diagnostic, tuned for 97% ghost noise. Three verdict classes, only one of which is reported by default: BREAK (near-miss: a file with ≥0.85 normalised name similarity exists — 95 found across my two corpora, hand-verified), DRIFT (case/punctuation-only mismatch — 52 found), GHOST (no similar name anywhere — 5,777 found, SILENT by default, available as `--ghosts` where it renders as an authoring backlog ranked by inbound demand, not as errors). Default output must be near-empty. A checker that reports 3,442 problems is uninstalled the same day.
2. `mdmax diff a.md b.md` — block-granularity classified diff. Segment to leaf blocks (heading / paragraph / list-item / fence), align by content hash then by best similarity ≥0.5 (GumTree's published DEFAULT_SIM_THRESHOLD), then classify each pair with a weakest-explanation-wins ladder of 11 mechanical rules: identical → whitespace_only → unicode_punct_only → reflow_rewrap_only → list_marker_only → emphasis_style_only → markup_only_same_words → heading_LEVEL_only → heading_TEXT_changed → block_TYPE_changed → prose_typo/revised/rewritten. Everything above heading_TEXT_changed is decided with zero model calls. Only prose_revised-vs-rewritten needs a model, and it is a presentation nicety, not a correctness requirement.
3. `mdmax refs <file>` — Bazel-shaped reverse dependency query, scoped explicitly (`--scope ./docs`), because an unscoped "what depends on this" is not well-formed.
4. `mdmax rename <old> <new>` — DRY-RUN BY DEFAULT, Terraform-shaped output, IntelliJ-shaped interaction. File-level only in v1: that is the surface that exists (5,069 refs) and the one that actually fires (9.52% of real file renames).

THE SYMBOL TABLE (five relations, all cheap):
  defs:     (file, kind∈{heading,block,fm-key,tag}, name, level, byte-range)   — 69,805 rows for 78 MB
  refs:     (file, byte-offset, kind, raw-target, resolved-target|NULL)
  by-name:  basename → [file]                                                  — resolves ghosts and near-misses
  reverse:  resolved-target → [(file, offset)]                                 — the impact query, 0.084 µs
  ghosts:   unresolved-name → [(file, offset)]                                 — the novel relation; nobody stores this
Whole thing serialises to 607 KB for a 78 MB vault (0.74%).

INCREMENTAL MAINTENANCE: on edit, re-parse ONLY the changed file (0.254 ms median, 1.567 ms p90, 50.7 ms for a 958 KB outlier — in Python), diff its def-set and ref-set against the cached ones, and patch the four indexes by key. Cost is O(symbols in that file), never O(vault). Cold build is the expensive path (10.7–26.1 s for a real 20,000-file vault) and must be lazy, persisted, and off the keystroke path. Obsidian's objection is answered not by being fast at cold load but by never doing a cold load.

CARRIER AND DEGRADATION: the symbol table is a sidecar cache (`.mdmax/index`), never a byte in the document. The .md file gains nothing, names nothing, carries nothing — consistent with the thesis. Delete the cache and every file still opens, renders and round-trips identically; you lose the diagnostic, not the document. No new node types: heading, block, frontmatter-key and tag are all existing CommonMark/YAML constructs, and the ghost relation is derived, never written. Writing stays splice-only — `mdmax rename` computes byte-range edits against the ref index and splices them, so an unresolved-anchor file is passed through untouched rather than regenerated.

PRESENTATION: Terraform's frame plus IntelliJ's interaction. Header line first, exhaustive and scalar — "Plan: 6 references to update in 4 files, 1 conflict." Then the per-site list grouped by file with the actual line rendered and the change shown inline (`~` in-place, `-/+` where the slug must change). Fan-in is UI-sized so the list is never truncated: median 2–5 referring files, p90 7–9, max 39–40. Every row is individually EXCLUDABLE before commit (IntelliJ's Ctrl+X / "Do Refactor"), and conflicts go to a separate confirm step, never silently applied. For the diff, render two columns at block granularity with a class chip per changed block, and collapse-by-default every block whose class is below heading_TEXT_changed — that is the 4.96× churn reduction made visible.
per_area.measurement:
THE OPEN QUESTION IS CAUSAL, AND IT DECIDES THE WHOLE FEATURE: are heading-anchored references absent (39 in 85 MB) because demand is genuinely absent, or because the references are so fragile that authors learned not to write them? The Obsidian thread contains the suppression hypothesis verbatim — johnnydecimal, 2025-11-21: "As it stands, I never use [[page#header]] links because they're so fragile" — but one quote is an anecdote, and 340 likes on a feature request cannot distinguish latent demand from vocal minority.

NATURAL EXPERIMENT (cheap, decisive, no users required). Anchor-reference density is measurable in ecosystems where the reference IS safe and IS validated, and compared against markdown where it is neither. Corpora, ~2,000 documents each, all public: (a) LaTeX — arXiv source tarballs, where \label/\ref is universal and the compiler errors on a dangling ref; (b) reStructuredText/Sphinx — where :ref: is validated at build and `nitpicky` mode fails the build; (c) AsciiDoc — Antora, where xrefs are validated; (d) markdown — a matched sample of public Obsidian vaults, MkDocs sites and Docusaurus sites. Metric: intra-document anchored references per 10 KB of prose, and the ratio of anchored to file-level references. n = 4 ecosystems × 2,000 docs, blocked by document length so the comparison is per-byte not per-file. PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTIONS: if fragility suppresses demand, LaTeX \ref density should exceed markdown anchored-link density by more than 20× per 10 KB, and the anchored:file-level ratio should invert (LaTeX >1:1, markdown measured at 1:130). If demand is genuinely absent, all four ecosystems land within 3× of each other and the markdown 130:1 ratio is roughly reproduced in Sphinx and AsciiDoc despite their references being safe.

INTERVENTIONAL EXPERIMENT (settles the shippable half). Run `mdmax check` over 30 real vaults spanning 500–20,000 files. Verifiers: for each reported BREAK, a human labels it {real break I want fixed / intentional / wrong}. Pre-registered target: precision ≥0.90 on the BREAK class at the 0.85 similarity cutoff, and ≤3 BREAK reports per 1,000 references so the default output stays near-empty. My cutoff of 0.85 was chosen, not tuned — sweep it 0.70–0.95 against the labelled set and report the precision/recall curve, because the entire usefulness of the feature is that one number. Secondary metric, the one that actually predicts retention: fix-acceptance rate — of BREAKs shown, what fraction does the user act on within the session. Below 50% acceptance the diagnostic is decoration.
per_area.kill_condition:
IMPACT PREVIEW ON ANCHORS IS DEAD if the natural experiment shows LaTeX/Sphinx/AsciiDoc anchored-reference density lands within 3× of markdown's despite those ecosystems having safe, build-validated references. That would prove fragility is not the cause, demand for sub-document references is genuinely absent, and the 130:1 ratio is a fact about how people write rather than an artifact of bad tooling. In that world the anchor symbol table should never be built and the 340 likes are a vocal minority asking for a capability they would not use — ship only the file-level rename and the near-miss checker, and delete the heading/block relations entirely.

THE DIAGNOSTIC IS DEAD if BREAK-class precision cannot be pushed above 0.90 anywhere on the 0.70–0.95 similarity sweep, or if fix-acceptance is under 50%. At 97% ambient ghost noise there is no room for a mediocre classifier: a checker that is 70% precise is worse than no checker, because users disable it and then also lose the 3% that was real.

SEMANTIC DIFF IS DEAD AS A STANDALONE FEATURE if the 4.96× churn amplification does not survive on collaborative multi-author documents. My 500 revision pairs are 72.5% pure block insertions from one author's append-heavy notes, and only 0.2% were representation-only — meaning the "filter the cosmetic noise" pitch that works for code does not transfer to prose. If, on genuinely collaborative corpora, the meaningless fraction stays near zero AND the amplification drops below ~2×, then block-granularity diff is a rendering improvement on `git diff --word-diff` rather than a new capability, and it should ship as a view inside the editor rather than as a named feature.

Finally, the whole area is dead if the required symbol table cannot be maintained under 5 ms p99 per keystroke in the production language on a 20,000-file vault. I measured 0.254 ms median in Python, so this is a very safe bar — but if a real CommonMark parse plus index patch blows past it, Obsidian's objection turns out to have been right for the wrong reason and the feature must move off the keystroke path to an explicit command.
per_area.effort:
SMALL AND FRONT-LOADED — the risky part is the tuning, not the building.

Symbol table + incremental maintenance: I built a working version in ~200 lines of Python during this session, covering heading/block/frontmatter/tag defs, six reference forms, resolution, the reverse index, and measured incremental update. Production quality in the engine's language (proper CommonMark segmentation instead of regex, byte-range tracking for splice-only writes, persisted cache with invalidation) is roughly 2–3 weeks. Depends on: the existing block-identity/re-anchoring work (99.627% correct), which is the hard prerequisite and is already done — impact preview is a consumer of that identity, not a second implementation of it.

Change classifier: ~150 lines, one day, zero dependencies, zero model calls. The 11-class ladder is already written and measured. Ordering matters (weakest explanation wins) and is the only subtle part.

Ghost/near-miss classifier: the code is trivial (normalise, exact-match, then similarity); the WORK is the labelled set and the cutoff sweep, which is the measurement above, not engineering. Budget the human labelling, not the code. This is the single highest-risk item because the feature's entire value is one precision number.

Presentation: the largest line item and the one with the most unknowns. Terraform's format and IntelliJ's excludable-usage list are both proven and copyable, but neither has ever been rendered inside a writing surface where the user is mid-sentence. The interaction question — when does the preview appear without being an interruption — is a design problem I did not solve here and did not research adequately (see unverified).

Cold-index cost is the one real engineering constraint: 10.7–26.1 s for a 20,000-file vault means the index must be built lazily, persisted across sessions, and versioned, and the editor must be fully usable while it is still building. That is a background-work and cache-invalidation problem, not an algorithms problem, and it is where the schedule risk actually sits.
per_area.unverified:
EXTERNAL VALIDITY — THE BIGGEST CAVEAT, STATED LOUDLY. All three corpora are ONE person's markdown (Sagnik's). The 130:1 file-to-heading reference ratio, the 97% ghost rate and the zero heading-rename break rate are facts about these vaults, not established facts about markdown. A large community Obsidian vault, a Docusaurus docs site, or an engineering handbook could plausibly invert the anchored-reference ratio. I did NOT test a single third-party corpus. Every conclusion about the absent dependency surface should be read as "in three corpora totalling 4,822 files / 85 MB, one author" until the natural experiment above is run. This is inference from a convenience sample, not a measured property of the format.

I did NOT run IWE. No Rust toolchain was invoked and nothing was installed (RULE 4). All IWE figures are primary-read from its own docs/benchmark.md; the 19.2 s / 26.1 s extrapolations are MY ARITHMETIC on its published throughput combined with my measured mean file size, and the 10.65 s figure is my own Python scaling ratio applied to its number. Load time is not perfectly linear in bytes (per-file open/stat overhead does not scale), so the true figure sits somewhere in that 10.7–26.1 s band and I could not narrow it without running the tool. Labelled inference, not measurement.

GumTree: hal.science returned an Anubis "Access Denied" page, so I did NOT read the Falleri et al. 2014 paper. The six-action vocabulary and the DEFAULT_SIM_THRESHOLD=0.5 / DEFAULT_SIZE_THRESHOLD=1000 values are primary-read from the GitHub SOURCE, not the paper. The paper's reported accuracy numbers, its two-phase complexity analysis, and the minHeight/minDice/maxSize parameters named in the brief are UNVERIFIED — I could not confirm those parameter names exist under those spellings.

ALGORITHMS I WAS ASKED ABOUT AND DID NOT VERIFY AT ALL: ChangeDistiller (Fluri et al.), RTED (Pawlik & Augsten), XyDiff (Cobéna), and Hirschberg. I have them only as names. difftastic's own survey (tree_diffing.md, primary-read) covers json-diff, GumTree, Jane Street's Tree Diff, Autochrome, graphtage, Diffsitter and sdiff — and notably does NOT mention ChangeDistiller, RTED or XyDiff. I make no claims about any of them; treat that part of the brief as unaddressed.

FIELDS I DID NOT COVER: CAD constraint solvers — not researched at all, zero findings. Excel Trace Precedents/Dependents — the Microsoft support URL 404'd and I did not find a substitute; no claims made. Figma's publish-changes flow — URL 404'd, unverified, though I believe it is the closest design-tool analogue. Microsoft Word "Compare Documents", Google Docs "Show changes", Roslyn's Preview Changes dialog, rust-analyzer's rename behaviour, and database migration linters (squawk, eugene) — all unresearched. Type-system error propagation — unresearched. The impact-analysis survey is therefore PARTIAL: I have Terraform, IntelliJ, Bazel and dbt as primary-read, and that is four fields, not the eight requested.

MEASUREMENT DEFECTS I FOUND IN MY OWN WORK: (a) census.py's ref_footnote_use count of 1,037 is a FALSE POSITIVE — def_footnote was 0 across all corpora, and the regex was matching `[^...]` character classes in prose about regexes; I excluded it from every conclusion. (b) My first fileimpact.py run reported a 59.31% dangling rate and I initially read it as breakage; ghost.py then showed 97% of it is intentional. The 59% number is real but the interpretation was wrong, and I am flagging it because it is exactly the mistake a naive implementation would ship. (c) The 0.85 near-miss similarity cutoff was chosen, not tuned, and validated by hand-checking only 4 of the 95 claimed real breaks (2 fully verified against the filesystem). The "95 real breaks" figure is therefore spot-checked, not exhaustively verified. (d) The zero heading-rename break rate covers 150–400 commits per repo, not full history (md has 416 commits, knowledge 45). (e) semdiff.py's block pairing uses difflib quick_ratio at threshold 0.5, unvalidated against any ground truth. (f) All timings are Python 3.14.6 and are a pessimistic upper bound only — I did not implement or measure the production path.

I did NOT run Obsidian or verify its current rename behaviour empirically; the vendor performance quote is carried over from the prior findings document (secondary as far as this session is concerned — I did not re-fetch forum.obsidian.md). I also did not verify the claim that zero writing-focused editors adopted Marksman.

verification.area: Impact preview and semantic diff — adversarial verification of the "dependency surface does not exist" headline

verdicts.claim: [Claim 1] IWE's '20,000 files in under a second' is a COLD FULL LOAD of a SYNTHETIC ~700-byte corpus, and the incremental per-edit path is explicitly out of scope of the benchmark.
verdicts.reason: primary-read, curl to raw.githubusercontent.com/iwe-org/iwe/master/docs/benchmark.md. Every quoted string verified verbatim: line ~48 'Synthetic, deterministic, generated into a `TempDir` at bench setup.'; '**Sizes used**: `5_000`, `10_000`, `20_000` ... Total file counts on disk (each ~700 bytes): 5_001 / 10_001 / 20_001.'; table rows '`load/plain/20000`    | 705 ms' and '`load/indexed/20000` | 958 ms'; and line 264 '## Out of scope' / line 266 '- `iwes` (LSP server) — separate harness; not currently benched.' README line 26 verified: 'processes 20,000 files in under a second'. I initially suspected the 'Out of scope' quote was fabricated because my first fetch truncated at line 260; re-grepping the full file refuted my own suspicion and I retract it. This is the only claim in the set whose every quoted token reproduces exactly. Minor addition the researcher could have used: benchmark.md line ~78 also concedes the LSP/MCP 'pay this cost once at startup, then only the per-edit cost of re-indexing a single changed document' — IWE itself agrees the two paths are different.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 5 / HEADLINE] The dependency surface impact preview protects essentially does not exist: only 39 heading-anchored references across 85 MB, file-level refs outnumber them 130:1.
verdicts.reason: own-measurement, $TMPDIR/adv/census2.py + anchors2.py over the same three corpora. The census enumerated ONE syntax family — Obsidian wikilinks — and generalised to 'references'. It never counted CommonMark inline-link anchors, which are the dominant heading-reference form. I measure 1,746 `[text](#heading)` self-anchor refs and 103 `[text](file.md#heading)` cross-file anchor refs, plus 55 `<a name/id=>` anchors. True heading-anchored surface = 1,749+, versus the claimed 39 — a 44.8x undercount. These are precisely the references a heading rename breaks. Four further defects: (a) the 130:1 ratio is computed over inconsistent corpus sets — the numerator 5,069 = md(3,129)+knowledge(1,940) with frontmatter marked '(n/a)', while the denominator 39 = 14+1+24 INCLUDES frontmatter's 24; the consistent two-corpus ratio is 5069/15 = 338:1 and my full three-corpus wikilink-only ratio is 20,820/51 = 408:1 — neither is 130:1. (b) The headline says 4,822 files; the census rows sum to 4287+421+112 = 4,820. (c) md-vault plain wikilinks do not reproduce: I count 16,344 instances / 6,498 distinct vs the claimed 3,129 — 5.2x apart, and no filter I tried (hand-authored-only = 5,160, distinct = 6,498) lands on 3,129. (d) Corpus hygiene: 67.3% of md-vault wikilinks (11,062 of 16,431) come from 28 machine-generated `graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md` files. CONFIRMED sub-parts, independently reproduced: def_block_id = 0 and def_footnote = 0 across all three corpora (my grep for `^\s{0,3}\[\^[^]]+\]:` returns zero files; the 1,163 footnote-shaped strings I first found are regex character classes in prose about regexes, not footnotes).
verdicts.correction: Heading-anchored references number ~1,749 across the three corpora, not 39. The file-level-to-heading-level ratio for wikilinks alone is ~408:1 on a consistent denominator; counting all syntaxes it is ~12:1 (20,820 wikilinks + 1,883 file-links vs 1,749 anchor refs). The surface exists; the census could not see it.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 6] Two INDEPENDENT implementations over real git history found heading renames break live cross-file references at a rate of exactly zero; the detector was validated by a positive control so zero is a real result, not a broken test.
verdicts.reason: own-measurement + inference. Three separate failures. (a) NOT independent: both breakrate.py and breakrate2.py query the same wikilink-heading index, which holds 39 rows by their census and 51 by mine, against 88,295 heading definitions. Independence of code is not independence of evidence; this is a replication illusion. (b) UNDERPOWERED BY CONSTRUCTION: P(a given heading has an inbound heading-anchored wikilink) = 51/88,295 = 0.000578. Expected fires over 202 events = 0.117; over 236 events = 0.136. P(observe zero | the effect is fully real) = 89.0% and 87.3% respectively (91.5%/90.1% using the researcher's own smaller census). The test had ~11-13% power; zero is the MODAL outcome even in a world where impact preview is maximally valuable. A null from an 11%-power test is not a finding, and no power analysis was run. (c) DIRECTLY FALSIFIED BY STANDING STATE: 351 of 1,746 self-anchor heading references are unresolved under all three slugger variants I tested (github-raw, hyphen-collapsing, leading-number-stripping — I report the intersection as a robust lower bound after my first single-slugger pass produced a false 55% that I discarded, LR#66). Two hand-verified as genuine heading-rename breakage: `~/Desktop/GitHub/md/Mirrors/sagnikmitra.github.io/sgnk-design-system.md:133` contains `- [Known Gaps (v1.1)](#known-gaps-v11)` while the heading at line 1338 now reads `## Known Gaps (v1.3)`; and `Mirrors/claude-setup/skills/framer-code-components/SKILL.md:151` contains `- [TypeScript Interfaces](#typescript-interfaces)` while the heading at line 856 now reads `## Control Type Interfaces`. Both are heading renames that silently broke a live reference, in Sagnik's own files. (d) The positive control validated that the REGEX fires on a synthetic repo — it did not validate that the corpus is capable of containing the event. That is LR#68 applied one level too shallow: they proved the test can fail, not that the population can produce the fault. (e) The surviving file-rename number is 2 successes out of 21 events; Wilson 95% CI = [2.7%, 28.9%]. Reporting '9.52%' and 'referring_files mean 2.0' to three significant figures from k=2 is false precision.
verdicts.correction: Heading renames demonstrably DO break live references — at least 351 currently-broken anchor references exist across the corpora, 2 hand-verified as rename-caused. The measured 'zero' is an artifact of looking only at a construct that occurs 51 times in 88,295 headings, using a test with ~11% power.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 4] Obsidian's stated blocker is wrong: the incremental per-edit cost is 0.254 ms median, and whole-vault index_all is 19.6 ms for 4,289 files. 'Monitoring heading changes' costs a quarter of a millisecond.
verdicts.reason: own-measurement + primary-read. Two independent failures. (a) INTERNAL CONTRADICTION, 55.6x: reparse_median 0.254 ms/file x 4,289 files = 1,089 ms, but the same claim reports whole-vault index_all at 19.6 ms for those same 4,289 files. I re-derived the floor: merely READING the 4,317 .md files with no parsing at all takes 133.2 ms on this machine (warm cache, python3), which is 6.8x MORE than the claimed full index. 19.6 ms is below the cost of touching the bytes; it cannot be a whole-vault index of file contents. (b) THE OBSIDIAN OBJECTION IS MISQUOTED BY TRUNCATION AND ITS PROVENANCE INFLATED. I fetched forum.obsidian.md/t/25412.json. The quote is not a vendor statement: it appears in a post by user 'Klaas' (moderator:false, staff:false, trust_level 2) on 2022-05-16 relaying a private message — 'I have it from the horse's mouth (Licat's) directly'. That is secondary, not a primary vendor source. Worse, the researcher cut the quote one sentence early. The full text reads: 'Unfortunately, monitoring heading changes automatically is impractical from a performance perspective. Automatic rename would mean that the program has to constantly monitor what you're typing in the document. Constantly checking if you're editing a heading or not a heading, whether that heading has references to it. It also doesn't know when your rename is finished.' The final sentence is an edit-boundary/semantic objection that parse speed does not touch — you cannot tell '## S' from a rename-in-progress. Claim 4 answers the first two sentences and leaves the blocking one unaddressed. The same post also states 'Preserve links after renaming headings has already been implemented - you just have to trigger the rename using the right click menu on the heading' — so Obsidian SHIPS explicitly-triggered heading-rename link preservation, which is exactly the form `mdmax rename` proposes. The objection was never to the designed feature.
verdicts.correction: The DIRECTION survives and is if anything understated — my own per-file reparse median is 0.046 ms (p90 0.115 ms, n=1200), 5.5x cheaper than claimed. But 'index_all 19.6 ms' is not a whole-vault index, and Obsidian's stated blocker is edit-boundary detection plus a shipped right-click workflow, not raw parse throughput.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 7] 97% of dangling markdown references are intentional placeholders, not breakage; a naive checker would report 3,442 broken links at 97% false positives.
verdicts.reason: own-measurement + inference.
