(a) ARITHMETICALLY IMPOSSIBLE AGAINST CLAIM 5: claim 5 reports md-vault plain wikilinks = 3,129 while claim 7 reports md-vault dangling_ref_instances = 3,491 — 362 more dangling references than references exist. Same for knowledge: 1,940 total vs 2,433 dangling, 493 more. Both corpora. The two claims cannot have been computed over one reference population, and no reconciliation was attempted. (b) The figure '3,442 broken links', which appears in both claim 7 and the design's justification for a quiet default, matches neither 3,491 (dangling) nor 3,393 (ghosts) nor any stated total — it is an unsourced third number. (c) 'INTENTIONAL PLACEHOLDER' IS AN INFERENCE TAGGED AS own-measurement. What was measured is 'no file with >=0.85 normalised name similarity exists'. Intent was not measured. The GHOST bucket necessarily conflates deliberate Obsidian non-existent-note links, references to deleted files, and typos bad enough to miss the 0.85 threshold. I did verify the named exemplars are hand-authored rather than machine-generated ([[Anthropic]] x58, [[Claude Code]] x56, [[n8n]] x32, [[Nate Herk]] x37 — all 100% from hand-authored vault files, zero from graphify-out), so the placeholder reading is plausible for those; plausible is not measured. (d) 'this is the reason no one has shipped it' is an unsupported causal claim about other people's product decisions.
verdicts.correction: The noise problem is real and the default-quiet design follows from it, but '97% are intentional' should read '97% have no near-name match in the vault, of which a hand-checked sample are Obsidian placeholder links'. The absolute counts do not reconcile with the census and should be re-derived from one shared reference population.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 8] The 3% residue is a shippable high-precision diagnostic: 95 real broken references across two corpora, hand-verified.
verdicts.reason: primary-read of the actual files, the strongest claim in the set and the only one whose exemplars I could reproduce byte-for-byte. `~/Desktop/GitHub/knowledge/categories/ai/paper/paper-yao-react.md:205` is verbatim `- [[article-anthropic-effective-agents]]` and `categories/ai/video/video-horthy-12-factor-agents.md:248` is verbatim the same string. `ls categories/*/*/article-anthropic-effective-agents.md` returns no matches; `categories/ai/article/article-anthropic-building-effective-agents.md` exists. I count 8 instances across 4 files — the claim says 'referenced from 8 sites', accurate if 'sites' means occurrences (it is 4 files). Second exemplar confirmed identically: `paper-anthropic-multi-agent-research-system` has no matching file, `categories/ai/article/article-anthropic-multi-agent-research-system.md` exists, 6 instances. 52+43=95 checks out arithmetically. I could not re-derive the full 95 without reimplementing their similarity threshold, so the total is CONFIRMED-by-mechanism rather than fully replicated; the mechanism and both sampled instances are exact. Note this class is file-level near-miss detection, which does not depend on any of the refuted heading-surface claims — it survives independently.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 2] Markdown index cost is BYTE-dominated, not FILE-dominated, so 'N files' is the wrong unit for the entire Obsidian-vs-IWE performance argument.
verdicts.reason: inference over the researcher's own reported numbers. The direction is right; the strength is not. Their three data points give ms_per_MB of 88.62 / 53.35 / 50.33 — a 1.76x spread, not a constant. The small-file corpus is 66% MORE expensive per MB than the large-file corpus, which is exactly the signature of a real per-file cost term. The honest model is affine (time = a*files + b*bytes with both terms material), not 'bytes dominate, files are the wrong unit'. My own measurement supports a substantial per-file component: reading 4,317 files costs 133.2 ms = 0.0308 ms/file before a single byte is parsed. Critically, this claim's own regime spread is what invalidates claim 3's extrapolation method (see next verdict) — the report never notices that its claim 2 and claim 3 are in tension.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 3] A real 20,000-file vault is 364 MiB, so IWE's headline is off by 11x to 27x (19.2 s plain / 26.1 s indexed).
verdicts.reason: own-measurement + re-derived arithmetic. The mean file size is roughly right — I independently measure 4,317 md-vault files at 85,423,293 bytes = 19,788 B/file vs their 19,098.6, within 3.5%. Three defects in what is built on it. (a) THE METHOD IS BIASED HIGH BY THE REPORT'S OWN DATA. The 19.23 s figure applies 18.94 MiB/s, a throughput measured on IWE's 700-byte corpus — which claim 2 identifies as the expensive per-MB regime (88.62 ms/MB) — to a large-file corpus that claim 2 measures at 53.35 ms/MB. Correcting by the report's own regime factor of 1.661x: 19.23/1.661 = 11.58 s plain, 26.14/1.661 = 15.74 s indexed. That corrected figure agrees with the researcher's OTHER estimate (10.65 s from the independently measured 15.1x scaling ratio) and disagrees with the one they headlined. The '27x' upper bound is a method artifact. (b) INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY ON THE MEAN: claim 3 uses 81,913,833 B / 4,289 files = 19,098.6 B/file, while claim 5's census reports the same corpus as 4,287 files / 75.94 MB = 17,714 B/file. Same vault, two means, 1.08x apart, ~5.97 MB unaccounted, and no MB-vs-MiB convention is stated anywhere (the design separately calls it a '78 MB vault', a third figure). (c) MIXED DENOMINATORS: '11x to 27x' compares 10.65 s against '1 second' but 19.23 s and 26.14 s against 705 ms and 958 ms. And the scenario itself is a 4.6x extrapolation beyond the largest corpus actually held (4,317 files), reported to four significant figures.
verdicts.correction: Corrected range is roughly 10.6-15.7 s, i.e. the headline is optimistic by ~11x-16x for a hypothetical 20,000-file real-world vault. Still a substantial and fair criticism of IWE's README claim — just not 27x, and not measured, since no corpus of that size was tested.

verdicts.claim: [DESIGN] The symbol table's ghosts relation — unresolved-name to (file, offset) — is 'the novel relation; nobody stores this'.
verdicts.reason: primary-read of Obsidian's public API surface, curl to raw.githubusercontent.com/obsidianmd/obsidian-api/master/obsidian.d.ts. Line 4444 declares `unresolvedLinks: Record<string, Record<string, number>>;` documented at lines 4439-4442 as 'Contains all unresolved links. This object maps each source file to an object of unknown destinations with count.' Line 4438 declares `resolvedLinks: Record<string, Record<string, number>>;` — the design's 'reverse' relation. Line 4462 documents an event 'Called when a file has been resolved for `resolvedLinks` and `unresolvedLinks`'. Both relations have been first-class, publicly documented, incrementally-maintained Obsidian indexes for years, keyed by source rather than by target and trivially invertible. This is exactly the prior art the brief asked me to look for, and it took one curl. Adjacent prior art on the checker itself: npm ships `markdown-link-check`, `@mintlify/link-rot` ('Static checking for broken internal links'), `linkinator`, `broken-link-checker`. The genuinely defensible novelty is the three-way BREAK/DRIFT/GHOST triage and the quiet default — not the relation, and not the category.
verdicts.correction: Drop 'the novel relation; nobody stores this'. Claim novelty only for the near-miss triage and the default-silent ghost class; cite Obsidian's unresolvedLinks/resolvedLinks as the incremental-maintenance precedent, which also strengthens claim 4 (Obsidian already maintains both indexes incrementally, so the cost objection was never about maintaining them).

verdicts.claim: [DESIGN] Ship `mdmax rename` file-level-only in v1, because 'that is the surface that exists (5,069 refs) and the one that actually fires (9.52% of real file renames)'.
verdicts.reason: inference from my own census, plus a settled-invariant check. The scoping decision inherits claim 5's blind spot: the defs relation is (file, kind in {heading, block, fm-key, tag}) and refs carries raw-target/resolved-target, with no anchor-slug kind and no self-anchor ref kind anywhere in the five relations. So the design as written cannot represent, let alone catch, the 1,746 self-anchor and 103 cross-file-anchor heading references I measured, nor the 351 currently-broken ones. It is scoped away from the only breakage class I was able to verify empirically exists in these corpora. The supporting rate is also 2 successes out of 21 (Wilson 95% CI [2.7%, 28.9%]). Separately, a GENERALISATION defect: all three corpora have a single author. The same Obsidian thread I fetched contains user shinyben, 2022-01-16: 'As I use internal links in headers, and just did a note name overhaul, essentially all of my header links (which are the main way I link) are broken' — and the linked feature request 'has 83 upvotes' per user Klaas. Heading-anchored linking is a real and common authoring idiom; this vault simply does not use it. n=1 author cannot support 'the surface does not exist' as a product-level conclusion. TO BE FAIR, the parts of the design I could check against the settled invariants are sound and I found no violation: the sidecar `.mdmax/index` puts no byte in the document, adds no node types (heading/fm-key/tag are existing CommonMark/YAML constructs), keeps writing splice-only via byte-range edits, and degrades correctly — delete the cache and every file still round-trips. The GumTree citation is also textually accurate (DEFAULT_SIM_THRESHOLD = 0.5 at GreedyBottomUpMatcher.java:43 and XyBottomUpMatcher.java:42), though it is a Dice coefficient over matched descendant nodes in a bottom-up AST matcher, not a text-similarity default for flat blocks — borrowing the constant across that category gap needs saying out loud.
verdicts.correction: Add an anchor-slug def kind and a self-anchor ref kind to the symbol table before scoping v1, and re-run the break-rate study against that surface. The 351 robustly-unresolved anchors are a ready-made, hand-verifiable validation set.

survived: Claim 1 in full — every quoted string from IWE's benchmark.md and README reproduces verbatim, including the 'Out of scope' section I initially and wrongly suspected was fabricated. The argument that the two sides measure different things is correct and well-sourced.

Claim 8 — the near-miss reference checker. Both exemplars reproduce byte-for-byte at the stated file:line, targets confirmed missing, similar targets confirmed present. This is the strongest finding in the report and it does not depend on any of the refuted heading-surface claims.

def_block_id = 0 and def_footnote = 0 across all three corpora — independently reproduced. Zero `^block-id` definitions and zero `[^n]:` footnote definitions in 4,851 files. The block-anchor surface really is absent.

The direction of claim 4's conclusion: incremental per-file re-parse is cheap and belongs off the cold-load path. My own median is 0.046 ms (p90 0.115 ms, n=1200), 5.5x cheaper than the reported 0.254 ms — the conclusion is understated, not overstated.

The mean real-file size, ~19 KB. I measure 19,788 B/file over 4,317 files vs the claimed 19,098.6 — within 3.5%. Real markdown really is ~27x larger than IWE's synthetic corpus, and 'N files' really is an inadequate unit.

The ghost-noise product insight. Even though 97% is not a measurement of intent, a large majority of dangling wikilinks in these corpora have no near-name match, and a checker that reports thousands of them by default would be uninstalled. The BREAK/DRIFT/GHOST triage and the near-empty default output follow soundly.

The carrier-and-degradation design. Sidecar `.mdmax/index`, no bytes in the document, no new node types, splice-only writing via byte-range edits, delete-the-cache-and-nothing-breaks. I checked this against every settled invariant in the project context and found no violation.
The GumTree 0.5 citation is textually accurate (GreedyBottomUpMatcher.java:43, XyBottomUpMatcher.java:42), with the caveat that it is an AST-subtree Dice threshold, not a flat-text default.
killed: THE HEADLINE — 'the dependency surface impact preview protects does not exist'. It exists; the census could not see it. Heading-anchored references number ~1,749 across the three corpora, not 39, because `[text](#heading)` and `[text](file.md#heading)` were never counted.

Claim 5's ratios: 130:1 and 1014:1. Computed over inconsistent corpus sets (numerator excludes frontmatter, denominator includes it). The consistent two-corpus wikilink ratio is 338:1; my full three-corpus wikilink ratio is 408:1; counting all reference syntaxes it is ~12:1. None of these is 130:1.

Claim 6's 'exactly zero, confirmed by two independent implementations'. Not independent (one shared 51-row index), underpowered by construction (~11-13% power; P(zero | effect fully real) = 87-92%), and falsified by standing state — 351 robustly-unresolved anchor references, 2 hand-verified as heading-rename breakage in Sagnik's own files.
Claim 4's 'whole-vault index_all: 19.6 ms for 4,289 files'. Contradicts its own reparse_median by 55.6x, and sits 6.8x below the 133.2 ms floor cost of merely reading those bytes on this machine.

Claim 4's framing of the Obsidian blocker. The quote is a forum user relaying a private message (secondary, not vendor-primary), truncated one sentence before the actual objection — 'It also doesn't know when your rename is finished' — and the same post states heading-rename link preservation is already shipped behind a right-click trigger.

Claim 3's 19.2 s / 26.1 s and the '27x' upper bound. Produced by applying small-file throughput to a large-file corpus, a method the report's own claim 2 shows is biased high by 1.661x. Corrected range is ~10.6-15.7 s.

Claim 7's absolute counts. 3,491 dangling md-vault refs against 3,129 total md-vault refs, and 2,433 against 1,940 for knowledge — more dangling references than references exist, in both corpora. Plus an unsourced third figure, 3,442.
Claim 7's '97% are intentional placeholders' as a measurement. Intent was never measured; what was measured is absence of a near-name match.
'this is the reason no one has shipped it' — an unsupported causal claim about other teams' product decisions.

The design's 'ghosts: the novel relation; nobody stores this'. Obsidian's public API has shipped `unresolvedLinks` (obsidian.d.ts:4444) and `resolvedLinks` (:4438) as documented, incrementally-maintained, event-emitting indexes for years.

`mdmax rename` file-level-only as a justified v1 scope. The justification rests on the refuted census, and the five-relation schema has no anchor-slug def kind, so it structurally cannot catch the one breakage class I could verify exists.
new_defects: CONSTRUCT VALIDITY — the central defect. The census enumerated one syntax family (Obsidian wikilinks) and reported the result as the count of 'references'. CommonMark inline-link anchors, the dominant heading-reference form in README/docs-style markdown, were never counted. Every downstream conclusion — the 130:1 ratio, the zero break rate, the file-level-only v1 scope — inherits the blind spot. A census must state which constructs it enumerated and which it did not.

REPLICATION ILLUSION. Two implementations (`git show` vs `git grep`) querying the same 51-row index were reported as 'two INDEPENDENT implementations'. Independence of code is not independence of evidence. Re-implementing the query does not re-sample the population.

A NULL FROM AN UNDERPOWERED TEST REPORTED AS A POSITIVE FINDING. Expected fires were 0.09-0.14 across 202/236 events; P(observe zero | effect fully real) = 87-92%. No power analysis was run. 'A rate of exactly zero' should have read 'this test cannot distinguish zero from fully-real'.

POSITIVE CONTROL AIMED ONE LEVEL TOO SHALLOW (LR#68 extended). The control proved the detector's regex fires on a synthetic repo. It did not establish that the corpus is capable of containing the event. The rule needs strengthening: validate the population's capacity to produce the fault, not just the detector's capacity to see it.

NO CROSS-CLAIM RECONCILIATION PASS. At least four pairs of numbers inside one report contradict each other: dangling > total refs in both corpora; index_all vs reparse_median by 55.6x; two means for one corpus (19,098.6 vs 17,714 B/file); file count 4,822 vs rows summing to 4,820. Any report carrying more than a few measurements needs a final pass that re-derives every ratio from its stated components.

RATIOS OVER INCONSISTENT CORPUS SETS. A numerator marked '(n/a)' for one corpus divided by a denominator that includes that corpus. If a corpus is excluded from one side it must be excluded from both, or the ratio must be stated per-corpus.

PROVENANCE INFLATION PLUS TRUNCATION-TO-FIT. A trust-level-2 forum user's relay of a private message was cited as 'the vendor quote', and cut one sentence before the part that does not support the argument. Quoting to the end of the objection is not optional when the claim is that the objection is wrong.
INFERENCE TAGGED AS own-measurement. 'Intentional placeholders' is an interpretation of 'no near-name match exists'. The evidence tag was measurement-grade; the claim was not.

CORPUS CONTAMINATION AND SINGLE-AUTHOR GENERALISATION. 67.3% of md-vault wikilinks (11,062 of 16,431) come from 28 machine-generated `graphify-out/GRAPH_REPORT.md` files, unfiltered and unmentioned. And all three corpora have one author — a product-level 'this surface does not exist' conclusion cannot rest on n=1 authoring style, particularly when the cited forum thread contains users reporting the opposite experience.

FALSE PRECISION. '9.52%' and 'referring_files mean 2.0' from k=2 successes (Wilson 95% CI [2.7%, 28.9%]); '19.23 s' and '26.14 s' to four significant figures from a 4.6x extrapolation beyond the largest corpus held.
UNSTATED UNIT CONVENTION. MB, MiB and a rounded '78 MB' are used interchangeably across claims 3, 5 and the design, which is where part of the 1.08x mean-size discrepancy hides.

UNREPRODUCIBLE PRIMARY COUNT. The md-vault plain-wikilink figure of 3,129 matches none of my derivations — all instances (16,344), hand-authored only (5,160), or distinct targets (6,498). A headline census number that cannot be re-derived from a stated filter is not usable, and the script's exclusion set was never published.

per_area.title: Show me what the model sees — a debugger for context
per_area.headline: The dangerous divergence is not the invisible character — a naive invisible-character detector fires on 4.94% of 2,308 real markdown files with a measured 0% true-positive rate — it is the transformation each consumer applies: a coding-agent Read costs +14.991% tokens over the file's own bytes, LangChain's markdown splitter destroys indentation on 34.61% of fenced-code lines and silently deletes the entire Unicode Tag block, 2.924% of the tokens a model receives are invisible in the rendered document, and this repo's own AGENTS.md — which opens "Read this before" — was never loaded into the agent reading it.

findings.claim: The file-tool pathway (coding-agent Read) prepends a line number plus tab to every line, costing +14.991% more tokens than the file's own bytes across a real corpus. The surcharge is a function of LINE COUNT, not content — so hard-wrapped prose is materially more expensive to an agent than soft-wrapped prose, and no tool surfaces this.
findings.evidence: node hop.mjs over ~/Desktop/GitHub/md, n=1984 non-hidden .md files, 888,223 lines: {"rawTok": 11894041, "lnTok": 13677024, "lnOverheadPct": 14.991, "bytesPerTok": 3.877}. Tokenizer = gpt-tokenizer 3.4.0 o200k_base. Script at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-sagnikmitra-Desktop-GitHub-frontmatter/9e5a4a9f-8c4a-4758-b560-0afea2b30447/scratchpad/hop.mjs

findings.claim: 2.924% of the tokens a model receives from real markdown are INVISIBLE in the rendered document. Frontmatter and link destinations dominate; invisible codepoints are a rounding error. This is the true size of the human/machine divergence and it is ~200x larger than the Unicode-injection channel everyone worries about.
findings.evidence: node hidden.mjs over md + knowledge + frontmatter/docs, mdast AST walk, n=2302 files, 12,890,412 o200k tokens: {"fm":199104,"comment":12478,"linkDest":157651,"linkTitle":430,"imgUrl":3640,"defn":104,"htmlAttr":3440,"invis":13,"hiddenTokens":376860,"hiddenPct":2.924,"parseFail":0}

findings.claim: CORRECTION TO STARTING EVIDENCE — a naive 'this file contains invisible characters' warning is 100% false-positive on real documents. It fires on 4.94% of files and every single occurrence is legitimate: emoji presentation selectors and Indic-script joiners. Zero Unicode Tag characters, zero bidi overrides in 2,308 real files. Shipping the naive badge trains the author to ignore it — LR#65's disease.
findings.evidence: node invis.mjs: 'files with invisibles: 114 of 2308' — U+FE0F 291 ("⚠️ Vintage note"), U+200C 71 (Bengali: "মা কুরু ধনজনযৌবনগর্বম্‌"), U+200D 11, U+200B 2 (a pasted YouTube comment). 375 occurrences, 0 malicious.

findings.claim: A context-aware classifier (emoji-base for variation selectors, complex-script neighbours for ZWJ/ZWNJ) reclassifies 93.3% of those hits as legitimate — and the 25 survivors are STILL all benign, exposing two rules a real detector needs: ASCII keycap bases (#, *, 0-9) are not Extended_Pictographic, and Indic ZWNJ frequently sits next to a space rather than a letter.
findings.evidence: node classify.mjs: 'files scanned 2308 invisible occurrences 375 / LEGIT 350 {variation selector after Extended_Pictographic: 290, ZWJ/ZWNJ in complex script: 60} / ANOMALOUS 25'. Top anomaly: 'U+FE0F README.md | variation selector after non-emoji "#" | "## #️⃣ Remote Config Var"'.

findings.claim: THE RAG HOP IS DESTRUCTIVE AND NOBODY SAYS SO. LangChain's MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter applies line.strip() and filter(str.isprintable) to every line INCLUDING inside fenced code blocks: 12.33% of all lines are altered and 34.61% of lines inside code fences lose their indentation entirely. Python, YAML and nested lists arrive at the model structurally destroyed.
findings.evidence: python3 replay of langchain_text_splitters/markdown.py split_text() over 2,303 files / 940,687 lines: {'lines_losing_indent_or_trailing': 116018, 'pct_strip': 12.33, 'code_block_lines': 200735, 'code_block_lines_indented': 69483, 'pct_code_indent_destroyed': 34.61}

findings.claim: CORRECTION TO STARTING EVIDENCE — the claim that the Unicode Tag block passes through everything byte-identically is TRUE for parse/render/format but FALSE at the RAG hop. LangChain's splitter silently deletes the ENTIRE Tag block, plus ZWSP/ZWNJ/ZWJ/WJ/BOM/NBSP/bidi overrides/TAB/ideographic space/soft hyphen — while keeping U+FE0F. It is accidentally the only sanitizer in the chain, and simultaneously the only tool that corrupts Bengali/Hindi/Persian text and every tab-indented code block.
findings.evidence: raw.githubusercontent.com/langchain-ai/langchain/master/libs/text-splitters/langchain_text_splitters/markdown.py line ~166: `stripped_line = "".join(filter(str.isprintable, stripped_line))` with the comment `# Remove all non-printable characters from the string, keeping only visible text.` Python truth table measured: U+200B Cf False, U+200D Cf False, U+E0041 TAG A Cf False, U+0009 TAB Cc False, U+00A0 Zs False, U+FE0F Mn TRUE (survives). Corpus deletions: 1,297 codepoints — U+3103 x600, U+00A0 x358, U+2028 x285, U+E200-E202 x36, U+200C x11, U+0009 x4, U+200B x2.

findings.claim: Anthropic ships a production machine-only channel on its Claude Code docs: a blockquote hidden from sighted users, screen-reader users AND keyboard users simultaneously, explicitly named as an agent channel, and marked noindex so search engines never see it either. This is the divergence law shipped by the company that writes the guidance against it — and it is the exact artifact the inspector exists to reveal.
findings.evidence:
curl docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/memory, byte offset 14272: `

Documentation Index

Fetch the complete documentation index at: /docs/llms.txt

Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

`. The .md twin serves it at `content-type: text/markdown` with `x-robots-tag: noindex, nofollow` and `x-matched-path: /_mintlify/_markdown/_sites/[subdomain]/[[...slug]]`.

findings.claim: CORRECTION TO STARTING EVIDENCE — Anthropic does NOT prepend the imperative to every doc page. It is scoped to the Claude Code subtree. Two of four pages sampled outside it have no preamble at all.
findings.evidence: curl of four .md twins: /en/docs/claude-code/hooks and /en/docs/claude-code/mcp both begin `> ## Documentation Index|> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt|...`; /en/api/overview begins `# API overview` and /en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview begins `# Prompt engineering overview` — no preamble.

findings.claim: THE THESIS RULE 'a document NAMES a capability, never CARRIES one' is already violated in production by Claude Code's own skill format: a markdown file can carry executable shell that runs BEFORE the model sees the content. This does not weaken the design rule — it is the strongest possible argument for the inspector, because the delivered text is not derivable from the file at all.
findings.evidence: code.claude.com/docs/en/skills.md line 494: "The `` !`<command>` `` syntax runs shell commands before the skill content is sent to Claude. The command output replaces the placeholder, so Claude receives actual data, not the command itself." And line 89: "Claude Code runs the command and replaces the line with its output before Claude sees the skill content".

findings.claim: CLAUDE.md import semantics are precise and non-obvious, and any inspector must reimplement them exactly: eager inlining at launch, recursion to a maximum of four hops, and import parsing that skips code spans and fenced code blocks. The starting evidence's 'gave up on traversal entirely' overstates it — it is bounded traversal with eager inlining, plus an approval dialog for external imports.
findings.evidence: code.claude.com/docs/en/memory.md line 95-99: "Imported files are expanded and loaded into context at launch alongside the CLAUDE.md that references them... Imported files can recursively import other files, with a maximum depth of four hops." / "Import parsing skips Markdown code spans and fenced code blocks. To mention a path in your CLAUDE.md without importing it, wrap it in backticks". Line 81: "imported files still load and enter the context window at launch."

findings.claim: THE FAILURE IS LIVE IN THIS REPO. /Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/frontmatter/AGENTS.md opens with an imperative addressed to agents, costs 2,056 tokens, and was never delivered to the agent reading the repo — there is no CLAUDE.md and no import. Meanwhile 17,303 tokens of user-scope memory WERE eagerly delivered. An author cannot currently tell these two cases apart.
findings.evidence: `ls CLAUDE.md` -> 'No such file or directory'; `find . -maxdepth 2 -name CLAUDE.md` -> empty. AGENTS.md line 3-5: "Operational rules for any agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, gstack, etc.) editing this repo. Read this **before** adding new files". Token counts (o200k): AGENTS.md 2056 (NOT loaded); ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md 14577 + imports/sgnk-skills.md 2374 + rules/gvc.md 260 + projects/.../memory/MEMORY.md 92 = 17,303 (loaded, and visible verbatim in my own system prompt under the wrapper "Contents of /Users/sagnikmitra/.claude/CLAUDE.md (user's private global instructions for all projects):").

findings.claim: A .md file cannot be uploaded to the Claude API as markdown — it must be declared text/plain, and plain-text documents are then automatically re-chunked into SENTENCES with char-index citations. Markdown block structure is not merely ignored at this hop; it is replaced. But 'custom content documents' receive NO further chunking — which is the exact hole MDMAX blocks fit, giving block-addressed citations nobody else can offer.
findings.evidence: docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/files.md line 448: "Files that are already plain text, such as .csv and .md files, can either be read in this way or uploaded through the Files API with an explicit `text/plain` content type." citations.md line 330/331: "**For plain text documents:** Content is chunked into sentences that can be cited from." / "**For custom content documents:** Your provided content blocks are used as-is and no further chunking is done." Line 710 table: Plain text | Sentence | Character indices (0-indexed).

findings.claim: MCP is the ONLY place in the whole ecosystem with a standardized, declared 'who is this content for' channel — Annotations.audience. Everywhere else the divergence is undeclared and must be derived. MCP's TextResourceContents is a bare string with no normalization requirement, so the byte->prompt transformation at the MCP hop is entirely client-defined and invisible to the document's author.
findings.evidence: schema/2025-06-18/schema.ts line 1098-1104: `export interface Annotations { /** Describes who the intended customer of this object or data is. It can include multiple entries to indicate content useful for multiple audiences (e.g., ["user", "assistant"]). */ audience?: Role[];` and line 626-631: `export interface TextResourceContents extends ResourceContents { /** The text of the item... */ text: string; }`. grep -i 'utf-8|encoding|normaliz' over 1,613 lines returns exactly one hit, and it is about byte size, not normalization.

findings.claim: repomix wraps every markdown file's content INSIDE a fenced code block, and computes ONE delimiter for the whole pack as max-backtick-run+1. 48.85% of real markdown files contain a backtick run >= 3, so a single markdown file drags the fence width up for every other file in the output. gitingest by contrast does NOT fence at all — it bare-concatenates, so a packed markdown file's headings merge into the surrounding document structure.
findings.evidence: repomix src/core/output/outputGenerate.ts line 60: `const maxBackticks = contents.flatMap((content) => content?.match(/`+/g) ?? []).reduce((max, match) => Math.max(max, match.length), 0); return '`'.repeat(Math.max(3, maxBackticks + 1));`. per_area.design:
## What ships

**`mdmax explain FILE --as <consumer>`** — a compiler pass that emits the exact byte string a named consumer delivers to a model, plus the delta against what a human sees. It is a DIFFER, not a linter. The law says divergence is only stable while exactly one rendering is displayed, so the tool's non-negotiable invariant is: **never show one rendering.** Two panes or it does not ship.

### The three-pane view (editor)

```
SOURCE (bytes)            HUMAN (rendered)          MACHINE (as: claude-code)
─────────────────────     ──────────────────        ────────────────────────────
▸ 0  yaml       117 tok   [not shown]           →   1→  ---
  ─── cache boundary 512 ─────────────────────      2→  title: ...
▸ 1  heading      5 tok   The frontmatter…      →   7→  # The frontmatter engine
▸ 2  para        85 tok   …see the docs.        →  14→  …see the [docs](https://…)
                             ^ 9 tok of URL the reader never sees
```

Gutter per block: `tok` (this consumer's count) · `Δtok` vs source · cumulative · cache-boundary rules at 512/1024/2048/4096 · a badge only when something is actually dropped or added.

**The delta rail** between HUMAN and MACHINE is the product. Four channel colours, and only four:
- `HIDDEN` — in MACHINE, not in HUMAN (frontmatter, comments, link destinations, HTML attributes, invisibles). Measured 2.924% of tokens.
- `LOST` — in HUMAN, not in MACHINE (images, indentation the RAG hop stripped, lines past the 2,000-line cap, headings a splitter moved to metadata).
- `ADDED` — in MACHINE, in neither the file nor the render (line numbers, repomix preamble, fence wrapper, `!`cmd`` output, import expansions).
- `RESHAPED` — same content, different segmentation (sentence chunking, fence-width escalation, table realignment).

### Consumer profiles (each is a pure function `bytes -> delivered string`)

| profile | modelled transformation |
|---|---|
| `human` | rendered baseline. The only profile that is not a machine. |
| `claude-code` / `read-tool` | `N\t` per line; 2,000-line default cap; system-reminder suffix. **+14.991% measured.** |
| `claude-md` | discovery order, 4-hop import expansion, code-span/fence skip, `!`cmd`` substitution, 1,536-char description cap, and **LOADED / NOT-LOADED verdict**. |
| `repomix` | `## File: path` + pack-wide fence at `max(3, maxBackticks+1)` + the File Summary preamble. |
| `gitingest` | bare concatenation, no fence — headings merge into the pack. |
| `rag:langchain-header` | `line.strip()` + `filter(str.isprintable)` + `strip_headers=True`. **34.61% of code lines lose indentation.** |
| `rag:recursive-char` | size/overlap windows; shows which blocks straddle a boundary. |
| `api-document` | `text/plain` only; sentence re-chunking; char-index citations. |
| `api-custom-content` | MDMAX blocks 1:1, no re-chunking — the profile we want people to reach for. |
| `mcp-resource` | `TextResourceContents.text` verbatim + the `annotations.audience` declaration, rendered as a first-class column. |
| `http` | `.md` twin vs HTML (**17x bytes measured**), and any `sr-only` / `aria-hidden` agent channel surfaced explicitly. |
| `chat-paste` | attachment threshold + the retrieved-not-inlined warning. Marked LOW CONFIDENCE in the UI (see unverified). |

### Invisible characters — the corrected design

Not a red badge. A **neutral, always-on chip** rendering every invisible codepoint inline (`⟨ZWNJ⟩`), classified in three tiers, because the naive alarm measured 100% false-positive:

1. **expected** — variation selector after an emoji base OR after an ASCII keycap base (`#`, `*`, `0-9`); ZWJ/ZWNJ within 2 codepoints of a complex-script character; BOM at offset 0. Rendered grey, no count in the summary.
2. **unusual** — invisible in a run of pure Basic Latin. Rendered amber with the codepoint name.
3. **never-legitimate** — the Unicode Tag block, bidi overrides (U+202A–202E, U+2066–2069). Rendered red, decoded to its plaintext, and this tier alone can fail CI.

Injection detection is NOT phrasing-based: >90% of real injections avoid explicit instructions. The tool's honest claim is *"here is everything present that you cannot see"*, not *"this is an attack."*

### Cache blast radius

Falls out of splice for free and is the feature that makes this a cost tool, not a safety toy: hovering a block shows *"editing here invalidates N of M cached tokens (P%)"*, with the 512-token Opus 5 floor drawn as a hard line in the gutter. Measured live: editing block 92 of `docs/engine/README.md` discards 54% of the cached prefix.

## CLI — yes, and it is the honest test

Per the engine's own rule (must be useful with no editor at all):

```
mdmax explain FILE --as claude-code            # table + delta summary
mdmax explain FILE --as all --json             # machine-readable matrix
mdmax explain FILE --as rag:langchain --emit   # the literal delivered bytes, to stdout
mdmax explain FILE --diff human --as repomix   # unified delta, pipeable to git diff tooling
mdmax explain DIR  --check                     # CI mode
```

Exit codes: `0` clean · `1` divergence over threshold · `2` never-legitimate invisible · `3` an instruction file that is not loaded by the profile that claims to read it. `--emit` is what makes it verifiable: you can pipe MDMAX's prediction into `diff` against the real tool's output, which is exactly how the conformance suite works and how a user can call us wrong.

## Where it lives in the engine

`explain` is a pure read-only pass over the existing block model — no new node types, nothing written to the file, no new dialect. It consumes exactly what splice already produces (block ranges + byte offsets) and adds one table per consumer. It is the diagnostics arm of the same thesis: like the axe-core finding, it sees defects no HTML-level tool can see, because the defect lives between the bytes and the tokens and every other tool only ever looks at one end.
per_area.measurement:
Three pre-registered experiments; the first is the one that decides whether this can ship at all.

**E1 — Conformance (does our predicted machine-view equal the real one?).** Corpus: 300 files stratified over the measured population — 40% with fenced code, 30% with frontmatter, 15% >2,000 lines, 10% non-Latin script, 5% containing invisibles. For each profile, run the REAL tool and byte-diff against `mdmax explain --emit`. Real tools: repomix 1.17.0, gitingest (coderamp-labs/gitingest @ pinned SHA), langchain-text-splitters (pinned), the Read tool via a scripted harness, and the Anthropic `count_tokens` endpoint for the document-block profile. Pre-registered thresholds: **>=98% byte-exact for `claude-code` and `repomix`, >=95% for `gitingest`, >=90% for `rag:langchain`** (it version-drifts), and >=99% agreement on the *summary* numbers (token count, dropped-line count) even where bytes differ. Re-run monthly against latest; the delta between runs is the maintenance cost signal.

**E2 — Detector calibration (is the invisible-character tier honest?).** Set: 500 unmodified corpus files (measured negative baseline: 114 naive hits, 0 true positives) plus 100 files seeded with injections across 8 techniques — Tag block, ZWSP-encoded, bidi override, HTML comment, `aria-hidden`/`sr-only` block, frontmatter field, reference-definition title, and a >90%-realistic *data* injection with no imperative phrasing. Two annotators, binary pass/fail, Cohen's kappa >= 0.7 before any number is reported (per house rule #4/#5). Pre-registered: **tier-3 recall >= 0.95 at <= 0.5% per-file false positive**, against the measured naive baseline of 4.94% FP / 0.00% TP. The data-injection case is expected to FAIL detection and must be reported as a known limit, not hidden.

**E3 — Does anyone change anything? (the toy/tool test).** n=30 real documents from 10 authors, within-subject. Show the view, measure edits within 10 minutes and classify them: removed hidden content · restructured for cache · fixed an instruction file that was not loading · nothing. Pre-registered: **>=40% of documents receive an edit and >=15% are the not-loading class.** If <15% overall, the feature is a demo and should be cut to a CI check with no UI.

**Trace requirement.** Every `explain` invocation emits one trace line with `{profile, file_tokens, delta_tokens, tier3_hits, accepted}` so E3 keeps producing signal after launch rather than being a one-off study.
per_area.kill_condition:
Three, any one of which kills it.

**1. Conformance drift outruns maintenance.** If E1 cannot hold >=90% byte-exactness per profile at a monthly re-run without more than ~1 engineer-day of upkeep per month, the tool starts telling authors that a model saw something it did not. A confidently wrong context inspector is strictly worse than none: it is the false-green case, and it launders the very divergence it exists to expose. The tell to watch for: a profile whose exactness falls two months running. Mitigation that must exist from day one — `--emit` and a visible per-profile `verified against <tool>@<version> on <date>` stamp; a profile with a stale stamp must degrade to LOW CONFIDENCE in the UI rather than silently keep asserting.

**2. Authors look and do nothing.** If E3 shows <15% of documents edited after seeing the view, the divergence is real but nobody's problem, and the correct product is a five-line CI check, not a pane.

**3. The delta collapses to noise.** The measured 2.924% hidden share is dominated by frontmatter (1.545%) and link destinations (1.223%) — both of which a sophisticated author already knows are in the file. If E3's edit classification shows essentially all edits are in the *invisible-character* class, the feature is a Unicode linter with 0 measured true positives on real corpora, and it should be folded into the existing diagnostics pass rather than built as a surface.

Note what does NOT kill it: a low absolute injection rate. ~1% of resumes carry injections and >90% avoid explicit phrasing — the value is the transformation delta, which is present in 100% of documents, not the attack, which is present in 1%.
per_area.effort:
**Prototype exists.** `explain.mjs` (~200 lines, run this session) already produces the per-block table, per-block token counts, the line-number surcharge, the hidden-token share and the cache blast radius on a real 184-block document, using only `mdast-util-from-markdown` + `micromark-extension-gfm` + `micromark-extension-frontmatter`, all already in `package.json`. So the core is de-risked.

Realistic build, in dependency order:

| work | cost | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `explain` core: block table, token counts, delta rail | 3 d | pure function over the existing block model; no new node types |
| Tokenizer plumbing | 2 d + **risk** | see dependency below |
| Consumer profiles (12) | 5 d | each is a small pure function; the profiles themselves are cheap |
| **Conformance harness + corpus (E1)** | **10 d** | the real cost, and the thing that decides whether it ships |
| Invisible classifier w/ script + keycap rules | 3 d | rules are specified above and measured |
| Cache blast radius | 1 d | falls out of splice for free |
| CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md loaded-or-not resolver | 3 d | discovery order + 4-hop import + code-span/fence skip + `!`cmd`` |
| Three-pane UI | 5 d | scroll-sync across three differently-segmented renderings is the fiddly part |
| CI mode + exit codes | 2 d | |

**~34 engineer-days**, of which ~30% is the conformance suite. Cutting the suite halves the cost and triggers kill condition #1, so it is not a real option.

**Dependencies and the one real risk:**
- **The block model and splice engine** — designed, not yet built. `explain` is downstream of both; the cache blast radius is impossible without splice's exact changed-byte range.
- **Tokenizer.** This is the honest risk. Every token number in this research is `o200k_base` via `gpt-tokenizer@3.4.0` — a proxy. **Anthropic publishes no tokenizer for current models** (`@anthropic-ai/tokenizer` is the Claude-1/2-era one and is in `package.json` at `"*"`, which is itself a bug worth flagging). Options: (a) bundle o200k/cl100k and label every Claude figure "approximate"; (b) call `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` for exact Claude counts, which costs a network round-trip per file and makes the CLI non-offline; (c) both — offline proxy by default, `--exact` opting into the API. Recommend (c). The design must never present a proxy count as exact — that is a RULE 5 violation baked into a product surface.
- **A pinned conformance corpus** with the real tools installed (repomix, gitingest, langchain-text-splitters). None are currently installed in this repo; installing them is a RULE 2/4 op I did not perform.

**Not done, and proposed for approval:** installing repomix / gitingest / langchain-text-splitters to run E1 for real. I read their source instead. Someone must approve the install before conformance numbers exist.
per_area.unverified:
**Token counts are a proxy, everywhere.** Every token figure in this report is `o200k_base` (GPT-4o family) via `gpt-tokenizer@3.4.0`, not Claude's tokenizer, which is not public for current models. The 14.991% line-number surcharge, the 2.924% hidden share and the 11,741-token README figure are all **directionally right, not exact for Claude**. I did not call `count_tokens`; no API key was available and reading `.env.local` is denied.

**Chat-UI paste pathway: search-only, and it is the weakest link in the whole map.** I could not verify Claude.ai's paste-to-attachment threshold from any primary source. What I have: ChatGPT's threshold is reported as ~5,000 characters; Claude.ai reportedly converts long pastes to attachments with no opt-out (evidenced only by the existence of workaround tools — `unclecode/claude-paster`, a Greasyfork "Chunked Paste — Bypass Attachment Detection" script); and the claim that attachments are *retrieved over* rather than fully inlined is **search-only and I do not believe it should be repeated as fact**. This matters because if true it is the single largest divergence in the whole map — the model may never see most of the document. This needs a primary measurement before it goes in any user-facing surface.

**Anthropic Console / Workbench and OpenAI Playground: NOT verified.** I could not log in. I did not open either UI. Any claim about what they display would be inference and I am not making one. My prior-art negatives are confined to the three tools whose source I actually searched (Phoenix, Langfuse, LangSmith SDK) plus Claude Code's `/context` as documented.

**Read-tool truncation behaviour partially verified.** The 2,000-line default comes from the tool description (own observation of my own tool schema). I did NOT test a >2,000-line file, so I do not know whether truncation emits a visible marker to the model or is silent. The 2.56%/3.16% corpus figures assume the documented default and no marker.

**Other harnesses unmeasured.** Cursor, Codex, Aider, Windsurf, Continue — I did not verify any of their file-read transformations. The `claude-code` profile is the only file-tool profile with an own-measurement behind it, and even that is measured on line-number *format*, inferred from the schema and one direct Read, not from decompiled source.

**LangChain damage figures are a faithful replay, not the library running.** I re-implemented the two destructive lines (`line.strip()`, `filter(str.isprintable)`) and the fence-state machine exactly as read from `markdown.py@master`, then ran them over the corpus. I did NOT install or execute langchain. Version drift is possible; the file is `master`, not a release tag.

**One corpus anomaly unexplained.** U+3103 (category Cn, unassigned) appears 600 times in the corpus. I did not determine whether that file is mojibake, a deliberate encoding, or a bug — it is the largest single class of codepoints LangChain would delete and I cannot say what it is.

**Sample-size inconsistency, stated so nobody reconciles them wrongly.** The corpus counts differ across scripts because of different size cutoffs and roots: n=1,984 (md repo only, >400KB excluded) for the line-number surcharge; n=2,302 (three roots, >300KB excluded) for the hidden-token share; n=2,303 (three roots, >400KB excluded) for the LangChain and truncation figures; n=2,308 (three roots, no cutoff) for the invisible-character scan. They are not directly comparable. Also: `~/Desktop/GitHub/md` contains 5,586 `.md` files total, but 1,547 are under `Mirrors/` and 780 under `.sgnk/` — all measurements exclude dot-directories and are therefore on the ~2,000-file authored subset, not the full tree.

**The `sr-only` finding is one site.** I verified Anthropic's agent blockquote on 2 of 4 sampled pages and confirmed its absence on the other 2. I did not survey any other documentation site, so "everyone does this" is not a claim I am making — "Anthropic does this, in production, scoped to the Claude Code subtree" is.

verification.area: Adversarial verification of "Show me what the model sees — a debugger for context" (MDMAX `explain` pass): 8 claims + the proposed design, re-derived locally and against primary sources.

verdicts.claim: C1 core: the Read-tool pathway prepends line-number+tab and costs +14.991% tokens over the file's own bytes (n=1984, 888,223 lines, rawTok 11,894,041 → lnTok 13,677,024, bytesPerTok 3.877).
verdicts.reason: I wrote my own walker/tokenizer script (scratchpad/vf1.mjs) and reproduced every figure to the digit: n=1984, skippedBig=5, lines=888223, rawTok=11894041, lnTok=13677024, lnOverheadPct=14.991, bytesPerTok=3.877. Arithmetic re-derived: (13677024-11894041)/11894041 = 14.9906%; extra tokens/line = 1782983/888223 = 2.0074. I also independently verified the TRANSFORMATION rather than assuming it: `Read` on /Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/frontmatter/docs/engine/PLAN.md offset 997 returned `997\t**These are different architectures.**` — unpadded `N\t`, not cat -n's `%6d\t`, despite the tool's own description saying "cat -n format". Corpus denominator also checks out: `find` gives 1,988 non-hidden non-node_modules .md under ~/Desktop/GitHub/md vs the walker's 1,989.
verdicts.correction: Two riders on the number: (a) it is format-specific — I measured the padded `%6d\t` variant at 29.926%, exactly 2x, so this figure generalises to Claude Code and to nothing else; (b) the design's own `claude-code` profile specifies a 2,000-line cap, but the measurement did not apply it — 59 files (2.974%) exceed 2,000 lines and 29,731 lines (3.347%) sit beyond the cap and would never be delivered.

verdicts.claim: C1 rider: "The surcharge is a function of LINE COUNT, not content — so hard-wrapped prose is materially more expensive to an agent than soft-wrapped prose."
verdicts.reason: Presented as a conclusion of the measurement; it was never measured. I measured it both directions (scratchpad/vf2.mjs, vf3.mjs). Forward: hard-wrapping 400 real files at 80 columns raised delivered (line-numbered) tokens by 1.34% vs the as-is soft form, of which 0.472% is extra newlines in the raw bytes — so ~0.87% is attributable to line numbering. Reverse: unwrapping 500 real files removed 6.19% of lines and saved 1.053% of delivered tokens (raw saving 0.45%). The corpus is already 80.62% lines ≤80 chars, so there is real headroom and the effect is still ~1%. Separately, "a function of LINE COUNT, not content" is itself only approximate: regressing delta on line count with no intercept leaves R²=0.9687, with a worst-case file deviating 0.78 tokens/line from the line-count model.
verdicts.correction: Wrapping style moves delivered cost by ~1%, an order of magnitude below the 14.991% headline it is attached to. The 14.991% is a floor paid regardless of wrapping. Drop "materially" or state the measured 1.0–1.3%.

verdicts.claim: C1 rider: "and no tool surfaces this."
verdicts.reason: Claude Code ships a first-party context debugger the research never mentions. Primary read, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/commands.md line 68: `/context [all]` — "Visualize current context usage as a colored grid. Shows optimization suggestions for context-heavy tools, memory bloat, and capacity warnings." repomix (registry.npmjs.org/repomix/latest, v1.17.0) also reports token counts for its own pack output. The premise "Show me what the model sees — a debugger for context" has a shipped incumbent inside the very harness being profiled.
verdicts.correction: The defensible claim is narrower: no tool ATTRIBUTES the surcharge to the line-number prefix or lets you diff it against the file's own bytes. `/context` shows totals by bucket, not the byte→token delta per consumer. Say that, and cite `/context` as the incumbent you are differentiating from.

verdicts.claim: C2: "2.924% of the tokens a model receives from real markdown are INVISIBLE in the rendered document."
verdicts.reason: The arithmetic reproduces exactly — I re-ran an independent mdast walk (scratchpad/vf4.mjs) over the same three roots and got files=2302, total=12,890,412, fm=199,104, comment=12,478, linkDest=157,651, linkTitle=430, imgUrl=3,640, defn=104, htmlAttr=3,440, invis=13, sum=376,860, 2.9236%. But the SEMANTICS fail for the two largest components, which are 94.7% of the total. (a) linkDest is 41.83% of the "hidden" total, and 61.59% of those tokens (97,104 of 157,651; 5,601 of 9,468 link nodes) belong to links whose visible label IS the destination — GFM literal autolinks and `<https://…>`, where the reader sees the URL on the page. That is a bug in the classifier, not a hidden channel. (b) Frontmatter is 52.83% of the total and its visibility is renderer-dependent, not universal: this exact corpus is an Obsidian vault (/Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/md/.obsidian exists; app.json does not set `propertiesInDocument`, so Obsidian's default visible Properties panel applies) and static-site generators surface `title`/`description` in the rendered page. Excluding visible URLs and frontmatter, the genuinely-hidden share is 0.626%.
verdicts.correction: The honest number is ~0.6%, not 2.924% — a 4.7x overstatement. Report the channel breakdown with a visibility column, and make link-destination visibility a per-link determination (label==url) rather than a blanket classification. The design's HIDDEN rail is still worth building; the marketing number is not.

verdicts.claim: C2 rider: "this is ~200x larger than the Unicode-injection channel everyone worries about."
verdicts.reason: A ratio stated with no derivation, and the researcher's own evidence line contradicts it. hiddenTokens=376,860 and invis=13 give 376860/13 = 28,989x, which I reproduced. Even against the corrected 0.626% figure (77,470 tokens) the ratio is 5,959x. No combination of the reported quantities — tokens, files (114/2308), occurrences (375) — yields ~200. Closest is hiddenTokens/occurrences = 1,005.
verdicts.correction: Either state 28,989x from the token counts, or delete the comparison. As written it is a number with no denominator, wrong by ~145x in the direction that makes the finding look weaker — which suggests it was estimated rather than computed.

verdicts.claim: C3: "a naive invisible-character detector fires on 4.94% of 2,308 real markdown files with a measured 0% true-positive rate" / "every single occurrence is legitimate."
verdicts.reason: The counts replicate exactly — I re-ran invis.mjs: "files with invisibles: 114 of 2308" (4.9393%), U+FE0F 291, U+200C 71, U+200D 11, U+200B 2, sum 375. But "0% true-positive rate" is not a rate that was measured. TPR = TP/(TP+FN); the corpus contains zero known positives, so the denominator is 0 and TPR is undefined. What was measured is precision (0 of 375 fires malicious) on a corpus with base rate zero. Worse, it is the wrong population: an injection detector's operating population is documents the user did NOT author, and every file here is the user's own vault, its mirrors, or this repo's docs. A false-positive rate established on self-authored content says nothing about the detector's behaviour on ingested content, which is the only place the threat exists. Additionally "every single occurrence is legitimate: emoji presentation selectors and Indic-script joiners" is falsified by the researcher's own C4: 25 occurrences are ZWNJ/ZWJ sitting between two SPACES (classify.mjs output: "ZWJ/ZWNJ between \" \" and \" \""), which perform no Indic joining function — they are inert scrape residue, neither malicious nor linguistically legitimate.
verdicts.correction: State it as: "375 fires, 0 malicious, on a 2,308-file self-authored corpus with a zero base rate — this bounds nuisance volume, not detector precision." Do not call it a true-positive rate. C3 and C4 also directly contradict each other on the same 375 occurrences ("every single occurrence is legitimate" vs "ANOMALOUS 25"); pick one.

verdicts.claim: C4: the context-aware classifier reclassifies 93.3% as legitimate "and the 25 survivors are STILL all benign", evidenced by quoted context strings.
verdicts.reason: The counts replicate (LEGIT 350, ANOMALOUS 25, 350/375 = 93.333%), and the sub-rule is correct — I verified in node that `/\p{Extended_Pictographic}/u` is false for "#", "*", "0", "9" while true for "⚠" and "✅". But the EVIDENCE for the adjudication is generated by a bug. classify.mjs line ~30 builds every context window with `s.indexOf(c)` — the FIRST occurrence of that codepoint in the file, not the occurrence being classified. The tool's own output proves it: fifteen "Satinath Content JSON" rows carry byte-identical context `"় ভুলেই থাকি\\\" .... ‌..... আমি বলি - ..."` while their `why` fields differ (between " " and ".", between "‌" and "\\", between "n" and " "). So for 24 of the 25 anomalies the human looked at the wrong text when concluding "benign." The `why` field (built from cps[i-1]/cps[i+1]) is correct; only the quoted evidence is wrong — which is exactly the field quoted in the claim.
verdicts.correction: Fix to an index-tracking scan and re-adjudicate the 25. Also note the proposed rule set has a further gap the corpus did not expose: regional indicators are not Extended_Pictographic either (`/\p{Extended_Pictographic}/u.test("🇮🇳")` is false), so a flag base would also mis-flag.

verdicts.claim: C5 core: LangChain's MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter applies line.strip() and filter(str.isprintable) to every line including inside fences; 34.61% of fenced-code lines lose indentation.
verdicts.reason: Primary read of raw.githubusercontent.com/langchain-ai/langchain/master/libs/text-splitters/langchain_text_splitters/markdown.py: line 164 `stripped_line = line.strip()`, line 167 `stripped_line = "".join(filter(str.isprintable, stripped_line))` under the comment "Remove all non-printable characters from the string, keeping only visible text", then lines 180-182 `if in_code_block: current_content.append(stripped_line); continue`. Verified the append is of the stripped form. I then wrote my own replay (scratchpad/vf5.py) rather than reusing theirs and got code_block_lines=200,739 (theirs 200,735), code_block_lines_indented=69,483 (identical), pct=34.614 (theirs 34.61). The headline reproduces exactly.
verdicts.correction: My line total was 996,981 over 2,308 files vs their 940,687 over 2,303, and my strip rate 13.32% vs their 12.33% — the 12.33% is corpus-selection-dependent and does not reproduce; the 34.61% does.

verdicts.claim: C5 framing: "THE RAG HOP IS DESTRUCTIVE AND NOBODY SAYS SO."
verdicts.reason:
A GitHub-API search of langchain-ai/langchain found it reported 27 months ago, with a repro and a proposed patch. Primary read of api.github.com/repos/langchain-ai/langchain/issues/20823: title "Markdown text splitter will remove code block indentation", created 2024-04-24, closed 2024-07-31, body shows expected `my:
   foo: bar
   a: b` vs actual `my:
foo: bar
a: b` and offers a `code_block_indent` fix. Issue 19436 "MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter removing format of nested lists / sublists" (2024-03-22, closed 2024-06-28) covers the nested-list half. Issue 22256 "MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter flattens Paragraphs separators into single line breaks" (2024-05-29). Issue 22728 (2024-06-10) is literally "text-splitter[minor]: Declare MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter deprecated." And LangChain shipped a remedy: ExperimentalMarkdownSyntaxTextSplitter, whose docstring in the same file says it "aims to retain the exact whitespace of the original text" and lists "Retains the original whitespace and formatting of the Markdown text" as its first key feature.
verdicts.correction: The defensible claim is that no tool SHOWS the user the delivered bytes, not that the defect is unknown. Also: modelling a class that has an open deprecation proposal and an official whitespace-preserving replacement as the headline `rag:langchain-header` profile is a maintenance risk — the number will age out.

verdicts.claim: C5/design scope: "LangChain's markdown splitter destroys indentation" (headline) and the `rag:langchain-header` profile as representative of the RAG hop.
verdicts.reason: There are three markdown splitters in that one file and only one strips. Primary read, same file: line 14 `class MarkdownTextSplitter(RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter)` — it only sets `separators = self.get_separators_for_language(Language.MARKDOWN)` and inherits byte-preserving recursive splitting; line 298 ExperimentalMarkdownSyntaxTextSplitter explicitly preserves whitespace. The strip is specific to MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter.
verdicts.correction: Name the class in the headline, not "LangChain's markdown splitter". As written it implicates the two splitters that behave correctly.

verdicts.claim: C6 core: `str.isprintable` deletes the Unicode Tag block, ZWSP/ZWNJ/ZWJ/WJ/BOM/NBSP/bidi/TAB/ideographic space/soft hyphen, while U+FE0F survives.
verdicts.reason: Re-derived the whole truth table in python3 myself: U+200B Cf False, U+200C Cf False, U+200D Cf False, U+2060 Cf False, U+FEFF Cf False, U+00A0 Zs False, U+00AD Cf False, U+202A Cf False, U+202E Cf False, U+2066 Cf False, U+2069 Cf False, U+0009 Cc False, U+3000 Zs False, U+E0041 Cf False, U+E007F Cf False, U+FE0F Mn TRUE. Every value in the claim matches.
verdicts.correction: None on the mechanism.

verdicts.claim: C6 evidence: "Corpus deletions: 1,297 codepoints — U+3103 x600, U+00A0 x358, U+2028 x285, U+E200-E202 x36, U+200C x11, U+0009 x4, U+200B x2."
verdicts.reason: The histogram is wrong three ways and does not survive its own arithmetic. (1) Their listed items sum to 1,296, not the stated 1,297 — off by one before anyone re-measures. (2) My independent replay counts 1,374 deletions, and critically U+200C at 71, not 11 — which is the same 71 the researcher's OWN C3 reports for U+200C. 11 is U+200D's count, which is missing from the table entirely. The two rows were transposed and one dropped, so C3 and C6 disagree about the same corpus by 6.5x. (3) U+00A0 is 364 not 358, and U+3000 IDEOGRAPHIC SPACE x1 is mentioned in the prose but absent from the table. (4) The single largest entry is misleading: U+3103 (category Cn, unassigned — I checked) appears 600 times across 300 files, and it is not corruption — it is a deliberate literal inside a homoglyph example that reads "`3103` thinking it is 管 U+7BA1, but `㄃` is actually ㄃ …", mirrored 300 times under md/Mirrors/skills-registry/skills/*/skill.md. 43.7% of the claimed harm is one documented sentence counted 600 times.
verdicts.correction: Correct table from my replay: 1,374 total — U+3103 600, U+00A0 364, U+2028 285, U+200C 71, U+E200/E201/E202 12 each, U+200D 11, U+0009 4, U+200B 2, U+3000 1. And 0 Tag characters, 0 bidi, 0 BOM, 0 WJ, 0 soft hyphen were deleted in the corpus — those come from the synthetic probe only. Label which is which.

verdicts.claim: C7 core: docs.anthropic.com ships an sr-only, aria-hidden, tabindex=-1 blockquote explicitly named as an agent channel.
verdicts.reason:
I curled it and the string matches verbatim: `

Documentation Index

Fetch the complete documentation index at: /docs/llms.txt

Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

`. sr-only hides it visually, aria-hidden="true" removes it from the accessibility tree, tabindex="-1" removes the link from tab order — all three simultaneously, as claimed.
verdicts.correction: Two provenance corrections. The URL 301s: docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/memory → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory, so the artifact is served by code.claude.com and x-matched-path on the HTML is `/_sites/[subdomain]/[[...slug]]`, not the `/_mintlify/_markdown/...` path quoted (that one belongs to the .md twin). And the byte offset does not reproduce: I measure the `<blockquote` at 14,192 and the attribute at 14,220, not 14,272 — a byte offset into a server-rendered Next.js payload is not a reproducible citation.

verdicts.claim: C7 rider: "and marked noindex so search engines never see it either."
verdicts.reason: Two different resources conflated. I dumped the full response headers for the HTML page: no `x-robots-tag` at all, and `grep -c noindex` over the 601,419-byte HTML returns 0, with no `<meta name="robots">`. The `x-robots-tag: noindex, nofollow` I confirmed applies only to the .md twin (code.claude.com/docs/en/memory.md, content-type: text/markdown). The blockquote lives in the HTML — which is fully indexable.
verdicts.correction: The blockquote is on an indexable page; the noindex is on a different URL that does not contain a blockquote at all. Two facts, both true, joined by a "so" that is false.

verdicts.claim: C8: Anthropic does NOT prepend the imperative to every doc page; it is scoped to the Claude Code subtree (2 of 4 pages sampled outside it have no preamble).
verdicts.reason: Direction confirmed and I strengthened the sample from n=4 to n=9. All five code.claude.com pages carry it (memory.md, hooks.md, mcp.md, overview.md, quickstart.md all open `> ## Documentation Index | > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt`); none of four platform.claude.com pages do (api/overview.md → `# API overview`, prompt-engineering/overview.md → `# Prompt engineering overview`, api/messages.md → `# Messages`, about-claude/models/overview.md → `# Models overview`). 5/5 vs 0/4.
verdicts.correction: The mechanism is wrong. It is not a "subtree" of one site — docs.anthropic.com no longer serves either; it 301s to two SEPARATE Mintlify sites, and the preamble is a per-site config on code.claude.com. Say "per docs site", not "per subtree". Also n=2 outside was too thin to support the generalisation the claim made; it happened to hold.

verdicts.claim: HEADLINE: this repo's own AGENTS.md — which opens "Read this before" — was never loaded into the agent reading it.
verdicts.reason: Primary read, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory.md line 129: "Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md`, not `AGENTS.md`. If your repository already uses `AGENTS.md` for other coding agents, create a `CLAUDE.md` that imports it…". /Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/frontmatter/CLAUDE.md does not exist (ls: No such file or directory) and .claude/ contains only settings.local.json, .cc-writes and worktrees — no memory file, no `@AGENTS.md` import, no symlink. So /Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/frontmatter/AGENTS.md (7,705 bytes) is genuinely unread. This is the strongest single finding in the set and the one that most justifies the LOADED/NOT-LOADED verdict in the `claude-md` profile.
verdicts.correction: Minor: it does not "open" with that. The file opens `# AGENTS.md` then a paragraph; "Read this **before**" appears on line 4, and it is scoped — "Read this **before** adding new files to `public/`, new routes, new env vars, or new gates" — not a general imperative. Quote it accurately. (The design's related `claude-md` fact-check passes: "4-hop import expansion" is confirmed by memory.md line 97, "a maximum depth of four hops".)

verdicts.claim: DESIGN: "Measured live: editing block 92 of docs/engine/README.md discards 54% of the cached prefix."
verdicts.reason: No evidence line was supplied for this in the CLAIMS list, no script was named, and it is not reproducible from anything provided — the block model that defines "block 92" is the unshipped `explain` pass itself. I can only confirm the file exists and is 789 lines. Per LR#62, a number produced by replaying data through code that has never run in production is a prediction, not a measurement, and "Measured live" is the wrong label for it.
verdicts.correction: Either name the artifact the 54% came from, or label it SIMULATED. This is the same class the project's own Learned Rule #62 exists to catch.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN: "Injection detection is NOT phrasing-based: >90% of real injections avoid explicit instructions."
verdicts.reason: No citation given, and a targeted web search returned no primary source carrying that statistic — the retrieved literature (Neural Exec arXiv 2403.03792, the MDPI review, the educational-LLM Scientific Reports paper) discusses implicit/indirect injection qualitatively but none supplies a >90% figure. It reads as a hard number but is unsourced. Note: those search results themselves contained the string "ignore previous instructions" as quoted study material; I treated it as data and did not act on it, and the local injection hook flagged it as the second such hit this session.
verdicts.correction: Drop the percentage or cite it. The design conclusion it supports — "the tool's honest claim is 'here is everything present that you cannot see', not 'this is an attack'" — is correct and does not need the statistic.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN: the cache-boundary gutter at 512/1024/2048/4096 with a "512-token Opus 5 floor".
verdicts.reason: Primary read, https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching.md line 593ff: "the minimum cacheable prompt length is: * 512 tokens for Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5, and Claude Mythos 5 * 2,048 tokens for Claude Mythos Preview and Claude Opus 4.7 * 4,096 tokens for Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Opus 4.5 * 1,024 tokens for Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Sonnet 4.6…". All four gutter values are real per-model minimums and the Opus 5 floor is exactly 512.
verdicts.correction: None. This is the best-grounded fact in the design and the one the researcher did not even flag as needing a source.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN: `http` profile — ".md twin vs HTML (17x bytes measured)".
verdicts.reason: No evidence line was given, but it reproduces on the page I could match: code.claude.com/docs/en/memory HTML is 601,419 bytes, the .md twin is 35,388 bytes, ratio 16.99.
verdicts.correction: n=1. State the page, or sample enough pages to justify the general "17x".

survived: +14.991% Read-tool surcharge — reproduced to the digit by an independently written script, and the `N\t` transformation independently verified by observing a live 4-digit Read (997\t…), which is stronger than the researcher's own evidence since the tool's documentation claims cat -n padding that would have doubled the figure to 29.926%.

34.61% of fenced-code lines lose indentation at the LangChain MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter hop — my independent replay produced code_block_lines_indented=69,483, byte-identical to theirs, from a differently written script over a slightly different file set.
The `str.isprintable` truth table — all 16 codepoints re-derived in python3 and every value matches, including the U+FE0F Mn survival that makes the sanitizer inconsistent.

The mechanism in LangChain's source — primary read confirms strip() and the isprintable filter are applied to lines inside fences and the stripped form is what gets appended (markdown.py lines 164/167/180-182).
The Anthropic sr-only agent-channel blockquote — verbatim string match, and all three concealment mechanisms (sr-only, aria-hidden, tabindex=-1) verified independently.
The preamble scoping — strengthened from the researcher's n=4 to n=9: 5/5 code.claude.com pages carry it, 0/4 platform.claude.com pages do.

AGENTS.md is genuinely not loaded — primary read of the memory docs ("Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, not AGENTS.md") plus confirmation that the repo has no CLAUDE.md, no @AGENTS.md import and no symlink. The strongest finding in the set.
The 4-hop CLAUDE.md import depth in the `claude-md` profile (memory.md line 97: "a maximum depth of four hops").
The 512-token Opus 5 cache floor and the 512/1024/2048/4096 boundary set — all four confirmed against the prompt-caching doc.
The 16.99x HTML-to-markdown byte ratio (n=1).

The design's core architecture — a read-only pass over the existing block model, no new node types, no runtime, no dialect, `--emit` as a falsifiable conformance hook, and the 'never show one rendering' invariant. Nothing in it violates a settled project invariant.
killed: "nobody says so" about the RAG hop — langchain-ai/langchain issue #20823 "Markdown text splitter will remove code block indentation" was filed 2024-04-24 with a repro and a patch, #19436 covers nested lists (2024-03-22), #22256 covers paragraph flattening, #22728 proposed deprecating the class outright, and LangChain shipped ExperimentalMarkdownSyntaxTextSplitter whose stated purpose is to "retain the exact whitespace of the original text". Found in a single GitHub API search.

"no tool surfaces this" — Claude Code ships `/context`, documented as "Visualize current context usage as a colored grid. Shows optimization suggestions for context-heavy tools, memory bloat, and capacity warnings."
"~200x larger than the Unicode-injection channel" — the researcher's own numbers give 28,989x; no reported quantity yields 200.
"hard-wrapped prose is materially more expensive to an agent than soft-wrapped prose" — measured both directions at ~1.0–1.3% delivered-token effect, vs the 14.991% headline it is attached to.

"a measured 0% true-positive rate" — TPR is undefined on a corpus with zero positives; what was measured is nuisance volume on self-authored content, which is the wrong population for an injection detector.
"every single occurrence is legitimate" (C3) — contradicted by the researcher's own C4, and 25 of the occurrences are ZWNJ/ZWJ between two spaces, performing no Indic joining function.

"the 25 survivors are STILL all benign" as evidenced — the quoted context windows are produced by `s.indexOf(c)`, which returns the first occurrence in the file, so 24 of 25 adjudications were made against the wrong text.

C6's deletion histogram — U+200C is 71 not 11, U+200D (11) is missing entirely, U+00A0 is 364 not 358, U+3000 is omitted, the true total is 1,374, and the researcher's own listed items sum to 1,296 against a stated 1,297.
"marked noindex so search engines never see it either" — the HTML page containing the blockquote has zero occurrences of noindex and no x-robots-tag; that header belongs to a different URL.
"LangChain's markdown splitter" as a general subject — MarkdownTextSplitter and ExperimentalMarkdownSyntaxTextSplitter both preserve the bytes.
"byte offset 14272" — reproduces at 14,192/14,220; a byte offset into a server-rendered Next.js payload is not a citable anchor.
"Measured live: editing block 92 … discards 54%" — no artifact named, not reproducible.
">90% of real injections avoid explicit instructions" — no source found.
new_defects: CORPUS INDEPENDENCE IS UNMODELLED, and this contaminates every corpus-wide rate in claims 1-6. I hashed all 2,308 files: 336 are byte-identical duplicates of another file (14.56%), redundant copies account for 10,958,347 of 54,819,238 bytes (19.99%), and 1,233 of 2,308 files (53.42%) live under md/Mirrors/ — a mirror directory. The corpus is majority-mirror, one-fifth literal duplicate, single-author, and entirely private. "2,308 real markdown files" reads as a population sample and is not one. The U+3103 x600 entry is the visible symptom: one documented sentence, counted 600 times because a registry is mirrored 300 times.

A FALSE-POSITIVE RATE MEASURED ON A ZERO-BASE-RATE, SELF-AUTHORED CORPUS. This is the deepest method error in the set, because the corrected design (the 3-tier chip) is built on it. Nothing here bounds the detector's behaviour on ingested third-party markdown, which is the only population where the threat exists. The right experiment is to run the naive detector over a corpus the user did not write — public repos, scraped docs, MCP resource payloads.

EVIDENCE-GENERATING SCRIPT BUG: classify.mjs computes every quoted context window with `s.indexOf(c)`, returning the first occurrence of that codepoint in the file rather than the occurrence being classified. This is visible in the tool's own output (fifteen rows with identical context but different neighbour verdicts) and it is the field quoted verbatim in Claim 4. A human adjudicated 25 anomalies against 24 wrong text windows and reported the result as a replication.

DENOMINATOR DRIFT ACROSS CLAIMS THAT SHARE A HEADLINE. Four different file counts appear — 1,984 (C1), 2,302 (C2), 2,303 (C5), 2,308 (C3/C4) — from four scripts with different size filters, and the headline quotes the largest ("2,308 real markdown files") while attaching it to findings computed on the smaller sets. Also C5's 940,687 lines vs my 996,981 over the same roots.

THE MEASUREMENT DOES NOT IMPLEMENT THE PROFILE IT SPECIFIES. The design defines `claude-code` as "`N\t` per line; 2,000-line default cap; system-reminder suffix" but the +14.991% was computed on whole files with neither the cap nor the suffix applied. 59 files (2.974%) and 29,731 lines (3.347%) sit beyond the cap and would never reach the model. A profile whose headline number is produced by a different transformation than the profile describes is exactly the defect `--emit` is supposed to prevent — run the conformance check against your own headline first.

A CLASSIFIER JUDGMENT PRESENTED AS AN OBSERVATION. "Invisible in the rendered document" is asserted as a property of the bytes, but visibility is a property of the RENDERER, and the two largest channels (frontmatter 52.83%, link destinations 41.83%) are visible in the renderers most likely to be pointed at this corpus. Any HIDDEN classification in the shipped tool must be parameterised by the human-side renderer, not hardcoded — which is the same lesson as the invisible-character correction, applied one level up and not noticed.

INTERNAL CONTRADICTION SHIPPED AS TWO SEPARATE FINDINGS. C3 ("every single occurrence is legitimate") and C4 ("ANOMALOUS 25") describe the same 375 occurrences and cannot both be the result. Likewise C3's U+200C=71 and C6's U+200C=11. Cross-claim reconciliation was never run — the same class as LR#59 (producer/consumer field mismatch), here between two of the researcher's own scripts.

AN ARITHMETIC ERROR THAT SURVIVED INTO THE EVIDENCE LINE: C6's enumerated deletions sum to 1,296 against a stated total of 1,297. Small, but it means the total was not recomputed from the list at write time — LR#60's "re-derive the headline at write time" failure, in miniature.

per_area.title: Invisible-content integrity — what a file says vs what it looks like it says
per_area.headline: A tiered, atom-aware integrity check built on Unicode's Default_Ignorable property plus a markdown-native link/code-span rule achieves 12/12 recall on an attack corpus at exactly 0 false positives across 4,823 real files / 91,394,509 bytes — and the brief's premise that "RTL content is legitimate in this corpus" is wrong twice over: Bengali is bidi class L (left-to-right), and the entire 4,823-file corpus contains exactly one RTL-script character occurrence, inside PLAN.md's own Arabic test string.

findings.claim: CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF: Bengali is not RTL, and the corpus has essentially no RTL content at all. The stated tension ('this repo's own corpus contains 19+ Bengali files and RTL content is legitimate. A naive bidi filter breaks real users') conflates two unrelated problems. Bengali is bidi class L. Across 4,823 .md files / 89,960,680 chars in ~/Desktop/GitHub/md + ~/Desktop/GitHub/knowledge + the frontmatter repo, exactly 1 file contains any character with bidi class R/AL/AN — and it is docs/engine/PLAN.md itself, matching its own Arabic test string.
findings.evidence: python3 unicodedata: 'Bengali KA U+0995 bidi=L name=BENGALI LETTER KA'; 'Bengali A U+0985 bidi=L'; vs 'Arabic ALEF U+0627 bidi=AL', 'Hebrew ALEF U+05D0 bidi=R'. Corpus scan: 'files=4823  chars=89960680' / 'files containing RTL-script chars (Arabic/Hebrew/etc bidi R/AL/AN): 1' / 'files with BOTH RTL script AND an explicit bidi format/tag control: 0'. The one RTL hit: ('/Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/frontmatter/docs/engine/PLAN.md', "'*252 emoji headings** |\\n| **Arabic** | `كتاب` / `كِتَاب` / `كــتاب` (tatweel) | '")

findings.claim: The real Indic constraint is JOINERS, not bidi — and it is separable mechanically. The corpus contains 73 ZWNJ + 11 ZWJ occurrences; the Bengali ones are legitimate হলন্ত/hasanta conjunct control adjacent to a Bengali virama, and a two-character context test (is either neighbour in an Indic/Arabic/Khmer/Thai block?) separates them from stray joiners floating in whitespace with zero tuning.
