verdicts.reason: primary-read + own-measurement. node_modules/micromark-util-normalize-identifier/index.js reproduces verbatim: .replace(/[\t\n\r ]+/g," ").replace(/^ | $/g,'').toLowerCase().toUpperCase(). I ran it end-to-end through the real micromark parser, not just the util: [Café(NFD)] vs [Café(NFC)]: /u → NOT-RESOLVED; বড় U+09DC vs U+09A1 U+09BC → NOT-RESOLVED; ज़ U+095B vs U+091C U+093C → NOT-RESOLVED; Å U+212B and K U+212A → RESOLVED. All three become MATCH under NFC. Blast radius confirmed: api.npmjs.org last-week micromark = 50,373,030, micromark-util-normalize-identifier = 46,171,455 — 8 figures, as claimed. This is the research's one genuinely solid technical contribution.

verdicts.claim: Claim 5's novelty framing — 'NEW AND UNCLAIMED', 'the single highest-leverage unclaimed defect'
verdicts.reason: primary-read. api.github.com search of commonmark/commonmark-spec (the same repo the research already cited for the spec text) returns issue #695 'Clarify link label matching', open since 2021-11-11. Its P.S. verbatim: "A better definition would likely have been `R5` as it would handle correctly identifiers in different normal forms (like é composed in one id and é decomposed in another one) but you'd need to import the Unicode normalization and associated machinery into the definition of CommonMark." Identical defect, identical é-composed-vs-decomposed example, five years old, still open. A single API query against a repo the researcher had already opened refutes the novelty claim.
verdicts.correction: The defect is real and verified, but it is a known, upstream-reported, five-year-old open spec issue (commonmark/commonmark-spec#695), not unclaimed territory. Cite it and add to it.

verdicts.claim: Claim 4 — remark-cjk-friendly is EAW-gated so it 'repairs NOTHING for Thai, Lao, Khmer, Burmese, Javanese, Balinese, which have the identical defect'; this is the specific unclaimed territory
verdicts.reason: own-measurement. The source quote itself is accurate (I downloaded micromark-extension-cjk-friendly-util 3.0.1 from registry.npmjs.org and dist/characterWithNonBmp.js reproduces cjkOrIvs verbatim). But the premise that all six scripts have the defect is false, and the researcher never ran the test. Under micromark 4: Thai นี่**สำคัญ**มาก → EMPH; **กรุงเทพฯ**เมือง → EMPH; **มากๆ**ครับ → EMPH; Lao ນີ້**ສຳຄັນ**ຫຼາຍ → EMPH; **ຫຼາຍໆ**ຄົນ → EMPH. All five natural constructs already work. Reason (python3 unicodedata): ฯ U+0E2F = Lo, ๆ U+0E46 = Lm, ໆ U+0EC6 = Lm — LETTERS, not punctuation, so they never trip the flanking rule. Thai and Lao have no native sentence-terminating punctuation in running prose. Only Khmer ។ U+17D4 (Po) and Burmese ။ U+104B (Po) actually reproduce the failure: **ខ្ញុំ។**បន្ទាប់ → LITERAL, **ကျွန်တော်။**နောက် → LITERAL.
verdicts.correction: 2 of the 6 named scripts (Khmer, Burmese) have the defect; Thai and Lao do not. Javanese/Balinese have Po marks so are plausible but were untested by both of us.

verdicts.claim: Claim 3 — the exact predicate is Unicode Line_Break class (LB=ID ∪ SA); Bengali/Devanagari/Arabic are AL and 'are not exposed'
verdicts.reason: The Unicode measurements reproduce perfectly — I parsed unicode.org/Public/16.0.0/ucd/LineBreak.txt and got ID = 172,421; SA = 757; AL = 26,679, and every probe codepoint matches (中=ID, あ=ID, 한=H3, ก/ກ/ក/က=SA, ཀ/ক/a=AL). But the design conclusion is wrong twice. (a) LB class is not the parser predicate: CommonMark flanking breaks on General_Category P or S on the character INSIDE the delimiter, which is script-agnostic — which is why Thai (SA) passes and Bengali (AL) fails. (b) 'Bengali/Arabic not exposed' is refuted by my own run: **সাদা শাড়ী।**আজো → LITERAL and **ملاحظة:**النص → LITERAL in both micromark and marked. The reframing also redirects attention from the script that is actually in the corpus to ones that are not: across 4,837 .md files / 93,590,395 chars in ~/Desktop/GitHub/md + knowledge + frontmatter I measured Bengali 288,887 chars in 25 files, and Thai/Lao/Khmer/Myanmar/Javanese/Balinese = 0 chars in 0 files.
verdicts.correction: The predicate is Unicode General_Category P|S on the inside character, letter on the outside — script-agnostic, exactly as PLAN.md §17.3 already states. LB class describes who is statistically likely to hit it, not what the parser tests.

verdicts.claim: Claim 2 — 'CORRECTION TO THE FRAMING GIVEN ME': the failure is punctuation inside the span with a letter outside, and Latin fails identically
verdicts.reason: primary-read of docs/engine/PLAN.md:1555ff. Every behavioural measurement reproduces (I re-ran all 17 constructs in micromark 4 + marked and got identical EMPH/LITERAL verdicts, including the Latin control this**bold.**next → LITERAL). But this is not a correction — PLAN.md §17.3 already says verbatim: "The failure condition is narrower and sharper than 'CJK has no spaces'. `**粗体**中文` works fine. What breaks is **punctuation inside the delimiter with a letter or ideograph outside it**". The research concedes this mid-claim ('PLAN.md §17.3 already states the correct condition') and still bills it as finding #2 and as the headline correction. Restating the design of record is not a research result.
verdicts.correction: Drop the 'CORRECTION' framing; the design of record already had it right. The scriptio-continua reframing the research adds on top is a regression, not a sharpening (see the Claim 3 verdict).

verdicts.claim: Claim 6 — 'CORRECTION: the CJK word-count undercount is far worse than the 1.7–2.0× in PLAN.md §17.5. On a real 80-file Chinese corpus it is 3.80×'
verdicts.reason: own-measurement, corpus substitution. The vuejs-translations/docs-zh-cn numbers reproduce essentially exactly — I downloaded the repo from codeload.github.com and got chars 295,117 (claimed 295,114), naive 19,885 (exact), Segmenter('zh-Hans') word-like 75,618 (exact), ratio 3.80× (exact). But PLAN.md:1643 states its scope explicitly: "Whole-file undercount on the vault's real Chinese files is 1.7×–2.0×". I measured that exact population — every file in md/knowledge/frontmatter with >200 Han chars, n=3 — and got naive 1,469 vs Segmenter 2,661 = 1.81×, squarely inside PLAN.md's stated range. PLAN.md's number is correct for what it claims. Substituting a 100%-Chinese translation repo for a Latin-dominant vault and calling the different ratio a correction compares two populations. Sensitivity confirms it is a population effect: all 125 files gives 4.08×, unstripped gives 2.36×.
verdicts.correction: Not a correction. Report it as a second, higher-CJK-density population: 1.81× on the vault, 3.80× on a fully-Chinese doc set. Both are true of different corpora.

verdicts.claim: Claims 7 and 8 — character-bigram indexing gives a measured 100.0% recall at every query position in both zh and ja, decisively beating Intl.Segmenter (82.0–90.6%) and the shipped tokenizer (47.6–51.8%)
verdicts.reason: inference + own-measurement — the 100% is a theorem, not a measurement. The protocol seeds queries as contiguous 2- and 3-character substrings of the gold document (init2/init3/mid2/mid3/fin2/fin3). For any query q of length ≥2 taken as a contiguous substring of document d, every bigram of q is by definition a bigram of d, so bigrams(q) ⊆ index[d] and AND-matching cannot miss d. The experiment cannot return anything but 100%. I reproduced it on 200 synthetic 400-char CJK documents: 100.0% recall, n=1200. The consequential untested case: perturb one character of each query (a typo, the case the shipped ladder's third pass `fuzzy: 1` exists to serve, confirmed at src/modules/vault/infrastructure/search-index.ts:305) and bigram-AND recall goes to 0.0%, n=1200. So the recipe is presented as a pure win over a ladder it would regress on. The shipped-ladder characterization itself is CONFIRMED — search-index.ts:297/299/305 is exactly AND+last-term-prefix → OR+last-term-prefix → OR fuzzy:1 — and the reported cell means re-derive (ZH split 51.783, JA split 47.567, all values integer-consistent on the n=150 grid).
verdicts.correction: Report bigram recall as entailed by construction for substring queries, and re-run the comparison with perturbed/non-substring queries before treating it as a design answer. Otherwise the 100% figure carries no information about real search behaviour.

verdicts.claim: Design G3 — 'Every emphasis span MDMAX emits renders as emphasis in cmark-gfm, micromark, markdown-it and commonmark.js. Where the four disagree (S-category symbols), MDMAX emits the construct all four agree on'
verdicts.reason: own-measurement. The research supplied measurements from two engines (micromark, marked) and asserts a guarantee over four, one of which (cmark-gfm) is not installed here and was not tested by either of us. I built the missing arm — fetched markdown-it 15.0.0 and commonmark.js 0.31.2 tarballs from registry.npmjs.org — and swept 624 constructs (13 outside chars × 12 inside chars × 4 delimiters) across micromark 4.0.2 / marked / markdown-it / commonmark.js. Result: 46 disagreements, and ZERO of them are S-category. Every S-category case (+ $ = ~ ^ ©, inside and outside, Latin and CJK) had all four engines agreeing EMPH. All 46 divergences involve an EMOJI as the outside character, e.g. 😀__X__😀 and 😀**X。**😀 → micromark LIT / marked EMPH / markdown-it EMPH / commonmark.js LIT. Prevalence inverts the research's priority: emoji occur in 969 of 4,814 corpus files (20.1%), the six scripts named as the unclaimed territory in 0.
verdicts.correction: The S-category divergence is a cmark-gfm-vs-JS-engines claim inherited from PLAN.md §17.3 and remains untested here. The measured four-engine hazard is emoji-flanked emphasis, which is 20.1%-prevalent and currently unnamed anywhere in the design.

verdicts.claim: Design call site 5 — 'Ship this as an upstream PR to micromark — it is a one-line, spec-supported fix with an 8-figure blast radius'
verdicts.reason: primary-read of cmark's src/references.c via raw.githubusercontent.com. normalize_reference does cmark_utf8proc_case_fold + cmark_strbuf_trim + cmark_strbuf_normalize_whitespace — no Unicode normalization, exactly like micromark. So adding .normalize('NFC') to micromark would make micromark DIVERGE from cmark-gfm, i.e. from GitHub: [Café] would resolve locally and fail on GitHub. That is the precise hazard PLAN.md §17.3 already names — "A live WYSIWYG divergence with GitHub... The vault is stored on GitHub. Same bytes, two renderings" — and it contradicts the design's own G3. Spec issue #695 further shows this is a spec-level R4-vs-R5 case-fold question, so the change is a spec deviation, not spec-supported.
verdicts.correction: Do it in MDMAX's own read-side key() where it degrades correctly and touches nothing another engine sees, and file against commonmark-spec#695. Do not send it as a micromark PR framed as a conformance fix.

survived: Claim 1 in full — zero normalization / zero segmentation in the shipped product. All four grep counts reproduce exactly.

Claim 5's technical core — micromark's normalizeIdentifier is normalization-blind, verified end-to-end through the real parser, not just the util. Café/বড়/ज़ NOT-RESOLVED, Å/K RESOLVED, all fixed by NFC. Blast radius 50,373,030 weekly micromark downloads confirms '8-figure'.

Claim 3's Unicode data — LineBreak.txt 16.0.0 class totals ID 172,421 / SA 757 / AL 26,679 and every probe codepoint reproduce exactly. The data is right; only the design inference drawn from it is wrong.
Claim 4's source quote — micromark-extension-cjk-friendly-util 3.0.1 dist/characterWithNonBmp.js reproduces cjkOrIvs verbatim, EAW-gated as described.
Claim 6's vuejs-translations measurements — chars 295,117 vs claimed 295,114, naive 19,885 exact, Segmenter 75,618 exact, 3.80× exact. Only the 'CORRECTION to PLAN.md' framing fails, not the numbers.
Claim 2's behavioural matrix — all 17 emphasis constructs reproduce identically in micromark 4 and marked, including the Latin control this**bold.**next → LITERAL.

Claim 7's characterization of the shipped ladder — search-index.ts:297/299/305 is exactly AND+last-term-prefix → OR+last-term-prefix → OR fuzzy:1; and the reported cell means re-derive correctly (ZH split 51.783, JA split 47.567), with every rate integer-consistent on the stated n=150.

Design item 9's ICU premise — Node 24.6.0 Intl.Segmenter.supportedLocalesOf returns all of th, km, my, lo, bo and genuinely dictionary-segments them (Thai 32 chars → 9 words, Khmer 26 → 7, Burmese 38 → 8, Lao 30 → 6).
R-I18N-1's substance — never normalize stored bytes — is correct and consistent with the settled invariants, though it is PLAN.md's finding, not new.
killed: The headline's scriptio-continua reframing (LB=ID ∪ SA) as the predicate. The parser tests General_Category P|S on the inside character; Thai (SA) passes, Bengali (AL) fails. The reframing is narrower AND wrong, and it points away from the only non-Latin script actually present in the corpus.
'Thai/Lao/Khmer/Burmese/Javanese/Balinese have the identical defect' — Thai and Lao measurably do not; their ฯ/ๆ/ໆ are Lo/Lm letters, not punctuation. 2 of 6, not 6 of 6.

The whole 'specific unclaimed territory' as a differentiator, on prevalence grounds. Zero chars of all six scripts across 4,837 .md files and 93,590,395 chars of the project's own corpora. The research never reported a denominator for the opportunity it is sizing.
Claim 5's novelty. commonmark-spec#695, open since 2021-11-11, names the identical defect with the identical é-composed-vs-decomposed example.
'CORRECTION: far worse than PLAN.md's 1.7–2.0×'. I measured PLAN.md's own stated population and got 1.81×, inside its range. PLAN.md is right; the research changed corpora without saying so.

Bigram '100% recall' as an empirical finding. It is entailed by construction for substring queries; I reproduced it on random synthetic data and proved the mechanism. Under a one-character typo it is 0.0%.
G3's premise that the four engines disagree on S-category symbols. 624-construct sweep: 0 S-category disagreements, 46 emoji disagreements.
'A one-line, spec-supported fix' to micromark. cmark does not normalize either; the change would break GitHub parity — the exact failure mode PLAN.md §17.3 already flags and G3 forbids.
new_defects: ARITHMETIC, independently re-derived: the reading-time numbers are computed with the wrong operator. The research quotes the shipped code correctly in the same sentence — Math.max(1, Math.ceil(words/200)), EditorPane.tsx:58 — then reports 'zh reads 99 min by the shipped metric vs 378 min by Segmenter'. ceil(19885/200) = ceil(99.425) = 100, not 99. ceil(75618/200) = ceil(378.09) = 379, not 378. Both reported values are the FLOOR. The numbers were computed by hand instead of by running the quoted function — Learned Rule #59 exactly.
ARITHMETIC: the ZH Segmenter mean does not reproduce. The six cells 98.0/99.3/84.0/87.3/89.3/85.3 sum to 543.2, mean 90.533, which rounds to 90.5. Reported as 90.6.

A ratio whose definition is missing: the 5.64× / 9.40× 'CJK-char convention' figures do not reproduce. Counting CJK Unified Ideographs + Ext A over the identical 80 files gives 91,413 (4.60×), not 112,237 (5.64×). 'CJK-char' is never defined, so the figure is unfalsifiable as stated — while the 3.80× Segmenter figure beside it reproduces to the digit.

Unexplained subsetting on the load-bearing corpus. The repo has 125 .md files; the research used 80 and never says why or which. All 125 gives 4.08×, unstripped gives 2.36×. One cell of a four-cell sensitivity surface was reported as the result.

A ratio reported without its aggregation: 'median 7 candidates → 6 verified, precision 96.9%' (and JA 'median 34 → 31, precision 95.3%'). 6/7 is 85.7% and 31/34 is 91.2%. The precision figures are presumably post-filter over all queries rather than over the medians, but the two are printed adjacent as if they were the same computation, and no denominator is given for either.

Prior work inside the project presented as new design. R-I18N-1 and its Bengali evidence are PLAN.md:1485-1501 ('normalize for the HASH ONLY, never the bytes written'; 'lines changed by NFC: 77 of 437'), and PLAN.md:1523 already prescribes '.normalize("NFC") on the comparison key in slug generation, link-fragment...'. Call sites 1, 2 and 4 of the 'eleven' are the design of record. Only call site 5 is genuinely absent from docs/engine (grep for normalizeIdentifier / case fold returns nothing).

An internal inconsistency in the design's own numbers: design item 10 says localeCompare/.sort() is '12 hits today', while claim 1's measurement in the same document says 4. I measured 4. The 12 is unsourced.

Two engines measured, four asserted. Every behavioural result in claims 2 and 4 comes from micromark + marked, yet G3 is written as a guarantee over micromark, marked, markdown-it, commonmark.js and cmark-gfm. Building the missing arms took me ten minutes and immediately falsified G3's stated locus of disagreement.

A single unreplicated construct-level judgment is used to dismiss the project's own exemplars. 'Constructs those scripts do not naturally produce' is asserted about the Bengali and Arabic cases in PLAN.md §17.3 with no corpus evidence, no native-speaker check, and no frequency count — while the corpus contains 288,887 Bengali characters in 25 files and zero characters of the scripts the research promotes in their place.

per_area.title: The unit of exchange — message-level MDMAX and the human-paste hop
per_area.headline: The human-paste hop is not "lossy" — it is bimodal: the text/plain clipboard flavour destroys 100% of code fences, 99.8% of tables and 81% of hyperlink destinations while keeping 94.7% of the bytes, whereas the text/html flavour round-trips at 99–100%; but BOTH paths delete HTML comments and YAML frontmatter outright, so any message-level MDMAX metadata must live in visible prose — and the thing actually lost in a handoff is not prose structure at all but evidence, since 62.6% of the numbers and 69.7% of the file paths in a real AI final answer exist only in tool context that the copy drops.

findings.claim: The paste hop is bimodal, not uniformly lossy. Rendering real markdown in headless Chrome and reading the two clipboard flavours a full-message selection produces: the text/plain flavour annihilates structure, the text/html flavour preserves it almost perfectly. Over 600 real AI final-answer messages the text/html flavour passed through turndown+GFM recovered headings 3086/3086 (100.0%), tables 518/518 (100.0%), lists 1796/1796 (100.0%), blockquotes 761/761 (100.0%), fenced-code languages 3494/3494 (100.00%) and inline-link URLs 1193/1196 (99.75%).
findings.evidence: Own measurement, /private/tmp/claude-501/mdmax-msg/rich.mjs, Chrome 'Google Chrome.app' headless via puppeteer-core, Range.cloneContents() innerHTML -> turndown 7.x + turndown-plugin-gfm. Verbatim output: '##### RICH PATH: text/html flavour -> turndown+GFM  (n=600 AI messages)' / 'heading 3086 3086 100.0%' / 'table 518 518 100.0%' / 'inline links URL survives: 1193/1196 = 99.75%' / 'fenced blocks 6055, with lang 3494, lang recovered 3494 = 100.00%'.

findings.claim: On the text/plain path, ZERO fenced code blocks survive as code. Not a low rate — exactly zero, across two independent corpora totalling 21,054 fenced blocks. A pasted code fence becomes prose indistinguishable from the surrounding text, and its language annotation is gone.
findings.evidence: Own measurement, survive2.mjs (window.getSelection().toString() on the rendered message, re-parsed with remark-parse+gfm+math). Corpus A (1,200 real AI final answers >=500 chars): 'fenced code blocks: 6491 (with lang: 3783); body still parses as a code block after hop: 0 = 0.00%'. Corpus B (400 files from /Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/md, 5,586 .md found): 'fenced code blocks: 14563 (with lang: 11288); body still parses as a code block after hop: 0 = 0.00%'.

findings.claim: Inline markdown links lose their destination on the text/plain path. Only 19.38% of [text](url) URLs survive in AI messages and only 1.07% in real markdown documents — and those survivors are cases where the URL also appeared as literal text. Bare/autolinked URLs survive at 95.35% / 64.62% precisely because they are already literal text. Images survive at 0%: an ![alt](url) serialises to the empty string.
findings.evidence: Own measurement, survive2.mjs. Corpus A: 'links inline-style [t](url): 230/1187 URL survives = 19.38%' / 'links autolink/bare URL: 717/752 URL survives = 95.35%'. Corpus B: 'links inline-style [t](url): 18/1677 URL survives = 1.07%' / 'image 67 0 0.0%'. Direct probe (peek.mjs): IN '![alt text](https://x.com/i.png)' -> OUT ''.

findings.claim: HTML comments and YAML frontmatter are DELETED on both clipboard paths — they never reach the DOM, so there is nothing to select. This kills the obvious message-level design (carry provenance in <!-- --> or in frontmatter) at exactly the hop the product exists to serve. Blockquote markers, list markers, ordered-list numbering, task-list checkbox state and heading level are likewise unrecoverable on the plain path.
findings.evidence:
Own measurement, peek.mjs verbatim: html comment IN '"Visible.

<!-- MDMAX: provenance=x -->

More.
"' OUT '"Visible.

More."'; frontmatter IN '"---
title: T
id: 42
---

Body.
"' OUT '"Body."'; ordered list IN '"1. alpha
2. beta
3. gamma
"' OUT '"alpha
beta
gamma"'; task list IN '"- [ ] todo
- [x] done
"' OUT '" todo
 done"'; table IN '"| col | val |
|---|---|
| a | 1 |"' OUT '"col	val
a	1"'. Cross-checked in the rich path: the candidate envelope probe reports 'html-comment confidence  plain=no  rich=no '.

findings.claim: The plain-text hop destroys structure while preserving bytes — text/plain output is 94.7% of the source byte count. This is why the failure is invisible to humans and to naive byte-diff checks: nothing looks missing, but headings survive at 3.3%, inline code at 0.6%, strong emphasis at 0.4% and GFM tables at 0.2% (instance-level, over 1,200 real AI messages).
findings.evidence: Own measurement, survive.mjs / survive2.mjs on Corpus A: 'bytes: in=5996736 out=5679869 (text/plain is 94.7% of source bytes)'; instance table 'heading 3214 106 3.3%' / 'inlineCode 24620 158 0.6%' / 'strong 22023 90 0.4%' / 'table 551 1 0.2%'. These survival figures are UPPER bounds — a doc counts as surviving if any instance of the type reappears.

findings.claim: THE DECISIVE FINDING, and it reframes the problem: what a handoff loses is evidence, not prose. Across 741 real sessions with a substantive final answer, 62.6% of the distinct numbers, 69.7% of the distinct file paths and 49.0% of the distinct backtick identifiers in that final answer appear ONLY in tool-call context that a copy-paste drops. Median session: 50% of the final answer's distinct tokens are unverifiable by whoever receives the paste. A further 12.1% of numbers appear in neither the user's messages nor any tool result — computed, with the derivation never shown.
findings.evidence: Own measurement, /private/tmp/claude-501/mdmax-msg/dep.py over 2,500 sampled transcripts from ~/.claude/projects (13,908 .jsonl total). Verbatim: 'sessions': 741, 'nums': 13202, 'nums_only_tool': 8263, 'nums_nowhere': 1593, 'paths': 1030, 'paths_only_tool': 718, 'idents': 14199, 'idents_only_tool': 6955 / 'nums: 13202 distinct; only-in-tool-context 8263 = 62.6%; in neither user nor tool text 1593 = 12.1%' / 'paths: 1030 distinct; only-in-tool-context 718 = 69.7%' / 'median: 0.500'.

findings.claim: MCP has no slot to declare that a string is markdown, in ANY schema version — and the omission is pointed, not accidental. Six interfaces carry mimeType (Icon, Resource, ResourceTemplate, ResourceContents, ImageContent, AudioContent); ImageContent and AudioContent REQUIRE it. TextContent — the block that carries every tool result and every sampling message to the model — has exactly four fields and none of them is a media type. MCP can tell you a PNG is a PNG but cannot tell you whether a string is markdown, plain text, JSON or a diff.
findings.evidence: Primary read of raw.githubusercontent.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/main/schema/{2024-11-05,2025-03-26,2025-06-18,2025-11-25,2026-07-28,draft}/schema.ts. grep -ic markdown = 0 in all six (line counts 1117/1258/1613/2582/3197/3197). Extracted from 2026-07-28: 'TextContent fields = [type, text, annotations, _meta]' vs 'ImageContent fields = [type, data, mimeType, annotations, _meta]'. Source text: 'export interface TextContent { type: "text"; /** The text content of the message. */ text: string; ... }'.

findings.claim: A2A, by contrast, already has the slot and it is free. Part.media_type is field 7 and the spec comment states it applies to text parts too — so an A2A agent can legally emit `text/markdown; variant=MDMAX` today with zero protocol change. This is a hard asymmetry: goal G3 has a free ride on A2A and is structurally blocked on MCP.
findings.evidence: Primary read of raw.githubusercontent.com/a2aproject/A2A/main/specification/a2a.proto (812 lines, 35,942 bytes, grep -ic markdown = 0). Verbatim: 'message Part { oneof content { string text = 1; bytes raw = 2; string url = 3; google.protobuf.Value data = 4; } google.protobuf.Struct metadata = 5; string filename = 6; // The `media_type` (MIME type) of the part content (e.g., "text/plain", "application/json", "image/png"). // This field is available for all part types. string media_type = 7; }'

findings.claim: The IETF specified this exact problem in March 2016 and nobody uses the answer. RFC 7763 registers text/markdown with an optional `variant` parameter that is explicitly a non-binding hint; RFC 7764 §2 is titled 'Strategies for Preserving Media Type and Parameters' and enumerates six of them (map to filename, adjacent headers file, arm with MIME headers, local batch script, pre-process, rely on context), and registers eight variants including CommonMark and GFM. §2.6 predicts MDMAX's premise verbatim.
findings.evidence: Primary read of rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7763.txt and rfc7764.txt. RFC 7763: 'variant: An optional identifier of the specific Markdown variant that the author intended. The value serves as a "hint" to the recipient, meaning that the recipient MAY interpret the Markdown as that variant, but is under no obligation to do so.' RFC 7764 §2.6: '"Context" can be easily lost over time, and the trend of passing Markdown between systems -- taking them *out* of context -- is increasing.' RFC 7764 §1.4: 'Unlike complete HTML documents, [MDSYNTAX] provides no means to include metadata in the content stream... In general, the metadata must be supplied via supplementary means in an encapsulating protocol, format, or convention.' Registered identifiers: MultiMarkdown, GFM, pandoc, Fountain, CommonMark, kramdown-rfc2629, rfc7328, Extra.

findings.claim: RFC 7763's variant parameter has an adoption base rate as bad as llms.txt or worse: 173 code results across all of GitHub for the literal string 'text/markdown; variant=', ten years after registration. This is the closest available precedent for 'declare the dialect in the media type' and it says the declaration channel is not the bottleneck — nobody fills it in even where it exists.
findings.evidence: Own measurement via api.github.com/search/code?q=%22text%2Fmarkdown%3B+variant%3D%22 -> total_count = 173. Comparison queries: '"variant=CommonMark"' -> 343, '"variant=GFM"' -> 5748 (the latter is contaminated by vendored RFC copies and unrelated config keys).

findings.claim: CORRECTION to the established starting evidence: the MAST '37% inter-agent misalignment' figure is version-specific and the current version of the paper no longer states it. arXiv 2503.13657v2 says FC2 = 36.94%; v3 (current) removes the aggregate sentence entirely and its per-mode figures sum to 32.35%. More importantly, only three of the six FC2 modes are plausibly addressable by a richer message envelope, and they total 9.55% in v3 (13.48% in v2) — not 37%. The single largest FC2 mode is reasoning-action mismatch (13.2%), which no message format fixes.
findings.evidence: Primary read of arxiv.org/html/2503.13657v2 and v3. v2 verbatim: 'The distribution of failures across MAST's categories is relatively balanced (FC1: 41.77%, FC2: 36.94%, FC3: 21.30%, Figure 2)'. v3 verbatim: 'FC2 covers failures in agent coordination. These include unexpected conversation resets (FM-2.1, 2.20%), proceeding with wrong assumptions instead of seeking clarification (FM-2.2, 6.80%), task derailment (FM-2.3, 7.40%), withholding crucial information (FM-2.4, 0.85%), ignoring other agents' input (FM-2.5, 1.90%), or mismatches between reasoning and action (FM-2.6, 13.2%)'. Arithmetic: v2 2.33+11.65+7.15+1.66+0.17+13.98 = 36.94; v3 2.20+6.80+7.40+0.85+1.90+13.2 = 32.35; v3 (FM-2.2+2.4+2.5) = 9.55. Abstract confirms '1600+ annotated traces collected across 7 popular MAS frameworks' and 'high inter-annotator agreement (kappa = 0.88)'.

findings.claim: The OpenAI Agents SDK handoff claim is confirmed and sharper than stated. _SUMMARY_ONLY_INPUT_TYPES is exactly three entries; default_handoff_history_mapper returns a single assistant message; the transcript becomes a numbered plain-text list inside pseudo-XML markers. The decisive detail is the branch condition: _format_transcript_item falls through to json.dumps for ANY content containing a newline. Markdown is multi-line by construction, so a markdown-formatted turn is always JSON-escaped.
findings.evidence: Primary read of raw.githubusercontent.com/openai/openai-agents-python/main/src/agents/handoffs/history.py (635 lines). Verbatim: '_SUMMARY_ONLY_INPUT_TYPES = { "function_call", "function_call_output", # Reasoning items can become orphaned after other summarized items are filtered. "reasoning", }'; 'def default_handoff_history_mapper(transcript) -> """Return a single assistant message summarizing the transcript.""" ... return [summary_message]'; '_DEFAULT_CONVERSATION_HISTORY_START = "<CONVERSATION HISTORY>"'; 'if content is None or (isinstance(content, str) and not _contains_newline(content)): return _format_transcript_item_legacy(item) / return _format_transcript_item_json(item)'; 'def _contains_newline(value: str) -> bool: return "\n" in value or "\r" in value'. Companion file extensions/handoff_filters.py drops 26 item type strings and 11 RunItem classes.

findings.claim: That json.dumps branch fires on essentially every substantive AI message. Across 60,014 assistant text blocks from 10,396 real transcripts, newline presence rises monotonically with length: 0.8% for <200 chars, 71.5% for 500–1500, and 99.9% for 1500–5000. Any AI turn worth handing off takes the JSON-escaping path.
findings.evidence: Own measurement, extract.py + m2.py over ~/.claude/projects (13,908 .jsonl; 'files_read=10396 assistant_text_blocks=60014'). Verbatim bucket table: '0-200 35779 0.8%' / '200-500 12593 16.8%' / '500-1500 6866 71.5%' / '1500-5000 4013 99.9%' / '5000-inf 763 99.0%' for the 'newline' column. Table prevalence in the same buckets: 27.3% and 47.6% for the two largest.

findings.claim: The mechanical lossy-handoff detector's provably-correct tier finds almost nothing: over 6,325 real AI final answers, Tier-1 structural checks (unclosed fence, dangling footnote, dangling reference link, dead in-message anchor, unresolvable link target, unreachable image, hop-fragile carrier) fire on 0.14% of messages combined. Real AI output is structurally well-formed. Tier-2 lexical heuristics fire on 22.53%, dominated by one check: 17.55% of messages state a percentage with no denominator anywhere near it, and 84.5% of all 7,567 individual percentages lack an n within ±140 characters.
findings.evidence: Own measurement, detect2.mjs. Verbatim: 'messages with >=1 TIER-1 flag: 9 = 0.14%' / 'messages with >=1 TIER-2 flag: 1425 = 22.53%' / 'T2:pct_without_n 1110 17.55%' / 'T2:toolref_no_evidence 336 5.31%' / 'T1:unclosed_fence 3 0.05%' / 'T1:hop_fragile_carrier 3 0.05%' / 'percentages: 7567 seen, 6393 with no n nearby = 84.5%'.

findings.claim: The 'dangling pronouns to prior turns' check is much weaker than assumed and my first version of it was wrong. Explicit cross-turn deixis ('as I mentioned', 'the above result', 'per your last message') appears in only 0.26% of all assistant messages and 0.43% of substantive final answers. The mechanically detectable form is a message OPENING on a bare pronoun, which runs at 13.40% for substantive mid-conversation messages versus 6.15% for final answers — real, but 13% not 40%, and roughly 2x higher mid-conversation, which is where handoffs actually get cut.
findings.evidence: Own measurement over both corpora. Verbatim: 'ALL assistant text blocks (mid-conversation incl.) n= 60014 deixis=0.26% leading-pronoun-open=8.14%' / '  ...of those, >=500 chars n= 11642 deixis=1.01% leading-pronoun-open=13.40%' / 'FINAL answer per session n= 13016 deixis=0.22% leading-pronoun-open=4.66%' / '  ...of those, >=500 chars n= 6325 deixis=0.43% leading-pronoun-open=6.15%'.

findings.claim: Mechanical arithmetic verification of prose does NOT work, and I have to report this against my own first result. My initial checker reported 145/311 = 46.6% of checkable arithmetic statements failing. Inspection showed it was matching chained sums two terms at a time, treating A/B = C% as a raw division, and reading ISO dates as subtraction. After excluding dates, versions, table-cell crossings and legitimate display rounding, only 180 checkable statements exist in 6,325 messages and 14 are flagged — of which inspection shows most are still artefacts ('13/34=11' is an indicator label, '5 + 5 = 752' is a table row). The defensible conclusion is the inverse of the one I started with: you cannot recover a derivation from prose, so the format has to carry it.
findings.evidence: Own measurement, arith.mjs then arith2.mjs. First version: 'checkable arithmetic statements: 311, failed: 145 = 46.6%'. Sample false positives it produced: '"11.0/60.2 = 18.3%"', '"112/133 = 84.21%"' (the message text itself says 'the math checks'), '"22 + 24 + 23 + 19 + 17 + 14 + 18 = 137  ✓"'. findings.claim: Demand for the human-paste case is even thinner than the starting evidence admits. GitHub's entire population of cross-AI context-transfer extensions has single-digit stars: the search 'chatgpt claude context transfer extension' returns total_count=14 with a maximum of 3 stars; 'cross-AI context bridge' returns total_count=1 at 8 stars. Generic AI chat exporters do slightly better (16, 8, 6 stars) — meaning the market that exists is 'get my chat out as a file', not 'make the message self-describing'.

findings.claim: CORRECTION: C2PA A.8 does not exist. Appendix A of the C2PA 2.2 specification is 'Embedding manifests' and runs A.1 through A.6 (A.6 = ZIP-based formats); there is no A.7 or A.8. The strings 'copy and paste', 'copy-paste' and 'clipboard' appear ZERO times in both the 2.2 and the 1.3 specifications, and a code search across the c2pa-org GitHub organisation for 'copy and paste' returns 0 results. Whatever the 'C2PA A.8 targets copy-paste, marked under review' claim refers to, it is not in the C2PA technical specification and should not be cited as such.
findings.evidence: Primary read of spec.c2pa.org/specifications/specifications/2.2/specs/C2PA_Specification.html (839,508 bytes) — extracted heading list ends 'A.6.
