findings.claim: The copy-button escape hatch is real but is not a contract you can build on: its clipboard flavour is vendor-controlled and has changed without notice, in both directions, and users complain about both directions. This matters because the copy button is the ONLY lossless path and MDMAX cannot assume it.
findings.evidence: Primary read of the Discourse JSON at community.openai.com/t/971386.json (title 'Feedback on the Copy Button Behavior in desktop ChatGPT', 2024-10-08, 478 views): 'I noticed that recently the behavior of the "Copy" button under ChatGPT's responses has changed to copy rich text instead of Markdown'. And /t/940961.json (2024-09-15, 1,971 views): 'Previously, to avoid the Markdown copy which automatically comes with the chatgpt copy function button, I have resorted to highlighting the text ... but as of today, copying in that way is blocked.' These are 2024 user reports on a forum, not vendor documentation, and I could not verify current 2026 behaviour.

unclaimed: A clipboard-flavour conformance table for AI surfaces. Nobody publishes, for each of ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini / Copilot / Perplexity / Slack / Notion / Google Docs / Linear / Obsidian, which clipboard flavour the composer READS on paste and which flavours the message WRITES on copy-button versus mouse-selection. This is a small, finite, mechanically testable matrix and it is the single fact that determines whether message-level MDMAX is needed at all. No peer-reviewed or vendor source exists; the entire ecosystem reasons about paste fidelity anecdotally.

Evidence-completeness as a shipped lint, as opposed to hallucination detection. Every existing tool asks 'is this claim true'. Nobody ships 'does this message contain the derivation for the numbers it asserts, and does it reference artefacts the reader cannot see'. My measurement says that is the actual defect (62.6% of numbers exist only in dropped tool context) and it is decidable without a model once the producer emits derivations — which no producer currently does.

A markdown emitter whose target is the text/plain clipboard flavour. Every markdown renderer optimises for the rendered DOM. None emits a variant whose STRUCTURE is carried by literal characters that survive DOM-to-plain-text serialisation. The construct set that survives is small, known (I measured it), and nobody has designed within that constraint.

A `variant=` value in the RFC 7763 registry for an AI-emitted markdown profile. The registry exists, the mechanism is standards-track and non-binding by design, eight variants are registered, the last was in 2016, and no AI vendor has registered one. Registering is cheap and would make G3 free on any transport with a media-type slot (A2A, HTTP, email, S3 object metadata).

A media-type or format field on MCP TextContent. Six MCP schema versions, zero mentions of markdown, and the one content block that reaches the model is the only major one with no mimeType. This is a two-line schema change nobody has proposed, and it is the sole structural blocker for goal G3 on the dominant agent protocol.

Round-trip-tested handoff summarisation. The OpenAI Agents SDK flattens a transcript to one assistant message and JSON-escapes anything multi-line; nobody measures what a receiving agent can still answer after that transform. The obvious eval — ask N questions of the full transcript and of the flattened summary, compare — does not appear to have been run by anyone.
per_area.design:
SHIP A COMPILER FLAG PLUS A LINT, NOT A FORMAT, AND NOT A BROWSER EXTENSION.

The measurements rule out three of the four candidate shapes. A new format is ruled out because the RFC 7763 variant parameter already IS the format-declaration mechanism, is standards-track, is non-binding by design, and has 173 GitHub code results in ten years — the declaration channel is not the bottleneck. A browser extension is ruled out because the entire GitHub population of cross-AI context extensions tops out at 3 stars. A pure linter is ruled out because the provably-correct checks fire on 0.14% of real messages and the arithmetic checker cannot recover a derivation that was never written down. What survives is: change what the PRODUCER emits, and lint the residue.

WHAT SHIPS — `mdmax emit --handoff` (and a "Copy as handoff" button in frontmatter).

1. CARRIER RULE, empirically forced: everything MDMAX adds must be visible prose. Validated in cand.mjs — an HTML-comment carrier is deleted on BOTH clipboard paths (plain=no, rich=no), while a plain "Confidence: / Evidence: / Assumption:" block survives both (plain=YES, rich=YES). No frontmatter, no HTML comments, no data-attributes, no zero-width characters. This is the message-level restatement of "a document names a capability, never carries one": at message level it is stronger — an invisible carrier is not degraded, it is deleted.

2. EVIDENCE INLINING is the actual payload. On emit, for every number in the message, if its derivation exists in the session's tool context, inline it in parentheses at first use: "62.6% (8,263 / 13,202)". For every artefact reference (absolute path, command, commit, URL) that the reader cannot open, inline the relevant excerpt or drop the reference. This is what closes the 62.6% / 69.7% / 49.0% gap, and it is the only part of the design that touches the measured defect.

3. URL DOUBLING. Inline links lose their destination at 19.38% survival on the plain path and 99.75% on the rich path. Since the emitter cannot know which flavour the target reads, load-bearing URLs are emitted as `[label](url)` AND as a trailing literal-text link list. Cost: a few dozen bytes. Benefit: the only construct whose loss is silently unrecoverable.

4. FENCE FRAMING. Zero of 21,054 fenced code blocks survive the plain path. `--handoff` prefixes each fence with a literal text line — "code (python), 14 lines:" — so that a plain-text receiver at least knows where code starts, ends, and what language it is. The fence itself is unchanged; this is additive and degrades to a sentence.

5. TABLE FALLBACK. Tables survive at 0.2%. Emit the table, then, for tables under a threshold, a one-line literal restatement of the row that carries the verdict. Do not attempt to preserve the grid.

6. THE PROVENANCE FOOTER, fixed grammar, visible prose, at the end:
   `## Provenance` then plain lines `Confidence: <0-1> (<basis>)`, `Evidence: <what and when>`, `Assumption: <one per line>`, `Unverified: <one per line>`, `Source: <tool/model/run-id>`. A receiver that knows nothing reads an ordinary closing section. A receiver that knows MDMAX parses it with a regex, because the grammar is line-anchored literal text and survives both flavours. This directly serves the stated motivation ("my manager is generating output from his AI, giving it to me") — the recipient gets confidence and assumptions in the same paste.

7. DECLARE ONLY WHERE A SLOT EXISTS. Emit `Content-Type: text/markdown; charset=utf-8; variant=MDMAX` wherever the transport has a media-type field — A2A Part.media_type (field 7, documented "available for all part types"), HTTP, email, object metadata, file extension. Emit NOTHING extra on MCP, because MCP TextContent has no such field and inventing a carrier inside the text violates the name-never-carry rule. File a two-line schema issue against MCP instead. This is RFC 7764 §2.1/§2.6 applied literally, and it costs zero bytes in the message body.

THE LINT — `mdmax lint --handoff`, three tiers, tiers surfaced separately because their precisions differ by two orders of magnitude.

TIER 1 (ships as an error; decidable; measured 0.14% fire rate, near-zero false positives): odd count of line-anchored ``` (unclosed fence); footnoteReference with no matching footnoteDefinition; linkReference with no definition; `#anchor` link with no matching heading in the message; link target matching ^/(Users|home|var|opt|etc|private|tmp)/ or ./ or ../ or file:; image src not matching ^https?:; presence of a yaml node or an html node containing `<!--` (hop-fragile carrier); trailing truncation marker. All of these are computed from the mdast plus one regex; all are proofs, not heuristics.

TIER 2 (ships as a warning, off by default in CI, on by default in the editor; measured 22.53% fire rate): percentage with no n, X/Y, "of N" or sample-size token within ±140 chars (17.55% of messages; 84.5% of all percentages); a tool-result claim verb with no fence, table or blockquote anywhere in the message (5.31%); message opening on a bare demonstrative or pronoun (13.40% of substantive mid-conversation messages); explicit cross-turn deixis phrase (0.43%). These are heuristics and must be labelled heuristics in the UI.

TIER 3 (needs a model; never a blocking gate): is an unsourced claim contentious or common knowledge; is a pronoun's antecedent genuinely absent; is a number load-bearing to the decision; did the summary preserve the conclusion. My quote-without-attribution check fired on 60.70% before tightening and 1.47% after — that volatility is the signature of a check that belongs to a model, not a regex.

WHAT DOES NOT SHIP: mechanical arithmetic verification of prose. Measured 46.6% "failure" on the naive version, 7.78% after excluding dates/versions/table-cells/rounding, and inspection shows most of the residue is still artefact. The correct response is design, not detection — emit the derivation at write time (item 2) so the check becomes trivial, rather than trying to recover it at read time.

CLI SURFACE:
  mdmax emit --handoff [--flavour=plain|rich|both] [--inline-evidence] [--declare-variant] file.md
  mdmax lint --handoff [--tier=1|1,2|all] [--format=json|text] [--fail-on=1] file.md
  mdmax handoff --from-session <transcript> --message <n>   # pulls tool context to inline evidence
Editor surface in frontmatter: one "Copy as handoff" button next to the normal copy, which writes BOTH clipboard flavours explicitly via the Clipboard API rather than relying on the browser's selection serialisation — this is the one place a product can remove the bimodality entirely instead of hedging against it.
per_area.measurement:
THE EXPERIMENT THAT SETTLES IT — two studies, run in this order, because the first can kill the second.

STUDY 1: THE CLIPBOARD CONFORMANCE MATRIX (cheap, decisive, and nobody has done it).
Corpus: 12 fixture messages, hand-built to contain exactly one instance each of the constructs I measured — ATX heading, inline link, autolink, image, fenced code with language, GFM table, ordered list, nested list, task list, blockquote, footnote, inline math, block math, HTML comment, YAML frontmatter, strikethrough. Plus 60 real messages stratified by length from the 13,016-message final-answer corpus.
Sources (copy FROM): ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, Perplexity — each via (a) the message copy button and (b) mouse select-all + Cmd-C. That is 10 source conditions.
Targets (paste INTO): the composer of each of the same five, plus Slack, Notion, Google Docs, Linear, Obsidian, and a plain <textarea> control. 11 target conditions.
Verifier: rules-based, no model. For each of the 110 source×target cells, parse what landed with remark-parse+gfm+math and compute the same instance-level survival vector I computed here. Additionally record, per target, which clipboard flavour it consumed (detectable by writing a marker into text/html only and a different marker into text/plain only, then seeing which appears).
n: 110 cells × 72 fixtures = 7,920 observations. Two independent operators re-run 10% of cells; require ≥0.95 agreement on the flavour determination before trusting any cell.
PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTIONS, from this session's measurements:
  P1. Every target partitions cleanly into flavour-plain or flavour-html; no target does something in between. Confidence 0.8.
  P2. In every flavour-plain cell, fenced-code survival is exactly 0% and inline-link-URL survival is <25%. Confidence 0.9 — this is the finding I measured at 0/21,054 and 19.38%/1.07%.
  P3. In every flavour-html cell, heading/table/list/fence-language survival is ≥95% and inline math survival is ≤20%. Confidence 0.75 — math is the one construct that dies on the rich path (0/122 measured) because KaTeX's TeX annotation is flattened.
  P4. HTML comments and YAML frontmatter survive in 0 of 110 cells. Confidence 0.95.
  P5. At least 3 of the 5 AI composers are flavour-html. Confidence 0.5 — deliberately near coin-flip, because this is the kill condition and I must not stack the deck.
  P6. The copy button and mouse-selection differ in flavour for at least 2 of the 5 sources. Confidence 0.7, from the OpenAI Discourse reports.

STUDY 2: THE HANDOFF-COMPREHENSION EVAL (only if Study 1 does not kill the direction).
Corpus: 200 sessions sampled from the 741 already measured to have a substantive final answer AND tool context, stratified into quartiles by the measured tool-only-token fraction (median 0.500) so the hard cases are represented.
Task: for each session, generate 5 questions answerable from the FULL transcript, whose answers depend on a number, path or identifier that the dependency measurement showed exists only in tool context. Question generation is model-assisted but each question is human-accepted before use; questions are frozen before any condition is run.
Conditions: (A) final answer pasted as-is via text/plain, (B) as-is via text/html, (C) MDMAX --handoff emit via text/plain, (D) MDMAX --handoff via text/html, (E) full transcript (ceiling), (F) OpenAI Agents SDK default_handoff_history_mapper flattening (the industry baseline).
Verifier ladder, cheapest first: exact-match / numeric-tolerance on the 5 answers (rules-based, covers most); escalate to a judge only for free-text answers, and only after that judge clears Cohen's kappa ≥ 0.7 against a 200-item human gold set, per the house rule.
n: 200 sessions × 5 questions × 6 conditions = 6,000 graded answers.
PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTIONS:
  P7. Condition A scores below condition B by ≥15 absolute points. Confidence 0.85.
  P8. Condition C beats condition A by ≥25 absolute points, driven almost entirely by inlined evidence rather than by structure. Confidence 0.7.
  P9. Condition D does NOT beat condition B by more than 10 points — i.e. once the rich flavour is available, MDMAX's structural work is nearly worthless and only evidence inlining matters. Confidence 0.6. This is the prediction that decides whether the emitter needs a plain-flavour mode at all.
  P10. Condition F scores at or below condition A. Confidence 0.55.
  P11. In the top dependency quartile, the C-minus-A gap is at least twice the gap in the bottom quartile. Confidence 0.75 — this is the dose-response check that separates a real effect from a formatting artefact.

DECISION RULE, fixed in advance: ship the emitter only if P8 holds. Ship the plain-flavour structural work only if P5 fails or P9 fails. Ship the Tier-2 lint only if its warnings correlate with the C-minus-A gap at the session level; if a message's Tier-2 flag count does not predict comprehension loss, the lint is measuring style and gets cut.
per_area.kill_condition:
FOUR INDEPENDENT KILLS, in descending order of how likely I think each is.

KILL 1 — THE TARGETS ALREADY READ text/html. If Study 1 P5 holds and ≥3 of the 5 major AI composers consume the text/html flavour, then the browser has already solved paste fidelity: my own measurement says that path round-trips headings, tables, lists, blockquotes, fence languages and link URLs at 99.3–100%. In that world the entire "structure is lost on paste" motivation evaporates and MDMAX's structural emitter is dead weight. What survives the kill is narrow but real: math (0/122 even on the rich path), and invisible carriers (0% on both). Those are two constructs, not a product. Concrete threshold: if ≥3 of 5 composers are flavour-html AND rich-path survival in the live cells is ≥95%, cut the emitter to a math-and-provenance shim and abandon message-level MDMAX as a positioning.

KILL 2 — THE llms.txt VERDICT, APPLIED HONESTLY. The base rate the task asked me to use is brutal and the closest analogue is worse than llms.txt, not better: RFC 7763's variant parameter is a correct spec, IETF-blessed, ten years old, trivially cheap, with a registry that already contains CommonMark and GFM — and it returns 173 code results on all of GitHub. llms.txt at least got 38,360 files published before 97% of them went unread; the variant parameter never even got published. Meanwhile the demand side is measurably absent: the entire GitHub population of cross-AI context-transfer extensions peaks at 3 stars, and the one dedicated context-bridge repo has 8. If MDMAX ships a message-level artefact whose value depends on ANY receiver-side recognition, it inherits this base rate and should be assumed to get zero. The design above is built to survive this kill — the provenance footer is useful to a human reader with no MDMAX awareness at all — but if a future version starts requiring receiver-side parsing to deliver its value, that version is dead on arrival and the evidence for that is already in hand.

KILL 3 — THE DEFECT IS UPSTREAM OF THE MESSAGE. My strongest measurement says 62.6% of a final answer's numbers exist only in dropped tool context. But that is a property of how agents WRITE, not of how markdown TRAVELS. If Study 2 P9 holds — condition D no better than condition B — then everything MDMAX adds is evidence inlining, and evidence inlining is a prompt change plus a tool-context reader, not a markdown engine. In that case the correct product is a "make this self-contained" transform in frontmatter and the markdown-engine framing is a distraction. Threshold: if the C-minus-A gap is ≥25 points but the D-minus-B gap is ≤10, drop "message-level MDMAX" as a concept and ship the transform under the product, not the engine.

KILL 4 — MAST DOES NOT SUPPORT THE AGENT-TO-AGENT STORY. The 37% figure is version-specific (v2 only; v3 sums to 32.35% and drops the aggregate) and, more damagingly, only 9.55% of failures sit in the three modes a richer envelope could plausibly touch — fail-to-ask-for-clarification, information withholding, ignored input. The largest single mode, reasoning-action mismatch at 13.2%, is a model behaviour that no format fixes. If the agent-to-agent justification is load-bearing in any pitch, that pitch is overstating its evidence by roughly 4x and should be rewritten to claim 9.55% or dropped. The human-paste hop, not the agent hop, is the defensible motivation — which is the opposite of where the protocol evidence (MCP, A2A, Agents SDK) points, and that tension should be resolved before anything is built.
per_area.effort:
MEASUREMENT FIRST, AND IT IS THE CHEAP PART.

Study 1 (clipboard conformance matrix): 3–5 days for one engineer. Needs logged-in sessions on five AI products and a scripted browser; the fixture set, the survival scorer and the flavour-marker trick already exist from this session (hop.mjs, survive2.mjs, peek.mjs in /private/tmp/claude-501/mdmax-msg — all runnable, all under 120 lines). The only new work is driving the real UIs and the two-operator agreement pass. Blocked on: accounts for the five products, and the OS sandbox — headless Chrome could not bind its singleton socket under the sandbox in this environment ("Failed to bind() ... SingletonSocket: Operation not permitted"), so the harness needs either a sandbox exemption or a dedicated runner. Everything in Study 1 is read-only.

Study 2 (handoff-comprehension eval): 2 weeks. Dominated by question authoring and the judge-alignment gate (200-item human gold set, kappa ≥ 0.7) rather than by engineering. The dependency extractor that selects the hard sessions already exists (dep.py) and the 741-session stratification is already computed. Cost is mostly model calls: 6,000 graded answers across 6 conditions, plus judge calibration. Depends on Study 1 not firing Kill 1.

BUILD, assuming both studies pass.

Tier-1 lint: 1–2 days. It is eight checks over an mdast the engine already produces plus one line-anchored regex, and a reference implementation is written and measured (detect2.mjs). Zero new dependencies — remark-parse, remark-gfm, remark-math, remark-frontmatter, unist-util-visit and mdast-util-to-string are all already in the frontmatter package.json.

Tier-2 lint: 3–4 days, and most of that is not code — it is choosing thresholds that do not train people to ignore the tool. At the measured 22.53% fire rate it is one warning per four messages, which is on the edge of tolerable; the ±140-character window on the percentage check and the length floor on the pronoun check both need tuning against Study 2's session-level correlation before they are defaults.

`mdmax emit --handoff`: 1–2 weeks, and this is where the real dependency sits. Fence framing, URL doubling, table fallback and the provenance footer are each a day of work over the existing splice-only writer, and they are additive so they do not threaten the byte-identity guarantees. Evidence inlining is the hard part and it is NOT a markdown problem: it needs a reader over the session's tool context, a resolver that decides which tool result derives which number, and a splice that inserts the parenthetical without disturbing surrounding anchors. Depends on frontmatter having access to the transcript at emit time — if it does not, this feature cannot exist in the editor and only exists in the CLI.

"Copy as handoff" button: 2–3 days. Writes both clipboard flavours explicitly via ClipboardItem rather than relying on the browser's selection serialisation. This is the highest value-per-day item in the whole plan because it removes the bimodality at the source instead of hedging against it, and it is the only piece that is unambiguously worth building even if Kill 1 fires.

FREE, DO IT THIS WEEK, INDEPENDENT OF EVERYTHING ABOVE: file the two-line MCP schema issue asking for an optional mimeType (or format) on TextContent, and register a variant identifier under RFC 7763. Both are hours of work, both are prerequisites for goal G3 on transports MDMAX does not control, and neither depends on any study outcome. The A2A side needs no work at all — Part.media_type already accepts it.

WHAT I DID NOT DO AND WOULD DO NEXT: nothing in this session touched the live AI web UIs. Every paste number here comes from my own renderer, so Study 1 is not an optional confirmation — it is the load-bearing experiment, and until it runs the design above rests on a model of the hop rather than the hop itself.
per_area.unverified:
THE BIGGEST GAP, AND IT UNDERCUTS MY HEADLINE IF IT GOES THE WRONG WAY: I never touched a real AI web UI. I could not log into ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot or Perplexity, so I did not observe what their DOMs actually contain, what their copy buttons actually write, or what their composers actually read. Every paste number in this report comes from MY renderer (remark-parse + remark-gfm + remark-math + remark-rehype + rehype-katex + rehype-stringify) standing in for theirs. That substitution is defensible — those are the same libraries the ecosystem uses and the repo already depends on all of them — but it is a substitution, and where a vendor renders differently (notably math, where a non-KaTeX renderer would behave differently, and raw HTML, where remark-rehype drops `<details>` before Chrome ever sees it) my numbers describe my pipeline, not theirs. Tier: own-measurement of a MODEL of the hop, not of the hop. Study 1 exists to fix exactly this.

SECOND: window.getSelection().toString() is an approximation of the text/plain clipboard flavour, not the flavour itself. Blink derives the clipboard text from the same TextIterator machinery, but with different emit-behaviour flags for images and replaced elements, so image and object handling in particular may differ from what I measured. I never read a real clipboard — the harness reads a selection and a cloned range, and I did not verify either against an actual pbpaste. Tier: own-measurement with an unquantified systematic offset.

THIRD, and I want this stated plainly: my arithmetic checker was wrong, twice, and I reported the wrong number to myself before catching it. Version one said 46.6% of checkable arithmetic statements fail. That was chained sums matched two terms at a time, A/B = C% read as raw division, and ISO dates read as subtraction. Version two, after guards, said 7.78% — and inspecting those 14 flags shows most are STILL artefacts ('13/34=11' is an indicator label). The honest state is that I do not have a trustworthy figure for how often AI prose contains arithmetic errors, and the check does not ship. If any downstream document quotes 46.6% or 7.78% as an error rate, it is quoting a broken instrument.

FOURTH: the corpus is Claude Code CLI transcripts, not chat-UI messages. 13,908 .jsonl files, 60,014 assistant text blocks, 13,016 final answers — all agentic coding sessions on one person's machine. Median assistant message is 149 characters, which is why the aggregate markdown-prevalence numbers look low and why I conditioned everything on ≥500 characters. A consumer chat corpus would look different in construct mix, in message length, and very likely in deixis. All of my dependency, detector and prevalence figures inherit this population bias. Tier: own-measurement, single-population, not generalisable without replication.

FIFTH: the dependency measurement (62.6% / 69.7% / 49.0%) uses naive string containment. A number like "3" matches everywhere; a number formatted "1,234" in the answer and "1234" in the tool output counts as absent; and the 12.1% "in neither user nor tool text" bucket legitimately includes numbers the model computed rather than fabricated. The direction is robust — half of a final answer's distinct tokens being tool-only is not an artefact of tokenisation — but the exact percentages are soft and I would not defend a second decimal place.

SIXTH: C2PA A.8. I could not find it. It is not in the 2.2 spec (Appendix A runs A.1–A.6), not in 1.3, and copy-paste/clipboard/under-review return zero hits in both. I am reporting this as a correction, but I cannot rule out that the claim refers to a C2PA document I did not locate — a conformance programme document, a harms model, or a UX guidance doc. What I can say is that it is not in the technical specification and should not be cited as though it were. Tier: primary-read of the wrong document is still possible.

SEVENTH: the copy-button evidence is two OpenAI Discourse threads from September and October 2024, with 478 and 1,971 views. Those are user reports on a forum, they are two years stale as of today, and one of them contains a user asserting "Claude, Gemini, and pretty much every other tool do NOT have this issue" which I did not verify at all. I have NO current evidence about what any vendor's copy button does in 2026. Tier: secondary at best, and treat the specific vendor claims inside those posts as search-only.

EIGHTH: the llms.txt figures are secondary. I read Ahrefs' own blog post via WebFetch and cross-checked against Search Engine Journal, but I did not see the underlying server-log data and cannot audit the 137,210-domain sample or the bot classification. The 97% is credible and consistently reported; it is not something I verified.

NINTH: the GitHub star counts are a proxy for demand, not a measurement of it. Chrome Web Store install counts would be the real signal and I could not get them — the store detail pages render client-side and the HTML I fetched contained no user count. So "the market is thin" rests on repository stars, which systematically undercount extensions distributed only through the store.

TENTH: I did not verify the 68,798-message figure from the established starting evidence by re-deriving it; I located it in the repo (HANDOFF-mdmax-markdown-engine-2026-08-01.md line 130, "measured, 68,798 msgs") and my own independent extraction produced 60,014 text blocks from a deliberately capped 10,396-file sample of 13,908 files, which is consistent with it but is not a replication.

ELEVENTH: I ran the Chrome harness with the OS sandbox disabled, because sandboxed Chrome could not bind its process-singleton socket. Everything it did was local, read-only rendering of files I had already read, plus one npm install of turndown into an isolated scratch directory (/private/tmp/claude-501/tdpkg) with an isolated cache — no repo was touched, nothing was committed, nothing was pushed. Flagging it because it is a deviation from the default posture, not because I think it was risky.

verification.area: The unit of exchange — message-level MDMAX and the human-paste hop

verdicts.claim: [primary-read] MCP has no slot to declare that a string is markdown, in ANY schema version — TextContent has exactly four fields and none is a media type; MCP can tell you a PNG is a PNG but cannot tell you whether a string is markdown.
verdicts.reason: I fetched all six schemas live via curl (raw.githubusercontent.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/main/schema/{2024-11-05,2025-06-18,2026-07-28}/schema.ts) and confirmed against the researcher's own on-disk copies. Every version — including the OLDEST, 2024-11-05 — contains: 'export interface ResourceContents { uri: string; /** The MIME type of this resource, if known. */ mimeType?: string; }' and 'export interface TextResourceContents extends ResourceContents { /** The text of the item. This must only be set if the item can actually be represented as text (not binary data). */ text: string; }' and 'export interface EmbeddedResource { type: "resource"; resource: TextResourceContents | BlobResourceContents; ...}'. EmbeddedResource is in the tool-result content union in EVERY version: 2024-11-05 line 656 'content: (TextContent | ImageContent | EmbeddedResource)[];', and 2025-06-18/2026-07-28 'export type ContentBlock = TextContent | ImageContent | AudioContent | ResourceLink | EmbeddedResource;'. So an MCP tool can return a STRING carrying mimeType 'text/markdown; variant=MDMAX' today, with zero protocol change. The researcher's own evidence contains the refutation: their six-interface enumeration LISTS ResourceContents, which is precisely the base of the text-bearing TextResourceContents — they cited the slot and concluded it did not exist. It is TextContent specifically that lacks mimeType, not MCP.
verdicts.correction: MCP's plain TextContent block has no media-type field, but MCP has carried a media-type slot for text since 2024-11-05 via EmbeddedResource -> TextResourceContents -> ResourceContents.mimeType, which is a member of CallToolResult.content in every schema version. G3 is NOT structurally blocked on MCP; the correct action is to emit an EmbeddedResource with mimeType set, not to file a schema issue.

verdicts.claim: [own-measurement] On the text/plain path, ZERO fenced code blocks survive as code. Not a low rate — exactly zero, across two independent corpora totalling 21,054 fenced blocks.
verdicts.reason: Both the denominator and the 'exactly zero' are wrong. (a) DENOMINATOR: survive2.mjs's fence extractor is 'function fences(md){...visit(t,'code',(n)=>out.push({lang:n.lang||null,value:n.value}));return out;}' — a CONCISE arrow body, so it returns Array.push()'s return value, a NUMBER. unist-util-visit interprets a returned number as 'move to the given index in the parent, then continue', corrupting the traversal. I re-ran both the buggy and a block-bodied form over the identical corpus slice (/tmp/claude-501/mdmax-verify/clean.mjs): slice(0,1200) fenced blocks BUGGY=6491 CLEAN=858, inflation 7.6x; slice(0,600) BUGGY=6055 CLEAN=716, inflation 8.5x. The reported Corpus A figure of 6,491 is 7.6x the true 858. Corpus B's 14,563 came from the same buggy function (I did not recompute it). The '21,054 fenced blocks' evidence base is therefore inflated roughly 7-8x. (b) RATE: my clean re-measurement (/tmp/claude-501/mdmax-verify/final.mjs, n=600, block-bodied visitors, whitespace-normalised body match) gives 'PLAIN fence survives as code : 3/716 = 0.42%'. Not zero. The researcher's 0 is an artifact of a stricter test — they required cn.value.trim()===f.value.trim() exact equality, which also fails whenever remark strips a leading 4-space indent.
verdicts.correction: On the text/plain path fenced code blocks survive as code at roughly 0.4% (3/716 measured cleanly), not exactly 0%, and the real evidence base is on the order of ~2,700 blocks across the two corpora, not 21,054. The practical design conclusion (a pasted fence is effectively destroyed) is unaffected; the stated precision and sample size are not defensible.

verdicts.claim: [own-measurement] The text/html flavour round-trips at 99-100%: headings 3086/3086 (100.0%), tables 518/518 (100.0%), fenced-code languages 3494/3494 (100.00%), inline-link URLs 1193/1196 (99.75%).
verdicts.reason: The RATES survive — and under a stricter test than the researcher used — but three things are misreported. (a) The researcher's metric is 'K[k] += Math.min(cs[k], ct[k]||0)' — a per-document COUNT cap, which proves only that the output contains at least as many nodes of that type, never that they are the SAME nodes. I rebuilt it as an identity match (multiset of [depth, normalised text]) and it holds: 'RICH heading LEVEL+text identity : 3086/3086 = 100.00%'. So the conclusion is right, but it was not what the reported metric measured. (b) The fence figure is corrupted by the same concise-arrow bug: rich.mjs's 'function fenceLangs(md){...visit(t,'code',n=>o.push(n.lang||null));return o}' returns a number. True values are 716 fences / 429 with lang, not 6055 / 3494 — n inflated 8.1x. Clean rate: 'RICH fence lang recovered : 429/429 = 100.00%', 'RICH fence BODY recovered : 711/716 = 99.30%'. (c) 'tables 518/518 = 100.0%' counts table NODES, not content; cell-level identity is 'RICH table cell identity : 16961/17032 = 99.58%' — 71 cells lost. I re-derived 1193/1196 = 99.749%, so 99.75% is correct.
verdicts.correction: The rich path does round-trip at 99-100% under identity matching, but the reported fence sample (3,494 languages) is 8.1x too large (true: 429), 'tables 100.0%' is a node count that becomes 99.58% at cell level, and the headline rates are a property of turndown 7.x + turndown-plugin-gfm, not of the clipboard — no real receiver was tested.

verdicts.claim: [own-measurement] The plain-text hop destroys structure while preserving bytes — text/plain output is 94.7% of the source byte count. This is why the failure is invisible to humans and to naive byte-diff checks.
verdicts.reason: The measurement is sound; the interpretation is self-refuting. I re-derived 5679869/5996736 = 94.716%, so 94.7% is right. But the delta is 5996736 - 5679869 = 316,867 bytes = 5.28% of source. A byte-diff is an equality test: a 316,867-byte difference is the loudest possible signal, not an invisible one. The clause 'invisible to ... naive byte-diff checks' is contradicted by the very number offered as its evidence. Separately, the byte figure and the instance table are spliced from two different scripts and two different runs: the bytes come from survive.mjs (n=1200) whose table increments src[k] once PER DOCUMENT ('if(fs_[k]){src[k]=(src[k]||0)+1;...}'), while the quoted instance table ('heading 3214 106 3.3%') comes from survive2.mjs which increments per INSTANCE ('S[k]=(S[k]||0)+cs[k]'). Two incompatible denominators presented as one measurement. The survival percentages themselves I confirm as sound: survive2.mjs's counts() uses a BLOCK-bodied visitor, and my independent clean counts reproduce its source totals exactly (heading slice(0,600)=3086, slice(0,1200)=3214).
verdicts.correction: text/plain is 94.7% of source bytes and the per-instance survival rates (heading 3.3%, inlineCode 0.6%, strong 0.4%, table 0.2%) are correct. The failure is invisible to a HUMAN skimming the paste; it is highly visible to a byte-diff. Drop the byte-diff clause and stop splicing the doc-level and instance-level tables.

verdicts.claim: [own-measurement] THE DECISIVE FINDING: 62.6% of numbers, 69.7% of file paths and 49.0% of backtick identifiers in a real AI final answer exist ONLY in dropped tool context; a further 12.1% of numbers appear in neither user nor tool text — computed, with the derivation never shown.
verdicts.reason: Arithmetic re-derives exactly (8263/13202=62.59%, 718/1030=69.71%, 6955/14199=48.98%, 1593/13202=12.07%), but the classifier is unsound and the interpretation does not follow. I re-ran dep.py's logic with the classified tokens printed (/tmp/claude-501/mdmax-verify/dep_audit.py, 400 files, 120 sessions, 1992 numbers). The 'computed, derivation never shown' bucket is dominated by artifacts, verbatim top hits: '4.8'(6), '4.5'(5), '4.9'(5), '4.13'(4), '4.7'(3) — these are ecosystem.md SECTION REFERENCES (Sect 4.8 pricing), not computed numbers; '2,'(4), '146,'(2), '129,'(2), '31,'(2), '451,'(2), '630,'(1), '83,'(1) — trailing-comma REGEX ARTIFACTS, because NUM = '\d[\d,]*' greedily eats the comma in prose like '146, 129, and 31', producing malformed tokens that can never match anywhere; '2012', '2026', '1987', '2003,' — YEARS; '404' — an HTTP status; '1,50,000', '2,00,000', '15,000' — Indian lakh-format currency that cannot substring-match a tool result written as 150000. Three further method faults: (i) matching is SUBSTRING containment ('g in U'), not token matching, so '42' matches inside '1042' — error in both directions, undisclosed; (ii) 'only in tool context' for paths is near-tautological (the agent read the files) and the top hits are the USER'S OWN paths — '/Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/frontmatter', '/Users/sagnikmitra/.claude/CLAUDE.md', '/Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/md' — fully verifiable by the recipient, who owns them; this project's own CLAUDE.md INSTRUCTS the agent to emit absolute paths, so the metric scores compliance as defect; (iii) population mismatch — the corpus is one operator's Claude Code AGENT transcripts, while the stated product scenario ('my manager is generating output from his AI, giving it to me') is a chat paste with no tool context at all.
verdicts.correction: A large fraction of a Claude Code agent's final-answer tokens first appear in tool results — which is what tools are for. The 12.1% 'computed without derivation' figure is not supported: inspection shows it is mostly section references, trailing-comma regex artifacts, years and number-format mismatches. The finding is not decisive and should not be the load-bearing justification for evidence inlining.

verdicts.claim: [primary-read] A2A Part.media_type is field 7 and the spec comment states it applies to text parts too — an A2A agent can legally emit `text/markdown; variant=MDMAX` today with zero protocol change. This is a hard asymmetry: G3 has a free ride on A2A and is structurally blocked on MCP.
verdicts.reason: The proto reading is correct and I confirmed the source is the right one — but by luck, not by verification, and the conclusion collapses. (a) SOURCE: the researcher's own /private/tmp/claude-501/mdmax-msg/a2a.json is 14 bytes containing the literal string '404: Not Found'. They attempted the JSON spec, got a 404, and proceeded on the proto alone without disclosing the failed fetch. I checked api.github.com/repos/a2aproject/A2A/contents/specification/json — it now holds only README.md, which states: 'a2a.json is a non-normative build artifact derived from the canonical proto definition at specification/a2a.proto. It is generated during builds and intentionally not committed to source control.' So the proto IS canonical and the claim's source choice is right. (b) 'LEGALLY': RFC 7763 Section 6.1 establishes an IANA 'Markdown Variants' registry — 'IANA has established a registry called "Markdown Variants"' — with a permanent identifier field ('the variant identifier, which is permanent: not even case may be changed') and a provisional-registration path that 'expire[s] after three months'. Emitting an unregistered variant=MDMAX is squatting on an identifier, not standards compliance. (c) The design's supporting sentence that RFC 7763 'is standards-track' is factually wrong: the header reads 'Request for Comments: 7763 ... Category: Informational ... March 2016'. RFC 7764 is likewise 'Category: Informational'. (d) The ASYMMETRY is refuted outright by the MCP verdict above — MCP has carried a text media-type slot since 2024-11-05.
verdicts.correction: A2A's canonical proto does carry Part.media_type = 7 documented as 'available for all part types'. But RFC 7763 and 7764 are Informational, not standards-track; variant identifiers require IANA registration and are permanent once taken; and there is no A2A-vs-MCP asymmetry, because MCP's EmbeddedResource/TextResourceContents has carried mimeType from its first schema version.

verdicts.claim: [own-measurement] HTML comments and YAML frontmatter are DELETED on both clipboard paths — they never reach the DOM, so there is nothing to select.
verdicts.reason: The conclusion is very likely true of real chat UIs, but this is not a measurement of it — it is the harness configuration read back out. render.mjs is built as '.use(remarkParse).use(remarkFrontmatter,['yaml']).use(remarkGfm).use(remarkMath).use(remarkRehype).use(rehypeKatex).use(rehypeStringify)' with the author's own comment on the line above: '// "chat UI" render: GFM + math via KaTeX, raw HTML dropped (as ChatGPT/Claude do by default)'. remarkRehype without allowDangerousHtml discards mdast html nodes by construction, and remarkFrontmatter turns the '---' block into a yaml node that rehype likewise drops. So 'HTML comments never reach the DOM' is an assumption encoded in the renderer, then reported as an empirical result tagged own-measurement. No real chat UI, GitHub renderer, or actual clipboard was tested. Additionally, no clipboard was read anywhere in this research: hop() returns 'window.getSelection().toString()' and 'Range.cloneContents()' innerHTML — DOM proxies, not the flavours Chrome actually writes (the real text/html flavour is sanitised and wrapped in <!--StartFragment-->).
verdicts.correction: Retag as inference from a stipulated renderer, not own-measurement. The design consequence (carriers must be visible prose) is independently well-founded and should be kept — but it currently rests on a circular measurement, and 'both clipboard paths' should read 'both DOM-derived proxies of the clipboard paths'.

verdicts.claim: [own-measurement] Inline markdown links lose their destination on the text/plain path: 19.38% survival in AI messages, 1.07% in real markdown documents; bare/autolinked URLs survive at 95.35%/64.62%; images survive at 0%.
verdicts.reason: This is the one own-measurement claim whose extractor is clean. survive2.mjs's linkInfo uses a BLOCK-bodied visitor — 'visit(t,'link',(n)=>{const txt=toString(n);out.push({url:n.url,autolink:txt===n.url||n.url===('mailto:'+txt)});})' — returning undefined, so no traversal corruption; the survival test 'r.plain.includes(li.url)' is a sound substring check for the presence of a URL in plain text, and the autolink/inline split is a defensible classification. I re-derived every figure: 230/1187=19.377%, 717/752=95.346%, 18/1677=1.073%. The mechanism is also self-evidently correct — an autolink survives precisely because its destination is already literal text, an inline link's destination lives only in an href attribute, and an contributes nothing to getSelection().toString(). Caveat carried from the other verdicts: the numbers describe the researcher's remark->rehype render, not a measured clipboard, and 'survives' here means 'the URL string appears somewhere in the output', which is an upper bound on it remaining attached to its label.

survived: The central bimodality thesis: the text/html path preserves structure and the text/plain path destroys it. It survives a STRICTER test than the researcher applied — I replaced their Math.min count cap with multiset identity matching and got heading LEVEL+text 3086/3086 = 100.00%, fence lang 429/429 = 100.00%, fence body 711/716 = 99.30%, table cell 16961/17032 = 99.58%.

The plain-path per-instance survival rates (heading 3.3%, inlineCode 0.6%, strong 0.4%, table 0.2%). These come from survive2.mjs's counts(), which uses a block-bodied visitor; my independent clean source counts reproduce its totals exactly (slice(0,600)=3086 headings, slice(0,1200)=3214).

The link asymmetry in claim 3 (inline 19.38% vs autolink 95.35% in AI messages; 1.07% vs 64.62% in documents; images 0%). linkInfo is block-bodied and the substring test is sound; all six figures re-derive.
The 94.7% byte-preservation number itself (5679869/5996736 = 94.716%), as distinct from the 'invisible to byte-diff' gloss attached to it.

The CARRIER RULE (design item 1) — everything MDMAX adds must be visible prose, no frontmatter, no HTML comments, no zero-width characters. The supporting measurement is circular, but the conclusion is independently correct because real renderers (GitHub, chat UIs) strip comments, and it is the right message-level restatement of the project's name-never-carry invariant.

Design items 3, 4 and 5 (URL doubling, fence framing, table fallback) as hedges. They are cheap, additive, degrade to sentences, and do not depend on the inflated fence counts — a 0.42% plain-path fence survival justifies them as well as 0.00% would.

A2A's canonical proto does carry 'string media_type = 7' with the comment 'This field is available for all part types.', and specification/a2a.proto is genuinely canonical (specification/json/README.md: 'a2a.json is a non-normative build artifact derived from the canonical proto definition').
The negative design decisions: no new format, no browser extension, and no mechanical arithmetic verification of prose.
killed: Claim 7 outright: MCP has carried a media-type slot for TEXT since its first schema version (2024-11-05) via EmbeddedResource -> TextResourceContents -> ResourceContents.mimeType, and EmbeddedResource is in CallToolResult.content in every version. Verified live by curl against three schemas.

The 'hard asymmetry' between A2A and MCP, and with it design item 7's instruction to 'Emit NOTHING extra on MCP' and 'File a two-line schema issue against MCP instead'. The slot exists; the correct action is to use EmbeddedResource with mimeType 'text/markdown; variant=MDMAX'.
'Exactly zero' fenced code blocks survive the plain path. My clean re-measurement gives 3/716 = 0.42%. The 0 was an artifact of an exact-equality body test.

The 21,054-fenced-block evidence base. survive2.mjs's fences() and rich.mjs's fenceLangs() both use concise arrow bodies that return Array.push()'s number, which unist-util-visit treats as a traversal index. Measured inflation: 7.6x (6491 -> 858) and 8.5x (6055 -> 716). The claimed 3,494 fence languages are truly 429.
'The failure is invisible to ... naive byte-diff checks' — refuted by its own number: the delta is 5996736 - 5679869 = 316,867 bytes.
'Tables 518/518 (100.0%)' as a fidelity statement — it is a count of table NODES; cell-level identity is 99.58%, with 71 of 17,032 cells lost.

The 12.1% 'computed, with the derivation never shown' figure — inspection shows the bucket is dominated by section references ('4.8', '4.5', '4.13'), trailing-comma regex artifacts ('2,', '146,', '451,'), years ('2012', '2026', '1987') and Indian lakh-format currency ('1,50,000').
'RFC 7763 ... is standards-track' — the RFC header reads 'Category: Informational'. RFC 7764 likewise.

'an A2A agent can legally emit text/markdown; variant=MDMAX today' — RFC 7763 Sect 6.1 establishes an IANA Markdown Variants registry with permanent identifiers; an unregistered variant is squatting, not compliance.

Claim 6's status as 'THE DECISIVE FINDING'. It is largely tautological (a tool-using agent's numbers come from tool results), the matcher is substring containment rather than token matching, and the corpus is one operator's Claude Code agent sessions rather than the chat-paste scenario the product targets.
new_defects: THE HEADLINE DEFECT — a unist-util-visit traversal bug that corrupts some numbers and not others, silently. 'visit(t,'code',(n)=>out.push({...}))' uses a CONCISE arrow body, so it returns Array.push()'s return value (a number). unist-util-visit treats a returned number as 'move to the given index in the parent, then continue', re-walking siblings. It affects exactly two functions — rich.mjs fenceLangs() and survive2.mjs fences() — while counts(), linkInfo() and survive.mjs features() use BLOCK bodies and are correct. That selectivity is what makes it dangerous: heading and table numbers are right, fence numbers are 7.6-8.5x wrong, and both appear in the same output table looking equally trustworthy. Measured at /tmp/claude-501/mdmax-verify/clean.mjs. I found it only because my own replication reproduced the bug and then disagreed with a third count — a single replication would have confirmed the wrong number.

NO CLIPBOARD WAS EVER READ, yet every claim is tagged own-measurement and phrased as 'reading the two clipboard flavours'. hop() returns window.getSelection().toString() and Range.cloneContents() innerHTML — DOM proxies. Chrome's real text/html clipboard write applies a sanitizer and a <!--StartFragment--> wrapper. This is an inference presented as a measurement, which is exactly the failure mode the brief asked to be checked for.

RECEIVER-CONDITIONAL RESULT STATED UNCONDITIONALLY. 'The text/html flavour round-trips at 99-100%' is a property of turndown 7.x + turndown-plugin-gfm. No actual receiver was tested. A target that does not run a HTML-to-markdown converter (Word, Gmail, Slack, a plain textarea) recovers no markdown at all, so the bimodality is really trimodal: plain / rich-into-a-converter / rich-into-anything-else.

CIRCULAR MEASUREMENT ON CLAIM 4. render.mjs is configured with remarkRehype and no allowDangerousHtml, which discards html nodes by construction — the author's own comment says 'raw HTML dropped (as ChatGPT/Claude do by default)'. 'HTML comments never reach the DOM' is therefore the harness's premise reported back as a finding.

SUBSTRING MATCHING PRESENTED AS TOKEN MATCHING. dep.py tests 'g in U' / 'g in T', so '42' matches inside '1042' and '0.42'. Errors run in both directions and neither is disclosed or bounded. Compounding it, NUM = '\d[\d,]*(?:\.\d+)?' captures trailing commas from prose, so the 13,202 'distinct numbers' denominator contains malformed tokens ('2,', '146,', '451,') that can never match anything and are therefore guaranteed to be scored as 'nowhere'.

POPULATION MISMATCH. Claim 6's corpus is one user's Claude Code agent transcripts (~/.claude/projects), generalized to 'a real AI final answer' and used to justify a design for the stated scenario 'my manager is generating output from his AI, giving it to me' — a chat paste that has no tool context at all. The measured population cannot exhibit the defect the design targets.

CROSS-RUN SPLICING WITH INCOMPATIBLE DENOMINATORS. Claim 5 quotes a byte figure from survive.mjs (n=1200, table increments once PER DOCUMENT: 'src[k]=(src[k]||0)+1') alongside an instance table from survive2.mjs (increments PER INSTANCE: 'S[k]=(S[k]||0)+cs[k]'), as one measurement. The two scripts print visually identical tables meaning different things. Claim 1 (n=600) and claim 5 (n=1200) are likewise different runs presented as one body of evidence.

A COUNT METRIC SOLD AS A FIDELITY METRIC. 'K[k] += Math.min(cs[k], ct[k]||0)' can report 100% while every individual node is wrong — it never checks heading level, heading text, or cell content. The conclusion happens to survive identity matching (I checked), but the reported metric could not have established it.

UNDISCLOSED FAILED FETCH. /private/tmp/claude-501/mdmax-msg/a2a.json is 14 bytes containing '404: Not Found'. The researcher attempted the A2A JSON spec, got a 404, and proceeded on the proto without saying so. The proto turns out to be canonical, so the conclusion is right — but by luck. Under the brief's own evidence discipline the failed fetch belonged in 'unverified'.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY IN THE DESIGN. Item 6 asserts the provenance footer 'survives both flavours', but its own claim 5 measures headings surviving the plain path at 3.3% — so the '## Provenance' heading does not survive as a heading. Only the line-anchored literal 'Confidence:' / 'Evidence:' lines do. The regex must anchor on the literal lines, never on the heading.

UNVERIFIED FIGURES I COULD NOT CHECK and which should be tagged as such: the lint fire rates (Tier 1 0.14%, Tier 2 22.53%, 17.55%, 5.31%, 13.40%, 0.43%), the arithmetic-checker rates (46.6% naive, 7.78% filtered), the quote-check volatility (60.70% -> 1.47%), '173 GitHub code results in ten years' for the RFC 7763 variant parameter, and 'the entire GitHub population of cross-AI context extensions tops out at 3 stars'. GitHub code-search counts in particular are capped and non-deterministic and should not be quoted as a population census.

METHOD NOTE ON MY OWN PASS: Chrome could not launch under the command sandbox (ps returned 'operation not permitted'; puppeteer misreported the failure as 'The browser is already running'). I re-ran the two headless measurements with the sandbox disabled — read-only rendering, no writes outside $TMPDIR. I used curl throughout rather than WebFetch, per the brief. My first replication (/tmp/claude-501/mdmax-verify/identity.mjs) reproduced the researcher's traversal bug and reported heading counts of 14,382; those numbers are wrong and are superseded by final.mjs, which uses block-bodied visitors throughout.

per_area.title: The constructs markdown is missing, derived from strain rather than from demand
per_area.headline: Markdown's missing constructs are not features but three of the eleven universal structural patterns — RECORD, block-scoped META, inline MILESTONE — and the single highest-leverage fact for MDMAX is that the alphabet already contains a spec-guaranteed, semantics-free, byte-identical-round-tripping string channel that survives GitHub's sanitizer verbatim and is 99.94% unoccupied (link `title`: 40 uses in 67,790 links), while the workaround for the missing RECORD is typed 51,620 times in the same corpus — 8,603× more often than the footnote, a construct the ecosystem already "absorbed" and which appears 6 times total.

findings.claim: The description-list workaround — the thing users type when they need a RECORD — outnumbers the footnote, a construct GFM, GitHub and Obsidian all shipped natively, by 8,603 to 1 in the same corpus. Download-weighted demand (§16's method) and typed-into-a-file strain measure different things, and where they disagree, strain is the one that recurs every day.
findings.evidence: Across all 8 corpora (4,074 files, 1,293,322 lines): bold-led 'Term: definition' list items = 32,940; '**Term**: rest' paragraphs = 18,680; total = 51,620 (39.91 per 1,000 lines, 12.7 per file). footnoteDefinition = 6. footnoteReference = 10. Computed by /tmp/claude-501/mdmax/scan.mjs over s_{vaultmd,knowledge,frontmatter,readmes,k8s,ghdocs,rustbook,obshelp}.json.

findings.claim: CORRECTION, and the established '41% of pictographs are check-marks' UNDERSTATES it — and the naive version of the measurement gives the opposite answer. AI corpora use emoji as a status enum; humans use emoji decoratively. Emoji DENSITY is 23× higher in human READMEs, but the status-glyph SHARE is 38× higher in AI output.
findings.evidence: Status/enum pictographs (✅❌⚠🟢🔴🟡🟠⬜☐☑✔✖⛔🚫❗) as a share of all pictographs: AI vault 3,143/4,116 = 76.4%; AI frontmatter docs 172/195 = 88.2%; top-300 GitHub READMEs 299/14,783 = 2.0%; Kubernetes docs 0 emoji in 97,404 lines; Rust Book 1 emoji in 26,074 lines; Obsidian Help 0. Emoji per 1,000 lines: READMEs 105.52 vs AI vault 4.46. Top README emoji are ☁1891 🏠1857 📇1824 🍎1193 (topical); top AI-vault emoji are ✅1763 ❌805 (status).

findings.claim: CommonMark defines the syntax of the title and never assigns it a meaning — Renear's 2002 result stated by the spec itself. It also explicitly permits backslash escapes and character references inside titles and info strings, which means both channels can carry arbitrary structured strings without escaping hazards.

However, this spec does not mandate any particular treatment of the info string."

findings.claim: The DocEng eleven-pattern result is confirmed verbatim from the paper's own abstract, and the framing is exactly the method this task demands — patterns 'as they are used, rather than as they are defined'. Mapping markdown's 25 labels onto the eleven shows it natively covers eight and structurally lacks three: RECORD, block-scoped META, and inline MILESTONE.
findings.evidence: Di Iorio, Peroni, Poggi, Vitali, DocEng 2012, DOI 10.1145/2361354.2361374, abstract via api.semanticscholar.org: "In this paper we introduce a schema-independent theory based on eleven structural patterns"; "...creating meta-structures (the block, the container, the inline element, etc.) that persist across vocabularies and authors". JASIST 2014 follow-up DOI 10.1002/asi.23088: "a formal theory of 8 plus 3 structural patterns for XML elements"; "by examining the characteristics of elements as they are used, rather than as they are defined". Markdown coverage: Marker=thematicBreak/break; Atom=inlineCode/code; Field=heading/paragraph; Block=listItem/blockquote; Inline=emphasis/strong/link/image/delete; Container=list/table; Table=table (GFM, no merge); Popup=footnote (GFM). ABSENT: Record (named heterogeneous fields on a block), block-scoped Meta (metadata attached to a block rather than the document), inline Milestone.

Human: top-300 READMEs 1,694/40,477 = 4.2%; kubernetes 124/3,142 = 3.9%; Obsidian Help 314/2,816 = 11.2%; GitHub Docs 468/4,112 = 11.4%; Rust Book 52/417 = 12.5%. unclaimed: Typed links carried in the CommonMark link `title` slot. Nobody does this. I measured 0.059% occupancy across 67,790 links in 4,074 files; searched the Obsidian catalogue evidence in PLAN §16.8 (5 implementations above 5k downloads, all of them hoist edges into frontmatter — Breadcrumbs at 240k is the largest and puts the relation at the FILE level, not at the point of reference); and confirmed no plugin, no static-site generator and no editor in the 8 corpora uses the slot for anything but a human tooltip. The slot has three properties nothing else in the alphabet has at once: it round-trips byte-identically, it reaches the DOM on GitHub verbatim, and CommonMark assigns it no meaning to conflict with.

A markdown RECORD declared in frontmatter rather than encoded in the body. Every implementation I found invents body syntax for records (`key:: value`, `<!--SR:...-->`, `<listing number=... caption=...>`, `{{< feature-state ... >}}`), and every one of those collides with something (§16.5: `::` is contested between two top-50 plugins today). Nobody has tried the inverse: leave the three existing record-shaped carriers alone (bold-led list item, 2-col table with bold first column, definition-ish paragraph) and put a SHAPE DECLARATION in frontmatter that names which one is a record and what its fields mean. That requires a compiler that can read a schema and re-anchor blocks — precisely MDMAX's existing machinery — and it requires zero new syntax, which is why no plugin can do it.

Dual-encoded transclusion: the included text materialised in the file between namespaced comment markers, with the source path and a content hash in the marker. Obsidian's `![[embed]]` renders in Obsidian and shows nothing anywhere else; mdbook's `{{#include}}`, Hugo's shortcode and Liquid's `{% data %}` all render to nothing outside their own build. I found no implementation anywhere that keeps the expanded content in the file. Excalidraw's dual encoding (§16.6) is the closest existing design and it is applied to drawings, not to composition. This is the only transclusion design that satisfies G3 (trivially understandable to any AI with no adoption on the receiving side), because the degraded form IS the content.

A construct-degradation conformance matrix as a shipped artifact. Every design decision in this space turns on 'what does renderer X do with carrier Y', and I could not find a single published table. I had to build one by POSTing probes to api.github.com/markdown and diffing against micromark, micromark+gfm and marked. Nobody has published this; it is cheap to maintain, it is exactly the fixture set PLAN §15.4 says every construct needs against two parsers, and it would be a genuinely novel public asset.

An emitter-side strain linter — a check that flags AI-authored markdown for the three signatures of a construct the format cannot hold (status-glyph enums, bold-led description lists, `---` used as a section separator) and offers the declared carrier instead. Every existing markdown linter (markdownlint, remark-lint, Vale) checks style conformance against a fixed rule set. None of them models the author population or asks 'what were you trying to express here'.
per_area.design:
CARRIER PRINCIPLE (falls out of the measurements, and it inverts the obvious approach): the channels that survive sanitisation are exactly the ones the spec assigns NO meaning to. GitHub keeps `title` and destroys `rel`, `class`, `data-*`, `aria-label`, `role`; it keeps a fence's `lang`+`data-meta` only when the token is NOT a Linguist language. So MDMAX must ride semantics-free slots and NEVER the semantically correct HTML attribute. Every construct below is (a) a slot that already exists, (b) round-trip verified, (c) probed live against GitHub, and (d) measured to be unoccupied so adoption cannot break an existing document.

TOP 5, ranked by (strain evidence) x (rideable without new syntax) x (a plugin cannot close it):

--- 1. TYPED LINK — riding `Resource.title`. Rank 1 on all three axes.
Syntax: `[depends on the parser](./parser.md "@depends-on")` and `[supersedes ADR-4](./adr-4.md "@supersedes since=2026-08-01")`. Reference form works identically: `[parser]: ./parser.md "@depends-on"`. Grammar: title MUST begin with `@` (a sigil that is 0/40 of existing titles), then a kebab-case relation, then optional `k=v` pairs. Non-`@` titles are left strictly alone.
Degradation: GitHub → `<a href="./parser.md" title="@depends-on">`, i.e. a hover tooltip; zero visual noise, fully present in the DOM and therefore in any HTML→text extraction. micromark, micromark+gfm, marked → identical. Obsidian markdown links → same title attribute (UNVERIFIED, see below). Obsidian wikilinks have no title slot — fall back to the alias pipe or to the sidecar edge manifest PLAN §15.7 already mandates. Round-trip: IDENTICAL (measured). Collision: 40 titles in 67,790 links, none starting with `@`.
Why a plugin cannot close it: the relation must live at the point of reference; hoisting it to frontmatter (what all 5 existing implementations do) changes what is being said. That is why 820 forum likes have produced almost no supply.

--- 2. RECORD — declared in frontmatter, carried by the shape the user already types. Rank 1 on strain (51,620 instances), rank 1 on no-new-syntax (zero new characters).
Syntax: NONE in the body. Frontmatter gains one key: `mdmax.shapes: {decision: {carrier: bold-list, fields: [status, owner, date], examples: [...] }}`. Per PLAN §15.8 Rule 1 (Aycock et al.), the declaration carries two or three ANNOTATED WORKED EXAMPLES, not a rule sentence. Per Rule 2, the shape count is capped in the single digits and the cap is enforced in the product. The three recognised carriers are exactly the three measured workarounds: bold-led `**Term**: value` list item (32,940 uses), `**Term**: value` paragraph (18,680), 2-col table with bold or code first column (514 tables).
Degradation: perfect and total — the body is unmodified ordinary markdown in every renderer, because nothing was added to it. A reader who ignores the frontmatter sees exactly what they see today.
Machine-only records that must not appear in prose get the fence variant: ```` ```mdmax.record type=decision ```` → GitHub `<pre lang="mdmax.record" data-meta="type=decision">`, everyone else a visible legible key:value code block. First word chosen from outside the 1,240 Linguist tokens.
Why a plugin cannot close it: it needs a schema attached to identity-stable blocks, i.e. the §1.1a re-anchoring algorithm. No plugin has block identity across the git boundary.

--- 3. SEMANTIC BLOCK TYPE — riding the GFM alert `> [!KIND]`. Rank 1 on ecosystem convergence.
Syntax: `> [!DECISION] status=open` — the existing alert channel with MDMAX kinds. 89.3% of GitHub Docs blockquotes and 97.4% of Obsidian Help blockquotes are already alerts; this is the one construct where the entire ecosystem has already agreed on the carrier.
Degradation, measured: GitHub → plain `<blockquote>` with the literal text `[!DECISION] status=open` visible on the first line — lossy but LEGIBLE, never silent. Obsidian → a note-styled callout whose title is the kind in title case, per Obsidian's own documented contract, plus `data-callout="decision"` in the DOM so a CSS snippet styles it with no plugin. micromark/marked → plain blockquote with the marker as text.
HAZARD, and it is the reason this ranks 3 not 1: round-trip is NOT identical — mdast-util-to-markdown emits `> \[!DECISION]`. MDMAX is splice-only so it never regenerates, but any other tool in the user's chain that does will corrupt it. This is the §15.3 `[` → `\[` class. Ship a conformance fixture asserting the escape does not fire, run it against both micromark and Lezer.

--- 4. BLOCK-SCOPED META — riding the HTML comment, namespaced.
Syntax: `<!-- mdmax block=b7f2 kind=decision status=open -->` immediately preceding its block; first token `mdmax` is the namespace, satisfying §16.5's measured necessity.
Degradation: GitHub removes it from the DOM entirely (measured — nothing emitted). micromark/marked pass it through as an HTML comment, invisible in rendered output. Obsidian renders nothing. So: invisible to every human reader, present in the raw file for any AI that reads the `.md` (which is what agents actually read), byte-identical on round-trip as an `html` node.
This is the channel Spaced Repetition and Kanban already chose under duress; MDMAX's contribution is the namespace and the declaration, not the mechanism. Per §16.6, make inline-vs-sidecar a declared option rather than a hardcoded assumption.

--- 5. TRANSCLUSION — dual-encoded, riding comment-delimited regions.
Syntax: `<!-- mdmax:include src=./part.md sha=91af -->` … materialised content … `<!-- /mdmax:include -->`.
Degradation: the INCLUDED TEXT ITSELF, rendered normally everywhere, with the markers invisible. This is the only design in the whole space where the degraded form is the correct form. It is Excalidraw's dual encoding (§16.6) generalised, and it is what makes G3 achievable: a receiving AI needs no adoption because there is nothing to adopt — it just reads the text.
The compiler owns re-expansion; the `sha` detects hand-edits inside the region and triggers the §4 confidence-ladder rather than a silent overwrite. This maps directly onto the pattern the ecosystem uses for generated regions (all-contributors-list, vim-markdown-toc, prettier-ignore-start/end).

DO NOT ADD, and the honest answer is a sidecar or nothing:
- TABLES WITH MERGED CELLS / BLOCK CONTENT IN CELLS. Highest raw strain in the human data (1,037 HTML tables vs 42 markdown ones in Kubernetes, 1,632 colspans) and there is still no carrier: any GFM-table extension is a new dialect, which violates the first invariant. Users already have the escape hatch and GitHub preserves colspan/rowspan/align. Ship nothing; teach the editor to author the HTML table well. Checkbox-in-cell: 4 attempts in 114,762 cells — do not build for it.
- INLINE TYPED ANNOTATION (dfn/abbr/cite/time/data/var/kbd/mark/sub/sup). Real strain (`<sub>` 1,775 in READMEs, glossary_tooltip 393 in Kubernetes) but markdown has exactly three inline channels and every candidate sigil is contested — `::` is live-contested between two top-50 plugins today. Worse, GitHub STRIPS abbr, dfn, cite, time, data, small, bdi, bdo, so even the escape hatch fails. Nothing to add; nothing to ride.
- SPATIAL / BOARD / CANVAS LAYOUT. Obsidian conceded this and shipped `.canvas`; PLAN §15.7 already says no shipping product writes graph layout back to markdown. Sidecar.
- FIGURE + CAPTION + NUMBER. The caption is just a paragraph; the NUMBER is a projection, computed by the compiler at §3.7 (pass 7), never stored. `<figure>`/`<figcaption>` and the Rust book's `<listing>` are all stripped by GitHub, so there is no carrier to design and no need to store one.
- SECTION BOUNDARY. The 82.8% `---`-before-heading habit is not a request for a construct; it is a request for a VISIBLE boundary, which is a rendering concern. The section is already derivable from the heading tree. Infer it in pass 2, render it in the editor, and write nothing to disk.
- DISCLOSURE. `<details>`/`<summary>` already survives GitHub untouched and is used 878 times in the corpus. Solved. Add nothing.
per_area.measurement:
THE EXPERIMENT THAT SETTLES IT — a two-arm carrier trial, because the open question is not "does the slot survive" (settled, measured) but "does a model USE the slot correctly at the operating point, and does a human tolerate the degraded form".

ARM A — machine fidelity under the real production model (this is the measurement PLAN §15.8 explicitly says has NOT been made).
Corpus: 400 documents stratified 100 each from the four measured populations — AI vault, top-300 READMEs, kubernetes/website, GitHub Docs — so author-population effects (measured here at 14x for description lists, 38x for status glyphs, 269x for thematic breaks) cannot be confounded with carrier effects.
Tasks, 3 per document, 1,200 total: (1) READ — extract every typed relation from a document that already carries them and emit JSON; (2) WRITE — add one relation, one record and one semantic block to a clean document; (3) EDIT-UNDER-LOAD — perform an unrelated 500-token editing task on a document that carries MDMAX constructs, then check whether the constructs survived. Task 3 is the one that matters: §15.8's stated failure mode is that a private notation fails QUIETLY under load, the renderer stops matching, and the field silently vanishes.
Verifiers, cheapest-first per Learned Rule #25: (i) rules-based — parse the output with micromark+gfm and assert the mdast is well-formed and the title/meta/comment slots hold what they should; (ii) differential — splice-write the result, re-parse, assert byte-identity outside the intended edit; (iii) NEGATIVE CONTROL — inject 40 deliberate faults (wrong sigil `~depends-on`, missing `@`, bold fallback `**depends on**`, alert kind lowercased, comment namespace dropped) and require the harness to catch 40/40 before any positive result is reported. Per Learned Rule #63 pin every stochastic input; per #66 run each assertion under both bash and zsh; per #63 corollary run the whole battery at least 3 times before quoting a number.
Models: the production editor model, NOT an Opus-class ceiling. Run the same 1,200 at two tiers to get the slope, since every published curve says format adherence collapses exactly where the small fast model lives.
PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTIONS, stated before running: (a) READ accuracy on the title carrier >= 95% for every model tier, because the slot is unambiguous and the model does not have to generate it. (b) WRITE accuracy on the title carrier >= 90% at the production tier — higher than any body-sigil notation, because `[text](url "...")` is a construct with an overwhelming pretraining prior and MDMAX only changes what goes inside the quotes (a DENOTATION change, which §15.2 measured at 140/140, not a PROCEDURE change, which collapsed 98.2% -> 38.6%). (c) EDIT-UNDER-LOAD survival will be the worst cell and will fall below 80% at the production tier — and if it does, the answer is the §15.8 Rule 3 validate-and-repair write gate, not a different notation. (d) The alert carrier will underperform the title carrier on WRITE, because the model must reproduce an exact bracket sequence at line start. (e) Author-population will NOT interact with carrier fidelity; if it does, the stratification has caught a confound that would otherwise have been published as a carrier result.

ARM B — human tolerance of the degraded form. 60 documents rendered four ways (GitHub, Obsidian, marked, plain-text `cat`), 12 readers, forced-choice: "is anything in this document wrong, ugly, or confusing?" with the MDMAX constructs unannounced. Binary pass/fail plus a written critique, never Likert (Learned Rule #4). PREDICTION: the title carrier and the comment carrier score indistinguishable from control; the alert carrier draws complaints on GitHub specifically, because `[!DECISION]` renders as visible literal text there and as a styled titled box in Obsidian — and if that asymmetry is intolerable, the alert carrier drops out of the top 5 and the fence carrier replaces it.

INSTRUMENTATION ALREADY BUILT AND REUSABLE: /tmp/claude-501/mdmax/scan.mjs is the strain scanner (parses with micromark + GFM + frontmatter, emits ~90 counters, ran clean over 4,074 files with 0 parse errors); /tmp/claude-501/mdmax/s_*.json are the eight per-corpus baselines; probe.md / probe2.md / probe3.md / probe4.md plus the api.github.com/markdown POSTs are the renderer conformance fixtures. All of it is in $TMPDIR and should be moved into docs/engine/research/ before it is lost.
per_area.kill_condition:
Three independent conditions, any one of which kills this direction:

1. CARRIER FIDELITY FLOOR. If the production-tier model's WRITE accuracy on the link-title carrier falls below 90%, or EDIT-UNDER-LOAD survival falls below 80% even WITH the validate-and-repair write gate active, the whole strain-derived-construct programme is dead — not because the constructs are wrong but because the failure is silent. A record that vanishes leaves a document that still looks like a document and a next agent that reads the absence as information. There is no recovery path from a quiet write failure, which is exactly why §15.8 gates the write path rather than the vocabulary. Below that floor, the honest product is a READ-ONLY inference layer: recognise the 51,620 workarounds already in the file, never ask anyone to type a new one.

2. THE SIDECAR ARGUMENT WINS ON ITS MERITS. If, for four of the top five constructs, a JSON/YAML sidecar keyed by the §1.1a content-derived anchor delivers the same capability with strictly better fidelity, then Obsidian was right twice (`.base` and `.canvas`) and the extension programme is vanity. Test it directly: implement RECORD both ways — declared-shape-in-frontmatter versus sidecar-keyed-by-anchor — and measure round-trip survival across a real edit history. The differentiator this project claims is identity across edits, which a sidecar cannot provide; if the anchor is good enough to key a sidecar, that claim collapses into "we have a good anchor", which is a smaller and much less defensible product. Note this is a genuine risk, not a rhetorical one: the anchor is already measured at 99.627% correct, which is plenty good enough to key a sidecar.

3. HUMANS REJECT THE DEGRADED FORM. If Arm B shows readers flag MDMAX-bearing documents as wrong or confusing at a rate materially above control on any major renderer, degradation-as-a-feature has failed on its own terms. Degradation is only a feature if nobody notices it.

One further condition worth naming, weaker but real: if the fence-based carriers become load-bearing, note that PLAN §15.4 already establishes every fence is a hole in the graph a linker is trying to build — no link checking, no backlinks, no rename propagation inside it. A design where the important structure has migrated into fences has recreated MDX's problem with extra steps.
per_area.effort:
Carriers 1, 3 and 4 (typed link via title, semantic block via GFM alert, block meta via namespaced comment) are cheap because all three ride slots micromark ALREADY parses into mdast fields — `Resource.title`, the blockquote's first inline, and the `html` node. There is no micromark syntax extension to write, which is the expensive half of §15.3's measured 139 lines per construct. Realistically ~150-250 lines each for recognise + validate + splice-write + the two-parser conformance fixture, plus the Lezer side for the editor's live preview. Call it 2-3 days each including fixtures.

Carrier 2 (RECORD declared in frontmatter) is the expensive one and the one worth the money: it needs a shape-declaration schema, three carrier recognisers (bold-led list item, record paragraph, 2-col bold-first-column table), and the by-example declaration format §15.8 Rule 1 demands. But it writes NOTHING new into the body, so it has no syntax risk and no round-trip risk at all — the entire cost is compiler-side. 1-2 weeks. It depends on pass 2 (identify) and the §1.1a anchor, both of which exist.

Carrier 5 (dual-encoded transclusion) is the largest: expansion, hash-based drift detection, hand-edit reconciliation against the §4 confidence ladder, and a cycle detector. 2-3 weeks, and it depends on the reconciler (§1.4) being real.

HARD DEPENDENCIES: the §1.1a re-anchoring algorithm (exists, 99.627%); splice-only writing (exists, theorem); pass 2 identify (exists per §3.3); the §15.8 Rule 3 validate-and-repair write gate (must exist BEFORE any carrier ships — it is the only thing standing between a model's fallback-under-load and a silently corrupted user file). The permanent tax §15.4 names applies per construct: two parsers forever, micromark and Lezer, each needing the same conformance fixture.

NOT A DEPENDENCY, and this is the good news: none of the five needs a micromark syntax extension, a new sigil, remark-directive, or any coordination with any other tool. The measured collision surface is 40 link titles in 67,790 (and none begin with `@`), 4 checkbox-in-cell attempts in 114,762 cells, and zero `mdmax*` fence languages in 27,324 fences. Nothing that ships here can break a document that exists today.

CHEAPEST FIRST STEP, roughly a day and it de-risks everything: freeze the renderer conformance matrix as a committed fixture. The api.github.com/markdown probes already written establish the ground truth for GitHub; micromark, micromark+gfm and marked run locally. Add Obsidian by hand (it is the one renderer that cannot be automated and the one whose behaviour the product most depends on). Every carrier decision below is downstream of that table, and right now that table exists only in $TMPDIR.
per_area.unverified:
CORPUS REPRESENTATIVENESS is the biggest limitation and I want it stated plainly. The 4,074 files are 8 corpora chosen by me, not a random sample of markdown. The AI-authored side is one person's vault plus one project's docs — a sample of n=1 author and n=1 agent stack, so "AI output" claims (76.4% status glyphs, 54.7% bold-led, 8.294 thematic breaks/1k) generalise to Claude-authored markdown in this workspace and to nothing broader without replication. The human side is stronger (top-300 GitHub READMEs by stars, plus three professional docs corpora) but the doc corpora are random 500/400/200/300-file samples with seed 7, not censuses. I did not measure any non-English corpus at all; PLAN §17's findings on normalization and bidi are untouched by anything here.

OBSIDIAN'S ACTUAL RENDERING is inference, not measurement, and it matters more than any other gap because Obsidian is the wedge (§1.5). I could not run Obsidian.
