My early-cutoff evidence is Salsa's documentation, which is primary and sufficient for the design, but the paper that names and formalises the property was not read.

7. GitHub's API rate-limited me mid-session. Comby's language list was never retrieved, so "no structural search/replace tool covers markdown" was never established even before ast-grep contradicted its strong form. I also could not enumerate Ardour's or FreeCAD's file trees; the Ardour evidence is the single WebFetch quoted above and nothing else.

8. Two claims in the design section are reasoning, not measurement. That cyclomatic complexity has no prose analogue, and that CAD's constraint solver has no discrete counterpart, are both inference — I read no source arguing either. They are the two false-analogy calls I would most want a second opinion on.

9. The latency claim composes by extrapolation. PLAN §1.1a reports re-anchoring at ~41 ms for a 446 KB / 2,225-block document. I assert that whole-vault interface recomputation can sit inside Microsoft's <100 ms "instant" band; I did not measure the composition at 5,000 files, and P6 exists specifically to settle it.

10. Absence-of-feature claims rest on published feature lists, which is weak evidence. That Marksman lacks call hierarchy and incremental caching, and that IWE has no impact preview, comes from their READMEs and features.md — not from reading their source. A shipped-but-undocumented feature would falsify those claims cheaply.

11. Not covered at all, and named so the gap is visible: proof-assistant elaboration and refinement types beyond the holes primitive; W3C PROV and C2PA for provenance; ORCID/CRediT for contributor roles; JATS retraction markup; video NLE proxies and comping specifically (I have Ardour's playlist model but nothing on comping); remote build caching; sparse checkout; and git bisect, which I judged a weak analogue without evidence either way.

The block-id sub-claim is STRONGER than stated: I grepped all 5,587 .md files in ~/Desktop/GitHub/md including node_modules and dot-directories (the census walks only 1,989) and found 0 files declaring a block id. BUT the headline conclusion is refuted by a number in the researcher's OWN census output that they silently dropped. The census prints `intra_doc_anchor 1,581` — 1,581 same-file heading references across 35 files — and the 0.61% figure excludes them from BOTH numerator and denominator with no disclosure. Those 1,581 links ARE heading references and they ARE what breaks on a heading rename: 950 of them sit in three generated tables-of-contents (Mirrors/sgnkos/features.md 401, Zephyrus/ecosystem.md 335, Mirrors/hq/docs/ecosystem.md 335). verdicts.correction: Transclusion and declared-block-id substrate: empty, confirmed, and robust to the widest possible file set. Heading-reference substrate: NOT empty — 1,581 intra-document anchors in 35 files, undisclosed and excluded from both sides of the ratio. State the ratio as 0.61% CROSS-FILE sub-file references and 9.24% including intra-document heading anchors, and say which one the design depends on.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 2] Early cutoff is the highest-yield build-system transplant AND its yield is 8.6x sensitive to durability stratification — 69.1% structural vs 8.0% full interface unchanged, the entire gap being one low-durability key (`mirrored`, 207 of 362).
verdicts.reason: Re-ran scratchpad/ec2.py on ~/Desktop/GitHub/md at 416 commits: 'STRUCTURAL interface unchanged: 250 (69.1%)' / 'FULL interface unchanged: 29 (8.0%)' / mirrored=207 — exact reproduction. I attacked it twice and it survived both. (a) Bot-artifact hypothesis: I classified each commit by subject ('via sgnk-md', 'auto-sync', 'share: set public_slug', 'Upload attachment') and re-split. BOT 83 revisions -> 15.7% struct-same; HUMAN 279 revisions -> 237 struct-same = 84.9%, HIGHER than the 69.1% headline. Not a sync-bot artifact. (b) Location hypothesis: `grep -rl '^mirrored:'` returns 203 files, all under Research/, none under Mirrors/ — so the churning key is not itself mirror boilerplate. Arithmetic checks: 250/29 = 8.621x, 250/362 = 69.06%, 29/362 = 8.01%.
verdicts.correction: Two corrections, neither fatal. (1) 'the entire gap is one low-durability key' is 93.7%, not 100%: excluding `mirrored` alone moves full-interface-unchanged from 29 to 236, closing 207 of the 221-revision gap; 14 revisions remain unexplained (measured by re-running with per-key exclusion sets). (2) The 8.6x is measured against a baseline — every frontmatter VALUE inside the cross-file interface hash — that Design 1 never proposes and no compiler would build. It is the distance from the design to a strawman, not a sensitivity to a tuning knob. The honest statement is 'the proposed interface hits 69.1%', full stop.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 3] Excel deliberately does NOT implement early cutoff, so transplanting 'the spreadsheet' would import the weaker of the two available dependency engines.
verdicts.reason: curl'd learn.microsoft.com/en-us/office/vba/excel/concepts/excel-performance/excel-improving-calculation-performance (88,571 bytes) and probed the stripped text. All three quotes verbatim-confirmed: 'Excel continues calculating cells that depend on previously calculated cells even if the value of the previously calculated cell does not change when it is calculated.'; 'The smart recalculation engine in Excel tries to minimize calculation time by continuously tracking both the precedents and dependencies for each formula...'; 'For some complex workbooks, the time taken to build and maintain the dependency trees needed for Smart Recalculation is larger than the time saved by Smart Recalculation.' So the BEHAVIOUR claim is primary-read and sound. Two problems with what is built on top. (1) 'deliberately' is inference presented under a primary-read tag — the page documents behaviour and never states intent or a design decision. (2) The kill targets a straw man. The researcher's own P1 says the spreadsheet's transplantable contribution is the CELL ADDRESS — the stable coordinate. 'Importing the weaker of the two dependency engines' only follows if the transplant is the recalc engine, which P1 explicitly says it is not.
verdicts.correction: Excel's recalc engine lacks early cutoff (verbatim-sourced). Drop 'deliberately' — unsupported by the source. And scope the kill: it rules out transplanting Excel's RECALCULATION ENGINE, not 'the spreadsheet', whose addressing model is the P1 exemplar the researcher is relying on two paragraphs earlier.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 5] Microsoft publishes the exact latency budget a document compiler should be held to, and it is a four-band UX spec, not a vibe.
verdicts.reason: The four quotes are verbatim-confirmed on the same Microsoft Learn page I fetched. The framing is wrong on three counts. (1) Attribution: I curl'd nngroup.com/articles/response-times-3-important-limits/, which states verbatim 'The basic advice regarding response times has been about the same for thirty years [Miller 1968; Card et al. 1991]' and then gives the identical thresholds — '0.1 second is about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously', '1.0 second is about the limit for the user's flow of thought to stay uninterrupted', '10 seconds is about the limit for keeping the user's attention focused on the dialogue'. Microsoft is restating a 1968 HCI result via Nielsen 1993, not publishing anything. (2) 'Four-band' miscounts: Miller/Card/Nielsen give THREE thresholds; MS restates the same three. (3) 'Spec' is wrong in kind — on the MS page these bands are descriptive guidance for choosing Excel's automatic-vs-manual calculation mode, not a conformance budget anything is 'held to'. This is a search-result presented as a discovery: the well-known citation was one fetch away.
verdicts.correction: The 0.1s / 1s / 10s response-time limits are Miller 1968 and Card et al. 1991, popularised by Nielsen (Usability Engineering, 1993, ch.5); Microsoft's Excel page is a downstream restatement. Cite Miller/Card/Nielsen, call them three thresholds, and call them HCI guidance — the budget is legitimate, the provenance claim is not.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 6] The Figma-component / prefab transplant has essentially NO substrate — human-authored cross-file block duplication is 0.14–1.23%, and the 26% headline is an artifact of a machine-generated mirror.
verdicts.reason: scratchpad/dup2.py reproduces exactly: md human-authored 198/16,156 = 1.226%; md/Research 11/7,764 = 0.142%; knowledge 16/8,098 = 0.198%; frontmatter/docs 5/1,564 = 0.320%; full-md headline 12,972/49,286 = 26.32%. The obvious attack is that the block definition was chosen to produce a small number, so I swept it six ways: keeping code fences (which the researcher strips, and which are the most component-like content), lowering the minimum block length 40 -> 20 -> 12 chars, and splitting list items into separate units. Human-authored md moves 1.23% -> 1.44% -> 1.51% -> 1.71% -> 2.51% -> 2.52%; knowledge 0.20% -> 0.50%. Worst case is a 2x move on a number that needs to move ~20x to change the conclusion. The finding is robust and the machine-generated attribution is correct.
verdicts.correction: One presentation defect: each percentage is printed adjacent to a FILE count that is not its denominator. 'md/Research only: 218 files, 11 (0.14%)' invites the reader to compute 11/218 = 5.05%; the actual denominator is 7,764 distinct blocks. Print the denominator that produced the percentage.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 7] Duplication is at the TYPE level, not the instance level — 0/253 conformance to a shipped template, 39 distinct h2 skeletons over 199 notes with the largest two at 87 and 53 files, and one semantic section under three names across 167 files with ZERO links pointing at any of them.
verdicts.reason: Claim 7 is the one own-measurement claim that cites NO script path, so I rebuilt it. Reproduces: exact h2-skeleton match to templates/synthesis-note.md = 0, strict superset = 0, and the 8 template sections are as quoted. Does NOT reproduce: I count 51 distinct h2 skeletons (claimed 39) and the largest cluster is 83 files (claimed 87); the second at 53 matches. The alias enumeration is truncated and presented as complete — I find NINE variants of the 'how I'd apply this' section totalling 175 files, not three totalling 167 (88 + 61 + 18 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1). The 0/253 denominator includes 37 notes with no h2 heading at all, which cannot structurally conform; the eligible population is 216. And under name-normalisation, 4 of the 8 template sections appear in 78–86% of notes (connections 186/216 = 86.1%, open questions 185 = 85.6%, tl;dr 175 = 81.0%, key ideas 170 = 78.7%), so '0 conformance' is an artifact of demanding exact full-skeleton equality rather than a measure of divergence. Finally, 'ZERO links point at any of them' is mathematically forced, not observed: the whole knowledge corpus contains exactly 1 heading-targeted link (census: wikilink_heading 1, wikilink_block 0, md_relative_links_with_anchor 0). Zero links point at ANY heading. That is Claim 1 restated, presented as independent corroboration.
verdicts.correction: Directionally right and the inferred-over-declared conclusion stands, but restate as: 0 of 216 h2-bearing notes match the template skeleton exactly, while 4 of its 8 sections appear in 78–86% of them; 51 distinct skeletons, largest 83 and 53; the 'how I'd apply this' section appears under NINE names across 175 files. Delete the 'zero links' line — it carries no information.

verdicts.claim: [Claim 8] PLAN §1.3's open risk — that the flagship status schema-violation demo had zero real instances — now has a real, live instance: status n=575, OUTLIERS(3) including ('ACTIVE', 2), 3/575 = 0.52%.
verdicts.reason: The arithmetic reproduces (3/575 = 0.5217%) and the frontmatter parser is correct — I checked all 23 files that grep flags for `^status: ACTIVE|in-progress` and confirmed only 9 have it in real frontmatter and only 2 carry `ACTIVE` there, so the script is not undercounting. The finding still fails on two grounds I verified directly. (1) The two ACTIVE instances are the SAME DOCUMENT: Mirrors/tred/docs/ceo-roadmap-20260515.md and Mirrors/trade/docs/ceo-roadmap-20260515.md are byte-identical, md5 de9b4010c424eb57adb836e92b28767d for both. n=1 distinct document, not 2 — a rate confused with a count via a mirrored duplicate. (2) There is no enum to violate. Decomposing the 575 status values by top-level directory: Skills/ 368, all `active`, one generator emitting one constant; Research/ 203, all `done`, a second generator emitting a second constant; Mirrors/ 3; Zephyrus/ 1. `active` and `ACTIVE` never co-occur in any population. Under the researcher's OWN Design 4 — cluster by (heading skeleton, frontmatter key set) — a tred/trade ceo-roadmap is not a member of the Skills class, so `ACTIVE` is not a class outlier at all. Claim 8 and Design 4 contradict each other.
verdicts.correction: PLAN §1.3's open risk is NOT closed. The corpus contains one hand-written case-drift instance, in a machine-mirrored copy of a document from another repo, in a directory whose 'enum' is two disjoint generator constants. 571 of 575 values are written by two scripts. A 0.52% violation rate over that denominator measures generator determinism, not authoring discipline.

verdicts.claim: [Design 3 / Design 2] Typed holes surface via `workspace/diagnostic` — 'LSP already specifies it; nobody implements it for markdown'; and 'IWE already proves the CASCADE half' of referential actions.
verdicts.reason: A single curl refutes the 'nobody' clause. raw.githubusercontent.com/artempyanykh/marksman/main/README.md, verbatim: 'Using LSP protocol it provides completion, goto definition, find references, rename refactoring, diagnostics, and more' and 'Marksman provides diagnostics for wiki-links to detect broken references and duplicate/ambiguous headings.' docs/features.md lists as shipped: 'Find references for headings and links', 'Diagnostics for wiki-links', 'Rename refactor', 'Code Lens with # references on headings'. Marksman ships for Neovim, VS Code, Emacs, Sublime, Zed, Helix, BBEdit. So markdown LSP diagnostics exist today; heading-level find-references exists today; and rename-as-CASCADE has at least TWO implementations, not the one (IWE) the researcher credits. Marksman's 'duplicate/ambiguous headings' diagnostic is also direct prior art for part of Design 4.
verdicts.correction: Narrow the claim to what is actually novel: pull-based `workspace/diagnostic` (LSP 3.17) specifically, versus marksman's push-based publishDiagnostics — and say so explicitly rather than claiming nobody does markdown diagnostics. Design 2's genuine novelty is the DECLARED action and RESTRICT/deferred-checking, not CASCADE, which is shipped by both IWE and marksman.

survived: ZERO declared ^block-ids — strengthened under my own wider test: 0 files across all 5,587 .md in ~/Desktop/GitHub/md including node_modules and dot-directories, not just the 1,989 walked
Transclusion substrate is empty: 21 edges in md (0.13%), 0 in knowledge (0.00%) — reproduced exactly; the value-flow kill on the spreadsheet transplant stands

Claim 2's early-cutoff measurement: 250/362 = 69.06% structural vs 29/362 = 8.01% full, reproduced exactly, and it survived both attacks I mounted — the human-commit-only rate is 237/279 = 84.9%, HIGHER than the headline, so it is not a sync-bot artifact

Claim 6's no-instancing-substrate finding, robust under a six-way sensitivity sweep of the block definition (keeping code fences, min length 40->20->12, splitting list items): human-authored md moves only 1.23% -> 2.52%, knowledge 0.20% -> 0.50%

Claim 4: both Salsa quotes verbatim-confirmed via raw.githubusercontent.com — backdate.md ('Backdating is when we mark a value that was computed in revision R as having last changed in some earlier revision') and algorithm.md line 77 ('If a tracked function depends (transitively) only on high durability inputs... avoiding the need to traverse the input edges one by one')
Claim 3's three Microsoft quotes and Claim 5's four latency quotes: all seven verbatim-confirmed on the fetched page
Dead-code-elimination false analogy: 6 link reference definitions in md, 0 unused; 0 in knowledge — reproduced
The core organising principle (P1 stable coordinate + P2 dependency substrate) as an analytical frame; the CLASS A/B/C split is sound reasoning even where the CLASS A substrate number is wrong
killed: Claim 8 entirely — the two ACTIVE instances are one byte-identical mirrored document (md5 de9b4010c424eb57adb836e92b28767d), and the 575-value 'enum' is two disjoint generator constants (Skills/ 368x active, Research/ 203x done) in which `active` and `ACTIVE` never co-occur. PLAN §1.3's open risk is not closed.

Claim 1's headline CONCLUSION (not its numbers) — 1,581 intra-document heading anchors printed by the researcher's own census were excluded from both sides of the ratio undisclosed; including them gives 9.24%, 15.1x the reported 0.61%
Claim 5's attribution — the latency bands are Miller 1968 / Card et al. 1991 via Nielsen 1993, verbatim on nngroup.com; Microsoft publishes nothing here, and there are three thresholds not four bands
Design 3's 'nobody implements [LSP diagnostics] for markdown' — marksman ships diagnostics, heading-level find-references, rename refactor and duplicate-heading detection across eight editors
Design 2's implicit 'IWE is the only CASCADE implementation' — marksman is a second

Claim 7's specific counts: 87 files -> 83 measured; 39 skeletons -> 51 measured; 'three names / 167 files' -> nine names / 175 files; and '0/253' uses a denominator containing 37 notes with no h2 at all

CLASS A's 'the metadata plane is densely populated (36.3%)' as a reason to BUILD THESE — 81.3% of frontmatter-bearing files are two 100%-coverage generated trees; hand-authored frontmatter is 135 files, 6.8% of the corpus
Claim 2's '8.6x sensitivity to durability stratification' as a sensitivity — it is the distance to a baseline the design never proposes
new_defects: METHOD DEFECT, the load-bearing one: the machine-generated exclusion is applied selectively, always in the direction that supports the conclusion. Mirrors/Skills are excluded as 'machine-generated boilerplate' when that KILLS a transplant (Claim 6: 26.32% -> 1.23%), but relied upon when they SUPPORT one. CLASS A's 'metadata plane is densely populated (36.3% of md files carry frontmatter)' decomposes as Skills/ 369 of 369 = 100% and Research/ 218 of 218 = 100% — 587 of 722 frontmatter files, 81.3%, from two generators; Mirrors/ (1,233 files, the largest tree) is only 4.9%. Applying Claim 6's own exclusion consistently gives 135/1,402 = 9.63%, and hand-authored frontmatter is 6.8% of the corpus. Claim 8's status population is 64.5% Mirrors+Skills and its sole 'live instance' is a mirrored duplicate. Every conclusion that rests on 'the metadata plane is dense' needs re-deriving on the human-authored subset.

DESIGN DEFECT: Design 1 is unsound for Design 4 and would silently suppress Claim 8's own flagship finding. Design 1 defines the interface hash over '(heading list with levels, outgoing link targets, declared block ids, frontmatter KEY set)' and states 'Every cross-file query (backlinks, reference counts, schema check, outline of other files) depends only on the interface hash.' A change from `status: active` to `status: ACTIVE` alters no heading, no link, no block id and no KEY — the interface hash is unchanged, the file is BACKDATED, and every dependent including the schema check is skipped. The one defect Claim 8 exists to detect is the one Design 1 guarantees to miss.

CONCEPTUAL DEFECT: 'durability stratification' is not Salsa's durability. Salsa's algorithm.md line 77 (fetched) makes durability a fast path that preserves the edge — 'avoiding the need to traverse the input edges one by one'; the dependency still exists and the answer stays correct. Design 1 instead says LOW keys are 'excluded from the interface hash by construction', which DELETES the dependency. Any query that legitimately reads a LOW key returns a stale answer. Excluding a key nothing depends on is correct dependency scoping, not durability, and it does not need Salsa to justify it.

EVIDENCE DEFECT: Claim 7 is the only own-measurement claim with no cited script, and it is also the only one whose numbers failed to reproduce (87 -> 83, 39 -> 51, three variants -> nine). An own-measurement tag without a reproducible artifact is a secondary claim wearing a primary tag.

PRESENTATION DEFECT: ratios printed next to non-denominators. 'md/Research only: 218 files, 11 (0.14%)' reads as 11/218 = 5.05%; the real denominator is 7,764 distinct blocks. Same shape in the other three Claim 6 rows.

SCOPE DEFECT, disclosed here for completeness: the census walks 1,989 of the 5,587 .md files in ~/Desktop/GitHub/md — 1,547 are excluded from Mirrors/ alone because they sit under dot-directories (NOT node_modules, which I checked: 0 Mirrors .md files are under node_modules). The '2,262 files' figure is 1,989 + 273 and is not the corpus size. The exclusion is defensible but undisclosed. I re-tested the block-id sub-claim over the full 5,587 and it holds, so this does not change Claim 1's surviving half.

MINOR: the Salsa backdate quote is presented as verbatim but silently strips the source's reference-link brackets ('an older [memo] M' -> 'an older memo M'). Harmless here, but the evidence discipline says quote verbatim.

per_area.title: What to inline first — the context budget as a measured problem
per_area.headline: The single largest lever in the brief — "deleting near-miss content, up to 65% (GSM-NoOp)" — was refuted for frontier models in a March-2026 replication where only 12.4% of distractors survived a relevance audit and the audited drop was 0–2pp, statistically indistinguishable from zero; the near-miss effect survives only in RAG (Liu et al. Appendix B, Cuconasu +35%, Jin et al. hard negatives), and the correct reframing is not "models are distracted" but "inclusion is itself a relevance assertion the model correctly honours" — which makes MDMAX's job selection discipline, not model babysitting.

findings.claim: The brief's NoLiMa sentence is wrong on three counts: it is 32K not 128K, the baseline is <1K short-length not 32K, and the current paper says 11 of 13 models, not 10 of 12 (that was v1, superseded 2025-07-09 and again 2026-08-01). The error understates the finding — degradation appears at 32K, not 128K.
findings.evidence: arxiv.org/abs/2502.05167 (current): "We evaluate 13 popular LLMs that claim to support contexts of at least 128K tokens. While they perform well in short contexts (<1K), performance degrades significantly as context length increases. At 32K, for instance, 11 models drop below 50% of their strong short-length baselines. Even GPT-4o ... experiences a reduction from an almost-perfect baseline of 99.3% to 69.7%." v1 (arxiv.org/abs/2502.05167v1): "We evaluate 12 popular LLMs ... At 32K, for instance, 10 models drop below 50%". export.arxiv.org API: published 2025-02-07, updated 2026-08-01.

findings.claim: The brief's RULER figure ("only 4 of 10 models genuinely handle 32K") is the withdrawn v1 number. Current RULER evaluates 17 models and says only half hold up at 32K.
findings.evidence: arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654 (current): "We evaluate 17 long-context LMs with 13 representative tasks in RULER ... only half of them can maintain satisfactory performance at the length of 32K." v1: "We evaluate ten long-context LMs ... only four models (GPT-4, Command-R, Yi-34B, and Mixtral) can maintain satisfactory performance at the length of 32K." Updated 2024-08-06 and 2026-07-31.

findings.claim: The brief's Liu et al. number (52.9% at position 10 of 20) is misattributed — 52.9% is LongChat-13B at index 14 of 30 docs. The correct GPT-3.5-Turbo figure is 53.8%, and the real headline is far stronger than the brief states: in the 30-document setting GPT-3.5-Turbo is below its own closed-book score at 5 of 7 gold positions, and adding 29 non-gold documents costs 37.8pp versus the oracle.
findings.evidence: ar5iv Table 1: "GPT-3.5-Turbo 56.1% 88.3%" (Closed-Book, Oracle). Table 6 (20 docs): "GPT-3.5-Turbo 75.8% 57.2% 53.8% 55.4% 63.2%" for Index 0/4/9/14/19. Table 7 (30 docs): "GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) 73.4% 55.1% 50.5% 50.9% 51.8% 54.9% 63.7%"; its closed-book is 56.0%, so 55.1/50.5/50.9/51.8/54.9 are all below it = 5 of 7. Oracle 88.3% − 50.5% = 37.8pp (own arithmetic).

findings.claim: REFUTATION OF THE BRIEF'S LARGEST CLAIMED LEVER. A March-2026 replication of GSM-NoOp on GPT-4o, Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Haiku 4.5 reproduced the original collapse only on unaudited distractors; after auditing for genuine irrelevance, 88% of distractors were thrown out and the remaining drop was 0–2pp and statistically indistinguishable from zero.
findings.evidence: greaterwrong.com/posts/Ze4C99Dasj74YKCFh (Sturb, 5 Jun 2026): "Only samples GPT-5.5 classified as TRULY_IRRELEVANT were retained: 117 out of 945 (12.4%). The rest were excluded from primary evaluation because a reasonable solver might fold them into the calculation." ... "The two auditors disagree on borderline cases (κ = 0.32; 12% vs 36% kept), but every audited drop is statistically indistinguishable from zero." ... "only a minor decrease to the models' scores (0-2 percentage points, none statistically distinguishable from zero)." Also: "Apple did not release the GSM-NoOp dataset." Code: github.com/BenSturgeon/gsm-symbolic-revisited.

findings.claim: Even in the original paper, "up to 65%" was one 3.8B model, not the typical case — a detail the brief's phrasing loses.
findings.evidence: arxiv.org/html/2410.05229v2 §4.4: "there is a catastrophic performance decline across all tested models, with the Phi-3-mini model experiencing over a 65% drop, and even stronger models such as o1-preview showing significant declines." The "unrecoverable by in-context examples" claim is verbatim correct — "the significant drop in performance cannot be recovered, even when using the exact same question's variation as shots (NoOp-Symb) or when using different questions with different GSM-NoOp ... as shots" — but is immediately qualified: "Fig. 8(c) shows that some models can perform significantly better."

findings.claim: The near-miss result DOES generalise beyond arithmetic — but via an older, RAG-based literature that predates GSM-NoOp by 9–15 months and is untouched by the 2026 refutation. Liu et al. ran the exact ablation the brief needs.
findings.evidence: Liu et al. Appendix B, verbatim: "We also run multi-document question answering experiments with random Wikipedia documents as distractors, which allows us to ablate the impact of retrieved distractors (hard negatives) ... Although all models have higher absolute accuracy in this setting, they surprisingly still struggle to reason over their entire input context, indicating that their performance degradation is not solely due to an inability to identify relevant documents." Cuconasu et al. (arxiv 2401.14887) abstract: "the retriever's highest-scoring documents that are not directly relevant to the query (e.g., do not contain the answer) negatively impact the effectiveness of the LLM. Even more surprising, we discovered that adding random documents in the prompt improves the LLM accuracy by up to 35%." Jin et al. (2410.05983): "identifying the detrimental impact of retrieved 'hard negatives' as a key contributor."

findings.claim: Liu et al.'s Appendix B splits the brief's single lever into two independent mechanisms: near-missness sets the LEVEL, position sets the CURVE. You cannot fix lost-in-the-middle by cleaning near-misses, and you cannot fix near-misses by reordering. MDMAX needs both a selection policy and an ordering policy; either alone leaves the other loss on the table.
findings.evidence: Derived from Liu App. B ("higher absolute accuracy ... still struggle to reason over their entire input context") crossed with Jin et al. §4, which shows reordering helps only at large k. Both effects persist under the other's manipulation.

findings.claim: The sandwich/zigzag reorder that LangChain and LlamaIndex both ship is validated by exactly one paper, and only in the large-k regime — at small k the gain is explicitly negligible. Neither library cites that validation; both cite only the descriptive Liu et al. paper.
findings.evidence: Jin et al. ar5iv 2410.05983 §4: "retrieval reordering yields negligible improvements with smaller retrieval sets, but significantly and consistently outperforms the original ordering when the number of retrieved passages is large." Formula: "Order(d_i) = (i+1)/2 if mod(i,2)=1; (k+1)−i/2 if mod(i,2)=0". LangChain langchain_community/document_transformers/long_context_reorder.py: "Lost in the middle reorder: the less relevant documents will be at the middle of the list and more relevant elements at beginning / end. See: https://arxiv.org/abs//2307.03172" — no other citation. LlamaIndex core/postprocessor/node.py class LongContextReorder cites the same single URL. Both implement the identical alternating insert(0)/append.

findings.claim: 2026 work shows the U-shape is not universal and that the shipped reordering fixes can fail outright: in multimodal KB-VQA the shape flips to pure primacy by 16–26 points, and MMR, oracle reranking and rank-based reordering all leave the gap intact.
findings.evidence: arXiv 2606.16494 "Lost at the End: Primacy Bias in Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Question Answering" (verified live via export.arxiv.org API): "The shape flips from U to primacy: gold-at-first beats gold-at-last by 16 to 26 points on every reader-by-benchmark cell, an effect we call 'Lost at the End'. ... On a frozen reader, three retrieval-side fixes (MMR, oracle reranking, rank-based reordering) all leave the gap intact (no separable improvement)." Companion: arXiv 2606.27793 finds one-pass position-bias correction closes only 37% of the gap to iterative sorting.

findings.claim: The brief's Anthropic token figures are inflated because they were chars/4 estimates. Re-derived today with tiktoken o200k_base: the container is 1,210,912 tokens, not ~1.64M — the estimate was 35.4% high. Byte ratio 168.78x is correct; the decision-relevant TOKEN ratio is 137.2x. The container is 6.05x a 200K window and 1.21x a 1M window, not the ~8x and ~1.6x previously recorded.
findings.evidence: curl 2026-08-01: https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt = 38,847 bytes / 8,825 tokens / 174 entries / 1 H2 ("## Docs") / 174 of 174 carrying a description. https://code.claude.com/docs/llms-full.txt = 6,556,407 bytes / 1,210,912 tokens. 6556407/38847 = 168.78; 1210912/8825 = 137.21; 6556407/4 = 1,639,101 vs 1,210,912 → 35.4% overstatement.

findings.claim: A flat, depth-1 index has a measured breaking point: at Anthropic's production density (50.7 tokens/entry) it saturates a 200K window at ~3,943 entries. On a real personal vault the index alone is already 157% of a 200K window — the index IS the budget problem at vault scale, which llms.txt's one-level design cannot express.
findings.evidence: Own measurement, tiktoken o200k_base: 8,825/174 = 50.72 tok/entry → 200,000/50.72 = 3,943 entries. On ~/Desktop/GitHub/md + ~/Desktop/GitHub/knowledge (4,710 .md, node_modules excluded): total inlined 23,965,059 tokens; llms.txt-shaped index with descriptions = 314,481 tokens = 66.77 tok/entry = 157.2% of a 200K budget; name-only index = 206,304 tokens. Inline/index ratio 76.2x (with desc) and 116.2x (name only) — independently the same order as Anthropic's 137x.

findings.claim: KILLS THE OBVIOUS PRIORITY FUNCTION. Aider's PageRank-over-the-link-graph does not transfer to prose: 90.0% of a real 4,289-file vault is orphaned (no resolved in- or out-link), Gini of PageRank is 0.225 (near-uniform), and PageRank's top 174 files overlap the size-ranked top 174 by only 6 of 174. On a deliberately cross-linked corpus it works (48.0% orphans, Gini 0.542, top-174 = 80.6% of mass). Dense linking is guaranteed in code by imports; in prose it is an authoring discipline most vaults lack.
findings.evidence: Own measurement (scratchpad/graphrank.py, damping 0.85, 40 iterations, wikilinks + relative .md links resolved by filename stem). md vault: files=4289, wikilinks_seen=5432, edges_resolved=2174, orphans=3859 (90.0%), Gini=0.225, top-174 = 24.1% of PageRank mass, PageRank∩size top-174 = 6/174. knowledge vault: files=421, orphans=202 (48.0%), Gini=0.542, top-174 = 80.6%, overlap 103/174.

findings.claim: THE TOC COST IS NOW MEASURED, AND IT IS CHEAPEST EXACTLY WHERE IT MATTERS MOST. H1–H3 heading lines are 2.72% of a 24M-token corpus, and the fraction falls monotonically with document size: 8.11% of the smallest decile down to 1.97% of the largest (12,477–297,499 tokens), median 419 tokens absolute. So the TOC question is: spend ~2% for an unmeasured benefit.
findings.evidence: Own measurement, tiktoken o200k_base, 4,660 files ≥50 tokens, deciles by file size. Median TOC-tokens / median TOC-% / median h1-3 count by decile: d1 13/8.11%/2 … d6 82/4.08%/13 … d9 200/2.30%/27 … d10 419/1.97%/54. Corpus total 23,963,327 tokens, h1-h3 heading lines 652,369 = 2.72%.

findings.claim: A TOC IS A SELF-INFLICTED NEAR-DUPLICATE, and the corpus is already saturated with near-duplicates — which is the specific, testable mechanism by which a TOC could HURT, and nobody has tested it. 86.1% of heading occurrences already share their text with another heading; the single string "overview" appears 441 times. Adding a TOC doubles every heading string in every document.
findings.evidence: Own measurement over 4,710 files: heading texts 77,887 total / 17,950 distinct; 67,047 occurrences (86.1%) non-unique. Heading PATHS: 77,887 total / 27,778 distinct; 63,054 (81.0%) non-unique. Top repeats: overview 441, purpose 440, capabilities 439, dependencies 435, when to use 428. Paragraph blocks (≥40 normalized chars): 161,043 total, 134,714 (83.65%) exact normalized duplicates of another block. On the clean, human-authored 421-file knowledge corpus alone it is still 58.2% of headings and 16.71% of blocks. Chroma's own definition of the hazard: "Distractors are topically related to the needle, but do not quite answer the question" (research.trychroma.com/context-rot).

findings.claim: Humans essentially never write a table of contents into a markdown file — 0.64% of 4,710 files, and 0 of 421 in the clean corpus. Whatever MDMAX emits, an inline TOC is a construct with almost no precedent in the substrate it is imitating.
findings.evidence: Own measurement, regex `^\s{0,3}#{1,6}\s*(table of contents|contents|toc)\s*$` case-insensitive, fenced code excluded: 30 / 4,710 = 0.64%; 0 / 421 in ~/Desktop/GitHub/knowledge. Headings per file p50=10, p90=39, p99=96, max=756; files with zero headings 49 (1.0%).

findings.claim: THE MOST-DEPLOYED CODING AGENT SHIPS NO INDEX AND NO PRIORITY FUNCTION AT ALL — the vendor's own word is "naively". Claude Code's answer to "what to inline first" is one file eagerly plus grep, explicitly to avoid stale indexes. Its only shipped selection heuristic is a recency rule of k=5.
findings.evidence: anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents (2025-09-29), verbatim: "Claude Code is an agent that employs this hybrid model: CLAUDE.md files are naively dropped into context up front, while primitives like glob and grep allow it to navigate its environment and retrieve files just-in-time, effectively bypassing the issues of stale indexing and complex syntax trees." And: "The agent can then continue with this compressed context plus the five most recently accessed files." The same post states the knapsack objective verbatim: "good context engineering means finding the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of some desired outcome" — and hedges the whole structure question: "the exact formatting of prompts is likely becoming less important as models become more capable."

findings.claim: The other shipped budget policies are greedy and unprioritised. OpenAI Codex caps AGENTS.md at 32,768 bytes by default and consumes that budget first-come-first-served down the ancestor chain, truncating mid-file. Aider's repo map is a complete priority function (personalized PageRank + binary-search packing to 1,024 tokens) with, in its two canonical documents, zero published A/B.
findings.evidence: openai/codex codex-rs/core/config.schema.json: "project_doc_max_bytes": {"default": 32768, "description": "Maximum number of bytes to include from an AGENTS.md project doc file."}. codex-rs/core/src/agents_md.rs: `let mut remaining: u64 = max_total as u64;` … `if size > remaining { data.truncate(remaining as usize); }` … tracing::warn!("project doc exceeds remaining budget; truncating"). Aider aider/repomap.py: `map_tokens=1024`, `map_mul_no_files=8`, `padding = 4096`, `ranked = nx.pagerank(G, weight="weight", personalization=..., dangling=...)`, `personalize = 100 / len(fnames)`, `middle = min(int(max_map_tokens // 25), num_tags)` with `ok_err = 0.15` binary search. aider.chat/2023/10/22/repomap.html and website/docs/repomap.md contain no benchmark, no ablation and no on/off comparison.

findings.claim: llms.txt's reference implementation defaults to DROPPING the Optional section, and its size function measures characters, not tokens — so the one prioritisation mechanism in the spec is a boolean, and the one cost signal is in the wrong unit.
findings.evidence: AnswerDotAI/llms-txt llms_txt/core.py: `def create_ctx(txt, optional=False, n_workers=None)` and CLI `def llms_txt2ctx(fname:str, optional:bool_arg=False, ...)` — Optional excluded unless asked for. `def get_sizes(ctx): return {o.tag:{p.title:len(p.children[0]) ...}}` — `len()` over a string is characters. `_doc(kw)` also still contains a stray `print(dict(kw))` debug statement.

findings.claim: HELMET undermines every heuristic derived from needle tests — including the shuffled-haystack result the brief leans on. NIAH scores do not predict downstream performance, and the categories that do matter correlate poorly with each other.
findings.evidence: arxiv.org/abs/2410.02694: "we find that (1) synthetic tasks like NIAH do not reliably predict downstream performance; (2) the diverse categories in HELMET exhibit distinct trends and low correlations with each other; and (3) while most LCLMs achieve perfect NIAH scores, open-source models significantly lag behind closed ones when tasks require full-context reasoning." Chroma's shuffle claim is verbatim correct — "Across all 18 models and needle-haystack configurations, we observe a consistent pattern that models perform better on shuffled haystacks than on logically structured ones" — but the same page also says "Not all 18 models are included in each experiement due to context window or thinking_budget constraints", so "all 18" is the roster, not necessarily the n of that cell; and the manipulated text is the irrelevant HAYSTACK, not the content the model must use.

findings.claim: Two 2026 results argue for co-locating related content and against defensive prompt wording — both directly actionable for MDMAX and neither in the brief.
findings.evidence: arXiv 2601.02023 "Not All Needles Are Found" (verified via export.arxiv.org): "We identify two critical failure modes: Distributional Collapse, where performance degrades significantly when evidence is dispersed; and a Safety Tax, where anti-hallucination prompts cause over-conservative refusal of present facts and evidence, sharply reducing accuracy." Nearest measured structure-injection result: arXiv 2505.22950 StrucSum, "on ArXiv, it increases FactCC and SummaC by 19.2% and 8.0% points" — but "The ablation study shows that the combination of multiple strategies does not yield clear performance gains", i.e. stacking structure signals does not compound.

unclaimed: A document index that carries the COST of each entry. Anthropic's 174-entry index ships a title and a description but no size; llms.txt concedes size matters only in a Python function (get_sizes) that never reaches the file, and measures characters. Nobody publishes `- [title](path) (~4.2k tok): description`. The consumer is being asked to solve a knapsack while being shown only the value side. This is a few lines of code and it is the single cheapest unbuilt thing in the whole area.

An outline hoisted into the index rather than inlined into the document. Every system either inlines a TOC (books, Sphinx single-file builders) or ships titles only (llms.txt, Anthropic, gitingest). Nobody ships a third tier — heading paths for all documents, collected in the index — which costs the measured 2.72% once, gives sub-document routing, and avoids duplicating every heading string inside the document body where the near-miss density is already 86%.

A priority function that reports WHY each item was selected, per item, in the emitted artifact. Aider computes a PageRank and throws the reason away; repomix ranks by directory; Codex uses ancestor path order. No tool emits `included: README.md (special-file rule)`, `included: auth.md (heading-path match: "session")`, `omitted: legacy/ (rank 0.001, budget)`. Without this the selection is unauditable and the eval in section 5 below is impossible to run against a shipped system.

A graph-density gate on graph-based ranking. Aider assumes the link graph exists because in code it does. Nothing in the wild measures orphan rate first and falls back. The measured 90%-orphan prose case makes PageRank a no-op dressed as a ranking, and no shipped tool detects that condition.

Cross-document near-duplicate collapse at pack time. The literature says hard negatives are the poison and my corpus says 83.65% of blocks are exact normalized duplicates, yet every packer (repomix, gitingest, Codex, CLAUDE.md imports) concatenates verbatim. Nobody replaces the 441st copy of an '## Overview' section with a pointer to the first.

A budget policy that refuses rather than truncates. Codex truncates AGENTS.md mid-file at 32 KiB; repomix errors only when one leaf alone exceeds the limit. Asciidoctor's model — warn on stderr AND leave a visible breadcrumb in the output — has never been applied to LLM context packing, where a silently half-eaten document is strictly worse than an honestly omitted one.

Any measurement whatsoever of whether a table of contents at the top of a document helps a model. Two targeted searches returned nothing. The nearest neighbours are StrucSum (sentence graph signals, not an outline), Anthropic's contextual retrieval (per-chunk prefix for retrieval, not comprehension) and EDU compression. The brief's flag that this is untested folklore is confirmed, not merely unrefuted.

A k-threshold on reordering. Jin et al. proved the sandwich helps only at large k and is negligible at small k; LangChain and LlamaIndex both apply it unconditionally to any list handed to them, including k=3. Nobody ships the threshold, and the 2026 multimodal result shows at least one regime where the sandwich is worthless.
per_area.design:
WHAT SHIPS — three artifacts, all of them ordinary markdown, all degrading to something a human and an unaware AI read correctly.

(1) THE ROOT INDEX (`mdmax pack --index`). One line per document, Anthropic's measured production shape plus the one field nobody ships: `- [Title](rel/path.md) (~4.2k tok): one-sentence description.` Cost measured at 50.7 tok/entry (Anthropic) to 66.8 (auto-generated descriptions). Hard rule: refuse to emit a FLAT index past 2,500 entries — measured saturation is ~2,995–3,943 entries against a 200K budget, and a root that does not fit is not a root. Past the cap, group by directory into a two-level index and stop there; Sphinx's canonical example is :maxdepth: 2, Google refuses a third sitemap level, and my own vault's index is already 157% of a 200K window at 4,710 files. Cycle handling copies Sphinx exactly — an ancestor stack, not a global visited set, so a DAG with two parents pointing at one child still works — plus Asciidoctor's absolute depth guard as a second net.

(2) THE OUTLINE TIER (`--outline`, off by default). H1–H3 heading paths for every document, collected IN THE INDEX, not inlined at the top of each document. This is the design's one non-obvious move and it falls straight out of the measurements: the outline costs 2.72% of the corpus (1.97% median for large documents, 419 tokens), and hoisting it buys sub-document routing while avoiding the self-duplication hazard — inlining a TOC doubles every heading string inside a body where 86.1% of heading texts are already non-unique. Cost identical, hazard removed, and it is the arm the experiment in §5 can overturn.

(3) THE PACKED BODY (`mdmax pack --budget 128k`). Selection is an explicit, ordered, auditable policy:
  a. user-named paths (unbounded, never dropped),
  b. special files — README / AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / CONTRIBUTING / CHANGELOG, copying aider's `filter_important_files` list verbatim,
  c. lexical match of the request against title + heading path (BM25; the heading path is a free author-supplied context prefix, which is Anthropic's contextual-retrieval mechanism at zero LLM cost),
  d. link-graph rank ONLY IF the graph earns it — gate on measured orphan rate < 50%; at 90% orphans PageRank is a uniform distribution wearing a ranking's clothes, and its top-174 disagrees with a size ranking on 168 of 174 files,
  e. recency, as the terminal fallback (Claude Code's own k=5 rule generalised).
Near-duplicate collapse runs at pack time: normalize whitespace and punctuation, hash blocks, and replace repeats with `<!-- mdmax: identical to <path>#<anchor> -->`. This is the one intervention the near-miss literature unambiguously supports and the one my corpus says will actually fire (83.65% duplicate blocks vault-wide, 16.71% in the clean corpus).

ORDERING. Rank order below k=10; Jin et al.'s sandwich at k≥10. The threshold is the paper's own boundary ("negligible improvements with smaller retrieval sets"), and it is off by default for non-retrieval packs because the 2026 multimodal result shows a regime where the sandwich buys nothing at all.

DEGRADATION BEHAVIOUR. Never truncate mid-document — Codex's `data.truncate(remaining)` is the anti-pattern. Drop the whole document and leave Asciidoctor's breadcrumb, expressed as an HTML comment so it is valid CommonMark, invisible in every renderer, and legible to any model: `<!-- mdmax: omitted docs/legacy.md (~18.4k tok) — budget exhausted at 128k -->`. A consumer that knows nothing about MDMAX sees a normal markdown document with a linked index at the top. A consumer that does can read the trailing manifest. No new node type, no new opener, no runtime — the index is a list, the outline is a list, the breadcrumb is a comment.

CLI SURFACE.
  `mdmax pack [paths] --budget 128k --index|--full --outline --order rank|sandwich --explain --manifest out.json`
  `mdmax index [paths] --max-flat 2500 --depth 2 --sizes`
  `mdmax budget [paths]` → prints the knapsack before you spend it: total tokens, index cost, outline cost, orphan rate, duplicate-block fraction, and the depth at which a flat index stops fitting.
`--explain` puts the selection reason on every line; `--manifest` writes what was included, what was dropped, the priority score, and the rule that fired. That manifest is what makes §5 runnable against the shipped binary rather than a research fork.
per_area.measurement:
THE OBJECTIVE, FORMALISED FIRST (§3 of the brief). This is a knapsack with a measured cost side and an unmeasured payoff side, plus a term nobody models.
  maximize  Σ v(d_i | q, S)      subject to  Σ c(d_i) ≤ B
where c(d) = tokens(d), exactly measurable, and v is NOT separable — that is the whole difficulty. Three non-separabilities are now measured or cited: (i) POSITION, v depends on rank(i) within S (Liu et al.: 73.4% at index 0 vs 50.5% at index 9 of 30, same document); (ii) ADJACENCY, v(d_i) falls when S contains near-misses of d_i (Liu App. B, Cuconasu, Jin et al.); (iii) DISPERSION, v of a fact falls when its evidence is split across many members of S (2601.02023 "Distributional Collapse"). So the honest statement is: this is a QUADRATIC knapsack with a position-dependent objective, and every shipped system solves the LINEAR relaxation and hopes. A priority function therefore needs four inputs — a query-relevance score, a redundancy penalty against already-selected items, a position slot, and a per-item token cost — and the only one every tool actually has today is cost.

THE EXPERIMENT.

Corpus: the 4,710-file vault (~24M tokens, already characterised here: p50 1,552 tok, p99 81,753, top 1% holds 20.4% of mass, 86.1% non-unique headings) plus docs/engine of the frontmatter repo. Held fixed across all arms.

Tasks: 300 items, generated by CONSTRUCTION so every verifier is rules-based, not a judge (cheapest applicable verifier first). Three families, 100 each:
  T1 LOCATE-AND-QUOTE — a span is held out of the index; the model must return it verbatim. Verifier: exact normalized string match.
  T2 MULTI-HOP SYNTHESIS — an answer requires k∈{3,5} facts drawn from distinct documents, deliberately including at least one document whose heading path collides with a decoy's (the measured 86%-collision condition, weaponised). Verifier: all k required strings/numbers present AND the decoy's number absent. The decoy check is the near-miss measurement.
  T3 ABSENCE — the fact is genuinely not in the corpus. Verifier: correct refusal. This arm exists to catch the Safety Tax and to stop an arm winning by becoming credulous.

Arms — a 3×3×2 factorial plus two controls, all paired on the same 300 tasks:
  ROOT ∈ {none (grep-only, the Claude Code null hypothesis), flat index, index + hoisted outline}
  TOC ∈ {none, TOC inlined at top of every packed document, outline hoisted to index only}
  ORDER ∈ {rank, sandwich}
  Controls: full-inline-until-truncated (the naive baseline every tool actually ships), and random-selection-at-same-budget (the Cuconasu control — if random ties your priority function, your priority function is decoration).
Budgets: 8K, 32K, 128K. Models: 3, spanning at least two vendors, run at temperature 0.

Sample size: paired design, McNemar. To detect 5pp at α=.05 / 80% power needs 471 discordant-eligible pairs at 15% discordance, 628 at 20%, 942 at 30%. 300 tasks × 3 models = 900 paired observations per arm-contrast, which covers the 20% case and is marginal at 30% — so report the observed discordance and widen if it exceeds 25%. Bootstrap CIs must be TEMPLATE-CLUSTERED, not row-level: tasks generated from the same template are not independent, which is exactly the correction the 2026 GSM replication had to make. Every arm runs 3 times; one run is an anecdote.

PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTIONS (I commit to these so they can refute me):
  P1. Index + selective read beats full-inline-until-truncated at 8K and 32K by ≥10pp on T2, and the gap CLOSES to <3pp at 128K. If the index does not win at 8K it does not win anywhere.
  P2. Inlined TOC-at-top does NOT beat outline-hoisted-to-index on T1 or T2, and is WORSE on T2 by ≥2pp, because it doubles every heading string in a corpus where 86.1% of headings already collide. This is the sharp, falsifiable form of the untested folklore.
  P3. Sandwich beats rank order at 128K by ≥3pp and is indistinguishable (<1pp) at 8K — Jin et al.'s k-boundary, reproduced on documents rather than passages.
  P4. Near-duplicate collapse is worth more than any ordering change: ≥5pp on T2, larger than P3's effect.
  P5. Random-selection-at-budget beats no-selection-at-budget, replicating Cuconasu's direction on prose; if random also ties the priority function, report that loudly.
  P6. T3 (absence) accuracy FALLS as budget rises in every arm — more context, more confabulation.

KILL CRITERIA FOR THE EXPERIMENT ITSELF: if arm-to-arm variance across the 3 repeats exceeds the smallest effect being claimed, no result is reportable; if T1 saturates above 95% in every arm the task is too easy and must be re-cut before any conclusion about T2 is trusted.
per_area.kill_condition:
Three, in order of how likely each is to fire.

(1) THE INDEX IS THEATRE. If prediction P1 fails — index + selective read does not beat naive truncation at 8K/32K — MDMAX should stop building a root file and do what the most-deployed agent already does: ship good filenames and let the consumer grep. This is not a hypothetical alternative, it is Anthropic's stated design, in their own words: CLAUDE.md is "naively dropped into context" and everything else is glob and grep, chosen "effectively bypassing the issues of stale indexing". An index also carries a cost the null option does not: it goes stale the moment a file changes, which is a maintenance liability for a product whose core promise is that the file stays ordinary markdown.

(2) THE MODEL DOES NOT NEED HELP AT THE BUDGET USERS ACTUALLY HAVE. If P1's gap is already <3pp at 128K, then the entire selection apparatus buys nothing for any corpus under ~1M tokens, and the correct product is a packer with a byte counter, not a compiler with a priority function. Anthropic's own hedge points this way — "the exact formatting of prompts is likely becoming less important as models become more capable" — and the direction of travel across every result here is that 2024 failures shrink on 2026 models (the GSM-NoOp collapse went from 65% to statistically zero in eighteen months). Any MDMAX feature whose justification is a 2023–2024 measurement should be assumed to be decaying beneath it.

(3) THE PRIORITY FUNCTION CANNOT BEAT RANDOM. If P5's second clause fires — random selection at the same budget ties the ranked selection — then the ranking is decoration and MDMAX should ship budget enforcement, near-duplicate collapse and honest omission breadcrumbs, and nothing else. The 90%-orphan measurement already says the graph-based half of any ranking is dead on arrival for general prose; if the lexical half also fails to separate from random, there is no priority function to build.

The whole direction survives only if selection beats both truncation AND randomness at a budget somebody actually has.
per_area.effort:
SHIPPABLE TODAY, no new research: 3–5 days.
  - `mdmax budget` (token counting, orphan rate, duplicate-block fraction, flat-index saturation point): ~1 day. Every measurement in this report is already written and running in scratchpad/measure.py and scratchpad/graphrank.py; it is a port, not a build. Depends only on a tokenizer.
  - Index emission with size hints, the 2,500-entry flat cap, and Sphinx-style ancestor-stack cycle detection: ~1 day. Depends on the existing block/heading-path machinery the repo already has from the re-anchoring work.
  - Outline tier (heading paths into the index): ~0.5 day. Pure reuse of the same heading-path extraction.
  - Near-duplicate collapse + pointer replacement: ~1 day. Needs the canonicalization step §12 of the plan already requires for hashing, so it is nearly free once that lands.
  - Honest omission breadcrumbs, `--explain`, `--manifest`: ~0.5 day.
  - Ordering (rank / sandwich with the k=10 threshold): ~2 hours. It is fifteen lines; LangChain's is nine.

BLOCKED ON THE EXPERIMENT: the TOC placement default, the k threshold's exact value, and whether the lexical/graph blend weights are worth tuning at all. Ship the conservative arm (outline hoisted, sandwich off below k=10) and treat every one of those as a flag, not a decision.

THE EXPERIMENT: 2–3 weeks and real money. 300 constructed tasks with rules-based verifiers is the expensive part (~1 week of authoring, and it must be construction-generated or the verifiers become judges and the whole thing needs a κ≥0.7 alignment study first). The run itself is 300 tasks × 18 arms × 3 budgets × 3 models × 3 repeats ≈ 145,800 calls; at 128K budgets that is dominated by input tokens and is the single largest line item — prompt caching on the fixed corpus prefix is mandatory, not optional. Budget the pilot first: 50 tasks × the 4 most-separating arms, to measure the discordance rate before committing to the full n.

HARD DEPENDENCIES: a tokenizer (tiktoken is not installed in this repo's environment — I had to build a scratch venv; that is a real setup step, not an assumption). Nothing else. No new parser, no runtime, no registry — which is the point.
per_area.unverified:
WHAT I COULD NOT VERIFY, WITH ITS ACTUAL TIER.

- The Chroma "shuffled haystack" result is primary-read for the CLAIM but the supporting numbers live in figures I could not read from the HTML. I have the sentence verbatim and the roster of 18 models; I do NOT have the effect size, and the page itself says "Not all 18 models are included in each experiement", so the n of that specific cell is unknown. Treat "all 18" as the roster, not the sample. Anyone repeating this figure should say so.
- GSM-Symbolic's o1-preview NoOp drop: the paper says o1-preview shows "significant declines" and gives two qualitative failure examples, but the per-model NoOp numbers are in Figure 8, which is an image. I could not extract them. The only NoOp number I can state with a source is Phi-3-mini's ">65%" and GPT-4o's "94.9% to 63.0%", and the latter is the 2026 replication's characterisation of the original figure, not a quote from the paper's text — that one is SECONDARY, not primary-read.
- The 2026 GSM replication is a LessWrong post, not peer-reviewed, by a single author, on LLM-GENERATED distractors because Apple never released GSM-NoOp. Its own caveats are load-bearing and I am repeating them rather than smoothing them: auditor κ = 0.32 is weak agreement (12% vs 36% kept), and "These may be systematically easier or different from Apple's hand-crafted distractors." I did not run the code. I am treating it as strong enough to overturn the brief's headline because its unaudited arm reproduces the original effect — but a κ of 0.32 is thin ice and the honest posture is "the 65% claim is not safe to cite", not "the effect is zero".
- The three 2026 arXiv papers (2606.16494, 2606.27793, 2601.02023) are verified to EXIST and their abstracts are quoted verbatim from the arXiv API, but I read abstracts only, not full texts. Tier them primary-read-of-abstract; the 16–26pp primacy figure and the "three retrieval-side fixes leave the gap intact" claim are the authors' own summary, unaudited by me.
- The WebSearch snippet claiming 2026 work "proves the full U-shape is already present at random initialization" does NOT match the abstract of the paper it appears to be describing (2502.01951 says causal masking biases toward EARLIER positions and describes a trade-off with RoPE decay). I did not find a primary source for the random-initialization claim and I am not repeating it. Search-only, and probably wrong.
- Aider "has no published A/B" is an absence claim over two documents I read completely (website/docs/repomap.md and the 2023-10-22 blog post). I did NOT exhaustively search the aider repo's benchmark directory — a GitHub code-search attempt was rate-limited. So the correct statement is "no A/B in its two canonical documents", not "no A/B exists anywhere".
- Cursor's codebase indexing is entirely unexamined. It is closed and undocumented at the level this question needs; I did not attempt it and it is a genuine gap in the §4 production survey. repomix and gitingest were read in the repo's PRIOR research pass (docs/engine/research/wf-findings-2026-08-01.md) and I did not re-verify them this session — cite those two as the prior pass's primary-read, not mine.
- LlamaIndex's LongContextReorder: I read the class and traced the algorithm by hand and it is correct (highest-scored items land outermost). That trace is INFERENCE from reading code, not an executed test.
- The Cuconasu +35% figure is primary-read of the ABSTRACT only. I did not open the paper body, so I cannot say which dataset, which model, or which k that 35% is measured at. It should not be quoted as a general magnitude.
- My own corpus measurements: single-corpus, single-author, one machine. The md vault's near-miss numbers (86.1% / 83.65%) are inflated by ~400 template-generated skill files; I re-ran on the clean 421-file knowledge corpus and report both (58.2% / 16.71%). Use the second pair for any general claim. The PageRank measurement resolves wikilinks by filename stem, which will miss aliased and heading-anchored links and therefore UNDERSTATES edges — the 90% orphan rate is an upper bound on orphanhood, though the knowledge-corpus contrast (48%) was computed identically, so the comparison holds. Descriptions in my index construction are the first non-heading line of each file, which is fatter than Anthropic's curated 132-char median; that is why my 76.2x is lower than their 137.2x, and it is a measurement artifact, not a corpus difference.
- Everything about what a TOC does to model performance remains UNMEASURED. I searched for it twice, directly, and found nothing. I measured its cost precisely and its hazard mechanism plausibly. The payoff side is inference, and the shipped default in §design is labelled a default for exactly that reason."

verification.area: Context budget / "what to inline first" — adversarial verification of the 8 claims and the pack-design

verdicts.claim: HEADLINE: the brief's largest lever (near-miss deletion, 'up to 65%', GSM-NoOp) was REFUTED for frontier models by a March-2026 replication; only 12.4% of distractors survived a relevance audit; audited drop 0–2pp, indistinguishable from zero.
verdicts.reason: Every quoted string verifies verbatim in greaterwrong.com/posts/Ze4C99Dasj74YKCFh (I fetched and read the full post). The refutation still fails on five independent grounds. (1) NOT A REPLICATION — the post's own Caveats say: 'Apple did not release the original GSM-NoOp dataset... These may be systematically easier or different from Apple's hand-crafted distractors. We cannot make a direct apples-to-apples comparison on NoOp,' and its Conclusion asks that 'the NoOp dataset should be shared to allow true independent replication.' The source explicitly denies being what the claim calls it. (2) GENERATOR = SUBJECT — 'Claude Opus 4.6 generated a distractor clause for each of the 1,000 questions'; Claude Opus 4.6 is also one of the three models evaluated. The post controls for generator/auditor contamination ('Using a different model family from the generator') but never for generator/subject. (3) THE AUDIT REMOVES THE INDEPENDENT VARIABLE — filtering retained only TRULY_IRRELEVANT items and discarded AMBIGUOUS ones, i.e. exactly the near-miss cases (828 of 945 dropped). A claim about near-miss content cannot be tested on the residue left after near-misses are deleted; this is circular by construction. (4) UNDERPOWERED NULL — n=117 = 2.34% of the 5,000-item benchmark, template-clustered. I computed the paired 95% CI: at discordant rates 0.05–0.30 the half-width is ±4.05 to ±9.92pp, so an observed 2pp drop cannot exclude a true drop of 6.1–11.9pp; minimum detectable effect at 80% power is 5.8–14.2pp. The design is powered for the original 31.9pp effect (GPT-4o 94.9→63.0), not to establish a null. 'Indistinguishable from zero' here is absence of evidence. (5) SINGLE CLASSIFIER — see next verdict. Finally the claim is self-undermining: if 'inclusion is itself a relevance assertion the model correctly honours,' then a packer that inlines near-miss content degrades output. The mechanism is relabelled; the lever is intact.
verdicts.correction: An unreplicated, LLM-generated, LLM-audited, n=117 blog experiment shows frontier models are robust on distractors an auditor certified as unambiguously irrelevant, and does not constrain a 0–10pp effect. It refutes 'up to 65%'; it does not refute near-miss cost. Treat near-miss selection as an unquantified but live lever, not a dead one.

verdicts.claim: [primary-read] After auditing for genuine irrelevance, 88% of distractors were thrown out (117 of 945, 12.4% retained).
verdicts.reason: 117/945 = 12.38% is quoted correctly, but the headline and claim text present one auditor's output as 'a relevance audit' while the disagreement is demoted into the evidence field. The post: 'The two auditors disagree on borderline cases (κ = 0.32; 12% vs 36% kept).' The two auditors' retained sets differ by 2.9× (117 vs ~340 items). κ=0.32 is fair-at-best agreement and sits far below this workspace's own Learned Rule #4 threshold (Cohen's kappa ≥ 0.7 before a judge is wired into anything). A number produced by a filter whose two implementations disagree three-fold is not a measurement of the stimulus set; it is a measurement of GPT-5.5.
verdicts.correction: Between 12% and 36% of generated distractors were judged unambiguously irrelevant, depending on which model judged (κ=0.32). The 12.4% figure is one classifier's opinion and should never be stated bare.

verdicts.claim: [primary-read] NoLiMa: 32K not 128K, baseline <1K not 32K, 11 of 13 models not 10 of 12; v1 superseded 2025-07-09 and again 2026-08-01.
verdicts.reason: The substance is CONFIRMED verbatim — I fetched arxiv.org/abs/2502.05167: 'We evaluate 13 popular LLMs... While they perform well in short contexts (<1K)... At 32K, for instance, 11 models drop below 50% of their strong short-length baselines. Even GPT-4o... from an almost-perfect baseline of 99.3% to 69.7%.' And v1 verbatim: '12 popular LLMs... 10 models drop below 50%.' The provenance is fabricated by a parsing error. The arXiv abs page Submission history lists exactly three versions: v1 Fri 7 Feb 2025, v2 Wed 26 Mar 2025, v3 Wed 9 Jul 2025. There is no 2026-08-01 revision. The Atom API returns TWO <updated> elements: a feed-level one (2026-08-01T00:06:43Z — the timestamp of the researcher's own HTTP request, which is today) and an entry-level one (2025-07-09T14:35:23Z — the real last revision). The researcher read the feed-level element as the paper's.
verdicts.correction: NoLiMa's current version is v3, last revised 2025-07-09. Drop '2026-08-01'; it is the query timestamp, not a revision.

verdicts.claim: [primary-read] RULER: the brief's '4 of 10 models' is the withdrawn v1 number; current RULER evaluates 17 models, 'only half' hold at 32K; updated 2024-08-06 and 2026-07-31.
verdicts.reason: Content CONFIRMED verbatim from arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654: 'We evaluate 17 long-context LMs with 13 representative tasks in RULER... only half of them can maintain satisfactory performance at the length of 32K,' and v1: 'We evaluate ten long-context LMs... only four models (GPT-4, Command-R, Yi-34B, and Mixtral).' Two errors. (a) Same feed-timestamp defect: the Submission history shows only v1 2024-04-09, v2 2024-04-11, v3 2024-08-06. There is no 2026-07-31 revision. (b) 'Withdrawn' is wrong and non-trivially so — arXiv withdrawal is a specific status; v1 was superseded by revision and remains publicly served. Calling a superseded version 'withdrawn' overstates how discredited the brief's citation is.
verdicts.correction: RULER's current version is v3, last revised 2024-08-06. v1 is superseded, not withdrawn.

verdicts.claim: [primary-read] Liu et al.: 52.9% is LongChat-13B at index 14 of 30 docs; correct GPT-3.5-Turbo figure is 53.8%; below closed-book at 5 of 7 gold positions in the 30-doc setting; adding 29 non-gold documents costs 37.8pp vs the oracle (88.3 − 50.5).
verdicts.reason: I parsed all seven tables out of ar5iv 2307.03172 and re-derived every number. Three of four parts CONFIRMED: 52.9% appears exactly once in the paper, at LongChat-13B (16K), Index 14, 30-doc table ✓; GPT-3.5-Turbo 20-doc Index 9 = 53.8% ✓; and the 5-of-7 claim ✓ — the 30-doc row is GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) [73.4, 55.1, 50.5, 50.9, 51.8, 54.9, 63.7] against its own closed-book 56.0%, giving {55.1, 50.5, 50.9, 51.8, 54.9} = 5 below. The 37.8pp is wrong: it subtracts the 16K model's minimum (50.5) from the 4K model's oracle (88.3). Table 1 lists GPT-3.5-Turbo oracle 88.3%/closed-book 56.1% and GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) oracle 88.6%/closed-book 56.0%. The claim correctly uses 56.0 (16K) for closed-book in the same sentence, then switches models for the oracle — internally inconsistent within one sentence.
verdicts.correction: Within-model: 88.6 − 50.5 = 38.1pp, not 37.8pp.

verdicts.claim: [primary-read] The sandwich/zigzag reorder LangChain and LlamaIndex ship is validated by exactly one paper, and neither library cites that validation.
verdicts.reason: The citation audit is CONFIRMED — I read both sources. LlamaIndex core/postprocessor/node.py class LongContextReorder cites only 'https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172'; LangChain's _litm_reordering (now in langchain-ai/langchain-community, libs/community/langchain_community/document_transformers/long_context_reorder.py — the path given resolves 404 in langchain-ai/langchain) cites only 'https://arxiv.org//2307.03172'. I also simulated both and they ARE the identical algorithm at every k ✓. But 'validated by exactly one paper' is a universal negative that a single search refutes: Peysakhovich & Lerer, arXiv 2310.01427, 'Attention Sorting Combats Recency Bias In Long Context Language Models' (Oct 2023, a year BEFORE Jin) — 'perform one step of decoding, sort documents by the attention they receive (highest attention going last)... We find that attention sorting improves performance of long context models.' That is a validated document-reordering intervention. Also Hsieh et al., arXiv 2406.16008, 'Found in the Middle', mitigates the same positional bias 'outperforming existing methods by up to 15 percentage points.' Worse, attention sorting validates highest-relevance LAST, directly conflicting with the sandwich's highest-FIRST; the design adopts Jin without engaging the conflict.
verdicts.correction: Reordering-by-relevance has at least three validations (Peysakhovich & Lerer 2310.01427; Hsieh et al. 2406.16008; Jin et al. 2410.05983), and they disagree about which edge wins. Jin's large-k boundary claim stands; 'exactly one paper' does not.

verdicts.claim: [design] Ordering: rank order below k=10; Jin et al.'s sandwich at k≥10 — implemented as the alternating insert(0)/append both libraries ship.
verdicts.reason: NEW DEFECT the research missed while claiming to have read the code. The shipped library algorithm does NOT reproduce Jin's formula at even k, and k=10 — the design's own chosen threshold — is even. I simulated all three. Jin's Order(d_i)=(i+1)/2 for odd i, (k+1)−i/2 for even i gives at k=10: [d1,d3,d5,d7,d9,d10,d8,d6,d4,d2]. LangChain and LlamaIndex both give [d2,d4,d6,d8,d10,d9,d7,d5,d3,d1] — the single most-relevant document lands in the LAST position and d2 first. They agree at odd k (3, 5, 11) and diverge at every even k (6, 10). The edge assignment is not neutral: Liu's own 20-doc GPT-3.5-Turbo row shows Index 0 = 75.8% vs Index 19 = 63.2%, a 12.6pp primacy advantage, so even-k packs under the library implementation put the best document on the weaker edge.
verdicts.correction: If MDMAX cites Jin as validation it must implement Jin's formula, not copy the libraries — they differ at exactly the k the design switches on. Pick one and say which.

verdicts.claim: [design] The root index ships 'Anthropic's measured production shape plus the one field nobody ships' — a per-entry token count — and `mdmax budget` prints the knapsack before you spend it.
verdicts.reason: A 10-minute search refutes it. repomix (registry.npmjs.org/repomix, latest 1.17.0, 84 published versions, 'A tool to pack repository contents to single file for AI consumption') already ships all three of the design's differentiators. From its README: 'Token Counting: Provides token counts for each file and the entire repository, useful for LLM context limits'; `--token-count-tree [threshold]` renders a hierarchical directory tree with per-node token counts — which is precisely the design's two-level grouped index with '(~4.2k tok)' per entry; and `--token-budget <number>` 'Fail with a non-zero exit code when the packed output exceeds N tokens. Useful as a guard in CI pipelines and agent workflows' — which is `mdmax budget`. The design's novelty claim and much of its CLI surface are pre-existing prior art.
verdicts.correction: Drop 'the one field nobody ships'. Position MDMAX against repomix explicitly and state what the markdown-specific engine adds (block identity, splice-only writing, near-duplicate collapse) that a generic packer does not.

verdicts.claim: [design] Local corpus measurements: 83.65% duplicate blocks vault-wide, 16.71% in the clean corpus, 86.1% of heading texts non-unique, 4,710 files = 157% of a 200K window.
verdicts.reason: None of these reproduce and none states its denominator or definition. FILE COUNT: the design says 4,710; the project brief itself says 4,312; I count 5,586 raw, 3,244 excluding hidden paths, and 1,989 excluding hidden + node_modules (1,270 .md files live under node_modules, 2,313 under hidden dirs). Four different numbers, no stated scope. DUPLICATE BLOCKS: on my 1,989-file scope I measure 78.39% of block occurrences appearing >1×, or 69.27% redundant copies; adding the design's own punctuation+case normalization moves it DOWN to 77.77%/68.37%. 83.65% falls outside all four definitions I tried. Clean corpus: frontmatter 11.06%/10.21%, knowledge 11.54%/10.65% — neither is 16.71%. HEADINGS: 'heading texts non-unique' reads as distinct texts, which I measure at 31.47% (H1–H6) and 30.61% (H1–H3); the occurrence-weighted reading gives 79.71%/79.53%. 86.1% matches neither. The 157% figure additionally switches operands: it uses the expensive 66.8 tok/entry constant while the same paragraph names 50.7 as 'Anthropic's measured production shape'. At 50.7 and the brief's own 4,312 files the index is 109%, not 157% — the headline is inflated ~44% by constant selection, the same operand-swap defect as claim 3.
verdicts.correction: Every corpus ratio must ship with (file set, glob exclusions, normalization, numerator definition, denominator) or it is not a measurement. Re-run with the scope pinned and both per-entry constants reported.

verdicts.claim: [design] Refuse a flat index past 2,500 entries because measured saturation is ~2,995–3,943 entries against a 200K budget; past the cap, group by directory into a two-level index.
verdicts.reason: I re-derived it: 200,000/50.7 = 3,944.8 and 200,000/66.8 = 2,994.0, so the design's 3,943 and 2,995 are right to the unit. But 'saturation' is defined as the index consuming 100% of the context window — the point at which zero tokens remain for the documents the index points at. That is not a saturation point, it is a degenerate one, and the cap derived from it inherits the error: 2,500 entries costs 126,750–167,000 tokens, i.e. 63.4%–83.5% of a 200K window, leaving 33K–73K for all content. Second gap: the stated remedy does not remedy. Grouping 4,710 files 'by directory into a two-level index' still emits 4,710 leaf entries unless the second level elides leaves — the cap fires but the token cost does not fall.
verdicts.correction: Set the cap from an index BUDGET FRACTION (e.g. index ≤ 10–15% of the window), not from the window itself; and specify whether the two-level index elides leaves or merely groups them, because only elision reduces cost.

verdicts.claim: [inference] Liu et al.'s Appendix B splits the lever into two independent mechanisms: near-missness sets the LEVEL, position sets the CURVE; both effects persist under the other's manipulation.
verdicts.reason: The Appendix B quote is verbatim ✓ ('Although all models have higher absolute accuracy in this setting, they surprisingly still struggle to reason over their entire input context, indicating that their performance degradation is not solely due to an inability to identify relevant documents'). But the inference rests on prose only — Appendix B is a single figure (Figure 13) whose numbers the researcher never extracted, so 'sets the LEVEL' has no magnitude attached and 'both effects persist under the other's manipulation' is asserted, not shown. The paper also supplies a caveat the claim omits, one sentence before the quoted text: 'Note that in this setting, the the document containing the answer can often be identified with simple heuristics (e.g., lexical overlap with the query).' Random-distractor vs retrieved-distractor therefore differs in gold-document findability as well as in near-missness, so it is not a clean isolation of one mechanism.
verdicts.correction: The two-policy conclusion (MDMAX needs both selection and ordering) is reasonable engineering, but it is an inference from confounded prose, not a measured mechanism split. Label it as such.

survived: NoLiMa content, verbatim from arxiv.org/abs/2502.05167: 13 models, 11 below 50% of short-length baseline at 32K, GPT-4o 99.3% -> 69.7%; and v1 verbatim said 12 models / 10 models. The brief's '128K / 10 of 12' framing is genuinely wrong and genuinely understates the finding.

RULER content, verbatim from arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654: current version evaluates 17 models, 'only half of them can maintain satisfactory performance at the length of 32K'; v1 said ten models / four models (GPT-4, Command-R, Yi-34B, Mixtral). The brief cites a superseded number.

Liu et al. attributions: 52.9% occurs exactly once in the paper and it is LongChat-13B (16K) at Index 14 in the 30-document table; GPT-3.5-Turbo at Index 9 of 20 documents is 53.8%. Both re-derived from the parsed tables.
Liu et al. 30-document setting: GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) is below its own 56.0% closed-book score at 5 of 7 gold positions (55.1, 50.5, 50.9, 51.8, 54.9). Independently recomputed.

GSM-Symbolic §4.4 verbatim: 'with the Phi-3-mini model experiencing over a 65% drop' — the headline number is one small model, and the 'cannot be recovered' quote is verbatim and correctly qualified by 'Fig. 8(c) shows that some models can perform significantly better.'

All three RAG citations verbatim: Liu Appendix B, Cuconasu et al. 2401.14887 abstract ('adding random documents in the prompt improves the LLM accuracy by up to 35%'), Jin et al. 2410.05983 abstract ('identifying the detrimental impact of retrieved "hard negatives" as a key contributor').

Jin et al. §4 verbatim: 'retrieval reordering yields negligible improvements with smaller retrieval sets, but significantly and consistently outperforms the original ordering when the number of retrieved passages is large' — and the Order(d_i) formula is transcribed correctly.

LangChain and LlamaIndex do implement the identical alternating insert(0)/append, verified by simulation at k=3,5,6,10,11 — they agree with each other at every k — and both cite only arxiv 2307.03172 and no validation paper.

Near-duplicate collapse is the design's best-supported intervention. My own measurement on the md vault (1,989 files, node_modules and hidden excluded) finds 78.39% of block occurrences appear more than once and 69.27% of all block occurrences are redundant copies. The exact figure the design quotes does not reproduce, but the phenomenon is real and large.

The reframing 'inclusion is itself a relevance assertion the model correctly honours' is a genuinely good reading of the GSM-NoOp evidence and is well supported by the post's own examples — it just implies the opposite operational conclusion from the one drawn.
killed: The headline word 'refuted'. The cited work is, by its own Caveats section, not a replication and not apples-to-apples; its author asks for the real replication to still be run.

'A March-2026 replication of GSM-NoOp' — the post ran in March 2026 and posted 5 Jun 2026, but Apple never released GSM-NoOp, so no replication of it has occurred. The stimulus set was re-created, not replicated.
