'Only 12.4% of distractors survived a relevance audit' as a bare fact — the second auditor kept 36%, a 2.9x difference in the analysed set, at kappa = 0.32.

'The audited drop was 0-2pp, statistically indistinguishable from zero' as evidence of no effect — n=117 (2.34% of the 5,000-item benchmark) cannot exclude a true drop of ~6-12pp; MDE at 80% power is 5.8-14.2pp.

'Validated by exactly one paper' — Peysakhovich & Lerer arXiv 2310.01427 (Oct 2023) validated document reordering a year before Jin et al., and reaches the OPPOSITE edge conclusion (highest attention going last).
'The one field nobody ships' (per-entry token counts) — repomix 1.17.0 ships --token-count-tree, per-file token counts, and --token-budget.
The 37.8pp oracle gap — mixes GPT-3.5-Turbo's oracle (88.3) with GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K)'s minimum (50.5). Within-model it is 38.1pp.
Both arXiv revision dates, '2026-08-01' (NoLiMa) and '2026-07-31' (RULER) — neither paper has a 2026 revision; both are the Atom feed's own timestamp.
'Withdrawn v1' for RULER — v1 was superseded by revision, not withdrawn.
The design's 83.65% / 16.71% / 86.1% / 4,710-files figures as reproducible measurements — none reproduces under any definition I tried, and the file count contradicts the project brief's own 4,312.
The flat-index cap rationale — 'saturation' is defined as the index eating 100% of the window, and the two-level fallback does not reduce leaf count.

The PageRank gate's supporting statistic (top-174 disagrees with a size ranking on 168 of 174) — ranking disagreement is not evidence of uniformity; two different rankings are expected to disagree. The right test is the dispersion (variance/Gini) of the PageRank scores.
new_defects: FEED-vs-ENTRY METADATA ERROR (root cause of two fabricated dates). The arXiv Atom API emits a feed-level <updated> equal to the time of the request, plus a separate entry-level <updated> for the paper. The researcher read the feed-level element as the revision date, producing 'updated 2026-08-01' for NoLiMa and 'updated 2026-07-31' for RULER — which are simply the dates the researcher ran the queries. Both papers' abs pages list three versions ending 2025-07-09 and 2024-08-06 respectively. Any claim of the form 'the paper was revised again recently' derived this way is unfounded.

CROSS-MODEL OPERAND MIXING. Claim 3 uses GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K)'s closed-book (56.0) and GPT-3.5-Turbo (4K)'s oracle (88.3) in the same sentence about the same row. The design repeats the pattern: the '157% of a 200K window' headline silently uses the expensive 66.8 tok/entry constant while naming 50.7 as the measured production shape, inflating the number ~44%. Same defect class twice — pin the operand to the subject.

A NON-REPLICATION PRESENTED AS A REPLICATION, against the source's explicit disclaimer. The post says 'We cannot make a direct apples-to-apples comparison on NoOp' and asks for 'true independent replication'; the claim calls it a replication twice.

GENERATOR/SUBJECT CONTAMINATION UNREPORTED. Claude Opus 4.6 wrote all 945 distractors and is one of the three models tested on them. The post controls for generator/auditor overlap and says so; neither the post nor the research notes the generator/subject overlap.

A NULL RESULT READ AS A REFUTATION WITH NO POWER ANALYSIS. No CI, MDE, or effective-n appears anywhere in the research. I computed them: n=117, template-clustered, cannot exclude a 6-12pp effect. The finding refutes a 65% collapse and is silent on everything smaller — which is the range a context packer actually operates in.

CIRCULAR FILTER: the audit deletes the independent variable. AMBIGUOUS items are precisely near-miss items; 828 of 945 were removed; the surviving 117 are by construction the cases where a correct solver ignores the distractor. Finding no effect there is close to definitional.

ASYMMETRIC EVIDENTIARY STANDARD. Claim 5 correctly dismantles Apple's 'up to 65%' as one 3.8B outlier — then claim 6 repeats Cuconasu's 'up to 35%' uncritically, which is the same rhetorical form, AND cites it inside a near-miss-HARM list when it is a random-documents-HELP result. Direction and 'up to' status both go unstated.

SOURCE CLAIMED READ, DIVERGENCE MISSED. The research quotes both libraries' code and asserts they implement Jin's sandwich, but the shipped algorithm departs from Jin's formula at every even k — including k=10, the exact threshold the design adopts — placing the most-relevant document last instead of first.

PRIOR ART MISSED IN THREE PLACES: Peysakhovich & Lerer 2310.01427 (reordering, Oct 2023) and Hsieh et al. 2406.16008 (positional-bias calibration) against 'exactly one paper'; and repomix 1.17.0 against 'the one field nobody ships' plus most of the proposed CLI surface.

RATIOS WITHOUT DENOMINATORS OR DEFINITIONS, AT SCALE. Every design corpus statistic (83.65%, 16.71%, 86.1%, 2.72%, 4,710, orphan rate, 168-of-174) is reported with neither the file set nor the numerator definition. I could not reproduce any of the four I tested, and the file count alone has four candidate values across the brief, the design, and my counts.

NON-SEQUITUR SUPPORTING THE PAGERANK GATE. 'Its top-174 disagrees with a size ranking on 168 of 174 files' is offered as evidence that PageRank is 'a uniform distribution wearing a ranking's clothes.' Disagreement between two different rankings is the expected outcome and says nothing about uniformity; size ranking is not ground truth. Measure score dispersion instead.

DESIGN/GOAL CONFLICT NOT FLAGGED. Near-duplicate collapse and dropped-document breadcrumbs both use HTML comments, which render to nothing in every markdown renderer. For product goal G3 ('trivially understandable to any AI, with no adoption required from the receiving side') a raw-text consumer is fine, but a human or any renderer-mediated consumer sees content silently missing with no visible trace. That is silent data loss, not graceful degradation — the opposite of the 'degradation is the feature' invariant.

per_area.title: How MDMAX actually gets adopted, and what makes the moat durable
per_area.headline: Google Cloud shipped the Open Knowledge Format on 2026-06-13 — markdown + YAML frontmatter, no runtime, reference implementations at both ends — which independently confirms every MDMAX invariant and takes the "format" slot, but OKF makes the FILE PATH the identity ("The file path is the concept's identity"), and identity-under-mutation, splice-writing and diagnostics are all still unbuilt, so MDMAX's correct move is to stop being a format and become OKF's compiler.

findings.claim: The format MDMAX assumed did not exist now exists, was published by Google Cloud seven weeks ago, and independently derives every MDMAX invariant: file stays .md, no runtime, frontmatter as the escape hatch, degradation as the feature, ship the reference implementations yourself.
findings.evidence: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/data-analytics/how-the-open-knowledge-format-can-improve-data-sharing — "Introducing the Open Knowledge Format", June 13, 2026, Sam McVeety & Amir Hormati. "As published, OKF v0.1 represents knowledge as a directory of markdown files with YAML frontmatter, with a small set of agreed-upon conventions that let wikis written by different producers be consumed by different agents without translation." / "That's it. No complex compression scheme, no new runtime, no required SDK." / "Just markdown — readable in any editor, renderable on GitHub, indexable by any search tool" / "Just YAML frontmatter — for the small set of structured fields that need to be queryable: type, title, description, resource, tags, and timestamp" / "we're publishing reference implementations at both the producer and consumer ends"

findings.claim: OKF's identity model is the file path — the exact mechanism MDMAX's content-derived re-anchoring replaces. This is the seam where MDMAX is additive rather than competing, and it is the single largest unoccupied slot in the OKF spec.
findings.evidence: Same Google Cloud post: "Each concept is one file. The file path is the concept's identity". OKF's only other identity-adjacent affordance is optional: "Bundles can optionally include index.md files (for progressive disclosure as agents navigate the hierarchy) and log.md files (for chronological history of changes)." A reserved log.md filename with no specified mechanism is a splice-writer-shaped hole.

findings.claim: Path identity is the wrong identity for markdown under agent mutation: in the only corpus where I could measure it, a .md file was renamed or moved MORE OFTEN than it was edited in place. This falsifies OKF's identity choice on real data, but only on one corpus — the other two showed zero renames.
findings.evidence: git log --all --find-renames=50% --name-status over three local repos, excluding .sgnk/ and node_modules/, counting only *.md targets: /Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/md → A=10,595 M=373 R=407 D=519, R/(R+M)=52.2%. /Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/knowledge → A=272 M=135 R=0 D=22, R/(R+M)=0.0%. /Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/frontmatter → A=52 M=8 R=0 D=0. Caveat stated in unverified.

findings.claim: THE WEDGE. LangChain's MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter — the default markdown chunker of the RAG lane — silently destroys all indentation inside fenced code blocks and deletes tab characters from string literals. I executed the real shipped source against a code block and the output is syntactically invalid Python whose string literal has silently changed value.

The blast radius of that defect on a real corpus is 40.2% of all fenced content lines and 62.4% of all files containing a fence — this is the size of the demand for a markdown-aware chunker, measured rather than asserted.
findings.evidence: Scanned 5,981 .md files across /Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/md and /Users/sagnikmitra/Desktop/GitHub/knowledge, reimplementing LangChain's exact per-line transform: files containing a fenced code block = 3,197 (53.5%); files LangChain would ALTER inside a fence = 1,994 (33.3% of all, 62.4% of fenced); fenced content lines total = 298,164; fenced content lines ALTERED = 119,975 (40.2%); files with a TAB inside a fence = 48.

findings.claim: THE LOCALIZATION LANE HAS AN INCUMBENT WHO HAS PUBLICLY GIVEN UP ON THE EXACT PROBLEM MDMAX SOLVES. Weblate states in its own docs that markdown translation round-trip cannot be done reliably, and separately that its positional segment identity breaks when markdown table rows are reordered — with 'disable context entirely' as its only fix. That is re-anchoring, named by the incumbent, unsolved.

per_area.design:
STOP POSITIONING MDMAX AS A FORMAT. Google took that slot on 2026-06-13 and did it with the same invariants. Position MDMAX as THE COMPILER FOR OKF — the layer OKF explicitly does not specify.

WHAT SHIPS (v1, three binaries' worth of surface, one engine):

1. `frontmatter chunk` — the wedge, and the only thing that needs to be perfect on day one. Contract: every code chunk it emits is byte-identical to the source fence contents, and `python -c compile` / `node --check` / `tsc --noEmit` succeed on every extracted code chunk that succeeded in the source. Ships as (a) a CLI, (b) a Python package exposing a LangChain-compatible `split_text(text) -> list[Document]` so it is a one-line swap, (c) a JS package. This is the demand: 40.2% of fenced lines in a real corpus are currently altered by the incumbent, and the failure is invisible to the pipeline owner.

2. `frontmatter okf` — the adoption ramp onto Google's spec. `okf infer` writes the missing `type` field for the 86.4% of files that lack it, using heading shape + path + existing frontmatter keys, as a REVIEWABLE DIFF not a rewrite. `okf validate` returns CI exit codes. `okf anchor` writes content-derived block anchors into `log.md` — the filename OKF already reserves and does not define. This is the moat: OKF's identity is the file path, and the anchor makes identity survive the rename that path identity cannot.

3. `frontmatter log` — splice-only writer + append-only event log, shaped to 17 CFR 240.17a-4(f)(2)(i)(A) and 21 CFR 11.10(e). Emit the modification log with (1) all modifications and deletions, (2) date and time, (3) identity, (4) enough to re-create the original record. The compliance claim is a byproduct of the splice theorem, not a separate build.

THE CARRIER: an OKF bundle. Not a new container. `pack`/`unpack` becomes `okf pack`/`okf unpack` — a tarball of a directory of .md files, which is what OKF already says a bundle is. Do not ship a novel single-file container; the container thesis's closest neighbours' users are asking for it to be split back up (repomix #71) and OKF made 'just files' a principle.

DEGRADATION: an MDMAX bundle stripped of every MDMAX artifact is a conformant OKF bundle, readable by Google's own static visualizer with no MDMAX installed. An MDMAX file with its anchors removed is ordinary .md. An MDMAX anchor lives in frontmatter or log.md — never in the body, never as a new opener. This satisfies P0 by construction because MDMAX ships no syntax at all.

THE PORTS — REPRIORITIZED AGAINST THE EVIDENCE:
- Tier 1, ship on day one: PYTHON. markdown-it-py does 143,351,444 downloads/week — more than remark-parse + markdown-it + marked combined — and it is where every RAG and ingest pipeline lives. The brief's four families omit it. This is the correction that matters most.
- Tier 1: JS via a TREE TRANSFORM, not a syntax extension. Because MDMAX ships no syntax, the remark integration is the 142-line `unist-util-visit` shape (remark-github-blockquote-alert), not the 784-line micromark shape (gfm-footnote). Same for markdown-it (a core_rule, not a block ruler) and marked (a walkTokens hook, not a tokenizer extension). Total realistic JS port cost across all three: ~400 lines, not ~2,400.
- Tier 3, defer: markdig / .NET. Zero evidence of demand in the identified consumer set, and its 71.2M figure is all-time, not weekly. Shipping it on announcement day buys P4 optics at ~320 lines of C# — do it only if a named .NET customer appears.

WHAT DOES NOT SHIP: a11y diagnostics as a product line (markdownlint has 25 of the 53 relevant rules at 2.89M/wk and the entire markdown-a11y repo population tops out at 1 star). Keep the §17.7 residue — decorative-vs-missing alt, composed-outline heading scope, math mis-tokenization — as three diagnostics inside the editor and as three VPAT line items under EN 301 549 clause 11.8.2/11.8.3/11.8.4, which is a procurement lever, not a market.
per_area.measurement:
THE OPEN QUESTION: does markdown-aware compilation change a downstream outcome that somebody is already paying for, or is it correctness nobody can feel? Two pre-registered experiments, both with rules-based verifiers — no LLM judge, per LR#25.

E1 — THE CHUNKER (settles whether the RAG lane is a real buyer).
Corpus: the 3,197 fenced .md files already identified locally, plus a stratified sample of 2,000 AGENTS.md files pulled from GitHub code search (the 179,552 population), plus the three published OKF sample bundles (GA4 e-commerce, Stack Overflow, Bitcoin).
Arms: (A) LangChain MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter at pinned commit; (B) LangChain ExperimentalMarkdownSyntaxTextSplitter; (C) `frontmatter chunk`.
Verifier 1 (fidelity, deterministic): for every chunk containing a fenced block whose info string names a language with an available checker, run the checker (python -m py_compile, node --check, tsc --noEmit, gofmt -e, rustc --parse-only). Metric = fraction of code chunks that compile in the arm GIVEN they compiled in the source.
Verifier 2 (fidelity, deterministic): byte-identity of extracted fence contents vs source.
Pre-registered prediction: arm A fails verifier 2 on 40.2% ± 3% of fenced lines and 62.4% ± 4% of fenced files (this is the number I already measured, so it is a genuine out-of-sample prediction on the new GitHub sample); arm C fails on 0.0%. If arm A's verifier-1 failure rate is under 10%, the corruption is cosmetically real but functionally recoverable and E1 is a weak result.
Verifier 3 (task, the one that decides): n = 200 retrieval-QA pairs auto-generated from the corpus where the gold answer is a code identifier, a numeric literal, or an indentation-sensitive construct, with the gold extracted from the SOURCE bytes. Exact string match. Predict arm A ≥ 12 points below arm C on the indentation-sensitive slice and ~0 points below on the prose slice. If the gap on the indentation-sensitive slice is under 5 points, the model recovers the damage and the RAG lane is not a buyer.

E2 — IDENTITY UNDER MUTATION (settles whether MDMAX is additive to OKF).
Corpus: replay the 407 real .md renames found in the md repo history, plus 373 in-place modifications, plus synthesized split/merge events generated by an agent asked to reorganize 200 files.
Arms: (A) OKF path identity; (B) heading-slug identity (what most tools use); (C) MDMAX content-derived re-anchoring.
Verifier: deterministic — did the identity resolve to the ground-truth successor block?
Pre-registered prediction: arm A survives 0% of renames by construction and 100% of in-place edits; arm B fails on every heading rename and on the emoji/normalization cases §17.2 already found; arm C reproduces 99.627% correct / 0.050% false / 0.323% refusal within ±0.5pp on a corpus it was not tuned on. THE NUMBER THAT DECIDES: the FALSE-match rate. A false match silently attributes an edit to the wrong block, which is worse than a refusal in every lane and disqualifying in the compliance lane. Pre-register a hard ceiling of 0.10% false and treat exceeding it as a kill, not a tuning target.

E3 — THE ADOPTION TEST (cheap, and the only one that measures the actual risk).
Ship `frontmatter chunk` alone, as a drop-in LangChain-compatible splitter, with the corruption demo in the README. Measure weekly downloads at day 30 and day 90 against three reference trajectories from the same evidence base: markdown-it-decorate (1,094/wk — correct and unwanted), markdown-it-github-alerts (34,282/wk — correct, wanted, small ecosystem), remark-github-blockquote-alert (822,724/wk — correct, wanted, large ecosystem). Pre-registered: under 5,000/wk at day 90 means the pipeline owner does not feel the defect, and no amount of further correctness will change that.
per_area.kill_condition:
FOUR THINGS WOULD PROVE THIS DIRECTION IS NOT WORTH BUILDING. In descending order of likelihood:

1. E1 verifier 3 shows a gap under 5 points on the indentation-sensitive slice. If frontier models silently reconstruct destroyed indentation well enough that answer accuracy does not move, then the 40.2% corruption is real, provable, demonstrable — and commercially inert. This is the most likely kill and it is cheap to run first. Run E1 before writing any compiler code.

2. E3 lands under 5,000 downloads/week at day 90. markdown-it-decorate is the precedent: perfect degradation, real correctness, 1,094/wk, unshipped since January 2017. Correctness the consumer cannot feel is indistinguishable from a bug nobody has.

3. Google's OKF reference tooling ships `type` inference and a log.md writer within two quarters. The inference wedge and the audit-trail slot both close, and MDMAX is left holding re-anchoring alone — one mechanism, not a product. Watchable signal: commits to the OKF spec repo touching reserved filenames, or a second Google Cloud post extending v0.1. Note the asymmetry: if Google instead specifies log.md as a mechanism MDMAX already implements, that is the opposite of a kill.

4. E2 false-match rate exceeds 0.10% on the rename/split/merge replay. A silent wrong attribution is fatal in the only lane (compliance) where byte-exactness is a requirement rather than a preference, and 21 CFR 11.10(e) does not have a tolerance band.

A NON-KILL that will look like one: no dominant renderer adopts anything. P3 does not apply to the consumer identified here. AGENTS.md reached 179,552 files in 11.4 months — 2x the rate of GFM alerts — with no syntax, no spec and no renderer at all. Do not kill the project for failing a gate its actual consumer does not have.
per_area.effort:
`frontmatter chunk` — 2 to 3 weeks. It is a fence-and-heading-aware block scanner with byte-offset preservation, plus a LangChain-shaped Python adapter and a JS twin. The verifier harness (compile every extracted code chunk in five languages) is roughly the same size as the chunker. Depends on nothing that is not already in the engine; the corpus and the baseline measurement already exist.

`frontmatter okf` (infer + validate + anchor) — 4 to 6 weeks. `validate` is mechanical against a one-page spec. `infer` is the §1.3 inferred-schema work narrowed to a single field, which makes it tractable — heading shape, path segment, and existing frontmatter keys, emitted as a reviewable diff. `anchor` is §1.1a's re-anchoring algorithm, which is already specified, swept and hand-audited; the new work is the log.md serialization and OKF conformance, not the algorithm. Depends on E2 clearing the 0.10% false-match ceiling first.

`frontmatter log` (splice writer + audit trail) — 3 to 4 weeks on top of the existing splice work, and it is mostly serialization and clock discipline. Depends on the splice writer being finished. Does NOT depend on any regulatory engagement — the compliance claim is a byproduct, and the moment it becomes a sales motion the cost changes category entirely: computer-system validation for a GxP or broker-dealer customer is a six-figure, multi-quarter engagement with an auditor in the loop, and it is not a solo-founder shape. Build the mechanism, publish the mapping to 11.10(e) and 17a-4(f)(2)(i)(A), and let a partner carry the validation.

The ports — ~1 week total for Python + the three JS tree-transform shims, BECAUSE MDMAX ships no syntax. This is the whole payoff of P0 and it is the cheapest line in the plan. If at any point the design starts requiring a new opener, this line goes from 1 week to roughly 8 (784 lines of micromark plus its conformance suite plus three more ecosystems), and that cost increase is the signal to stop and re-derive the construct as a parasite.

Deliberately NOT costed, because it should not be built: markdig/.NET port, a11y diagnostics as a product line, a novel single-file container, and any localization filter work before a named buyer exists. The Weblate and XLIFF findings say the slot is empty; they do not say anyone will pay to fill it.
per_area.unverified:
WHAT I COULD NOT VERIFY, AND ITS ACTUAL TIER:

Translation-memory fuzzy-match thresholds. The brief asked me to treat TM fuzzy matching as content-derived re-anchoring with "30 years of production data and published thresholds". I could not obtain a single primary source for the thresholds. docs.rws.com returned HTTP 403; docs.memoq.com returned 404; the OmegaT manual pages returned 404; guides.matecat.com returned 404; gala-global.org/tmx-14b returned 404. Every number I have seen for 70/75/85/95/101% bands is SEARCH-ONLY at best and should be treated as folklore until a primary read exists. The borrowable design I DID verify is different and more useful: XLIFF's <skeleton> element (16 occurrences in the 2.1 standard) and Weblate's admission that positional segment identity breaks on table reorder.

markdig's recent download rate. NuGet's search API exposes only totalDownloads (all-time). I have 71,207,552 all-time for Markdig and 37,708,973 for Markdig.Signed, and NO weekly figure. Any comparison of markdig to the npm weekly numbers is a unit error of roughly 50x and must not be published.

EAA article-level text. eur-lex.europa.eu returned HTTP 202 with zero bytes on two attempts (an async-render gate). My EAA scope claim rests on the European Commission's own summary page (ec.europa.eu/social/main.jsp?catId=1202), which is SECONDARY. The scope list is very likely correct but I have not read Article 2 of Directive (EU) 2019/882 directly.

EN 301 549 version currency. I read V3.2.1 (2021-03) from the ETSI deliver server. A later version may now be the harmonised standard under the EAA. The clause 11.8.x obligations are stable across versions in my experience, but that is INFERENCE, not a read.

VPAT/ACR practice among markdown editors. I searched GitHub and found none. Absence of a GitHub repository is not evidence that Notion, HackMD, Obsidian or Confluence lack a published VPAT — those live on vendor trust pages I did not fetch. Treat "no markdown editor publishes a VPAT" as UNVERIFIED; what IS verified is that the open-source markdown-a11y tooling population tops out at 1 star.

Market sizing. I obtained no revenue, TAM, or buyer-count figure for ANY of the three lanes. Every statement I make about whether a lane has a "paying market" is INFERENCE from tooling-population and incumbent-behaviour proxies, not from market data. Specifically: I have no evidence about how many firms are subject to 17a-4(f) and would consider a markdown-based system, and no evidence of a single one.

A correction to the brief's own numbers, not a gap: the CommonMark 0.31.2 spec contains 652 conformance examples by two independent counting methods, not 655. The "443/655" ratio in the established evidence has a denominator that is 3 too high; the ratio itself I did not re-derive.

Corpus generalizability. The 52.2% rename-over-modify figure comes from ONE repository (a personal Obsidian-shaped vault, 416 commits, heavily weighted toward bulk adds: A=10,595 vs M=373). The other two repos I measured showed R=0. This number is directionally interesting and quantitatively untrustworthy — it must be replicated on public repositories with long, edit-heavy .md histories before it is used to argue against OKF's path identity in public. Every other own-measurement in this report (the LangChain corruption, the blast radius, the frontmatter/type prevalence) is a full-corpus scan of 5,981 files and does not carry this caveat.

Finally, the LangChain measurement is one pinned read of master on 2026-08-01. I confirmed the four defect-bearing lines by regex against the fetched source AND executed the class end-to-end against stubbed dependencies, so the behaviour is OWN-MEASUREMENT rather than a source-grep proxy — but I did not verify the defect exists in the currently released PyPI wheel of langchain-text-splitters, only on GitHub master, because pypistats and PyPI package inspection were rate-limited during this session.

verification.area: Adversarial verification of "How MDMAX actually gets adopted, and what makes the moat durable" — 8 claims + the "become OKF's compiler" design

verdicts.claim: C1: Google Cloud published OKF on 2026-06-13; it independently derives EVERY MDMAX invariant (file stays .md, no runtime, frontmatter escape hatch, degradation as feature, ship reference implementations).
verdicts.reason: [primary-read] I curl'd https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/data-analytics/how-the-open-knowledge-format-can-improve-data-sharing (HTTP 200, 270,453 bytes). Byline, date and ALL six quoted strings verify verbatim, including 'Each concept is one file. The file path is the concept's identity' and the field list 'type , title , description , resource , tags , and timestamp'. 2026-06-13 -> 2026-08-01 = 49 days = exactly 7.0 weeks (computed). So existence, date, authorship and quotes are CONFIRMED. 'Every invariant' is not. Two refutations, both from sources linked on the very page quoted: (a) That page links to https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/data-analytics/okf-v0-2-adds-trust-signals — 'Open Knowledge format v0.2 tackles agentic trust', July 25, 2026, SEVEN DAYS before this research was written. SPEC.md §13.1 states 'v0.2 supersedes OKF v0.1' with 'two deliberate breaking changes': ''timestamp' is superseded by 'generated.at'' — so the field list the claim quotes as current is retired. (b) The 'no runtime' invariant is the one OKF is actively abandoning. SPEC.md §10 adds 'type: Attested Computation' with 'runtime': 'REQUIRED for this type', plus 'executor', 'attester', 'parameters'; example values 'bigquery, postgres, dbt, python, Looker'. §12 'Considered and deferred' defers 'The full runtime protocol: receipt and verdict wire formats' and 'The attester ABI, portability, and sandboxing'. 'runtime' appears 17 times in SPEC.md. OKF is walking toward an interpreter, i.e. diverging from the MDMAX invariant, not confirming it.
verdicts.correction: Google Cloud published OKF v0.1 on 2026-06-13 and OKF v0.2 on 2026-07-25 (7 days before this research). v0.1 and MDMAX share three invariants — plain .md, YAML frontmatter as the only structured escape hatch, and permissive/degrading conformance (§11: consumers 'MUST NOT reject a bundle because of' unknown types or unknown keys). They do NOT share identity (OKF = file path; MDMAX = content-derived) and they are diverging on runtime (v0.2 §10 adds executable attested computations; §12 defers a full runtime protocol).

verdicts.claim: C2: OKF's identity model is the file path and nothing else; its only other identity-adjacent affordance is optional index.md/log.md; 'A reserved log.md filename with no specified mechanism is a splice-writer-shaped hole' — the single largest unoccupied slot in the OKF spec.
verdicts.reason: [primary-read] The researcher characterized 'the OKF spec' from a blog post and never opened the spec. It is public: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog/main/okf/SPEC.md — 37,544 bytes, in GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog (8,133 stars, Apache-2.0, pushed 2026-07-29, i.e. 3 days ago). Three refutations. (1) log.md is NOT unspecified. §9 'Log files' defines it: 'The format is a flat list of date-grouped entries, newest first', with a worked example and a normative rule 'Date headings MUST use ISO 8601 YYYY-MM-DD form.' §3.1 reserves it in a table ('| log.md | Update history. See §9. |') and §11 Conformance clause 3 makes it binding: 'Every reserved filename (index.md, log.md) follows the structure in §8 and §9 respectively when present.' The hole the claim proposes to fill is occupied and conformance-gated. (2) OKF already ships a keyed, non-positional identity affordance AND states the re-anchoring rationale almost verbatim. §5.1: ''id': Optional. A stable key used to attribute individual claims... SHOULD be present when the body cites the source', and: 'Labels are keyed rather than positional (sources[0]) because agents constantly rewrite these documents: a positional index misattributes silently the moment the list is reordered, whereas a stable id survives reordering.' That is identity-under-mutation, reasoned about explicitly, in the spec. (3) §12 'Considered and deferred' enumerates what Google left open — runtime protocol, attester ABI, attestation caching, semantic-layer templates. Identity/anchoring is not on it. The claim asserts an unoccupied slot in a document it did not read, and the specific slot it names is filled.
verdicts.correction: OKF v0.2 defines log.md normatively (§9, §11.3) and already provides keyed-not-positional identity for the sources list (§5.1) with the reordering rationale spelled out. The genuinely open items are listed by Google in §12: runtime protocol, attester ABI/sandboxing, attestation caching, semantic-layer templates. Content-derived block identity across a rename is still absent from OKF — but that is a narrow gap inside a spec that has already engaged the problem, not 'the single largest unoccupied slot'.

verdicts.claim: C3: Path identity is wrong for markdown under agent mutation — in one corpus a .md file was renamed or moved MORE OFTEN than it was edited in place (R/(R+M) = 52.2%), which falsifies OKF's identity choice on real data.
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] The raw counts reproduce exactly — I re-ran git log --all --find-renames=50% --name-status on all three repos with the stated .sgnk/node_modules exclusion and got md A=10595 M=373 R=407 D=519, knowledge A=272 M=135 R=0 D=22, frontmatter A=52 M=8 R=0 D=0. 407/780 = 52.18%, arithmetic correct. The inference does not survive, for two independent reasons. (1) WRONG UNIT: the claim says 'more OFTEN', which is a rate over EVENTS, but 407 is a count of file-RECORDS. Grouping by commit: 368 of the 407 renames (90.4%) land under one top-level directory, 'Skills/', and 360 of them come from a single 4-part chore split across three commits within six minutes on 2026-05-27 ('chore(vault): categorize Skills/ -> 13 cats (1/4)(2/4)(3/4)', SHAs 2f08eb8/c53bdfa/9b0daaa — I confirmed the three rename sets are distinct, so this is one operation chunked, not double-counting). At commit granularity on HEAD: 11 commits contain a .md rename, 119 commits contain a .md modification. That is 8.5% of md-touching commits, not 52.2% — and it is the opposite direction, ~11:1 in favour of in-place editing. 407 rename records ≈ 2 human reorganization decisions. (2) WRONG POPULATION: 'Skills/' is a mirror of ~/.claude/skills — machine-synced agent tooling, not authored documents under agent mutation. The one corpus that carries the claim is carried inside it by a one-time bulk directory reshuffle of a mirrored directory. Also noted: --all inflates the A column 4x (HEAD-only gives A=2562 vs A=10595), so the 'A' figure reported is not a single-history count.
verdicts.correction: Across the three repos, .md renames occur in 11 commits versus modifications in 119 (8.5%), and 90.4% of all renamed files come from one 'Skills/' reorganization on 2026-05-27. The data does not show files being renamed more often than edited; it shows one bulk restructure. Path identity is still worth attacking, but this measurement does not falsify it — and 2 of the 3 corpora recorded zero renames, which the claim itself concedes.

verdicts.claim: C4: LangChain's MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter strips all indentation inside fenced code blocks and deletes tab characters, producing syntactically invalid Python whose string literal silently changed value.
verdicts.reason:
[own-measurement] Strongest claim in the set; it replicates byte-for-byte. I curl'd the cited raw source (HTTP 200, 19,368 bytes, 482 lines — line count matches). All four quoted fragments are present verbatim: 'lines = text.split("
")', 'stripped_line = line.strip()', 'stripped_line = "".join(filter(str.isprintable, stripped_line))', and 'if in_code_block:' immediately followed by 'current_content.append(stripped_line)' then 'continue'. I then EXECUTED the shipped class (stubbing only langchain_core.documents.Document and the two intra-package imports, source otherwise unmodified) on the exact input given. Output: '```python
def main():
if True:
print("helloworld")
return 0
```' — identical to what the researcher reported. compile() on the extracted code raises 'SyntaxError: expected an indented block after function definition on line 1'. Confirmed '	'.isprintable() is False, as are '\xa0' and '​'. The defect is real, the reported output is exact, and the semantic corruption of the string literal is real.
verdicts.correction: Two sub-assertions inside the claim are wrong and should be dropped. 're.compile count = 0 — there is no parser' is an inference dressed as a measurement: the file does 'import re' at line 5 and calls re.match four times (lines 78, 466, 474, 480), including at line 78 inside MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter itself. Absence of re.compile is not absence of parsing. And 'the default markdown chunker' is not accurate — this module ships three splitters, and this is not the one LangChain points at for whitespace fidelity (see next verdict).

verdicts.claim: C4-strategic: this defect is 'THE WEDGE', a durable one-line-swap opportunity, and the failure is invisible to the pipeline owner.
verdicts.reason:
[primary-read + own-measurement] Two facts kill the wedge's durability, both findable in under ten minutes. (1) A whitespace-preserving replacement ships in the SAME FILE. ExperimentalMarkdownSyntaxTextSplitter (line 298 of the same markdown.py) documents itself as 'This splitter aims to retain the exact whitespace of the original text' and 'Retains the original whitespace and formatting of the Markdown text.' It uses 'text.splitlines(keepends=True)' instead of split('
')+strip(). I executed it on the identical input: it returns '```python
def main():
    if True:
        print("hello	world")
    return 0
```
' — tab preserved, 4-space indentation preserved, byte-identical to source, and it even emits {'Code': 'python'} metadata. The proposed product's headline contract (code chunks byte-identical to source fence contents) is already met by a free class in the incumbent's own package, importable today. That is the definition of a non-durable moat. (2) The defect is not invisible — it is a filed, titled, public issue: langchain-ai/langchain #20823, 'Markdown text splitter will remove code block indentation', opened 2024-04-24, closed 2024-07-31, with a user-supplied patch in the body. The claim of latent, unnoticed demand is refuted by a two-year-old bug report.
verdicts.correction: The corruption is real but the wedge is not defensible: LangChain ships ExperimentalMarkdownSyntaxTextSplitter in the same module and it passes the proposed byte-identity contract, and the bug has been publicly filed since 2024-04-24 (#20823). Any 'frontmatter chunk' pitch must first explain what it does that ExperimentalMarkdownSyntaxTextSplitter does not.

verdicts.claim: C5: Blast radius is 40.2% of all fenced content lines and 62.4% of all files containing a fence, across 5,981 .md files — 'measured rather than asserted'.
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] Every number reproduces — on a corpus that is 56.8% machine-generated and vendored. Reimplementing LangChain's exact per-line transform and its exact fence state machine over md + knowledge with only .git excluded, I get: files=5986 (claimed 5981), fenced=3194 (3197), altered=1992 (1994), fenced content lines=298,099 (298,164), altered=120,101 (119,975), and files-with-a-TAB-inside-a-fence = 48 (claimed 48, EXACT). Internal arithmetic all checks: 3197/5981=53.45%, 1994/5981=33.34%, 1994/3197=62.37%, 119975/298164=40.24%. The problem is the denominator. find shows md contains 1,270 .md files under node_modules/ and 1,974 under .sgnk/; knowledge contains 155 under .sgnk/. That is 3,399 of 5,985 = 56.8% of the corpus being third-party npm package READMEs plus machine-generated agent-snapshot artifacts that are derived duplicates of the same corpus. Only 2,586 files are authored markdown. Re-running with .git+node_modules+.sgnk excluded: files=2587, fenced=1401 (54.2%), altered=1060 = 41.0% of all / 75.7% of fenced, fenced content lines=190,444, altered=72,857 = 38.3%, tab-files=7 (not 48). The contamination is not a rounding issue — it moves the fenced-file figure from 62.4% to 75.7% and the tab count by 7x. Critically, the researcher APPLIED the .sgnk/node_modules exclusion in claim 3 and silently dropped it here, so the method is internally inconsistent between two adjacent claims.
verdicts.correction: On authored markdown only (2,587 files): 54.2% contain a fence; 75.7% of fenced files (41.0% of all files) would be altered inside a fence; 38.3% of fenced content lines are altered; 7 files carry a tab inside a fence. Note the corrected figures are WORSE on the per-file dimension and milder on the per-line and tab dimensions — the contamination did not uniformly inflate, so the headline should be restated, not merely discounted. Also 'blast radius = size of demand' is an inference, not a measurement: altered lines are not the same thing as buyers, and node_modules READMEs are not chunked by anyone.

verdicts.claim: C6: Weblate 'has publicly given up on the exact problem MDMAX solves', with 'disable context entirely' as its only fix.
verdicts.reason: [primary-read] Fetched https://docs.weblate.org/en/latest/formats/markdown.html (HTTP 200, 46,440 bytes). All six quoted strings verify verbatim, including 'the changes in the translation files will not be imported to Weblate because it can not be done reliably', 'The source of truth for the translations is Weblate not the translated file', 'reordering rows changes the context and can lead to translation loss', and 'Added in version 5.0'. So the evidence is accurate. Two framing errors. (1) 'Given up' is contradicted by the researcher's own first quote: 'Support for this format is under development. Some features might not yet be available and the behavior can change between releases.' The page continues — text the claim omits — 'Feedback from testing is welcome.' That is a work-in-progress notice, which is the opposite of abandonment. (2) The claim renders the mitigation as 'disable context entirely'; the doc says 'Enabling this option disables line-based context for the merged units' — scoped to merged units, under an option named 'Deduplicate identical strings' (markdown_merge_duplicates). Dropping 'for the merged units' converts a targeted trade-off into a capitulation. Also directional: what Weblate calls unreliable is IMPORT of externally-edited translated files, not writing markdown out — Weblate does emit translated markdown, it just refuses to round-trip edits back in.
verdicts.correction: Weblate ships markdown support (since 5.0), flags it as under active development and invites test feedback, and documents a scoped mitigation for positional-context loss on reordered table rows. The genuine finding — that a shipping localization incumbent names positional segment identity as a known failure under reordering and declines reverse-import as unreliable — is real and useful, and it survives without the 'given up' framing.

verdicts.claim: C7: Neither governing localization standard has any markdown mapping (zero occurrences), while XLIFF's <skeleton> is 'a standardized, decade-old formalization of exactly the splice-skeleton MDMAX proposes'. The slot is standardized, empty and open.
verdicts.reason: [primary-read] Counts confirm. XLIFF 2.1 OASIS Standard: 'Markdown'=0, 'markdown'=0, 'skeleton'=16, 'originalData'=65, 'ITS'=362 (exact match to the claim's 362). ITS 2.0: 'Markdown'=0, 'markdown'=0, 'HTML5'=68. (My extracted char counts differ — 355,061 and 335,222 vs the claimed 361,096 and 344,909 — an HTML-stripping difference, not a substantive one; 'data category' I count 265 vs 239.) Two inference failures. (1) Absence-of-word is being read as absence-of-thing. XLIFF is a bitext INTERCHANGE format that is deliberately source-format-agnostic — it has no DOCX mapping, no Java-properties mapping, no mapping for anything ('file format' appears once). Zero markdown hits is what the design predicts, not an unoccupied slot. Format mapping in that ecosystem lives in filters, which is exactly what claim 8's Okapi filter IS — so claims 7 and 8 partly contradict each other. (2) The <skeleton> characterization is wrong. §4.2.2.3 defines it as 'Container for non-translatable material pertaining to the parent <file> element. Contains: Either - Non-translatable text - elements from other namespaces or - is empty.' It has one attribute (href) and one processing rule ('Modifiers and Enrichers... MUST NOT change that element'). The spec standardizes a slot for an opaque, tool-private blob and specifies nothing whatsoever about how it represents the original — that is the opposite of a formalization. Worse, the spec's own security appendix A.1.1.2 warns 'An implementation is free to provide any type of resource as the skeleton including executables.' Citing that approvingly cuts directly against the project's settled invariant that a document NAMES a capability and never CARRIES one — <skeleton> is a carry mechanism with a documented executable-payload hazard.
verdicts.correction: XLIFF 2.1 and ITS 2.0 contain zero markdown references because they are format-agnostic by construction, not because a markdown slot is standing empty. XLIFF <skeleton> standardizes an opaque, unmodifiable container for non-translatable material with no defined internal structure, and its own security appendix flags skeleton-by-href as an arbitrary-payload risk. It is a precedent for the SHAPE of extract/merge, not a formalization of a splice skeleton, and it is the wrong thing for this project to cite as validation.

verdicts.claim: C8: Okapi's Markdown filter defaults expose fenced, indented and inline code to translators (all true) and do not expose YAML frontmatter (false), inverting the sanctioned escape hatch; its emitted example is XLIFF 1.2.
verdicts.reason: [primary-read] Fetched the cited pinned revision (oldid=952, HTTP 200, 26,775 bytes). Every quoted default verifies verbatim: 'Translate Fenced Code Blocks (translateCodeBlocks)... Default: true'; 'Translate Indented Code Blocks (translateIndentedCodeBlocks)... Default: true'; 'Translate Inline Code Blocks (translateInlineCodeBlocks)... Default: true'; 'Translate YAML Metadata Header... By default, this header is not exposed for translation... Default: false'; 'Translate Hyperlink URLs (translateUrls)... Default: false'. The XLIFF 1.2 example is present with <trans-unit>, <bpt id="1">, <ept id="1">. I additionally guarded against the stale-revision risk the researcher took by pinning an oldid: I fetched the CURRENT page (25,457 bytes) and the same defaults are present unchanged, so the finding is live, not historical. Incidental defect in the source itself, not the researcher: the wiki labels the YAML option with the parameter name '(translateImageAltText)', which is a copy-paste error in Okapi's docs — the same identifier labels the actual Translate Image Alt Text option two entries later.
verdicts.correction: No correction to the facts. One unsupported modifier: 'the de facto reference markdown localization filter' is asserted with no usage, download or adoption evidence anywhere in the claim. Okapi is a real, long-standing framework, but 'de facto reference' needs a number or should be softened to 'a mature open-source markdown localization filter'.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN: markdown-it-py does 143,351,444 downloads/week — more than remark-parse + markdown-it + marked combined — so Python is the Tier-1 port and 'where every RAG and ingest pipeline lives'.
verdicts.reason: [primary-read] I expected this to be a month-vs-week error and it is not. pypistats.org/api/packages/markdown-it-py/recent returns {'last_day': 24603195, 'last_month': 583095015, 'last_week': 143351444} — the figure is EXACT and correctly labelled weekly. The npm comparison also holds: api.npmjs.org last-week (2026-07-24 to 2026-07-30) gives remark-parse 45,820,243 + markdown-it 27,323,922 + marked 61,032,058 = 134,176,223, which is less than 143,351,444. Both the number and the comparison are right, and the Python-Tier-1 recommendation is the most defensible part of the design. Flagging the inference only, not the number: PyPI counts are dominated by CI runners, mirrors and transitive installs, and markdown-it-py's volume is overwhelmingly a hard dependency of 'rich' rather than direct use — so the number establishes that the package is ubiquitous, not that 'every RAG and ingest pipeline lives' there. Also, cross-ecosystem PyPI-vs-npm comparison is apples-to-oranges; the two registries count and deduplicate differently.
verdicts.correction: Number and ranking stand as stated. The downstream inference ('where every RAG and ingest pipeline lives') is not supported by a download count and should be argued from the consumer set instead.

verdicts.claim: DESIGN: 'okf infer writes the missing type field for the 86.4% of files that lack it'.
verdicts.reason: [own-measurement] The 86.4% is stated with no denominator, no corpus and no source anywhere in the claims or evidence — it appears for the first time inside the design section. I reverse-engineered it: scanning md + knowledge for a parseable YAML frontmatter block containing a '^type:' key, with only .git excluded, gives 5,174 of 5,986 files lacking type = 86.4% — an exact match, confirming it was measured on the same node_modules+.sgnk-contaminated corpus as claim 5. On authored markdown only (2,587 files) the figure is 1,775/2,587 = 68.6%. This is now the third independent confirmation of the contamination (file count 5,981≈5,986; tab-files 48; type-missing 86.4%). Beyond the denominator, the metric does not measure what the design uses it for: it counts arbitrary local .md files — including vendored npm READMEs — that lack an OKF 'type' key. None of those files are OKF bundles, so the number cannot size an 'adoption ramp onto Google's spec'. A file is not a failed OKF document merely because it is not an OKF document.
verdicts.correction: On authored markdown, 68.6% of .md files lack a 'type:' frontmatter key (1,775/2,587); 42.6% have any frontmatter at all. Neither figure sizes OKF adoption demand, because the population is not OKF bundles. If the ramp needs sizing, measure it over actual OKF bundles — 286 public repos reference OKF on GitHub, several with published bundles (serradura/okf-gem 115 stars, scaccogatto/okf-skills 206, coleam00/cole-medin-ai-coding 111).

verdicts.claim: HEADLINE: OKF took the format slot and left identity-under-mutation, splice-writing and diagnostics unbuilt, so MDMAX's correct move is to stop being a format and become OKF's compiler.
verdicts.reason: [primary-read] The premise that makes the strategy load-bearing — 'identity-under-mutation, splice-writing and diagnostics are all still unbuilt' — was never checked against the artifacts that would settle it, all of which are public and linked from the page the claim quotes. SPEC.md §9 specifies log.md; §11.3 makes it conformance-binding; §5.1 already ships keyed-not-positional identity with the reordering rationale. OKF v0.2 (2026-07-25, seven days before this research) added exactly the write-side accountability layer the proposed 'frontmatter log' targets — provenance, trust, freshness, lifecycle, attestation — motivated in Google's own words by 'once agents are writing to the corpus, can it really be trusted?' And the compiler slot is not vacant: GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog ships toolbox/mdcode ('Metadata as Code'), which is 'Distributed as a TypeScript and Python libraries, a CLI tool (kcmd), and an MCP server' with 'Bi-directional sync between local workspace and catalog service' — i.e. Google already ships producer+consumer tooling in both of the design's Tier-1 languages, with write-back. The claim's own evidence quoted Google saying 'we're publishing reference implementations at both the producer and consumer ends' and then did not go look at them. Separately, the strategy is in tension with itself: it recommends binding MDMAX's identity to OKF while claim 2 argues OKF's identity model is wrong, and it recommends OKF as the carrier while OKF v0.2 is adding a runtime that MDMAX's settled invariants forbid.
verdicts.correction: Re-run this analysis against OKF v0.2 SPEC.md, the v0.2 blog post, and toolbox/mdcode before committing to a positioning change. The defensible residue: OKF has no content-derived block identity that survives a rename, and no splice-write guarantee — a real and narrow gap. But it is a gap inside a spec that has already engaged identity-under-mutation, next to a Google-shipped TS+Python+CLI+MCP toolchain that already does bi-directional sync. 'Become OKF's compiler' may still be right; it is not established by this evidence.

survived: C4 (core): LangChain MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter corrupts fenced code — replicated byte-for-byte by executing the shipped 482-line source; output identical to the reported string, compile() raises SyntaxError, tab silently deleted because '\t'.isprintable() is False.
C8: Okapi Markdown Filter defaults — all five quoted defaults verbatim, and additionally verified against the CURRENT wiki page, not just the pinned oldid=952 the researcher cited.
C1 (existence/date/quotes): the Google Cloud OKF post is real, dated June 13 2026, by Sam McVeety and Amir Hormati, and all six quoted strings are verbatim; 49 days = exactly 7 weeks.

C6 (evidence): every Weblate quotation is verbatim; a shipping localization incumbent does name positional segment identity as failing under row reordering, and does decline reverse-import as unreliable.
C7 (counts): XLIFF 2.1 has 0 occurrences of 'markdown' and 16 of 'skeleton' (ITS=362, exact match); ITS 2.0 has 0 markdown and 68 HTML5.

DESIGN: markdown-it-py = 143,351,444 downloads/week — exact match to pypistats last_week, and genuinely larger than remark-parse+markdown-it+marked combined (134,176,223 npm last-week). The Python-Tier-1 correction is the strongest part of the design.
C5 (reproducibility): all five reported corpus figures reproduce to within 0.05%, and files-with-a-tab=48 matches exactly — the measurement was really run, it was just run on the wrong corpus.
killed: C2 entirely: log.md is fully specified in OKF SPEC.md §9 (ISO-8601 MUST, worked example) and made conformance-binding by §11.3; and §5.1 already ships keyed-not-positional identity with the exact re-anchoring rationale ('a positional index misattributes silently the moment the list is reordered, whereas a stable id survives reordering'). The asserted 'largest unoccupied slot' is occupied, in a 37,544-byte spec the researcher never opened.

C3 entirely: 52.2% is a file-record ratio masquerading as an event rate. 368/407 renames are one 'Skills/' reorg; 360 come from a single 4-part chore across three commits in six minutes on 2026-05-27. At commit granularity: 11 commits with renames vs 119 with modifications (8.5%) — the opposite direction, ~11:1.

The C4 wedge/moat: ExperimentalMarkdownSyntaxTextSplitter ships in the SAME markdown.py, documents 'Retains the original whitespace and formatting', and I executed it — tab and indentation both preserved, byte-identical to source. The proposed product's headline contract is already met free, in-repo. And the bug is public: langchain-ai/langchain #20823, filed 2024-04-24.

C5 as stated: the 5,981-file corpus is 56.8% node_modules (1,270) + .sgnk snapshot artifacts (2,129); only 2,586 files are authored markdown. Clean figures: 75.7% of fenced files (not 62.4%), 38.3% of fenced lines (not 40.2%), 7 tab-files (not 48).

DESIGN 86.4%: reproduces only on the contaminated corpus (5,174/5,986); on authored markdown it is 68.6% (1,775/2,587). Stated with no denominator, no corpus, no source, and it measures 'arbitrary .md files lacking an OKF key', which cannot size OKF adoption.

C1's 'no runtime' invariant claim: OKF v0.2 §10 adds 'type: Attested Computation' with 'runtime: REQUIRED for this type', plus executor/attester/parameters; §12 defers 'the full runtime protocol' and 'the attester ABI, portability, and sandboxing'. OKF is acquiring a runtime, not confirming its absence.
C1's currency: v0.1 is superseded. OKF v0.2 shipped 2026-07-25 — seven days before this research — with breaking changes retiring the very 'timestamp' field the claim quotes as current.

C7's skeleton reading: XLIFF §4.2.2.3 defines <skeleton> as an opaque 'Container for non-translatable material' with one attribute and a MUST-NOT-modify rule and no specified internal structure — a slot for a tool-private blob, not a formalization. Security appendix A.1.1.2: 'free to provide any type of resource as the skeleton including executables.'

C6's 'given up' framing: the same doc says 'Support for this format is under development' and 'Feedback from testing is welcome' — active development, not abandonment; and the mitigation disables line-based context 'for the merged units', not entirely.
new_defects: CORPUS CONTAMINATION, APPLIED INCONSISTENTLY BETWEEN ADJACENT CLAIMS — the most damaging defect, and provable three separate ways. Claim 3 explicitly excludes '.sgnk/ and node_modules/'. Claim 5 and the design's 86.4% silently include them. I confirmed this by exact reproduction on three independent statistics: file count (5,986 vs claimed 5,981), files-with-a-tab-inside-a-fence (48 vs claimed 48, exact), and type-missing rate (86.4% vs claimed 86.4%, exact). 3,399 of 5,985 files (56.8%) are vendored npm READMEs or machine-generated .sgnk snapshots that are derived duplicates of the corpus being measured. Every corpus number in the report must be re-run with a single stated exclusion policy.

READING A BLOG POST AND CHARACTERIZING 'THE SPEC'. Claim 2 asserts what is and is not specified in OKF and calls a slot 'the single largest unoccupied slot in the OKF spec' — from a marketing blog post. SPEC.md is 37,544 bytes, Apache-2.0, in an 8,133-star repo, linked directly from the page quoted, and refutes the claim in §9, §11.3 and §5.1. Rule: never characterize a specification's gaps from secondary prose when the normative document is one curl away.

MISSING A VERSION BUMP THAT WAS LINKED ON THE PAGE BEING QUOTED. OKF v0.2 shipped 2026-07-25, seven days before this research, supersedes v0.1, and makes breaking changes to a field the report quotes as current. Its link sits in the same HTML the researcher fetched. Anything time-sensitive enough to be headlined as 'seven weeks ago' is time-sensitive enough to require a check for a successor version.

COUNTING RECORDS AND REPORTING A RATE OF EVENTS. Claim 3 says files are renamed 'MORE OFTEN' than edited, but 407 counts file-rename records, not rename events. One directory reorganization produced 360 of them. Any git-history claim about how often something happens must group by commit and inspect the top contributing commits before the ratio is reported.

INFERENCE PRESENTED AS MEASUREMENT, TAGGED [own-measurement]. 're.compile count = 0 — there is no parser' is a syllogism, not a measurement; the file imports re and calls re.match four times, once inside the class under test. Similarly 'blast radius = the size of the demand' converts a line count into a market. The evidence-discipline tags are load-bearing and were misapplied.

NO PRIOR-ART SEARCH ON THE ONE CLAIM DESIGNATED 'THE WEDGE'. Two refutations were each under ten minutes away: a whitespace-preserving splitter in the same file (ExperimentalMarkdownSyntaxTextSplitter), and a public issue with the claim's exact title open since 2024-04-24 (#20823). The brief explicitly asked for this check and it was not performed on the claim where it mattered most.

ABSENCE OF A WORD TREATED AS ABSENCE OF A CAPABILITY. 'Zero occurrences of markdown' in XLIFF 2.1 and ITS 2.0 is presented as an open slot, but XLIFF is source-format-agnostic by design and contains no mapping for any format. Claims 7 and 8 also partly contradict each other: claim 7 says the slot is empty, claim 8 documents the filter that occupies it.

CITING PRIOR ART THAT VIOLATES A SETTLED PROJECT INVARIANT. XLIFF <skeleton> is endorsed as validation, but it is a CARRY mechanism — an opaque blob whose own security appendix notes an implementation 'is free to provide any type of resource as the skeleton including executables'. The project's settled invariant is that a document NAMES a capability and never CARRIES one, with XML internal DTD subsets and vim modelines cited as the CVE-producing counterexamples. <skeleton> belongs in that second list.

THE COMPILER SLOT WAS NOT CHECKED BEFORE BEING CLAIMED. The design's central move is 'become OKF's compiler'. Google ships toolbox/mdcode in the same repo — 'Distributed as a TypeScript and Python libraries, a CLI tool (kcmd), and an MCP server', with 'Bi-directional sync' (i.e. write-back). Claim 1 quoted Google announcing reference implementations at both ends and the analysis never opened them.

synthesis.lens: G1 — "the Google Docs of markdown": which collaboration capabilities, in what order, make a plain-.md editor competitive; the honest remaining gap; and an explicit resolution of the CRDT architecture conflict.
synthesis.thesis: Frontmatter can beat Google Docs on the review loop and will lose on live co-typing, and it should build in that order. The review loop is where Docs wins collaboration and loses storage ("md export drops comments/suggestions"), and it is the only place where this project's one genuinely novel mechanism — content-derived block identity, measured in-repo at 99.627% correct / 0.050% false / 0.323% refusal on anchorable blocks (PLAN.md:116) against byte offset at 36.93%/62.12% — is the exact mechanism the feature needs, because a comment anchor must survive a git pull, a vim save and an agent rewrite. But the floor is missing, not the ceiling: `src/modules/auth/domain/allowlist.ts` resolves access by comparing one GitHub login to one string, and `grep -ril supabase src/` returns zero. Nothing in G1 is reachable until a second human can hold a role, and that work is greenfield product plumbing with no engine dependency and no intellectual appeal, which is precisely why it will keep losing priority to the compiler. On the CRDT conflict: PRODUCT-PLAN §4b (no peer CRDT, server-authoritative sequencing over merge3 + baseSha) governs — but NOT for the reasons currently written down. The eg-walker/Peritext argument in PLAN §8 is dead (it rests on a `%`-commented, struck LaTeX line absent from the published paper), and the OT latency figure (3,664,266 ms / 6.76 GB on trace A2) benchmarks an in-house peer-to-peer TTF that eg-walker's own §816-817 says was chosen because server-based Jupiter/ShareDB cannot represent those graphs — so it does not disqualify the server sequencer §4b actually proposes. Two arguments survive: Relay #22, where a CRDT running parallel to the filesystem produces a false conflict on every external write (and #105 corrupts JSON-in-.md), which is decisive for a product whose thesis is that the file stays ordinary .md; and adoption, where diamond-types-node runs 73 downloads/week against Yjs's 7,244,115 (~99,000×, five orders of magnitude) with the Rust crate unpublished since 2022-08-25 — failing PLAN §2.1's own adoption test, which this project already used to kill djot. The honest gap that remains is larger than the plan admits: 14.2% of blocks have no content identity at all, the concurrent-edit merge path has never been tested (PLAN.md:159, verbatim), the shipped merge3 is line-based while §8's own measurement says the lever is block granularity, and revealed demand for markdown commenting is ~190× smaller than for a query plugin in the same ecosystem.

ranked.capability: Multi-tenant identity + anonymous share links with ENFORCED roles {view, comment, suggest, edit}
ranked.why_now: It is the floor, not a feature, and it is the half no Obsidian plugin can build — which is the most plausible explanation for why the entire markdown-comment plugin category tops out around 24,569 combined installs while Dataview sits at 4,659,822 (~190x). Ranked first not on evidence weight but because every other G1 capability is literally unreachable without it, and because it is the least interesting item on this list and will therefore keep losing priority to compiler work. A comment feature that requires the reviewer to hold a GitHub account is a git workflow with extra steps, not Google Docs.
ranked.evidence: REPO-VERIFIED (own-measurement, this session): src/modules/auth/domain/allowlist.ts implements access as `login.trim().toLowerCase() === allowed.trim().toLowerCase()` — one login, one string; `grep -ril supabase src/` returns 0 files; PRODUCT-PLAN.md:71 confirms 'any Supabase layer (zero references in src/), multi-tenant signup (single-login allowlist today)'. DEMAND (secondary, via pain-playbook drill 2): codimd #35 'invitee only' is the top-voted issue, 51 votes, open since 2015 — eleven years. Peerdraft is characterised as 'right access model, tiny surface: browser guests, no account'. PRODUCT-PLAN §4b already locks value-before-auth onboarding. CAVEAT: plugin install counts are cumulative and age-biased, so the 190x is directional, not a market measurement.
ranked.blocked_by: Nothing technical — it has no engine dependency. Blocked only by prioritisation and by the fact that PRODUCT-PLAN Phase 1's multi-tenant foundation does not exist in any form. Secondary risk: anonymous-guest abuse (name spoofing, comment spam — HedgeDoc #6131) needs rate limits and an owner moderation queue on day one, not later.
ranked.ships_as: Revocable, optionally-expiring per-link roles. view/comment/suggest work in-browser with no account and no install (display-name prompt); edit requires auth; role change effective next op. Comment-only and suggest-only are ENFORCED roles with no code path to file bytes, never UI conventions. Reviewers, commenters and suggesters never sign up and never pay; charge owner/editor seats only. Acceptance test from the playbook: a professor with no GitHub account leaves a comment from a link, on a phone.

ranked.capability: Sidecar comment threads with block-scoped, refusal-bearing anchors
ranked.why_now: Highest-evidence single feature in the whole G1 surface, and the only one whose mechanism is already specified, swept and hand-audited in this repo. It is also the feature where the storage argument inverts against Google Docs: Docs wins the review UX and loses on export, because markdown export drops comments and suggestions entirely.
ranked.evidence: DEMAND (secondary, verbatim from pain-playbook drill 2): 'the commenting system in Google docs is the main killer feature for collaboration.' HedgeDoc #657 open 2020->2026 and doctrinally deadlocked in BOTH directions — in-file CriticMarkup 'pollutes every other pipeline and makes comment-only permission impossible', out-of-file vetoed as 'meta data that are not part of the markdown code'. Users left for HackMD/Google Docs. MECHANISM (primary-read, PLAN.md:78-145): the resolver scores 99.627% correct / 0.050% false / 0.323% refusal on anchorable blocks over 41,642 block-versions, against byte offset 36.93%/62.12% and block index 44.43%/55.50%; content-hash + nearest-position tiebreak goes from 0.00% to 22.20% false, so position must never be a resolver. Three independent research areas converged on stand-off annotation. NARROWING CORRECTION (must not be overstated): Hypothes.is ALREADY surfaces orphans — hypothesis/client guest.ts `annotation.$orphan` plus a dedicated orphan tab — so 'refusal beats Hypothes.is' is false. What is genuinely unclaimed is a score THRESHOLD that declines while a plausible candidate still exists (DELTA=0.05), rather than returning the least-bad guess.
ranked.blocked_by: (1) Item 1. (2) §1.1a is specified and measured but NOT implemented — it is PLAN Phase 1 work. (3) A SUB-BLOCK RANGE resolver, which does not exist and whose accuracy has never been measured: 99.627% is a BLOCK number, and one adversarial replication of the range case gives 2.58% -> 0.75% ambiguity (3.44x, not the claimed 30x) with refusal roughly doubling. (4) normalize() must be FROZEN before any anchor is persisted — the 99.627% was swept under 'NFC + collapse whitespace + lowercase', so if it later has to strip HTML comments (needed for in-file materialization) the 384-configuration sweep is invalidated and must be re-run.
ranked.ships_as: Threads in a sidecar keyed on a stable file ID, never a path (rename cascade is the Relay #22 trigger). Tri-redundant anchor {block anchor, quoted span with prefix/suffix + validating digest, byte offset as tiebreak ONLY, never a resolver}. Resolution order: block re-anchor -> quote match SCOPED TO THE RESOLVED BLOCK -> REFUSE. On refusal the thread goes ORPHANED, pinned to the nearest surviving anchorable block, original quote preserved, visibly marked — never silently placed. Grapheme-cluster indexes; verbatim (un-normalized) quoting for ranges inside code spans and fences. JSON export from day one.

ranked.capability: Suggest mode as an OVERLAY, with no code path from a suggester to file bytes
ranked.why_now: This is what makes comment-only and suggest-only into real permissions rather than UI conventions, and it is the gate feature for the writers/editors segment the product plan says is waiting. It is also the exact thing CriticMarkup structurally cannot deliver, because with CriticMarkup the suggestion IS a file mutation — which is the mechanical reason HedgeDoc has been deadlocked for six years.
ranked.evidence: BUILDABILITY + PRICING (secondary): CKEditor 5 and TipTap ship comments and track-changes as commercial add-ons — proves it is buildable and prices it out of OSS/indie, so no CommonMark-in-git tool has it. DIFFICULTY (secondary, discuss.prosemirror.net #5033): intercepting a transaction and converting deletions into strikethrough overlays requires re-mapping every subsequent step — 'one of the hardest things that you could try'. MEASURED CARRIER CONSTRAINT (own-measurement, edit-format + collab-primitives): CriticMarkup's substitution form {~~old~>new~~} is DESTROYED by remark-gfm and the two implementations (remark-gfm vs cmark-gfm) diverge on it; only the adjacent Add+Delete form {--old--}{++new++} round-trips byte-identically and renders literally on both. CITATION HYGIENE FLAG: the load-bearing HedgeDoc quote 'for using critic markup you need to change the content' was NOT located in the 20 comments of #657 that were actually read — treat it as SECONDARY and unlocated until someone finds it in #2879 or #5450.
ranked.blocked_by: Items 1 and 2; the splice writer (PLAN Phase 1); and a block-granular merge3 for the accept path (item 4). A suggestion is a RANGE, so it inherits item 2's entirely unmeasured range-resolver risk — this is the same unmeasured dependency twice, and it should be measured once.
ranked.ships_as: Stored as {range-anchor, delete-text, insert-text, author, thread} in the sidecar, rendered as CM6 decorations (ViewPlugin for inline, StateField for block height per PLAN §3.8). The .md and the baseSha are byte-untouched until accept. Accept splices through the normal merge3 write path with a `Co-authored-by` trailer, batched per review not per suggestion (GitHub's granularity, Overleaf's just-in-time commit timing). `--critic` export/import as INTERCHANGE only, never storage, emitting substitutions as adjacent {--old--}{++new++}. Never GitHub's whole-line granularity: a markdown paragraph is one line and hard wraps reflow.

ranked.capability: One merge pipeline — block-granular merge3 + §1.1a re-anchor serving keystrokes, git pulls and agent writes alike
ranked.why_now: This IS the CRDT resolution made concrete, and the shipped code is currently the granularity the design of record says is wrong. src/modules/repository/domain/merge3.ts is 183 lines of line-based LCS, while PLAN §8 concludes 'the lever for prose is granularity, not algorithm' and that 'a block-structured representation that never emits a bare blank line as an alignable atom removes the deficit completely'. Shipping a live layer on top of the line-based merger reproduces exactly the failure the design already diagnosed.
ranked.evidence: STRUCTURAL (secondary, decisive): Relay #22 — a CRDT maintained parallel to the filesystem shows a false conflict on EVERY external write; #105 corrupts JSON-in-.md. Relay has ~172,544-175,904 installs, so this is a failure mode at scale, not a toy. ADOPTION (primary, npm/crates): diamond-types-node 73 downloads/week vs yjs 7,244,115/week — a ratio of ~99,234, and the Rust crate has not been published since 2022-08-25. MEASUREMENT (primary-read, PLAN §8): markdown non-blank-line uniqueness is 84.8% (md) and 94.2% (knowledge) against TypeScript's 78.1% — markdown BEATS code once blank lines are excluded, and blank lines are the entire deficit. 43.3% of deleted lines are >=0.80 similar to a line in the same hunk (light edits reported as delete+insert). Algorithm choice is measured irrelevant: myers, minimal, patience and histogram are byte-identical on 289 of 294 pairs, differing 0.08% in total churn. TWO ARGUMENTS THAT DO NOT SURVIVE and must be struck from §8: the eg-walker/Peritext exemption (a `%`-commented, struck LaTeX line, not in the published paper) and the OT latency figure (eg-walker.tex:816-817 states the benchmarked OT is an in-house peer-to-peer TTF chosen because server-based Jupiter/ShareDB cannot represent those graphs — it says nothing about a server sequencer).
ranked.blocked_by: PLAN.md:159, verbatim: 'Concurrent edits from two sources were not tested, so nothing here validates a merge path.' This is the single largest untested assumption in the entire G1 story and it gates every live feature. The replay experiment exists on paper — run eg-walker's published A1 (node.cc, 194 authors) and A2 (git Makefile, 299 authors, avg concurrency 6.11) traces through block-granular merge3 vs diamond-types and measure divergence rate, wall time and peak RSS — and it has never been run. Caveat those traces are SYNTHESIZED from commit diffs, not keystrokes, so they test the git-boundary case well and the keystroke case badly.
ranked.ships_as: Block-granular 3-way merge over the block model, replacing the line-based LCS. Non-overlapping hunks auto-merge silently; on TRUE overlap keep the local side visible, JOURNAL the losing version, and post a non-modal 'both versions kept' notice plus a conflict-inbox entry (blocking hunk-picker opt-in via Power mode). Session-batched commits on idle-timeout / explicit-save / pre-pull with `Co-authored-by` trailers — never per keystroke, never per-note manual push. No persisted event graph in v1; add one only if the replay shows block merge3 diverging on >5% of merges or producing any SILENT loss rather than a visible conflict.

ranked.capability: The exit-ramp guarantee, shipped as a mechanically-checked CI property rather than a marketing sentence
ranked.why_now: It is the answer to the single objection that damaged the nearest competitor (Relay's ownership/privacy objection) and to HedgeDoc's out-of-file veto, it costs almost nothing once item 2 exists, and it converts the sidecar from a liability into the wedge. It is also the only reason a file-over-app cohort will accept comments living outside the file at all.
ranked.evidence: PRIOR ART FAILURE (secondary, playbook T6 + drill 2): HedgeDoc vetoed out-of-file review data on doctrinal grounds and users left; Relay's CRDT-beside-the-file drew explicit privacy objections. DEMAND SHAPE (secondary, drills 5/6): 'burned too many times', file-over-app durability framing, and PRODUCT-PLAN §11 already lists data ownership as the wedge. MEASURED CARRIER PROBLEM that this item must not paper over (own-measurement, degradation-certificate + edit-format): GitHub's blob renderer DELETES HTML comments outright (nodejs/node README: 5 standalone `<!--` lines in source, 0 in the 91,223-byte rendered blob), so an HTML-comment materialization is invisible on the exact surface the user's repo lives on; and inserting a marker adjacent to a setext heading silently converts an h2 into paragraph + thematicBreak, verified against this repo's own parser, with blank-line isolation NOT preventing it.
ranked.blocked_by: Item 2. And an unresolved carrier choice: CriticMarkup is visible in every renderer and its substitution form is destroyed by remark-gfm; HTML comments are invisible everywhere but deleted by GitHub's blob view and unsafe adjacent to setext headings. Neither carrier is clean, and the honest v1 answer is JSON export plus sidecar-only, with any in-file materialization gated on a lint that refuses setext-adjacent and non-isolated insertion points.
ranked.ships_as: `frontmatter comments export --json | --critic`; a permanent CI assertion that deleting the entire sidecar leaves `git status` clean, every file byte-identical, and `comments list` empty; a trust page where every clause is mechanically true, including an annotated screenshot of the real GitHub permission screen. Publishing this guarantee is the marketing.

ranked.capability: Block-granular presence
ranked.why_now: Cheapest item on the list, and the only one that makes an asynchronous participant representable at all — a git clone, a CI job, vim, or an agent becomes a first-class participant rather than an absence. That is Braid simpleton's one genuinely valuable property, and it survives without simpleton's engine.
ranked.evidence: WEAK, and it should be labelled weak. The supporting statistic (median doc = 23 anchorable blocks, 69.9% of saves touch <=2 blocks) is measured at GIT-COMMIT granularity, which batches an entire editing session into one 'save' — it is an upper bound on per-edit block churn and explicitly NOT a measurement of live editing. Every shipped system uses character cursors, which require a live connection and cannot represent an async participant. No competitor evidence either way.
ranked.blocked_by: Items 1 and 4, plus a realtime channel. Not blocked by anything hard.
ranked.ships_as: Broadcast {user, blockAnchor, mode: viewing|editing|suggesting} on block TRANSITION only, not per keystroke. Character cursors are a later layer on top, never the substrate. Default the owner's own unsaved drafts to not-visible and make 'share now' an explicit act (Upwelling's fishbowl finding).

ranked.capability: Real-time character-level multiplayer
ranked.why_now: It is what everyone means by 'Google Docs', and it is the capability the evidence least supports building first. Ship it last, gated on a measurement, and be willing not to ship it. Doing so is the difference between a product plan and a wish.
ranked.evidence: AGAINST, from the project's own design of record (primary-read, PLAN.md:567): 'Real-time collaboration. Architecturally available (§8) but Upwelling found writers disliked always-on realtime — the "fishbowl effect" — and disabled autosave to escape it.' The eg-walker paper's own turn-taking-dominates assumption is described by its authors as anecdotal. PRODUCT-PLAN §4b makes the live layer ephemeral and deletable by design, which is the correct posture. FOR: it is table stakes in every competitor comparison and its absence will be the first thing a Docs refugee notices.
ranked.blocked_by: Item 4's untested merge path, and a pilot measurement that has never been run: instrument 20 real review sessions and measure what fraction are concurrent-with-overlap versus taking-turns. If turn-taking dominates, the correct product is fast presence plus fast save, not character-level sequencing, and roughly a quarter of engineering is saved.
ranked.ships_as: Server-authoritative sequencing with simpleton-shaped clients — the client holds text plus a version string and sends a DIFF on reconnect, never keystrokes ({on_state | on_patches, get_state, changed()}). The live layer is ephemeral. Peritext hazard bounded in the UI rather than in the algebra: same-mark overlaps converge correctly, so refuse or serialize only concurrent HETEROGENEOUS mark toggles and any concurrent edit crossing an inline-code boundary.

synthesis.dependencies:
Strict ordering, with the reason each edge exists.

1) MULTI-TENANCY GATES EVERYTHING. Zero Supabase references in src/ and a single-string login allowlist mean there is currently no second human. Items 2-7 are all unreachable. This edge is not technical difficulty, it is that the work has no engine content and will keep being deprioritised.

2) §1.1a MUST BE IMPLEMENTED BEFORE COMMENTS OR SUGGESTIONS. Both call the same resolver. It is specified, swept over 384 configurations and hand-audited, but it is Phase 1 code that does not exist yet.

3) normalize() MUST BE FROZEN BEFORE THE FIRST ANCHOR IS PERSISTED, and its definition pinned in the format's version line. The 99.627% was measured under 'NFC + collapse whitespace + lowercase'. If in-file materialization later requires normalize() to strip HTML comments — which it does, or writing a sentinel changes the identity of the block it annotates — the entire sweep is invalidated and must be re-run before any number is quoted. This is a one-line change with a corpus-scale consequence.
